all.name: The Slow Kiln
all.pitch: A single continent of foraging tribes where nothing is an "item" — everything is a substance with a typed property vector, and invention is a process verb applied to substances, adjudicated by a local LLM that is only allowed to fill typed slots and is then audited by a mechanical conservation-law referee. The tech tree is the closure of {growing verb set} × {growing substance set} under laws you wrote once, and no one authored a single recipe.
all.world: 256×256 hex continent, 6–20 tribes of 8–40 agents. The substrate is SUBSTANCES, not items: every substance is a row `{id, name, emoji, phase, mass_per_unit, hardness, temp_K, energy_density_J, toughness, conductivity, opacity, reactivity, toxicity, workability, tags[]}`. You author ~24 primordials (flint, river clay, oak, birch bark, sinew, fat, ochre, reed, marrow…) and nine process verbs (STRIKE, HEAT, GRIND, SOAK, DRY, MIX, BIND, CUT, FERMENT). Terrain deposits substances; deposits deplete locally; seasons and a ~40-year drought cycle move what is available. Agents have calorie/warmth/injury/childbirth accounting and an inventory. Tags are typed: STATE / STRUCTURE / FUNCTION, and a FUNCTION tag carries an affordance — `FUNCTION:cuts` makes a substance usable as the instrument of CUT; `FUNCTION:seals` UNLOCKS A NEW VERB (SEAL) for whoever holds it. Verb invention is the second-order combinatorics: Arthur's "new domains".
all.invention_engine:
An attempt is `(verb, sorted[input substance ids], instrument?, ambient temp/wetness bucket)`. Five-stage adjudication, cheapest first:
1. EXACT CACHE. key = sha1(verb ‖ sorted inputs ‖ ambient bucket ‖ law_vector_hash) → `recipes` table in SQLite (WAL). Hit = zero cost. Negative results are cached too ("nothing happens") and are ~60% of the table.
2. SIGNATURE CACHE (the important one). Bucket each input into a coarse typed signature: (phase, hardness∈{0-2,3-5,6-8,9-10}, temp bucket, top-2 tags). If (verb, signature multiset) has ≥3 prior adjudications that agreed on an outcome class, apply the stored property-delta template deterministically and mint the result with a template-derived name. No model call. This is what makes cost sublinear in |substances|.
3. LOCAL ORACLE. llama.cpp server, Qwen3.5-4B Q4_K_M, GBNF grammar compiled from the property JSON schema via llama.cpp's json-schema-to-grammar. It cannot invent a free-form outcome: it emits `{outcome: TRANSFORM|COMBINE|NOTHING, props delta, ≤2 new tags each with declared type+affordance, name, 12-word why}`. Grammar makes the syntax free; the schema makes the semantics typed.
4. MECHANICAL REFEREE (pure code, no model). Mass: Σout ≤ Σin. Energy: HEAT can only raise temp_K by fuel energy_density / mass. Monotonicity: GRIND cannot raise hardness; DRY cannot raise a WET tag; nothing may simultaneously gain hardness, gain toughness and lose mass beyond an alloy budget. Tag legality: STRUCTURE tags require a structural verb in the attempt. On violation, one retry with the violated law quoted verbatim in the prompt; second violation → record NOTHING. This is the anti-nonsense mechanism and it runs at ~microseconds.
5. NIGHTLY ESCALATION. Rank the day's new recipes by consequence (Δ in tribe survival metrics attributable to them), send the top ~30 in ONE claude-haiku-4-5 Batch job for a better name, a lore line, and a property audit that can overrule the local model. This is also the chronicle voice.
all.why_unbounded: State is not a list of names; it is a point in a ~14-dimensional continuous property space crossed with the power set of a GROWING typed tag vocabulary, crossed with a growing verb set. Attempts available at any moment ≈ V·N²/2 (verbs × substance pairs), and each success can add a substance and, rarely, a verb — which multiplies the frontier rather than adding to it. Two-level combinatorics (Arthur: technologies are combinations, and new domains are the big jumps) means the reachable set is not enumerable in advance and I cannot tell you its size. Where it actually bottoms out: the tag vocabulary's semantic capacity. A 4B model has a finite number of distinct physical concepts; expect a few thousand genuinely distinct tags before new tags are synonyms of old ones. Also note the honest cache-economics wrinkle: pair space is quadratic, so cache hit rate would collapse as N grows — it doesn't, only because agents recombine what is in hand, which keeps the effective frontier local and small.
all.depth_ladder: WEEK 1: 24 primordials, 9 verbs. Within ~2 hours of sim time you get sharp flint, cordage, fire, cured hide — and at least one thing you did not author (HEAT(birch bark) → pitch is the classic first surprise). WEEK 2–4: heat chains. Charcoal raises the achievable temperature, which is a *technological variable*, not a stat you wrote; first ceramic; someone coins an AIRFLOW tag and a bellows-equivalent appears because the tag unlocks a verb. MONTH 2–3: metallurgy without you writing metallurgy — alloys are continuous property blends, so the space of alloys is literally continuous. First machine tool: a substance whose FUNCTION tag unlocks a verb only it enables, so a tool that makes tools becomes a bottleneck object worth killing for. MONTH 4–6: glass and optics, fermentation chains, medicine (toxicity-negating tags), recipes traded as secrets by specialists. WILDEST PLAUSIBLE: a nine-step composite from clay+ash+sinew with a property vector nobody planned (high toughness, low mass) that becomes load-bearing for every surviving tribe — and the chronicle can render its full nine-node ancestry DAG on your phone.
all.what_selects: Calories, warmth, injury, childbirth, winter. Substances deplete locally, so success creates its own scarcity (kilns exhaust nearby wood, forcing the charcoal invention — niche construction as a designed pressure). Raiding takes goods but not knowledge: a recipe spreads only by demonstration, requiring co-location for K ticks with a holder. When the last holder of a recipe dies, that lineage loses it — Henrich's Tasmania model implemented directly. Writing is a reachable invention that changes the loss rate, so the tribes can invent their own defence against forgetting, and you get to watch which one does it first.
all.changing_worlds: A 12-constant LAW VECTOR (gravity, atmospheric oxygen, water boiling point, ambient temp curve, ore abundance, decay rate…). New worlds are spawned by perturbing it; the law hash is part of every cache key, so results legitimately differ across worlds and the cache never lies about it. Within a world: volcanism and ice ages every ~3000 ticks shift what the ground gives, which strands technologies whose inputs vanished. Worlds can be seeded by migrants from another world, carrying a bottlenecked recipe subset into a place where half of it no longer works.
all.novelty_detector: Four independent scorers, each z-scored against a rolling 30-day baseline. (a) FIRST-EVER: canonical event signature absent from an `event_signatures` table. (b) KEYSTONE: the new node is an articulation point in the recipe DAG — removing it disconnects ≥5% of reachable tech (Tarjan, milliseconds). This is the best signal in the design: it detects "a technology everything now depends on". (c) MDL SHOCK: nightly compressed size of the tribe behaviour log drops >2σ (they learned to compress their lives = a real efficiency win). (d) REGIME CHANGE: CUSUM change-point on eight world aggregates (population, calorie surplus, tech depth, trade volume, max achievable temperature…). Push only if max z > 3, hard cap of 3 pushes/day, plus one guaranteed 07:00 digest so the coffee ritual never depends on a threshold firing.
all.phone_view: One hero card: giant emoji, the invented name, "FIRST EVER · night 41", a five-line ancestry chain as plain text (`flint → sharp flint → …`), a population spark, and one gauge — MAX ACHIEVABLE TEMPERATURE (K) — which is the single number that says how advanced the world is. Tap the card for the full ancestry DAG as inline SVG; tap the gauge for the chronicle. Five seconds tells you whether last night mattered; an hour of tapping through ancestry chains is a genuinely good evening.
all.hardware_use: llama.cpp server with Qwen3.5-4B Q4_K_M (~3.4 GB weights) + 8k ctx KV ≈ 5.5 GB — comfortable inside 8 GB with room for bge-small embeddings. `--parallel 4` continuous batching; a grammar-constrained adjudication is ~150 output tokens, so budget 1–2 s each → 2–4k novel adjudications/hour, ~30k overnight, which is far more than a warmed cache needs. The sim is node + SQLite on CPU; world state is under 200 MB, so 64 GB RAM is irrelevant here (that is fine — not every idea needs to use every resource). Cloud: ~200–300 Haiku 4.5 Batch calls/night. Haiku 4.5 is $1/$5 per MTok, Batch is 50% off, cached prompt reads ~0.1×: with a 2k-token cached system prompt that is roughly $0.0005/call → about $0.05–0.15 per night, $2–5/month. Do not run QLoRA here; there is nothing to finetune.
all.input_cadence: Zero required. Optional god-tier nudge: edit `worlds.yaml` to change a law constant, or hit a Tailscale endpoint from your phone to inject an event (meteor, a stranger arriving with a gift substance, a plague). Ten seconds, high leverage, entirely skippable.
all.tech: node + better-sqlite3 for the sim core and the whole world DB (WAL mode, one file per world — trivially backed up and diffed). Python only for the llama.cpp client and nightly analytics. llama.cpp with GBNF from json-schema-to-grammar. Anthropic Python SDK Batch API for the nightly chronicle. PWA: static build exported nightly to GitHub Pages, live build served over Tailscale. ntfy.sh topic for push (their PWA + Web Push means no app store, no Firebase). SHARED SUBSTRATE with ideas 5 and 6: the typed-substance schema, the referee, the lineage/event DB and the PWA chronicle are the same code.
all.first_weekend: SATURDAY: the property schema, 24 primordials, 9 verbs, the SQLite tables, the referee laws, and one grammar-constrained llama.cpp call. Build a CLI where YOU combine things and watch the referee reject the model's free lunches. SUNDAY: 12 dumb agents with hunger and an attempt policy (weight attempts by inventory × novelty), the recipe DAG, and a static HTML page listing FIRSTS. The delight moment lands Saturday night, before any agents exist: your conservation referee catches the model conjuring mass, quotes the law back at it, and the retry produces something better than you would have written.
all.six_months_later: An archipelago of law-vector variants; ~1,500–4,000 substances; 25–60 verbs; tribes with visibly divergent materials cultures; recipes as tradeable, stealable, losable secrets; an ancestry DAG that no longer fits on a screen. By then you are reading the chronicle for the sociology (who hoards, who teaches, who forgot) as much as for the chemistry.
all.honest_ceiling: The oracle is a plausibility engine, not physics — depth here is depth of narrative-and-property consistency, not truth, and a materials scientist would laugh at month four's metallurgy. Expect tag saturation at month 5–8: new tags start being synonyms, keystone events get rare, and the DAG grows wide instead of deep. New law vectors and harsher needs buy months, not forever. Two concrete failure modes to plan for: (1) if you let agents attempt arbitrary pairs, the quadratic pair space destroys your cache hit rate and your token bill; inventory locality is load-bearing, not flavour. (2) The 4B model writes boring names; without the nightly Haiku pass the chronicle is unreadable within two weeks.
all.research_notes: Verified by search: Infinite Craft's mechanic is exactly cache-then-LLM — every pair is checked against a database of prior combinations, only true novelties hit the model, and results are cached so all players see the same outcome (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite_Craft; https://www.conjecture.dev/research/building-an-infinite-craft-clone-with-tactics). Arthur O'Dwyer's analysis models the result as a directed hypergraph where each edge maps 1–2 vertices to exactly one vertex (https://quuxplusone.github.io/blog/2024/03/03/infinite-craft-theory/), and reports the scale problem honestly (>1M unique items, >10M recipes). Working open clones to crib architecture from: https://github.com/bufferhead-code/opencraft, https://github.com/ngruychev/finite-craft (explicitly runs on a laptop without a good GPU), https://github.com/CharlesFauman/infini-craft. Grammar-constrained decoding is production-ready in llama.cpp: GBNF plus a json-schema-to-grammar converter covering types, enums, required, additionalProperties, oneOf/anyOf (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/grammars/README.md) — and the docs make the key point that the schema constrains output but is NOT injected into the prompt, so you must describe the structure in the prompt too. Model sizing verified: Qwen3.5-4B Q4 is ~3.4 GB and is the standard pick for 8 GB machines; Qwen3.5-9B Q4_K_M at ~6.6 GB also fits 8 GB if you want a smarter oracle at lower throughput (https://benchlm.ai/best/local-llm, https://www.mayhemcode.com/2026/06/best-local-llms-for-4gb-6gb-and-8gb.html). Pricing checked against the current Anthropic model table: claude-haiku-4-5 $1/$5 per MTok, 200K ctx; Batch API 50%; prompt-cache reads ~0.1× and writes ~1.25×. Theory: W. Brian Arthur, *The Nature of Technology* (2009) for combination-and-domains; Kauffman's adjacent possible. Tasmania/knowledge-loss model: Henrich 2004 (https://www2.psych.ubc.ca/~henrich/Website/Papers/HenrichTasmania.pdf). Push: ntfy.sh is a PWA with Web Push and self-hostable (https://docs.ntfy.sh/releases/).

audit.name: The Slow Kiln
audit.ceiling: Two independent walls, both closer than the doc's 'month 5–8 tag saturation'. (a) VERB GROWTH IS NOMINAL. The whole second-order claim rests on FUNCTION:seals unlocking SEAL. But nothing in the referee knows what SEAL *does* — the referee only checks mass/energy/hardness monotonicity, which are verb-agnostic. A new verb is a new string in a prompt. Arthur's 'new domains' means new *mechanism*; here it means a new noun. So the multiplicative term in V·N²/2 never actually multiplies anything structural, and the frontier grows quadratically, not exponentially. (b) SIGNATURE CACHE EATS THE ORACLE. Stage 2 fires after 3 agreeing adjudications on a coarse bucket (phase, 4 hardness bins, temp bin, top-2 tags) — a few hundred buckets total. By week 3–4 essentially every attempt hits a stored property-delta template, and the system becomes a deterministic 14-D vector blender that mints interpolants with template names. 'Alloys are a continuous space' is not depth, it is a continuum of near-duplicates. Realistic: genuine surprise through ~week 3; recognisable-but-derivative through ~week 8; after that the DAG grows wide, never deep. Not 6 months.
audit.authored_content_risk: HIGH — the most important thing to say about this design. HEAT(birch bark) → pitch is presented as 'the classic first surprise'. It is not a surprise; it is retrieval. A 4B model has read the internet and holds a compressed copy of human material culture. The tech tree here is not authored by the designer — it is authored by pretraining, and the sim walks it in an inventory-constrained random order. That is strictly worse than a hand-authored tree in one respect: a hand-authored tree is at least consistent. The designer's own cost argument proves the point — 'agents recombine what is in hand, which keeps the effective frontier local and small' — a small local frontier over a prior-supplied answer key is exactly a tech tree being revealed. You cannot simultaneously claim the space is vast and that locality saves your cache; locality is what makes it affordable AND what makes it shallow. Genuinely non-authored content does exist here (continuous property trajectories the model never saw), but it is the least interesting layer and the LLM re-names it back into familiar categories.
audit.compute_honesty: HONEST — the strongest of the six on this axis, and the cost model is basically right. Corrections: 150 grammar-constrained output tokens on a 4B Q4 at realistic 5070 decode is ~3–4s single-stream, not 1–2s; GBNF adds measurable per-token overhead on a large schema grammar (the doc budgets none). 2–4k novel adjudications/hour needs --parallel 4 saturated and is a peak, not an average; 30k/night assumes 8h at peak. Haiku arithmetic checks out (~$0.0006/call, ~$0.20/night). The 8GB fit for Qwen3-class 4B Q4 + 8k KV is real. The 9B fallback claim is NOT: 6.6GB weights + KV + CUDA context on an 8GB card OOMs or thrashes.
audit.dubious_claims: 'Qwen3.5-4B/9B' — I cannot verify a Qwen3.5 release; Qwen3-4B is what I can confirm. Cited as verification: benchlm.ai and a mayhemcode.com post dated 2026/06 — content-farm sources presented at the same evidentiary weight as papers. '~60% of the table is negative results' is invented precision. Arthur O'Dwyer's hypergraph post is a personal blog cited alongside peer-reviewed work without distinction (the analysis is fine; the framing isn't). The llama.cpp GBNF / json-schema-to-grammar claims are correct, including the good catch that the schema is not injected into the prompt. Infinite Craft caching description is correct. Henrich 2004 is cited across four of these six ideas as settled; it is contested (Vaesen et al. 2016 PNAS; Read's critiques) and the population-size→complexity link does not replicate cleanly — building four designs on it as a load-bearing 'result' is a shared weakness.
audit.semantic_risk: MEDIUM-HIGH, and the referee does not address it. The referee catches conservation violations. Almost all nonsense in this system is *categorical*, not thermodynamic: GRIND(sinew, fat) → 'conductive resin, FUNCTION:seals' violates no conservation law and is pure drivel. The five listed laws (mass, energy, GRIND-hardness monotonicity, DRY/WET, tag legality) are a thin sieve over a very large space of plausible-sounding garbage. The nightly Haiku audit is the real anti-nonsense mechanism, and it only sees the top ~30 by consequence.
audit.one_change: Make verbs mechanical instead of lexical. Require every invented verb to be *defined* as a small program over the referee's own property algebra (a composition of existing operators with bound parameters, synthesised and validated against observed transformations), not just named by the LLM. Then a new verb genuinely enlarges the reachable set, tag→verb unlocking becomes real second-order combinatorics rather than vocabulary growth, and the signature cache can no longer flatten everything because new verbs create new signature spaces. This is the one edit that turns the design from 'Infinite Craft with conservation laws' into something with a real second level.

all.name: Ashcairn
all.pitch: Tribes whose every behaviour is a program in a tiny survival DSL, and whose entire technology is a library of named lambda abstractions that a compressor carves out of yesterday's successes each night. The technologies are literally the abstractions — they compound forever because each one shortens the description of everything built on it, and calories are the search budget, so compression is metabolism.
all.world: A deterministic 96×96 tile world with an honest small physics: heat diffusion, water, plant growth, wear, load. Tribes of 6–30 agents. The twist: an agent's behaviour is a PROGRAM in a stack DSL called SURV — about 40 primitives (`move`, `sense`, `take`, `put`, `hit`, `heat`, `wait`, `count`, `if`, `loop`, `nearest`, `carry_with`…). There is no scripted AI. What a tribe *knows* is a library of named lambda abstractions over SURV: `make_cordage`, `bank_the_fire`, `winter_cache`, `two_person_carry`. Objects exist, but they are inert until some program in the library knows what to do with them — knowledge is the primary asset and it is a data structure you can print.
all.invention_engine:
DreamCoder's wake-sleep loop, with Stitch as the compressor, embedded in a survival economy.
WAKE (all day, CPU, deterministic VM with a STEP BUDGET, never wall-clock): the world poses tasks (hungry, cold, this broke, the river moved). An agent solves by (i) retrieving library functions by embedding similarity on the task description (bge-small, 130 MB), (ii) enumerative/beam search over the library guided by a learned prior — start with a bigram over primitives, graduate to a 2-layer MLP; (iii) when search fails N times, and only then, the local 4B proposes a program SKETCH with holes that search fills. That is LILO's neurosymbolic split: LLM reaches concepts enumeration can't, symbolic compression consolidates them.
SLEEP-ABSTRACTION (nightly, ~10 min): take every program that succeeded today across all tribes and run **Stitch** (`stitch_core`, Rust with Python bindings) to find the abstractions that maximally compress the corpus. Any abstraction with compression gain above a bit threshold becomes a NEW NAMED PRIMITIVE with an inventor, a date, and a lineage. LILO's AutoDoc step: the local model writes its name and one-line docstring. That named primitive IS a discovered technology — it is in the library, it is inheritable, it is teachable, it is losable.
SLEEP-DREAMING: replay library functions against randomised worlds to train the search prior. This is the step that makes tomorrow's search reach deeper than today's, and it is why the thing compounds instead of plateauing at depth 2.
all.why_unbounded: Programs are unbounded, and the alphabet grows. Each new abstraction shortens the description length of a family of behaviours, which brings previously-unreachable behaviours inside the same search budget — that is the compounding DreamCoder actually demonstrated (it rediscovered classic list routines and physical laws from bare primitives). The space is not the bound; the bound is search budget × task-distribution richness, and the world generates the tasks, so as long as the world keeps changing the task distribution never freezes. This is the only engine here where the depth metric is a real number: abstraction depth in the library DAG, and bits saved.
all.depth_ladder: WEEK 1: 40 primitives grow to ~55. Abstractions like "walk to nearest X and take it" — trivial, but they were carved out, not written. WEEK 2–4: `keep_fire_alive`, `two_person_carry`; then the real milestone, the first abstraction whose body contains two other invented abstractions (depth 2). MONTH 2: depth 4–5 abstractions that read like practices — crop rotation, kiln tending, a division-of-labour protocol parameterised by role. MONTH 3–6: HIGHER-ORDER abstractions that take other abstractions as arguments — `repeat_until_stable(f)`, `teach(f, learner)`, `try_then_fallback(f,g)`. The moment a tribe invents a *method* rather than a technique is the moment this stops feeling like a toy. Tool-making programs whose output is an object whose use requires yet another program. WILDEST PLAUSIBLE: the library contains an abstraction that constructs abstractions — an invented apprenticeship protocol — and you can point at the exact night it appeared and the three ancestors it came from.
all.what_selects: VM step budget = calories. A behaviour costing 4000 steps eats more than one costing 900, so MDL compression IS metabolic efficiency — the single most elegant coupling in this document, and it means the compressor's objective and the survival objective are the same objective. Winter culls tribes with thin caloric margin. Libraries pass to children through a TRANSMISSION BOTTLENECK: only K functions can be demonstrated per season, so a large library is a liability for a small tribe (Henrich's Tasmania result falls straight out). Tribes with smaller, better-compressed libraries outcompete hoarders — which is a genuinely counter-intuitive dynamic you will watch happen.
all.changing_worlds: World-generation parameters mutate each era: rainfall, predator pressure, ore placement, a new organism with new affordances. Because the sim is CPU-cheap, run 3–5 worlds in parallel with different generators and let libraries migrate via a wanderer who can carry at most 5 functions across. A function that survives transplant into a differently-generated world is the strongest possible evidence that the abstraction is real rather than overfit — that is a genuine experiment your system runs on itself, nightly.
all.novelty_detector: MDL-native, so almost no false positives — the signal is a number of bits. Push when tonight's Stitch run produces an abstraction that is (a) in the top 1% of all-time compression gain, (b) arity ≥2 with a body containing ≥2 previously-invented abstractions (a composition-depth record), or (c) the first-ever higher-order abstraction. Second detector: a held-out task suite, auto-generated and never trained on, evaluated nightly — push when a task CLASS flips from 0% to >50% solved, which is a capability frontier crossing rather than a lucky run. Third: a LOSS alarm when an abstraction's speaker count hits zero.
all.phone_view: A library card. Tonight's new named function, its AutoDoc line, the bits saved, its three ancestors, and the pretty-printed body (5–8 lines of SURV — short by construction, because that's what compression means). Two sparklines: LIBRARY DEPTH and CALORIES PER SOLVED TASK (falling = they are getting good at being alive). Tap for the library DAG; tap a function to watch its program execute in the browser, because the VM is compiled to WASM and the PWA can replay any program from any night.
all.hardware_use: This is the honest CPU idea, and that is a feature: Stitch is Rust and fast, the SURV VM does millions of steps/sec, and 64 GB RAM lets you hold every program corpus from every night in memory for retro-compression experiments. GPU is used for three optional things: the 4B sketch proposer when search stalls, bge-small embeddings for retrieval, and — if you want the Ouroboros Forge flywheel inside a world — a weekly QLoRA on the sketch model using ONLY verified programs. Unsloth supports Blackwell/RTX 50-series (needs CUDA 12.8), and a 4B QLoRA fits 8 GB, but you must stop the inference server first and expect an hour of the laptop running hot. BENCHMARK HYGIENE, non-negotiable: fitness is VM step counts and material counts, never seconds — a thermally-throttling laptop would otherwise silently reshape evolution overnight and you would never find the bug.
all.input_cadence: None. Optional weekly: read the auto-generated UNSOLVED TASKS list over coffee and hand-write one task if something obvious is missing. This is the one idea where a five-minute weekly nudge measurably changes the trajectory, because the task distribution is the real bottleneck.
all.tech: Python for the wake-sleep orchestrator; `stitch_core` from PyPI for compression (POPL'23 algorithm, 3–4 orders of magnitude faster than DreamCoder's compressor); the SURV VM written once in Rust and compiled to both native (headless speed) and WASM (in-browser replay for the PWA); SQLite for library, lineage and corpus; llama.cpp + Qwen3.5-4B for sketches and AutoDoc; ntfy.sh push; PWA over Tailscale plus a nightly static export to GitHub Pages. SHARED SUBSTRATE with idea 4: the archive/lineage DB, the chronicle PWA and the push layer are the same.
all.first_weekend: SATURDAY: the SURV VM, 40 primitives, six hardcoded tasks, plain enumerative search with a depth cap. SUNDAY: pip install stitch_core, feed it the day's successful programs, print the top abstraction with its bit gain, add it to the library, re-run. The delight moment is unmistakable and arrives Sunday afternoon: the compressor names a subroutine you never wrote, and then Monday's search *uses* it to solve something it couldn't reach yesterday.
all.six_months_later: 300–800 named abstractions, depth 8–12, several tribes with divergent libraries, and a lineage view where the interesting fact is that a two-line function from night 12 sits underneath 60% of everything they now do. You will find yourself reading SURV like a language.
all.honest_ceiling: The hard cap is your primitive set and your world's task richness: if the 40 primitives cannot express chemistry, no amount of compression will invent chemistry. Compression gains flatten around 150–400 abstractions unless world complexity keeps growing — and growing it is the one real maintenance burden in this idea, so be honest with yourself about that. Enumerative search over a growing library also gets slower; the learned prior has to actually work, and a bigram prior will likely stall around depth 6, at which point you are writing a neural recogniser and this becomes a real ML project. DreamCoder's published results used serious compute; a laptop version will be slower and shallower. But the compounding is real, visible within 48 hours, and measured in bits — you will never have to wonder whether it is working.
all.research_notes: Verified: DreamCoder (Ellis et al., PLDI 2021) — iterative wake-sleep alternating between searching for solutions and refactoring shared abstractions into a library that guides future search (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3453483.3454080). Stitch (Bowers et al., POPL 2023) is the practical compressor: corpus-guided top-down synthesis, 3–4 orders of magnitude faster and 2 orders less memory than the prior compressor at equal-or-better compressivity, open source with Python AND Rust bindings (https://github.com/mlb2251/stitch, https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.16605, crate `stitch_core` at https://lib.rs/crates/stitch_core). LILO (ICLR 2024) is the neurosymbolic version I am copying: STITCH compression + LLM-generated AutoDoc producing an interpretable library of λ-abstractions, beating a language-guided DreamCoder on all three domains, with the explicit finding that LLM-guided search finds concepts enumerative search cannot while compression consolidates them into reusable abstractions (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.19791). Voyager for the skill-library-plus-auto-curriculum shape and its concrete numbers: skill library of executable code indexed by embeddings of natural-language descriptions, iterative prompting with environment feedback + execution errors + a self-verification call, 63 unique items over 160 iterations, 3.3× prior SOTA (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291, https://voyager.minedojo.org/). Successors exist if you want more ideas: Optimus-1's hierarchical knowledge graph memory, XENON's use of failed experiences to revise dependency knowledge. Unsloth on Blackwell/RTX 50-series is confirmed supported and needs CUDA 12.8; QLoRA on 8 GB handles up to ~11B (https://unsloth.ai/docs/blog/fine-tuning-llms-with-blackwell-rtx-50-series-and-unsloth). Tasmania/transmission-bottleneck loss: Henrich 2004 (https://www2.psych.ubc.ca/~henrich/Website/Papers/HenrichTasmania.pdf).

audit.name: Ashcairn
audit.ceiling: The task distribution, not the compressor — and the doc half-admits it in `input_cadence`. Stitch will happily compress whatever you feed it; a 96×96 survival world with hunger, cold, breakage and a moving river generates maybe 8–15 genuinely distinct behaviour families. Compression gain flattens when the corpus stops containing new recurring structure, and that happens at roughly 30–80 abstractions and composition depth 3–4, not '150–400' and not depth 8–12. Timeline: real compounding visible in 48h (true, and the best first-weekend payoff of the six), depth-2 abstractions week 2, depth 3 around week 4–6, then a long flat stretch where nightly Stitch runs return sub-threshold gains and you start hand-writing tasks to keep it moving. DreamCoder's published depth came from *staged, curated* task curricula across hundreds of tasks per domain; 'the world poses tasks' is a much thinner and much less compositionally structured curriculum than list-processing or LOGO.
audit.authored_content_risk: LOWEST OF THE SIX. Abstractions are genuinely carved out of behaviour by a compressor, with an inventor, a date, a bit-gain, and a printable body. Nothing about `make_cordage` was written by the designer. This is the only idea where 'discovery' survives the merciless reading. The one leak is the LLM sketch proposer: when enumeration stalls and the 4B proposes a program sketch, the LLM's prior about survival strategy enters the library — but it enters as *holes filled by verified search against a deterministic VM*, so it is checked, not asserted. That is the right containment.
audit.compute_honesty: HONEST — genuinely a laptop project, and correct about which parts are which. Stitch is Rust and fast at this corpus size; the VM does millions of steps/sec; 64GB for retro-compression is a real use. Two corrections. (1) 'A bigram prior will stall around depth 6' is optimistic by a factor of two or more — a bigram over primitives gives almost no guidance over a growing library and will stall at depth 2–3; you will be writing the neural recogniser in month one, and the doc should treat that as the plan, not the fallback. (2) The nightly training signal for that recogniser is thin: DreamCoder's dreaming phase worked because replay generated large synthetic corpora; with one small world you will overfit the prior to the current world's tasks, which is the exact opposite of what you need. The multi-world migration test is a good instinct and should be promoted from validation to training-data generation. QLoRA-on-8GB is a distraction here and the doc is right to make it optional; 'up to ~11B on 8GB' is marketing, not a usable configuration.
audit.dubious_claims: TWO REAL ERRORS. (1) 'MDL compression IS metabolic efficiency — the single most elegant coupling in this document.' This is a category error and it is load-bearing. Stitch minimises description length of the *corpus* (program size in AST nodes), not execution cost. A four-token abstraction can loop 40,000 VM steps. Compression and calories are not the same objective and will diverge immediately; Stitch will invent short, expensive abstractions and your survival selection will punish them, so the two halves of the engine fight. Fix by re-ranking Stitch's candidate abstractions by amortised step savings across the corpus before admitting them to the library. (2) 'Higher-order abstractions that take other abstractions as arguments — `repeat_until_stable(f)`, `teach(f, learner)` … an abstraction that constructs abstractions.' Stitch finds maximal-compression subtree patterns with *term* holes. It does not synthesise higher-order combinators, and it certainly does not produce metaprograms. You would need first-class functions in SURV *and* a corpus that already contains multiple hand-instantiated versions of the pattern before compression could abstract over it — at which point you authored it. The 'invented apprenticeship protocol' wildest-plausible is fantasy as described. Smaller: LILO's ICLR'24 result and Stitch's POPL'23 speedups are stated correctly; Voyager's 63 items / 160 iterations / 3.3× is correct; DreamCoder's physics-law rediscovery is correct but was a symbolic-regression domain, not a situated agent.
audit.semantic_risk: NEAR ZERO — the best of the six. Programs run or they don't; the VM is the adjudicator and it cannot be sweet-talked. Nonsense here manifests as *uninteresting* abstractions (a compressed pattern with no meaning a human would name), not as false ones, and the AutoDoc naming pass makes them look better than they are — which is a mild honesty risk in the chronicle, not in the mechanism.
audit.one_change: Replace world-posed tasks with an OMNI-EPIC-style auto-curriculum: a generator that proposes new tasks conditioned on the current library, gated by learning progress (push tasks just outside the frontier, retire ones solved or never solved). The compressor is not the bottleneck and never was — the task distribution is, and the design already concedes this by asking the human for one hand-written task a week. Automating that single loop is the difference between plateauing at depth 4 in month two and continuing to compound.

all.name: The Closure
all.pitch: A world made of reactions rather than things, where a settlement is alive only if its known reactions form a self-sustaining autocatalytic set closed over what the land freely gives — computed exactly, every tick, by the polynomial RAF algorithm. Invention is the discovery of a catalyst; the dramatic event is a CLOSURE, the moment a loop becomes self-sustaining, and its mirror is a cascade collapse when one catalyst goes extinct.
all.world: Six to twenty settlements on a geography that decides the FOOD SET F — the stuffs the land gives freely (sun, water, clay, reed, game, a seam of ore). Everything else is a STUFF produced by a REACTION `inputs → outputs, catalysed by C`. Materials, foods, tools and even practices are all stuffs of different types, treated uniformly. A settlement's knowledge is a set of reactions it has discovered. Its actual working technology is its maxRAF: the largest subset that is Reflexively Autocatalytic and Food-generated — every reaction catalysed by something the set produces or that is in F, every reactant reachable from F. Everything outside the maxRAF is knowledge they hold but cannot run: recipes for a machine they cannot build. That distinction — knowing versus being able — is the whole emotional core.
all.invention_engine:
Two coupled generators plus one exact algorithm.
(1) GENERATIVE REACTION GRAMMAR. Reactions are never enumerated up front. Typed rewrite operators (JOIN, SPLIT, SUBSTITUTE, REFINE, CATALYSE) generate candidate reactions from the *current* stuff set, so the candidate space grows with every discovery.
(2) LAZY CATALYSIS ORACLE. Whether stuff X catalyses reaction r is decided on demand: first by cheap typed compatibility rules (a hard hot thing catalyses a shaping reaction on a soft warm thing), and only for consequential cases by the local 4B under a GBNF grammar emitting `{catalyses: bool, efficiency 0..1, one-line why}`. Cached forever, keyed by (stuff signature, reaction signature, world chemistry seed). Because catalysis is the only thing the model decides, the token bill is tiny and the model's arbitrariness is confined to one relation.
(3) THE RAF FIXPOINT (Hordijk & Steel). Roughly fifty lines: repeatedly delete any reaction lacking a producible catalyst or a producible reactant until nothing changes; what remains is the maxRAF. Polynomial, runs per settlement per tick without noticing. Run it on the flow graph too (a simple relaxation or small LP) to get throughput.
INVENTION = an agent tries a candidate reaction; success adds it to the known set. The event worth caring about is when adding one reaction makes the maxRAF grow DISCONTINUOUSLY — twelve dormant reactions suddenly become runnable because the missing catalyst arrived. That is a closure, it is exactly computable, and it is the most satisfying thing a graph can do.
all.why_unbounded: The reaction grammar generates candidates from the current stuff set, so each new stuff multiplies candidates, and catalysis is a relation over stuff × reactions — quadratic in a growing set. Kauffman's core result is the reason this has structure rather than just size: as catalysis density crosses a threshold, RAFs appear as a phase transition, and every closure raises the local density, seeding the next transition in a new region. So progress is punctuated, not linear, which is precisely the "and then one day something wild" texture the builder asked for. Honest bound: the operator set of the grammar. With JOIN/SPLIT/SUBSTITUTE alone, stuffs are effectively strings over an alphabet — infinite, but structurally repetitive after a while. Adding an operator is the god-tier nudge that reopens the space.
all.depth_ladder: WEEK 1: the hearth closure. Fire is catalysed by dry tinder, which is produced by drying, which is catalysed by fire. Your first self-sustaining cycle, drawn as a highlighted loop, and it will genuinely delight you because you did not put it there — the grammar found it. WEEK 2–4: a pottery closure; then COUPLING, where one closure's waste is another's food, and the two become one bigger RAF. MONTH 2: parasitic sub-RAFs. Model ritual and story as reactions too: a practice that consumes surplus and catalyses cohesion is a real RAF member, so religion emerges as metabolism and can be analysed the same way. MONTH 3–6: CLOSURE TRADE — two settlements each holding half of a RAF, neither able to run it alone. That is the mechanical birth of interdependence, and therefore of politics, treaties and hostage-taking. WILDEST PLAUSIBLE: a RAF spanning three settlements that survives the loss of any one of them — a genuinely distributed, robust industry — and the inverse, a single catalyst's extinction cascading through 40% of the network in one night, rendered as an animation you will watch more than once.
all.what_selects: A settlement dies when its RAF cannot produce maintenance stuffs (calories, warmth, replacement tools) at the required rate; throughput comes from the flow relaxation on the RAF, so bigger and denser RAFs mean surplus, which means more people, which means more attempts per day and faster invention. That endogenous demographic feedback loop is the growth engine, and it runs in reverse just as well. Catalysts have HOLDERS (people, places, objects) — so the Tasmania effect is structural, not bolted on: a small settlement mathematically cannot hold a large RAF, because too many catalysts have a single point of failure.
all.changing_worlds: F is geography, so geography is physics here. Move the coastline, exhaust the ore seam, shift the climate and the same reaction knowledge yields a different maxRAF — knowledge that was technology becomes folklore. New worlds get a different F and a different CHEMISTRY SEED that biases the catalysis prior, so the same grammar builds a different periodic table. Migration is the cruelest and best mechanic in the design: a band carries its reaction knowledge to a new place and the RAF simply does not close there, and the maths tells you exactly which one missing catalyst is the reason.
all.novelty_detector: Closure events are the detector — this design gets its novelty signal for free from exact graph computation, with essentially zero false positives. Push on: the first-ever closure of a new sub-RAF; the largest single-night jump in maxRAF size; a FRAGILITY ALARM (a catalyst whose removal would collapse ≥30% of the RAF is now held by ≤2 people — a min-cut computation, and a genuinely suspenseful notification); and any collapse of >20%. Once closures become routine at month three, switch the statistic from "a closure happened" to "closure rate deviates >3σ" — the detector has to age with the world, and you should plan that from the start.
all.phone_view: One picture: the maxRAF as a small circular force-free graph laid out by ring depth, with tonight's new cycle glowing. Three numbers: RAF SIZE, THROUGHPUT, FRAGILITY (min-cut). One headline: "NIGHT 63 — charcoal closed the iron loop; 14 dormant reactions joined the working set." A glance tells you whether the civilization got bigger, faster, or more brittle. Tapping a node shows who holds that catalyst and what dies without them.
all.hardware_use: The lightest of the six. RAF fixpoint is polynomial and tiny at these sizes; candidate pools of millions of reactions fit comfortably in 64 GB RAM (this is the one idea where the RAM matters more than the GPU). The GPU runs the local 4B for catalysis adjudication, batched nightly rather than in the inner loop — a few thousand calls a night at ~200 tokens each is under an hour of GPU time. 8 GB VRAM is a complete non-issue. You could run this on a Raspberry Pi if you dropped the oracle.
all.input_cadence: Zero. Optional: hand-place a resource, or add one operator to the reaction grammar when things feel repetitive — that is the single highest-leverage twenty-minute intervention in the design.
all.tech: Python or node + SQLite. The RAF algorithm hand-rolled (~100 lines, a fixpoint loop; there is no need for a library and writing it yourself is the fun part). Reaction grammar as typed rewrite rules in a small module. llama.cpp GBNF for catalysis. Hand-rolled SVG graph rendering in the PWA — no chart library, the layout is a ring by production depth. ntfy.sh push, Tailscale-served PWA plus nightly GitHub Pages export.
all.first_weekend: SATURDAY: implement the RAF fixpoint against 30 hand-written reactions and a food set, and prove it finds the hearth loop and correctly refuses a loop with no external catalyst. This is a satisfying, fully-testable Saturday with a real algorithm at the end of it. SUNDAY: the generative grammar, the lazy catalysis oracle, and one settlement that tries things while you watch. Delight moment: the highlighted cycle appearing on its own, from reactions the grammar generated rather than ones you typed.
all.six_months_later: An economy where you can point at the exact reaction whose loss would end a civilization; settlements at war over a single catalyst; a browsable atlas of every closure event with its date and discoverer; and a phone view that is a living metabolic map of a society.
all.honest_ceiling: This is only as rich as the reaction grammar — the grammar is the game, and if it is boring the world is boring no matter how elegant the RAF maths. Catalysis assigned by an LLM inherits its arbitrariness; assigned by typed rules it inherits their finiteness; there is no third option and you will oscillate between them. Expect this to feel like an *economy and infrastructure* simulator rather than a cavemen-discovering-fire story unless you invest properly in the narrator — the maths is beautiful but it is not, by itself, a story. And closures stop being surprising around month three, so the novelty detector must be re-based onto rates, which is a real (if small) piece of maintenance.
all.research_notes: Verified: RAF sets are Hordijk & Steel's formalisation of Kauffman's collectively autocatalytic sets — 'reflexively autocatalytic and food-generated' — with a polynomial-time algorithm that detects whether a RAF exists in a general network of interacting entities, implemented and applied to Kauffman's original binary-polymer model (original paper: 'Detecting autocatalytic, self-sustaining sets in chemical reaction systems', J. Theor. Biol. 2004 — https://www.math.canterbury.ac.nz/~m.steel/Non_UC/files/research/autocatalytic-edited.pdf; structural theory and algorithms review: https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsif.2018.0808; tractable models: https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.03953; formal framework slides: https://members.elsi.jp/~sympo/1st_20130327/14_hordijk/src/28_3_10_hordijk.pdf). The 'general RAF setting is NP-hard but graph-theoretic restrictions give efficient polynomial algorithms' framing is from the Royal Society Interface review and is exactly the tradeoff you want. Artificial-chemistry neighbours worth reading before you commit to a grammar: AlChemy (Fontana & Buss, untyped lambda calculus) with a 2025 ALIFE paper on steering it via endogenous features that synthesises Church addition from simple primitives (https://direct.mit.edu/isal/proceedings/isal2025/37/28/134038); Combinatory Chemistry (Kruszewski & Mikolov) for combinator-based emergent evolution; Sayama's Hash Chemistry as a minimalist open-ended system (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.18027, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.12790); Buliga's chemlambda, a Turing-complete artificial chemistry with purely local reversible rewrites. Also relevant and encouraging: 'An Open-Ended Approach to Understanding Local, Emergent Conservation Laws in Biological Evolution' (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.03345).

audit.name: The Closure
audit.ceiling: Understand what RAF actually is: a *detector*, not a generator. The maxRAF fixpoint invents nothing — it reports which subset of an already-generated network is self-sustaining. So every claim about depth reduces to a claim about the five-operator rewrite grammar plus the catalysis oracle, and the elegant polynomial algorithm is downstream decoration. The grammar's honest description is in the doc itself: 'with JOIN/SPLIT/SUBSTITUTE alone, stuffs are effectively strings over an alphabet — infinite, but structurally repetitive.' That is the whole ceiling in one sentence. You will have 10^5 stuffs that are concatenations of clay/reed/ochre with no differentiating structure, and the RAF over them will be large and meaningless. Second and sharper wall: the design has one knob (catalysis density) and a narrow window. Kauffman's result is that RAFs appear *as a phase transition* in catalysis probability. Below the window nothing ever closes and the world is dead; above it, everything closes at once and closure stops being an event by week 2 — the doc says 'closures stop being surprising around month three'; I'd say week 3. You will spend the project hand-tuning the catalysis prior to stay in a band, which is designer intervention wearing a mathematics costume. Realistic: the hearth closure lands weekend 1 and it will genuinely delight; coupled closures by week 3; then an economy simulator that grows in size but not in kind.
audit.authored_content_risk: MEDIUM. The RAF layer is real, exact, and unauthored — closures genuinely are discovered, and 'which single catalyst's loss collapses 40% of the network' is a real computed fact, not a narrative. But the *content* of the network is (a) a designer-written rewrite grammar and (b) an LLM's vibes about what catalyses what. The grammar is a small authored object whose shape determines everything; the oracle is the same pretrained-prior-as-tech-tree problem as ideas 1/5/6, just confined to one boolean relation. The doc's own framing — 'assigned by an LLM it inherits arbitrariness; assigned by typed rules it inherits their finiteness; there is no third option' — is an accurate statement that the design has no answer to the central question.
audit.compute_honesty: HONEST on the arithmetic, DISHONEST about laziness. The RAF fixpoint is trivially cheap at these sizes, the memory claims are fine, and 'you could run this on a Pi' is true. But there is a correctness bug in the coupling of lazy catalysis with RAF closure: maxRAF is computed over a network whose *edges are mostly unqueried*. Whether reaction r is in the RAF depends on whether some producible stuff catalyses it — a fact you have deferred. So either you compute maxRAF over a network you know to be incomplete (and 'exactly computable' becomes false — your headline event is an artifact of query order), or you must eagerly adjudicate the entire frontier every tick, and the token cost is nowhere near 'a few thousand calls a night'. The doc never confronts this and it is the design's most concrete technical hole.
audit.dubious_claims: The complexity framing is garbled and inverted. Deciding whether a RAF exists and computing the maxRAF is polynomial in the *general* case (that is Hordijk & Steel's central result); what is NP-hard is finding *minimal/irreducible* RAFs and several constrained variants. The doc says the reverse — 'the general RAF setting is NP-hard but graph-theoretic restrictions give efficient polynomial algorithms' — which misdescribes the one paper the whole design rests on. Second: transferring Kauffman's phase-transition result to this world is unsound. That result concerns *random* catalysis at fixed probability in a binary-polymer model. Here catalysis is assigned by an LLM's semantic prior, which is strongly non-random and correlated with the rewrite grammar's own structure; the threshold theory simply does not carry over, and 'every closure raises local density, seeding the next transition' is asserted, not derived. Third, minor: chemlambda's rewrites are local but not reversible in general. Fourth: the Sayama Hash Chemistry arXiv IDs look mismatched to the described works, and the 2025 ALIFE AlChemy-steering paper is beyond what I can verify. Hordijk & Steel 2004 JTB and the 2018 Interface review are real and correctly attributed otherwise.
audit.semantic_risk: HIGH. 'Model ritual and story as reactions too: a practice that consumes surplus and catalyses cohesion' — that is relabeling, not mechanism, and it is the tell. When every kind of thing is a 'stuff' and every process is a 'reaction', the type system stops doing work and the graph stops meaning anything. Combined with string-concatenation stuffs, you get a large, precisely-computed, beautifully-rendered graph of nothing. The maths will remain exactly correct about a network that has ceased to be about anything.
audit.one_change: Kill the LLM catalysis oracle and make catalysis a deterministic function of the rewrite grammar's own type structure — i.e. give stuffs real internal structure (a term, not a string) and derive catalysis from structural matching. Then catalysis density becomes a tunable, principled parameter, the phase-transition theory you are citing actually applies, the network is self-consistent so maxRAF is genuinely exact, the lazy-adjudication hole disappears, and the grammar — which the doc correctly identifies as 'the game' — becomes something you can deepen with structure rather than with more string operators.

all.name: Sandwright
all.pitch: A falling-sand material world where the physics itself is the oracle — no LLM decides whether anything works — and technologies are spatial machine assemblies discovered by a MAP-Elites archive, with recurring sub-assemblies frozen into named modules that become the alphabet for the next generation of search. Arthur's "technology is combination" implemented literally in space, on the GPU, at thousands of blueprint evaluations per second.
all.world: A 2D cellular material world in the Powder-Toy / Noita lineage: 512×512 per region, ~30 material types, local rules for gravity, heat conduction, ignition, phase change, fluid flow, pressure, structural load, corrosion, and charge diffusion. Tribes of agents live on top of it and are relatively simple — this is the one design where the agents are not the interesting part; the MACHINES are. Every material behaviour is a rule you wrote once, and every consequence of those rules is something you did not write. Wood chars in low oxygen. Water boils and the steam has pressure. Ore reduces above a temperature you never labelled as a milestone.
all.invention_engine:
A technology is a BLUEPRINT: a small spatial arrangement of materials (say 24×24 cells) plus a control program (strike here, open that, wait) and declared PORTS (input cell region, output cell region). Three parts:
(1) NEEDS AS MEASURABLE OBJECTIVES. Agents pose objectives the physics can score: 'raise 1 kg water 3 m', 'hold 900 K for 200 ticks', 'cut a 5-cell notch in oak', 'keep this cell between 600 and 700 K unattended'.
(2) MAP-ELITES OVER BLUEPRINT SPACE. Archive keyed by behavioural descriptors — materials used, footprint, energy in, port topology, module count. Fitness = objective achievement per unit input. Mutation operators: spatial (grow, erode, mirror, translate), material substitution, control-program mutation, and crucially MODULE INSERTION — dropping a previously discovered blueprint in as a black box.
(3) MODULE ABSTRACTION — the compounding step. Any sub-assembly appearing in ≥K elite blueprints across ≥3 distinct objectives is frozen into a named MODULE with an interface: its ports plus a MEASURED TRANSFER FUNCTION (what comes out as a function of what goes in, fitted from simulation runs). Modules become primitives for future search. A bellows becomes a part. A furnace becomes a part. Furnace+bellows becomes 'hot furnace' — one part. Modules are what tribes teach, trade, steal, and lose.
all.why_unbounded: The space of spatial arrangements over 30 materials in a 24×24 blueprint is astronomically large, and unlike a token space it is GROUNDED: the physics adjudicates, so the nonsense-soup failure mode that haunts every LLM-crafting design simply does not exist here. Nothing can be invented that does not work, because working is defined by simulation. Compounding comes from modules-as-primitives — search operates over an alphabet that grows with every discovery, so the effective depth of what search can reach in a fixed budget increases monotonically. The real bound is the physics's expressive ceiling: you can only invent what the CA rules can express. That makes 'add one material rule' a legitimate, high-leverage god-tier nudge rather than a chore — each new rule measurably reopens whole regions of the archive, and you can watch archive coverage jump the next morning.
all.depth_ladder: WEEK 1: sharp edges, a fire pit that stays lit, a windbreak that actually changes local heat loss. WEEK 2–4: a water lift; a charcoal pile that requires oxygen starvation (a real emergent discovery in falling-sand chemistry that you will not have anticipated); a kiln that holds temperature. MONTH 2: bellows + furnace composite — the first two-module machine — then smelting, then the first machine that manufactures a part for another machine. MONTH 3–6: heat engines, because steam pressure is already in the CA; mechanical linkages; water-powered trip hammers; electricity if you put charge diffusion in from day one, which you should. WILDEST PLAUSIBLE: a self-regulating machine. MAP-Elites finds an arrangement that holds a kiln at temperature with no agent tending it — a thermostat discovered by search, not designed — which means the tribe has invented CONTROL, and you can watch it work pixel by pixel on your phone.
all.what_selects: Thermodynamics, all the way down. Fuel is finite and local, and the CA tracks the actual trees, so deforestation is a literal pixel event that forces the charcoal transition. Machines wear, corrode and fail; a tribe that cannot rebuild a module loses it, and rebuilding requires the modules that built it. Tribes compete for ore and fuel gradients. Machines that fail kill people — the physics does the killing, which is far more convincing than a damage formula. Population is search throughput: more people means more blueprint evaluations per day, so demography and invention rate are coupled in both directions.
all.changing_worlds: Regions with different geology and climate: a wet region makes fire tech expensive and water tech cheap, and the two regions develop visibly different engineering traditions from identical rules. Eras cycle — a volcanic era adds obsidian and sulfur, an ice age changes fluid behaviour and makes stored heat precious. And the honest non-stationarity lever: adding ONE new material rule every few weeks is your only maintenance ritual, it takes twenty minutes, and its effect on archive coverage is immediately measurable, which makes it satisfying rather than a chore.
all.novelty_detector: Archive-native. Push when (a) a previously empty MAP-Elites cell fills and its elite beats the global best on a new objective, (b) a new MODULE is frozen — module births are rare and always interesting, (c) an elite uses ≥3 modules (a compositional-depth record), (d) an objective unsolved for ≥14 days is solved. Then the best signal in this entire document: PHYSICS SURPRISE — a machine whose measured transfer function deviates >3σ from the linear composition of its constituent modules' transfer functions. That is, mechanically, 'the machine does something its parts do not predict', which is the operational definition of an emergent invention, and it is computable from data you are already collecting.
all.phone_view: A three-second looping WebP of the new machine actually running, autoplaying on the card, with its name, the objective it serves, and its module ancestry as three small icons. Nothing on earth explains a machine faster than watching it. Generation is cheap: render 90 CA frames to a canvas and encode. Below it, one number — ARCHIVE COVERAGE (% of descriptor cells filled) — and one counter, MODULES. Tap for the machine catalogue, which is the binge view: scrolling a catalogue of little looping machines your laptop invented is exactly the artifact worth building.
all.hardware_use: This is the only idea that uses the RTX 5070 for what it is actually good at, and it is a much better use of 8 GB than holding an LLM. The material CA is embarrassingly parallel: write it as a WebGPU/WGSL compute shader (or CUDA) and run hundreds of 256×256 test chambers concurrently in VRAM — 8 GB holds on the order of hundreds of chambers with double-buffered state, giving thousands of blueprint evaluations per second, which is what makes MAP-Elites actually converge on a laptop. Write the kernel in WGSL specifically so the same code runs in the browser for PWA replay. The local 4B is relegated to naming things and writing the chronicle, which is the correct job for it. BENCHMARK HYGIENE: fitness in CA ticks and material counts, never wall-clock — under thermal throttling a timing-based fitness would quietly select for machines that happen to be evaluated when the laptop is cool.
all.input_cadence: Near zero. The optional weekly ritual is 'add a material rule', which is genuinely fun and takes twenty minutes.
all.tech: WebGPU compute via wgpu (Rust) or a node/Deno WebGPU binding, so the CA kernel is literally shared between the headless runner and the PWA. MAP-Elites archive in SQLite + numpy; blueprint = a small integer tensor plus a control program. WebP/GIF encoding for the loops. llama.cpp for names and chronicle prose. ntfy.sh; PWA over Tailscale plus nightly static export to GitHub Pages. SHARED SUBSTRATE with idea 2: same archive/lineage DB, same chronicle PWA, same push layer. This idea also has the best physical-artifact story: a receipt printer (python-escpos over USB) printing one machine's blueprint as ASCII plus its name and date, every morning.
all.first_weekend: SATURDAY: falling-sand CA with 8 materials and heat, on the CPU first at 128×128 — do NOT start on the GPU, you want to debug the rules in a language you can print from. Add one fixed objective ('get this cell above 800 K'). SUNDAY: random blueprint mutation, a MAP-Elites archive with three descriptors, and a GIF of the best elite. The delight moment: search finds an oxygen-starved charcoal pile that your own rules permitted and you did not know about.
all.six_months_later: A catalogue of 50–200 modules with measured transfer functions; regional engineering traditions that diverged from identical rules; a phone feed of little machines that actually run; and the specific pleasure of scrolling a machine catalogue nobody designed.
all.honest_ceiling: It plateaus at your CA's physics, and that ceiling is closer than it feels: without pressure, electricity and some chemistry you top out at roughly 'medieval workshop', maybe 20–40 qualitatively distinct machine classes. A 2D CA also makes rotation and gears genuinely hard — either accept a world with no wheels-as-machines, or add a rigid-body layer, which is a serious project in itself. And MAP-Elites descriptor design is the real craft here; bad descriptors give you an archive full of near-duplicates that looks productive and is not. Budget for redesigning your descriptors at least twice, and for one weekend lost to a CA rule that is subtly non-conservative and quietly breaks every fitness measurement downstream.
all.research_notes: Verified: MAP-Elites is the standard illumination algorithm — a multi-dimensional archive of phenotypic elites over a user-defined feature/behaviour-descriptor space, producing the best solution of each type rather than one global optimum (Mouret & Clune 2015; overview https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/map-elites-algorithm). Extensions worth knowing before you design descriptors: Multi-Emitter MAP-Elites for convergence speed (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.05352), Multi-Objective MAP-Elites/MOME where each cell holds a local Pareto front (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.03715), and Multi-Objective QD in unbounded spaces — relevant because a growing module alphabet means your descriptor space is not fixed. Directly analogous precedent for QD over generative game systems: 'Quality Diversity in the Amorphous Fortress' evolving for complexity in 0-player games (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.02231) and micro RollerCoaster Tycoon open-ended gameplay-feature search (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04342). For the interestingness/task-generation half, OMNI-EPIC (ICLR 2025) is the reference architecture — a growing task archive of learned and failed tasks, a task generator conditioned on the archive, and an environment generator emitting environment code (https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15568, code at https://github.com/maxencefaldor/omni-epic); its explicit warning about agents optimising a metric rather than capturing interestingness is why my novelty detector here is grounded in physics deviation rather than a learned score. Theory: W. Brian Arthur, *The Nature of Technology* — technologies are combinations of prior technologies, encapsulated as modules with interfaces, which is exactly the module-freezing step. Physical artifact: python-escpos / python-printer-escpos drives USB ESC/POS thermal printers directly (https://github.com/shantanubhadoria/python-printer-escpos, https://pypi.org/project/escpos-thermal/).

audit.name: Sandwright
audit.ceiling: The CA's expressive ceiling, and it is much nearer than the depth ladder pretends. Falling-sand cellular automata are structurally incapable of rigid bodies, rotation, persistent multi-cell object identity, and load transfer through a mechanism. The doc flags this honestly in `honest_ceiling` ('rotation and gears genuinely hard') and then contradicts itself by listing heat engines, mechanical linkages and water-powered trip hammers in the month 3–6 ladder. A heat engine needs a piston: a rigid moving body with a seal, i.e. exactly the thing the substrate cannot represent. What this world can actually reach is the thermal/fluid/chemical family — fire pit, windbreak, charcoal pile, kiln, smelter, siphon/water-lift, still, maybe a self-regulating thermal loop if your rules happen to permit hysteresis. That is roughly 15–30 distinct machine classes, not 20–40, reached in 6–10 weeks. After that MAP-Elites keeps filling cells with near-duplicates and archive coverage keeps rising, which will *look* like progress on the phone and will not be.
audit.authored_content_risk: LOWEST OF THE SIX ALONGSIDE ASHCAIRN, and for the cleanest reason: no LLM is in the adjudication loop at all. The oxygen-starved charcoal pile really is a consequence of rules you wrote that you did not anticipate — that is authentic emergence, and the delight moment described for Sunday is real. The correct reading is that the designer authored a *generator* (the rule set) rather than a *catalogue*, which is the distinction the builder is actually asking for. The remaining authored content is objective specification: 'raise 1kg water 3m', 'hold 900K for 200 ticks' are hand-written goals, and the machine catalogue is therefore shaped by which objectives you thought to pose. That is a real but much milder version of the problem, and it is fixable with auto-generated objectives.
audit.compute_honesty: OPTIMISTIC BY ~10×, AND ONE CLAIM IS SIMPLY WRONG. 'The material CA is embarrassingly parallel' is false. Falling-sand movement has write conflicts — two source cells wanting the same destination — plus update-order dependence that produces the characteristic sand behaviour in the first place. Correct GPU implementations need Margolus/block partitioning or atomic conflict resolution, both of which change the dynamics relative to a sequential CPU implementation. This directly breaks the recommended plan ('debug on CPU at 128×128, then port to GPU'): your fitness landscape will shift under you at the port, and every archive elite found on CPU may be invalid on GPU. Throughput: memory is fine (a 256² chamber double-buffered is ~2MB, so hundreds fit in 8GB), but a branchy divergent falling-sand kernel gets nowhere near the arithmetic throughput of a clean kernel. At 500 chambers × 65k cells × ~500–1000 ticks per evaluation you are looking at ~10^10 cell-updates per batch; realistic is on the order of 10²–10³ evaluations/sec, not 'thousands'. Still enough for MAP-Elites — the design survives — but budget accordingly, and pin determinism early or your fitness measurements are unreproducible.
audit.dubious_claims: THE 'BEST SIGNAL IN THIS DOCUMENT' IS PROBABLY NOISE. 'PHYSICS SURPRISE — a machine whose measured transfer function deviates >3σ from the linear composition of its constituent modules' transfer functions.' In a CA with heat conduction, pressure and fluid flow, sub-assemblies are coupled non-locally through shared fields; non-additive composition is the DEFAULT, not the exception. Every multi-module machine will deviate from linear composition, so this detector fires constantly and carries no information. Worse, the same fact undermines the compounding mechanism itself: 'modules as black boxes with measured transfer functions' presumes interfaces that compose, and CA modules do not have them — a furnace's measured behaviour in isolation will not hold when a bellows is bolted to it, so MODULE INSERTION as a mutation operator is far weaker than advertised. This is the design's most serious hidden problem, and it sits precisely where the depth is supposed to come from. Also: 'electricity if you put charge diffusion in from day one' — charge diffusion is not circuits; you need conserved charge and a potential field solve, a different and much heavier component. Citation-level: MOME is Pierrot et al. (arXiv 2202.03057), not the ID given; Mouret & Clune 2015 and OMNI-EPIC (2405.15568) are correctly attributed; Arthur's modules-with-interfaces framing is used correctly and is the right theory for this design.
audit.semantic_risk: ESSENTIALLY ZERO, and this is the design's great virtue. Nothing can be invented that does not physically work, because working is defined by simulation. There is no drivel failure mode. The residual risk is the inverse: things that work but are not *interesting* — MAP-Elites archives fill with mechanically valid near-duplicates, and bad behavioural descriptors will make that look like productivity. The doc's warning to budget for redesigning descriptors twice is correct and probably still an underestimate.
audit.one_change: Add a rigid-body/mechanism layer above the CA — blueprints become jointed part-graphs (links, pivots, constraints) coupled to the cell field, rather than pure cell arrangements. This is the single edit that separates 'medieval kitchen chemistry' from 'machines', unlocks the entire month 3–6 ladder the doc already promises but cannot currently deliver, and gives module composition real interfaces (kinematic ports) instead of statistically-fitted transfer functions that don't compose. It is also a genuinely hard project — but it is the difference between a partial and a yes here, and no other change in this idea moves the ceiling at all.

all.name: Ninety-Nine Anvils
all.pitch: Dozens of small worlds running at once, each with its own LAW VECTOR that conditions both the mechanical referee and the LLM oracle, so the same combination is genuinely adjudicated differently under different physics — and the object of study is the difference between worlds. A shared ledger with nearest-law inheritance makes the token cost scale with consequence rather than with attempts, and anonymous web visitors act as gods, one omen per day.
all.world: 12–48 concurrent worlds, each a coarse 64×64 grid with a few hundred agents, sharing the typed-substance substrate from The Slow Kiln. Each world has a LAW VECTOR: 16 named continuous constants (gravity, oxygen fraction, water boiling point, decay rate, ore abundance, day length…) plus 6 boolean MYTHS that are injected into the oracle's system prompt and into the referee's parameters ('metals rust within a day', 'fire needs no air', 'the dead answer questions'). A myth is a physics constant and a cultural fact at the same time, which is the conceit that makes the whole thing sing. Worlds are born, run, and die; a dead world becomes an ASH WORLD you can still browse — the graveyard is a first-class feature.
all.invention_engine:
Infinite-Craft-style unbounded recipe space, made lawful and made cheap:
(a) TYPED SCHEMA + CONSERVATION REFEREE, shared with The Slow Kiln — the LLM fills typed property slots and mechanical laws audit it.
(b) LEDGER KEY = (canonical combo, LAW BUCKET), where the law bucket is a coarse quantisation of the 16 constants + 6 myths into ~64 buckets. Same combo, different bucket, different legitimate answer.
(c) NEAREST-LAW INHERITANCE — the cost trick. On a ledger miss, find the k nearest law buckets that HAVE adjudicated this combo; if ≥2 agree, adopt the result with confidence 0.8 and mark it PROVISIONAL. Provisional results are only re-adjudicated for real when a tribe's survival comes to depend on them. LLM calls therefore scale with CONSEQUENCE, not with attempts, which is what makes 40 worlds cost about the same as one.
(d) LAW DIVERGENCE OBJECTS. When the same combo yields materially different outcomes across two adjudicated buckets, that difference is promoted to a first-class browsable record with both results side by side. Comparative physics as a UI object; over months it becomes an atlas of how laws shape technology.
all.why_unbounded: Two axes multiply. The recipe space is the usual unbounded hypergraph (each combination can mint a new node, tamed but not bounded by the property schema). The LAW space is continuous and mutable, and worlds are cheap to spawn, so the system explores rule-sets as well as inventions — a civilization in a low-oxygen world builds a different tech tree from identical primordials. Formally the object being explored is a law-conditioned recipe manifold, and every new law bucket is a fresh slice of it. Honest bound: the LLM's cultural attractors (Infinite Craft's graph collapses toward meme-y sinks, and yours will too), plus the fact that law vectors only reach as far as the 16 constants you chose — the 17th constant is the god-tier nudge.
all.depth_ladder: WEEK 1: three worlds, identical 20 primordials, visibly different first tools by day 3 — that divergence alone is the proof-of-concept and it arrives fast. WEEK 2–4: twelve worlds plus a migration mechanic; the first recipe that is essential in one world and lethal in another. MONTH 2: a traveller caste; a queryable meta-ledger ('show me inventions that exist ONLY in high-gravity worlds' — a question no hand-authored tech tree can even express). MONTH 3–6: worlds FORKED from a snapshot with a single mutated constant, giving you true A/B physics on a running civilization; long-lived worlds developing distinct materials cultures; visitor-gods shaping worlds they have adopted. WILDEST PLAUSIBLE: a comparative-science page showing the same technology re-invented along three disjoint ancestral paths in three differently-lawed worlds — convergent technological evolution, discovered rather than authored, with the divergence points highlighted.
all.what_selects: Per-world survival as usual (calories, warmth, winter, raiding). But the distinctive layer is WORLD-LEVEL SELECTION: worlds are scored nightly on invention rate, divergence from siblings, and population stability, and the bottom 10% are retired and replaced by mutated forks of the top worlds. That is MAP-Elites applied to worlds, and it means your compute is continuously reallocated to whichever worlds are still surprising. It is the most direct structural answer to 'boring by week 2' in this whole document — boredom is measured and then killed.
all.changing_worlds: It is the premise, not a feature. Plus the perturbation layer: anonymous visitors to the public GitHub Pages site can spend one OMEN per day on any world — a weather event, a gift substance, a plague, or a line added to that world's SCRIPTURE, which is a text blob genuinely included in that world's oracle prompt. A guestbook that literally becomes law. This is cheap non-stationarity, a real reason for the artifact to be public, and the thing that makes a friend check in twice.
all.novelty_detector: (a) Cross-world CONTRADICTION with high consequence — the same combination, adjudicated for real in two worlds, giving outcomes that matter differently. (b) A world's first divergence from every sibling on a common recipe. (c) CONVERGENT RE-INVENTION: the same result reached by disjoint ancestral paths in ≥2 worlds (compare ancestor sets, Jaccard below threshold). (d) A world crossing a civilizational threshold no world has crossed. Score all four nightly, push the top 1–3. The comparative framing is what keeps this feed interesting: a single world's fiftieth invention is boring, but 'world 7 got there a completely different way' never is.
all.phone_view: A 4×3 grid of world tiles, each a 40×40 glyph encoding population, tech depth and mood as shape and colour — a dashboard of civilizations, readable in three seconds, with one tile pulsing for tonight's headline. This is the single best 30-second check-in view of the six ideas, because it shows you a whole portfolio at a glance. Tap a tile to fall into that world's chronicle; tap the headline for the divergence record with both outcomes side by side.
all.hardware_use: The sim is tiny and CPU-bound; the cost centre is adjudication. Local Qwen3.5-4B Q4_K_M under GBNF handles routine adjudication, and nearest-law inheritance means most misses never reach any model at all. Cloud usage is one nightly Haiku 4.5 Batch job for the ~300 most consequential adjudications plus the chronicle: at $1/$5 per MTok, 50% Batch discount, and a cached ~2k-token system prompt read at ~0.1×, that is roughly $0.0005 per call → $0.05–0.20 a night, call it $5/month. 8 GB VRAM is ample and you never need a bigger model, because the typed schema is doing the work the model would otherwise have to do. 64 GB RAM comfortably holds 48 world states plus the shared ledger in memory.
all.input_cadence: Zero. The only thing you may find yourself doing by hand is retiring a world you have grown tired of, which the selection layer would do for you anyway.
all.tech: node + SQLite: one DB per world plus one shared ledger DB (this separation matters — you will want to delete worlds). llama.cpp GBNF; Anthropic Batch API. A static PWA build published to GitHub Pages nightly so visitors need no Tailscale, plus the live build over Tailscale for you. ntfy.sh for push. The omen intake with no inbound ports: a Cloudflare Worker (or a GitHub Issues form) writes to a gist that your laptop polls every 10 minutes — laptop stays firewalled, world stays public. SHARED SUBSTRATE with ideas 1 and 6.
all.first_weekend: SATURDAY: one world — property schema, referee, local oracle, ledger. (If you build The Slow Kiln first, this Saturday is free.) SUNDAY: clone to three worlds with different law vectors, implement nearest-law inheritance, and render the three-tile dashboard. Delight moment: the same combination returning three different but internally coherent results, and the divergence record writing itself.
all.six_months_later: Dozens of ash worlds with epitaphs, a browsable comparative-physics atlas, a handful of long-lived worlds with genuinely distinct materials cultures, and a scripture page where a friend's joke from March has become three worlds' religion.
all.honest_ceiling: LLM cultural attractors are real and they erode divergence: the same model writes every world, so names and vibes converge over time no matter how you condition the prompt. Typed schemas and law-conditioned prompts slow this measurably; they do not stop it, and by month four you will see it. Breadth also trades against depth — forty shallow worlds are less moving than one deep one, and I expect you will cull to eight or twelve within two months and be happier for it.
