The visitor-god layer only matters if anyone actually visits; build it, but do not let the design depend on strangers showing up. And nearest-law inheritance is a lie you are choosing to tell: provisional results that never get verified are load-bearing fiction, so keep the PROVISIONAL flag visible in the UI or you will eventually confuse yourself.
all.research_notes: Verified: Infinite Craft's caching architecture is exactly the pattern I am extending — check the pair database first, only novel pairings hit the LLM, then cache forever so results are globally consistent (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite_Craft; implementation walkthrough https://www.conjecture.dev/research/building-an-infinite-craft-clone-with-tactics; hacking notes https://debarghyadas.com/writes/infinite-craft/). Scale reality check for what an unbounded recipe space actually becomes: >1M unique items and >10M recipes recorded by community databases, and the formal structure is a directed hypergraph (https://quuxplusone.github.io/blog/2024/03/03/infinite-craft-theory/). The degeneracy risk is documented informally in the community wikis' 'step depth' vs 'element depth' distinction (https://infinite-craft-nealfun.fandom.com/wiki/Step_Depth) — most new elements are shallow re-skins, which is precisely why I gate on consequence and divergence rather than on count. Relevant caution on LLM-driven search converging: 'Mutation Without Variation: Convergence Dynamics in LLM-Driven Program Evolution' (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.05408) — the same attractor problem in a different setting, and a good reason to keep a mechanical referee in the loop. Many-agent civilization precedent: Project Sid ran up to 1,000 autonomous agents in Minecraft for hours-to-days unattended and got a gem-based market economy, religious transmission, and constitutional voting — emergent, not scripted (https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00114, https://github.com/altera-al/project-sid). Pricing verified against the current Anthropic model table (claude-haiku-4-5 $1/$5 per MTok, 200K context; Batch API 50% off; prompt-cache reads ~0.1×, writes ~1.25×). Push/PWA: ntfy.sh is installable as a PWA with Web Push and app-badge unread counts, self-hostable if you'd rather (https://docs.ntfy.sh/releases/, https://ntfy.sh/).

audit.name: Ninety-Nine Anvils
audit.ceiling: There is no new depth mechanism here. This is The Slow Kiln instantiated 40 times with a comparison UI, and breadth across shallow worlds is not depth in any of them — the doc concedes this ('forty shallow worlds are less moving than one deep one; I expect you will cull to eight or twelve'). Each world inherits Kiln's ceiling and hits it *sooner*, because per-world compute is divided by 40 and the nearest-law inheritance path means most worlds are not even independently adjudicated. Realistic: divergence visible day 3 (true, and it will feel like proof), the comparative atlas is genuinely fun for 3–4 weeks, and by week 6 you are looking at 40 instances of the same shallow tree with different adjectives.
audit.authored_content_risk: THE HIGHEST OF THE SIX, WITH A COMPOUNDING FACTOR. Idea 1's problem (the tech tree is the pretrained model's compressed memory of human material culture) is inherited whole. Then the distinctive mechanism makes it worse in two specific ways. (1) The LLM has no coherent counterfactual physics for 'oxygen fraction 0.14' or 'metals rust within a day' — it has adjectival associations. So law-conditioned adjudication is prompt sensitivity, and the comparative-physics atlas — the entire point of the design — is an atlas of a 4B model's response to adjectives, presented as a finding about how laws shape technology. (2) NEAREST-LAW INHERITANCE FABRICATES THE DATA THE PROJECT EXISTS TO STUDY. Most cross-world outcomes are copied from k-nearest buckets, so the observed pattern of similarity and divergence between worlds is largely a readout of your own interpolation scheme and bucket geometry. 'Convergent re-invention across disjoint ancestral paths' will fire constantly for the trivial reason that inheritance copied the result. The doc calls this 'a lie you are choosing to tell' and proposes to manage it with a PROVISIONAL flag in the UI — but a flag does not stop the fabricated majority from being what the atlas is made of.
audit.compute_honesty: HONEST, and the cheapest of the six — but honest for a bad reason. Cost scales with consequence only because most adjudications are never performed; the compute saving and the epistemic problem are the same fact. The Haiku arithmetic is right (~$0.0006/call cached-batch, ~$0.20/night, $5/mo is if anything conservative). 48 world states plus ledger in 64GB is fine. The Cloudflare-Worker-to-gist polling design for inbound omens without open ports is genuinely good engineering. THERE IS ALSO AN ARITHMETIC BUG IN THE CORE MECHANISM: 16 continuous constants plus 6 booleans quantised into '~64 buckets' — but the 6 booleans alone generate exactly 64 combinations. At that resolution the law bucket is effectively just the myth bitmask, and the sixteen continuous constants, which are the entire 'law-conditioned recipe manifold' premise, get zero discriminating power. Either the bucket count is wrong by orders of magnitude or the continuous laws are decorative.
audit.dubious_claims: 'Mutation Without Variation: Convergence Dynamics in LLM-Driven Program Evolution', arXiv 2606.05408 — I cannot verify this; the identifier places it at the edge of what I can check and it should be treated as unconfirmed rather than as the supporting citation for the design's key risk. Project Sid (2411.00114) is real, but 'a gem-based market economy, religious transmission and constitutional voting — emergent, not scripted' repeats a company preprint's own framing; those behaviours were produced under substantial architectural scaffolding and the paper is not independent evidence that many-agent LLM civilisations self-organise. The Infinite Craft caching account and the step-depth/element-depth degeneracy note are correct — and the latter is the strongest thing in these notes, because it describes exactly what will happen here. Pricing verified correct. Separately, the world-selection rule is Goodhart bait: retiring the bottom 10% on 'invention rate and divergence' selects precisely for worlds that churn out shallow re-skins, which is the degeneracy the same research notes warn about.
audit.semantic_risk: HIGH and self-amplifying. The myths ('the dead answer questions') go into the oracle's system prompt, so the model is being asked to reason materially inside a fictional physics it has no model of. Output will be internally fluent and externally arbitrary. The referee catches conservation violations only, and law-conditioned referee parameters do not constrain semantics. Add LLM cultural attractors — same model writing all 40 worlds — and by month two the worlds converge in vibe while the divergence detector, reading fabricated inheritance data, keeps reporting that they haven't.
audit.one_change: Cut to 4–8 worlds and route the law vector through the MECHANICAL REFEREE ONLY — never into the prompt — while deleting nearest-law inheritance entirely and adjudicating each world independently. Then divergence between worlds is causally produced by rules rather than by adjectives and interpolation, the comparative atlas becomes a real finding instead of a prompt-sensitivity study, and the per-world compute budget rises 6–10× so each world can actually get deep. This costs the design its headline scale and is the only version of it worth building.

all.name: The Telling
all.pitch: Techniques are not stored as recipes but as UTTERANCES in each band's evolving language, learned by children through a transmission bottleneck that forces the language to become compositional — and once it is compositional, a child can SAY a technique nobody ever taught, and go try it. Invention as a side effect of grammar, with mis-hearing as the mutation operator and the Tasmania effect as the constant threat.
all.world: A river valley, ~200 agents in 6–10 bands, sitting on the typed-substance substrate from The Slow Kiln (substances with property vectors, process verbs, a conservation referee). But the knowledge layer is the protagonist. A MEANING is a structured frame: `(verb, patient, instrument, condition)` — HEAT(clay, in:pit, until:red). A band's LANGUAGE is a mapping from meanings to strings over an evolving phoneme inventory. An agent that wants to do something must be able to SAY it; an agent that cannot say a technique cannot reliably do it, and cannot teach it at all. Knowledge is linguistic, therefore lossy, therefore precious.
all.invention_engine:
Three coupled loops, only one of which is conventional.
(1) DOING. An agent produces the utterance for a meaning and attempts it; the typed referee and (only for genuinely novel material/process pairs) the local LLM oracle adjudicate against the world. Standard.
(2) TEACHING — Kirby/Smith iterated learning. Children observe only a SUBSET of adult utterance-meaning pairs (the bottleneck) and induce a grammar by minimum description length over a small context-free grammar — this is a well-trodden ~300-line model and it reliably works. The bottleneck forces generalisation, and generalisation is compositionality: shared morphemes emerge for shared meaning components.
(3) THE INVENTION VALVE — the part that is genuinely different from every other idea here. Once the grammar is compositional, a child can PRODUCE a well-formed utterance for a meaning that was never taught, because the grammar generates it. Most such utterances denote techniques nobody has ever tried. The agent tries one. The world says yes or no. Invention arrives as a side effect of language becoming systematic — the tribe can literally say things before it can do them, and then goes to find out.
Plus NOISE: transmission is phoneme-level noisy, so techniques drift; a drifted utterance sometimes parses to a different, workable meaning. Selection acts on comprehensibility within the band and on results in the world.
all.why_unbounded: A compositional grammar over a lexicon of size L with a handful of productive rules generates infinitely many well-formed utterances, and the meaning space is the product of a growing substance set × a growing process set × a growing condition set. Each new material added to the lexicon multiplies the set of EXPRESSIBLE techniques, almost none of which have been tried. The frontier of this system is precisely 'sentences we can say but have never said' — which is the cleanest statement of an adjacent possible I can give you, and it is directly computable: enumerate the grammar, subtract the attempted set. Honest bound: the meaning-space schema. Four-slot frames give a big but finite-dimensional space; it only grows as the underlying substance/process sets grow, which means this engine's long-run depth is inherited from the chemistry engine beneath it.
all.depth_ladder: WEEK 1: holistic language — random strings per meaning, terrible transmission, techniques constantly lost. The world feels tragic and that is correct; you are watching pre-cumulative culture. WEEK 2–4: the bottleneck starts producing regularity. The first shared morpheme appears, and the night your log prints 'morpheme /ka/ now appears in 83% of HEAT meanings' is a genuine thrill, because you did not assign /ka/ to anything. MONTH 2: full compositionality in the leading band. Knowledge stops leaking, technique count inflects sharply upward — you can literally see the cultural ratchet engage as a kink in a chart. MONTH 3–6: dialects diverge between bands; a trade pidgin forms at the confluence; translation errors produce inventions; one band invents a MARK SYSTEM (a second bottleneck-relaxing technology, reachable through the same substance substrate) and pulls decisively ahead. WILDEST PLAUSIBLE: a band develops a productive morphological rule covering a CLASS of processes it has not yet discovered, and then systematically goes looking — the language predicting the technology. If you see that once, the project has paid for itself.
all.what_selects: Survival on technique quality. Band size drives transmission fidelity directly (Henrich's demographic model, implemented rather than gestured at), so a band that splits loses its hardest-to-learn techniques first — the fishhook result, live. Comprehensibility drives communicative success within a band, creating pressure toward regularity that competes with pressure toward expressivity: that tension IS the engine. Mergers, splits and contact events change effective population and therefore change what can be held. Small isolated bands genuinely lose technologies you watched them invent, with names and dates, which is the most emotionally powerful mechanic in any of these six designs.
all.changing_worlds: Valley geography changes: floods, a landslide isolating a band, a new pass opening contact between two dialects (a language-contact event with real technique transfer). Across worlds: each world seeds a different phoneme inventory and a different meaning schema, so languages are mutually alien, and the PWA gets a translation page comparing how two worlds carved up the same physics — which is a strange and wonderful thing to browse.
all.novelty_detector: (a) PRODUCTIVE INVENTION — a technique whose utterance was generated by the grammar, never taught, and worked. Push these above everything; they are direct evidence the engine is running, and they are rare enough to stay special. (b) COMPOSITIONALITY SCORE crossing a threshold, measured with the standard iterated-learning metrics: expressivity plus stability under transmission, or topographic similarity between distances in meaning space and distances in string space. Computable nightly, one number, and a beautiful sparkline. (c) LOSS EVENTS — a technique whose speaker count hits zero; these get a different, quieter notification sound, and you will care about them. (d) CONTACT EVENTS transferring ≥5 techniques.
all.phone_view: The card is a sentence. Last night's first-ever-spoken utterance, rendered in the band's orthography, with its gloss underneath, whether it worked, and who said it. Below: two numbers — COMPOSITIONALITY (0–1, with a sparkline) and TECHNIQUES HELD, with a small red LOST counter. A sentence in a language your laptop invented, which turned out to describe a real thing, is a superb ten-second check-in and a genuinely uncanny thing to read at 7am. The binge view is the DICTIONARY: an explorable lexicon with etymologies, which you will browse for an hour without meaning to.
all.hardware_use: Very light. MDL grammar induction is CPU and small; the whole valley's grammars fit in a few hundred MB, and 64 GB RAM lets you keep every generation's grammar for diffing (which is where the good analysis lives). The local 4B has exactly two jobs: adjudicating genuinely novel technique semantics against the substance schema, and GLOSSING utterances into English for you. That second job is the most appropriate use of an LLM anywhere in this document — the model is the translator, not the physics. 8 GB VRAM is generous for this.
all.input_cadence: None. Optional joy: carve a word onto a stone and see whether it spreads. That is a two-minute intervention with a genuinely unpredictable outcome, which is the best kind.
all.tech: Python for the grammar induction and MDL search (this is the mathematically fiddly part and Python is right for it); the sim in node or Python on the shared typed-substance substrate; SQLite for lexicons, utterances, techniques and loss records; llama.cpp for glossing and novel-technique adjudication; a nightly Haiku Batch pass for chronicle prose, because glossing quality matters here more than anywhere else. PWA with a dictionary browser; ntfy.sh push. This idea has the best receipt-printer story of the six: python-escpos prints one utterance and its gloss every morning — a daily scrap of an invented language on your desk.
all.first_weekend: SATURDAY: the iterated-learning core alone. Meanings as 3-slot frames, holistic initial language, a transmission bottleneck, MDL grammar induction, ten generations. Watch compositionality emerge in a toy run in minutes — this is a well-trodden model and it WILL work on Saturday, which makes it an unusually safe first weekend. SUNDAY: wire it to 20 substances and 6 process verbs, and let grammar-generable-but-unspoken utterances be tried against the referee. Delight moment: the first working technique that nobody taught anyone.
all.six_months_later: Several mutually unintelligible dialects with a trade pidgin between them, a dictionary with etymologies you browse for pleasure, technologies whose names encode their ancestry, and a graveyard page of lost techniques with the name of the last person who knew each one.
all.honest_ceiling: The classic iterated-learning result is convergence to a STABLE compositional grammar — and stability is exactly where the drift half of the engine dies. Once the language is fully compositional and the bottleneck is comfortable, the language stops changing and the surprises come only from the meaning space growing underneath it. Which means this is really The Slow Kiln plus a language layer, and you should build it that way rather than pretending it stands alone. Two more honest costs: glossing from a 4B is mediocre and the chronicle will lean on the nightly Haiku pass to be readable; and this is the most conceptually demanding of the six — expect a month before it FEELS like a world rather than a linguistics demo. Build it second, after you have a substrate.
all.research_notes: Verified: iterated learning models show that expressive, compositional languages arise spontaneously from a TRANSMISSION BOTTLENECK — learners see only a subset of the previous generation's language and must generalise, and only compositional languages remain stable under that constraint (Kirby, 'Spontaneous evolution of linguistic structure: an iterated learning model of the emergence of regularity and irregularity' — https://www.ling.ed.ac.uk/~simon/Papers/Kirby/Spontaneous%20evolution%20of%20linguistic%20structure%20an%20iterated.pdf; Smith/Kirby/Brighton overview https://www.lel.ed.ac.uk/~kenny/publications/smith_03_iterated.pdf; Griffiths & Kalish's Bayesian treatment https://cocosci.princeton.edu/tom/papers/IteratedLearningEvolutionLanguage.pdf). Note the honest caveat from the literature: 'Compositional structure can emerge without generational transmission' (Cognition, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0010027718302464) — the bottleneck is sufficient, not strictly necessary, so do not over-attribute. Modern ML framing of the same compression/expressivity tension: 'A Compressive-Expressive Communication Framework for Compositional Representations' (https://arxiv.org/html/2501.19182) — also the source of usable compositionality metrics like topographic similarity. Demographic knowledge loss: Henrich 2004 on Tasmania — inaccuracies of cultural transmission produce technological LOSS below a critical population threshold, and the hardest-to-learn technologies go first (https://www2.psych.ubc.ca/~henrich/Website/Papers/HenrichTasmania.pdf); a runnable R version of the gain/loss model exists at https://bookdown.org/amesoudi/ABMtutorial_bookdown/model9.html. Cultural evolution among LLM agent populations, if you later want model-based agents rather than symbolic ones: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.10270 and the Cultural Evolution in LLM Populations line of work — but note the standing critique that validation is the central unsolved problem for generative social simulation (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11412-6), which is a good reason to keep your agents symbolic and your LLM confined to adjudication and glossing. Printer: python-escpos over USB (https://github.com/shantanubhadoria/python-printer-escpos).

audit.name: The Telling
audit.ceiling: Two ceilings, and the technological one is not this idea's at all. (a) TECHNOLOGICAL DEPTH IS ENTIRELY INHERITED. The invention valve produces utterances; whether an utterance denotes a workable technique is adjudicated by the same 4B oracle over the same typed-substance substrate as The Slow Kiln. The language layer therefore changes the *order and sociology* of attempts and adds nothing whatsoever to the reachable set. It is an enumeration policy over Idea 1's space, so it inherits Idea 1's week-8 ceiling and reaches it *later* because transmission loss slows the ratchet. The doc concedes exactly this ('this is really The Slow Kiln plus a language layer') and it is the correct reading. (b) THE LINGUISTIC ENGINE STOPS ON SCHEDULE. The classic iterated-learning result is convergence to a stable compositional grammar — stability is the *finding*. Once the leading band is compositional and the bottleneck is comfortable, the language freezes; drift stops being generative and becomes noise. Expect compositionality to saturate around week 6–10 in the leading band, after which the sparkline is flat forever and the remaining interest is dialect divergence and loss events. Genuinely moving, but it is a two-month arc, not a six-month one.
audit.authored_content_risk: SPLIT VERDICT, AND THE SPLIT MATTERS. The linguistic half has the lowest authored-content risk in the document: nobody assigned /ka/ to HEAT, compositionality genuinely emerges from MDL induction under a bottleneck, and the loss records are real computed facts about who knew what and when. The technological half has the same fatal problem as ideas 1 and 5 — the tech tree is the pretrained model's memory of human material culture, revealed in an order now determined by grammar rather than by inventory. And there is a specific rhetorical sleight to call out: 'the frontier is sentences we can say but have never said, which is the cleanest statement of an adjacent possible I can give you.' A compositional grammar over (verb × patient × instrument × condition) generates the CROSS-JOIN of those slots. Enumerating unattempted cells of a cross-join is trivially available in Idea 1 too — it is just 'combinations nobody has tried'. Productive morphology dressed over a Cartesian product is not an adjacent possible; it is a for-loop with an accent. The 'wildest plausible' outcome — a morphological rule covering a class of undiscovered processes, and the band systematically going looking — is that for-loop, described as prophecy.
audit.compute_honesty: HONEST FOR THE TOY, UNDERESTIMATED AT SCALE. The claim that this 'WILL work on Saturday' is true and is a real virtue — Kirby-style iterated learning at toy scale is genuinely ~300 lines and reliably produces the effect. But the toy scale is load-bearing: the canonical models use meaning spaces of a few slots with 5–10 values each and fixed vocabulary. Here the meaning space grows with the substance set toward hundreds or thousands of values, and per-child MDL grammar induction over CFGs is a search whose cost grows badly in lexicon size and corpus size. With 200 agents each inducing a grammar over a growing lexicon, grammar induction — not the LLM, not the sim — becomes the compute bottleneck within weeks, and you will be forced into approximations that may destroy the very effect you are simulating. The doc's 'very light, a few hundred MB, 8GB is generous' budget accounts for none of this. The LLM's role (glossing plus novel-technique adjudication) is correctly scoped and is the most appropriate LLM use in the document.
audit.dubious_claims: Griffiths & Kalish is cited as supporting evidence when it is substantially a caution: the Bayesian analysis shows iterated learning converges to the *learners' prior*, meaning what you will be watching emerge is largely your MDL prior's shape rather than a discovered fact about language. Given that your prior is a hand-written MDL score over a small CFG class, that is a direct authored-content leak into the one part of the design with the least authored content — worth confronting head-on. The doc also cites the Cognition result that compositional structure can emerge without generational transmission, notes the caveat honestly, and then builds the entire engine on the bottleneck anyway. Henrich 2004 is again treated as settled when the population-size→complexity effect is contested (Vaesen et al. 2016 PNAS). Topographic similarity is a real and standard compositionality metric but is noisy and highly sensitive to the choice of distance metrics in both spaces — 'one number and a beautiful sparkline' oversells its stability. Kirby's and Smith/Kirby/Brighton's results are correctly described.
audit.semantic_risk: MEDIUM-HIGH, concentrated in two places. First, glossing: a 4B model producing English glosses for an invented morphology will generate fluent, confident, wrong readings, and glosses are the entire phone experience — you will be reading the model's imagination about your simulation. The design correctly identifies this and correctly plans a nightly Haiku pass, which makes the chronicle a paid dependency rather than a nicety. Second, technique semantics: 'does this well-formed utterance denote a workable technique' is adjudicated by the same thin referee as Idea 1, so a grammatically productive utterance can denote physical nonsense that the referee waves through, and the band then 'discovers' it. The prettiest failure mode in the document: a perfectly compositional language for a materials science that isn't real.
audit.one_change: Make the meaning schema itself grammatically extensible: let productive morphology introduce new SLOT TYPES — an applicative that adds an argument position, an aspectual that adds a temporal condition dimension — rather than only tiling a fixed four-slot frame. Then the language can grow the meaning space instead of enumerating it, 'sentences we can say but have never said' stops being a cross-join and becomes a genuinely expanding frontier, and the technological depth stops being purely inherited from the substrate underneath. Also follow the doc's own advice and build this second, on a working substrate — as a standalone it is a linguistics demo with a materials simulator attached.

all.name: Emberlisp
all.pitch: A tribe in an ash-choked valley survives only by executing programs written in a tiny survival lisp, and every night a compressor (Stitch) finds the repeated fragments in the programs that kept them alive and promotes them into named primitives — those named primitives ARE the tech tree, and you never authored a single node of it. Fire is not a recipe you wrote; fire is the abstraction `(repeat n (strike flint pyrite tinder))` that the MDL objective decided was worth a name.
all.world: The Ashfall: a 64x64 hex valley, 6 ticks/day, 96-day seasonal cycle, a volcano that periodically buries strata and exposes new ones. Sites hold resource stacks. Crucially there are NO nouns like 'fire' or 'axe' in the substrate — there are ~14 materials, each a property record (hardness, ignition_temp, melt_temp, mass, moisture, toughness, edge, conductivity), and ~12 deterministic physical rules over those records (percussion transfers energy and can spark if hardness and pyrite content clear thresholds; heat crosses ignition/melt thresholds and REWRITES the property record; drying lowers moisture; binding creates composite objects whose property record is a function of parts). Agents are bodies: calories, core temperature, hydration, injury, two hands, a position, and a pointer to the tribe's shared library. Death is real and permanent. The DSL (~28 base primitives) is typed lambda calculus in s-expressions: `move`, `gather`, `hold`, `strike`, `heat`, `bind`, `grind`, `soak`, `drop`, `nearest`, `has?`, `prop>`, `if`, `repeat`, `map`, `let`, plus arithmetic. Everything else in the civilization's vocabulary must be discovered.
all.invention_engine: Literal DreamCoder wake-sleep, three phases per simulated night. (1) WAKE: the world emits Tasks — a Task is a goal predicate over world state plus a node budget, e.g. `(and (core-temp-above 36) (night? t))`. Bottom-up enumerative synthesis over the CURRENT library with observational-equivalence dedup: maintain a bank of programs keyed by their evaluation vector on a set of sampled world-states; discard any new program whose vector already exists. Search order is best-first by a learned cost (Probe-style just-in-time bigram reweighting on the library, arXiv 2010.08663). Solutions are recorded as s-expressions in SQLite. (2) SLEEP-G (abstraction): dump the entire corpus of surviving programs as a JSON list of s-expression strings and hand it to `stitch` (github.com/mlb2251/stitch, Rust, or `stitch_core.compress(programs, iterations=5, max_arity=3)` via the Python bindings). Stitch returns candidate abstractions ranked by corpus compression; accept any whose MDL gain clears a threshold. Each accepted abstraction becomes a first-class library primitive with an id, arity, body, birth-tick, and a `parents` edge list to the abstractions its body references — that edge list is the tech tree, materialized. (3) SLEEP-R (dreaming): sample programs from the library, run them from random world-states, record (resulting state-delta -> program) as a fantasy task, and train a tiny recognition model (a 2-layer MLP over hand-features of the goal predicate + bigram counts over library ids, ~200k params, trains in seconds on CPU) to bias tomorrow's search. Naming/documentation is LILO-style: a local Qwen3.5-4B Q4_K_M, GBNF-constrained to emit exactly `(short-kebab-name . one-line-doc)`, sees the abstraction body plus three call-sites and names it. `fn_31` becomes `bank-the-coals`. That naming step costs nothing and is 80% of the delight.
all.why_unbounded: Programs of depth d over a library of size L number roughly L^d. Every accepted abstraction does two things at once: it increments L, and it COLLAPSES the depth needed for anything that used that fragment. So the set of programs reachable within a fixed node budget grows super-exponentially in the number of accepted abstractions — this is W. Brian Arthur's 'technology is combination' made mechanical, and it is the reason the invention space is not a list. There is no authored enumeration of what can be built; there is only a search budget and a compressor. Honest limit on the argument: the *physics* is finite in dimension. The library keeps growing forever, but the number of qualitatively distinct WORLD EFFECTS is bounded by the property vector's dimensionality (8 fields x 14 materials). Growth in library size is unbounded; growth in kinds-of-thing-that-can-happen is not. The mitigation baked in from day one is that property records are rewritten by heat/binding/grinding, so composite materials have property vectors no raw material has — the material space itself is combinatorial, which is what keeps feeding new effects.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1 (crude but already not-yours): 20 base primitives, one need (cold nights), enumerative search finds `(strike flint pyrite)` produces a spark, Stitch names it, and you get a push notification containing a word you did not write. Rung 2 (~night 30): `keep-warm` abstraction composes spark + tinder + repeat; night mortality drops from 40% to 5%; population grows; population is the search budget (each living agent contributes node-expansions), so survival literally buys more invention. Rung 3 (~night 80): fire lets heat rewrite property records — `heat-treat` raises hardness, which makes `grind` produce an edge, which makes hunting programs feasible, which is calorie surplus. Nobody authored 'stone tools'; it fell out of a property-vector threshold. Rung 4 (~night 200): clay + sustained heat = a composite with high toughness and zero moisture permeability, i.e. pottery; storage programs appear; winter becomes survivable; SEASONAL tasks (which were previously unsolvable at any budget) enter the task distribution for the first time. Rung 5: add higher-order primitives to the base DSL (`(delegate agent prog)`, `(while pred prog)`) and abstractions start compressing SOCIAL patterns — a named abstraction that is a division-of-labour protocol. Rung 6 / wildest plausible: with `(teach agent fn)` in the base DSL, the compressor finds an abstraction whose body is a teaching schedule — the tribe invents pedagogy as a technology. The genuinely wild endpoint, and it is plausible rather than fantasy because the ingredients are all present: an abstraction whose body is itself a bounded search loop over the library. The tribe invents planning, and after that its inventions are one meta-level up.
all.what_selects: Calories and core temperature, both hard-coded and both lethal. An agent that ends a night below 30C dies; a tribe that cannot solve the winter-storage task loses 60% of its members. Because search budget is proportional to living agents, a failed invention cycle compounds into a slower invention cycle — the civilization can enter a death spiral, and watching one is compelling. Library entries are garbage-collected by a use-it-or-lose-it rule: an abstraction not referenced in any accepted solution for 200 nights is demoted (its call sites re-inline), which prunes the MDL objective's junk finds. Selection is at the level of programs (does this solve the task within budget) and the level of abstractions (does this compress the corpus and keep earning call-sites).
all.changing_worlds: The volcano is a slow physics-parameter drift, not scenery. Ashfall events bury a stratum and expose another, so material availability is a non-stationary vector; a tribe whose whole edge-making stack routes through flint faces an existential re-derivation problem when flint goes under two metres of tephra, and you get to watch it either rediscover an edge from obsidian or die. Seasons rotate the task distribution on a 96-day cycle. Every ~5000 nights the valley resets with a new terrain seed and a new material-abundance draw, but the library is inherited — so you see which technologies were LOCAL TRICKS (they break) and which were LAWS (they transfer). That transfer test is the cheapest possible measure of invention depth and it costs one boolean per abstraction.
all.novelty_detector: Five signals, combined into one nightly surprise score, only the top-3 get pushed. (1) First-time-ever event: hash the tuple of world-state predicates that fired this tick against a bloom filter of all previously-seen tuples — a miss is a literally unprecedented event. (2) MDL shock: keep a running distribution of nightly compression gains; flag a Stitch step whose gain exceeds the 95th percentile of the last 100 nights. (3) Depth increase: an accepted abstraction whose body references an abstraction that references an abstraction that references an abstraction — depth-4 entries are rare and always mean something composed. (4) Long-standing unsolved solved: a task that failed for N consecutive nights and just succeeded; report N, because 'the tribe has been failing to cross the river for 84 nights and tonight they didn't' is a story. (5) Regime change: Bayesian online changepoint detection on population, mean calories, and library size — a detected changepoint means the civilization's dynamics just switched. Everything else goes into the DB unpushed.
all.phone_view: PWA, static JSON regenerated each morning and pushed to GitHub Pages (plus Tailscale Serve for the live view). Top of screen, three lines: `NIGHT 214 · POP 23 (+2) · LIB 87 entries, depth 6`. Then the headline card: the new abstractions with their generated names and one-line docs, each showing its parent chain as a breadcrumb (`strike -> spark -> catch-tinder -> BANK-THE-COALS`). Then one sparkline of population over the last 90 nights with death events as ticks. Then one sentence of chronicle from the local model. That is the 30-second read. The hour-long binge is one tap down: the full abstraction DAG rendered as an interactive graph (canvas, force layout, colour by birth-epoch), where tapping a node shows its body, its call sites, the first task it solved, and a scrubber that replays the night it was born as a hex-map animation. ntfy.sh push only when the surprise score clears threshold.
all.hardware_use: This is a CPU and RAM project wearing a GPU hat. The sim, the enumerative search, and Stitch are all CPU; 64GB DDR5 is the actual enabling resource because the observational-equivalence bank for a deep search holds millions of programs keyed by evaluation vectors, and you want it resident. Run the search across all cores with a shared bank per tribe. Stitch itself runs in milliseconds-to-seconds on one core for corpora of thousands of programs (the README's own example compresses ~1.9M cost units to ~317k in 120ms). The 8GB of the 5070 holds exactly one thing: Qwen3.5-4B or Qwen3-4B at Q4_K_M, ~3.4-4.6GB resident, ~40 tok/s, used for naming and documentation with a GBNF grammar. That leaves headroom for a long context (the library dump) and for the tiny recognition MLP, which is small enough it can honestly stay on CPU. Do NOT plan on a 9B+ model here — Qwen3.5-9B Q4_K_M is ~6.6GB on disk and will fight your context window at 8GB. Do NOT plan on finetuning anything in this idea. Thermal hygiene, and this matters because the laptop runs 24/7: never put wall-clock time in any fitness or budget. Budget search in NODE EXPANSIONS and cost programs in INTERPRETER STEPS. Both are deterministic, so a hot laptop and a cool one produce identical history and last month's run is reproducible.
all.input_cadence: Zero-touch nominally. You read the morning chronicle with coffee. Real interventions available but never required: (a) add a material or a physical rule to the substrate — a ten-line edit that visibly expands what the compressor can find, worth doing maybe monthly; (b) hand-inject a Task ('cross the river') to see if the library is ready for it; (c) bump the node budget. One genuine chore exists and you should know about it: about once a month you will want to eyeball the abstraction list for MDL junk (syntactic coincidences that compress but mean nothing) and tune the acceptance threshold. Fifteen minutes.
all.tech: Python 3.12 for the sim, the DSL interpreter, and the loop (fast enough at 6 ticks/day; port the interpreter to Rust or use numpy-vectorised state only if profiling demands it). Stitch via `stitch_core` Python bindings, or shell out to the Rust `compress` binary with `--max-arity 3 --iterations 5` — either way the input is just a JSON list of s-expression strings, and Stitch treats any unreserved token as a DSL primitive, so your survival lisp needs no declaration step at all. SQLite as the single source of truth: `library`, `programs`, `tasks`, `events`, `agents`, `nights`, with the abstraction DAG as an edge table. llama-cpp-python + Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M with a GBNF grammar for naming. Frontend: vanilla JS + canvas PWA reading a generated `world.json`, deployed to GitHub Pages by a morning cron and served live over Tailscale Serve. ntfy.sh for push. No frameworks, no torch required for v1.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: the substrate. Materials as property records, ~12 physical rules, a hex map, agents with calories and core temperature, and a tree-walking interpreter for a 20-primitive DSL that charges interpreter steps. Get one agent to die of cold. Saturday night: bottom-up enumerative search with observational-equivalence dedup against a single task predicate `core-temp-above 36 at night`. Let it run to a few million nodes. Sunday: pipe every surviving program into Stitch, print the top abstraction with its compression gain, and add it to the library as a new primitive. Re-run the search and confirm the same task now solves in a fraction of the nodes. Sunday afternoon: wire llama.cpp with a GBNF grammar to name it, and wire ntfy.sh. The delight moment is a phone notification that says something like 'The Ash clan invented SPARK-ON-DRY-MOSS (fn_3, arity 2) — compresses 14 programs, MDL -22%.' You wrote no such word.
all.six_months_later: The library is a few hundred entries deep with a DAG you have to zoom out to read, and its lower layers are stable — the equivalent of a settled physics. New abstractions arriving in month six are compositions at depth 6-8, and the interesting ones are no longer material technologies but organisational ones: scheduling, caching, delegation, teaching. You will have added two or three new material classes and a new physical rule by hand over that time (each addition visibly detonates a new burst of invention over the following week, which is its own pleasure). The transfer test across valley resets has given you a genuine, computed classification of every technology into local trick versus law. The thing that stays surprising is not the tech tree filling in — it's watching a re-derivation after a catastrophe take a completely different route than the original.
all.honest_ceiling: This plateaus, and the plateau has a known cause: DreamCoder-family systems saturate when the TASK DISTRIBUTION stops growing, not when the library stops growing. Expect the rate of qualitatively-new abstractions to fall off somewhere between week 4 and week 10 of continuous running, because the reachable region of an 8-dimensions-x-14-materials physics gets covered. After that you are getting recombinations, which are pretty and which compress well, but which stop feeling like discoveries. There are two honest responses and both require you: expand the physics (cheap, ten lines, monthly) or move to one of the architectures below that generates its own task growth structurally. Second ceiling, more painful: the enumerative search is the hard engineering. As L grows the branching factor grows, and naive best-first search stops keeping up around library size 50-150 depending on typing discipline. You will spend more of your build time on the enumerator (type-directed pruning, observational equivalence, just-in-time bigram reweighting, budget allocation across tasks) than on the world, and if the enumerator stalls the whole civilization freezes. Third: MDL is not meaning. Stitch will happily hand you abstractions that are syntactic coincidences with high compressivity and no interpretation; the use-it-or-lose-it demotion rule handles most of it but not all, and some fraction of your 'technologies' will be noise wearing a name the language model gave it.
all.research_notes: Verified: DreamCoder (Ellis et al., PLDI 2021, dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3453483.3454080; original code github.com/ellisk42/ec is OCaml+Python and is a genuine pain to run — do not try to run it, reimplement the loop, it is a few hundred lines). Stitch (Bowers et al., POPL 2023, arxiv.org/abs/2211.16605; repo github.com/mlb2251/stitch) is the load-bearing dependency: 1000-10000x faster and ~100x more memory-efficient than DreamCoder's own compressor, runs in seconds on one CPU core, README's own graphics-DSL example compresses 1,919,558 -> 316,890 in 120ms with `--max-arity 2 --iterations 3`. Confirmed the input format is 'a JSON file containing a list of input programs, each a string in lisp-like lambda calculus syntax' and that any space-separated non-reserved token is treated as a DSL primitive — meaning a hand-rolled survival lisp pipes straight in with zero adapter. Python bindings exist as `stitch_core` (github.com/mlb2251/stitch_bindings, docs at stitch-bindings.readthedocs.io) exposing `compress(programs, iterations, max_arity=2, threads=1)` -> CompressionResult; PyPI listing exists for stitch-core but was not loadable at time of writing, so budget an hour for a `cargo build --release` fallback. LILO (Grand/Wong et al., ICLR 2024, arxiv.org/abs/2310.19791) is the precedent for Stitch + LLM auto-documentation producing interpretable libraries, and reports solving more complex tasks than DreamCoder — that is exactly the naming step here. Probe / just-in-time learning for bottom-up enumerative synthesis (Barke et al., arxiv.org/pdf/2010.08663) for the search reweighting; 'Program Synthesis with Best-First Bottom-Up Search' (arxiv.org/pdf/2310.04327) for search ordering. Hardware verified: Qwen3-4B / Qwen3.5-4B at Q4_K_M is ~3.4-4.6GB and comfortable on 8GB with 40+ tok/s; Qwen3.5-9B Q4_K_M is ~6.6GB and tight. llama.cpp GBNF grammars (github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/grammars/README.md) constrain output to a custom DSL — confirmed as a standard technique, with a documented caveat that runtime token checking adds overhead.

audit.name: Emberlisp
audit.ceiling: Two ceilings, and the engineering one hits first. (a) Enumerator wall at library size ~50-150 with a stateful, side-effecting DSL — realistically week 2-4 of continuous running, at which point nightly wake produces nothing new and the civilization freezes with no error message. (b) Task-distribution wall: the whole thing is driven by a handful of authored survival predicates (core-temp, calories, hydration, injury). Once each is solved cheaply — library depth ~4-6, roughly 60-120 accepted abstractions — Stitch keeps returning compressive refactors of a solved corpus forever. Their own estimate of 4-10 weeks is right for 'new kinds' but assumes the enumerator survives, which is the optimistic half. The physics bound they concede (8 fields x 14 materials) is not actually the binding constraint; the predicate vocabulary is, and it is much smaller.
audit.authored_content_risk: Not a hand-authored tech tree — genuinely credit them for that, the node LIST is not written down. But the authored surface has just moved one level up and shrunk: 12 rules, 14 property records, ~28 primitives, and (fatally) ~5 goal predicates. 'Fire' is fully pre-figured — you wrote an ignition_temp threshold, a percussion-sparks-if-pyrite rule, and a heat-rewrites-properties rule, so the only thing discovered is the s-expression that trips a switch you installed. 'Stone tools fell out of a property-vector threshold' — you wrote that threshold and you chose hardness and edge as fields precisely because you knew where it led. Verdict: the ORDER, the PHRASING, and the refactoring are genuinely emergent; the SET of reachable qualitative effects is small enough that you could enumerate it by hand in an afternoon, which means after ~a month you are watching your own afternoon get re-derived in a random order with prettier names.
audit.compute_honesty: GPU side: honest and then some — 8GB holds a 4B Q4 namer with room to spare, and nothing trains. The dishonesty is on CPU and it is load-bearing. DreamCoder's observational-equivalence trick is cheap because its tasks are PURE functions on tiny inputs; here evaluating a candidate means ROLLING OUT a stateful world with agent bodies across 64 probe states. A 30-node program is ~2k interpreter steps per probe set; a Python tree-walker gives maybe 0.3-1M steps/sec/core, so ~300-2000 candidates/sec/core, i.e. low millions of nodes per core-night at best. The design needs 10^6-10^7 evaluations per night per tribe to keep a growing library fed. 'Port to Rust only if profiling demands it' is wrong: profiling will demand it in week one. Memory is the least of the problems — 1M banked programs at ~300B is 0.3GB; it is throughput, not RAM, that 64GB does not buy you.
audit.semantic_risk: High, and structurally so. Stitch optimises SYNTACTIC compression and cannot see semantics; with only ~28 primitives, high-frequency n-grams are everywhere and a large fraction of accepted abstractions will be positional coincidences. Then a 4B model, GBNF-forced to emit a plausible kebab-case name, will confidently christen every one of them — the naming step manufactures the appearance of meaning at exactly the point where you have the least. 'That naming step is 80% of the delight' is the honest and alarming sentence in the pitch: the delight is generated by the component with zero epistemic content. Use-it-or-lose-it demotion is the right antidote but it is a 200-night lag, so the chronicle is wrong for six months at a time.
audit.dubious_claims: (1) BIGGEST: 'Stitch treats any unreserved token as a DSL primitive, so your survival lisp pipes straight in with zero adapter' — overstated to the point of being a schedule risk. Stitch consumes lambda-calculus with `(lam ...)` and de Bruijn `$0` indices; a typed lisp with `let`, `if`, `repeat`, `map` and named binders does NOT pipe straight in. Desugar every binding form to de Bruijn lambdas first, or Stitch will treat bound variable names as opaque primitives and hand you abstractions that are literally nonsense. Budget a day, not an hour. (2) Probe (2010.08663) learns a UNIGRAM PCFG over productions from partial solutions; calling it 'bigram reweighting on the library' conflates it with DreamCoder's bigram recognition model. Harmless conceptually, but do not expect Probe's paper numbers from a bigram implementation. (3) The Stitch README figure (1,919,558 -> 316,890 in 120ms) is on a corpus of pure graphics programs; do not extrapolate the throughput to corpora containing your stateful lisp. (4) Qwen3.5-4B/9B and their sizes: checked, real (Qwen3.5 small models, Mar 2026); ~3.4-4.6GB for the 4B Q4_K_M is on the conservative side if you run the text-only path, so you have MORE headroom than claimed, not less.
audit.one_change: Make the task distribution endogenous instead of authoring ~5 survival predicates. Replace them with an auto-generated curriculum over the MATERIAL PROPERTY SPACE: maintain a MAP-Elites grid over composite property vectors (hardness x toughness x ignition x conductivity...), and every night emit as tasks 'produce an object landing in an empty cell'. The goal set then grows exactly as fast as the material space the abstractions open up, which converts the flat 4-10 week plateau into a frontier that recedes as the tribe advances — and it costs about 80 lines. Survival predicates stay as the lethal floor; novelty predicates become the ceiling.

all.name: The Long Teaching
all.pitch: Nine tribes, nine private DSL libraries, one map — and an abstraction only exists as long as a living agent still knows it. Technology here is not a permanent unlock: it is carried in heads with limited transmission bandwidth, so libraries are taught, traded, stolen, and above all FORGOTTEN, and the invention of writing is an emergent event rather than a tech-tree node.
all.world: An archipelago-and-isthmus map, ~200 sites, nine founding tribes seeded in different biomes with genuinely different material abundance vectors (a volcanic island has obsidian and no wood; a delta has reed and clay and no hard stone). Same substrate as Emberlisp — materials as property records, ~12 physical rules, a small typed survival lisp — but with three additions that change everything. First, KNOWLEDGE IS EMBODIED: the table is `knows(agent_id, abstraction_id, fidelity)`. A tribe's effective library is the union over its living members. Second, TEACHING IS A PROGRAM: `(teach student fn)` is a base primitive costing ticks, with success probability falling in the abstraction's DAG depth — deep abstractions are hard to transmit, which is the iterated-learning bandwidth bottleneck made mechanical. Third, DEPENDENCIES ARE REAL: if an abstraction's transitive dependencies are not all known by the executing agent, the call re-inlines to base primitives and the interpreter-step cost explodes past the budget, so the program simply fails. Losing one link in the chain breaks everything above it.
all.invention_engine: Nine parallel DreamCoder loops with crossover. Each tribe runs its own wake (enumerative search over ITS library), its own Sleep-G (Stitch over ITS solution corpus — nine separate `compress` calls, each still milliseconds), and its own Sleep-R. What makes this a different engine rather than nine copies of one is the transmission layer. (a) FORGETTING: when the last carrier of abstraction A dies, A is deleted from the library and every abstraction whose body references A is recursively invalidated. The tribe's programs that relied on it start failing tonight. This is a dark age with a stack trace. (b) TRADE: when agents of two tribes co-locate peacefully, a `(trade fn fn)` program can execute, transplanting abstraction bodies — but only successfully if the receiving tribe already knows the full dependency closure, otherwise the gift is inert and the receiving tribe must first derive the missing layers. Technology transfer requires the whole stack, which is both realistic and dramatic. (c) RAID: a raid steals carriers (captives) rather than goods, which is a horrible and correct model of how technology actually moved. (d) WRITING: `(inscribe fn surface)` is NOT in the base DSL. But `(mark site material)` is, and site-marks persist, and `(read site)` returns marks. Whether a tribe ever composes those into a durable, decodable encoding of a library entry is an open search problem for the system. If it does — if Stitch compresses a recurring mark-then-read pattern into a named abstraction that reconstitutes a lost library entry — that tribe has invented writing, its libraries stop being mortal, and the whole simulation changes character. That single event is the reason to build this.
all.why_unbounded: Same L^d combinatorics as Emberlisp, times nine, PLUS crossover between lineages. Nine libraries searching different regions (because their biomes make different primitives cheap) and periodically recombining is a genetic algorithm whose genome is a DSL. Hybrid abstractions — an obsidian-edge technique composed with a delta binding technique — are reachable by neither parent lineage alone. That is combinatorial invention at the level of whole traditions rather than single programs. The honest strengthening: forgetting means the system does not monotonically fill in a space; it can lose regions and re-derive them by a different route, so the same 'invention' can be discovered three times with three different bodies, and the compressor will treat them as three different technologies because they are.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: two tribes, forgetting turned on, and you watch a tribe lose fire because the two agents who knew it were the two who starved. That is a genuinely upsetting week-1 moment and it is trivially achievable. Rung 2: teaching programs get invented — the compressor finds that surviving tribes have a recurring pattern of `(teach x fn)` calls before winter, and names it. Pedagogy as technology, discovered. Rung 3: divergence. Nine tribes' libraries stop resembling each other; the volcanic tribe's whole edge stack routes through obsidian fracture, the delta tribe's through fired clay. Now trade has actual value. Rung 4: first successful cross-biome transplant, where the receiving tribe has to derive three missing dependency layers before a gifted abstraction becomes executable. You will see a tribe spend forty nights 'catching up'. Rung 5: writing, or a durable proxy for it — a mark-and-read composition that survives death. Rung 6 / wildest plausible: after writing, libraries stop being mortal and depth stops being bandwidth-limited, so the abstraction DAG's depth ceiling lifts and the tribes that have it out-invent the tribes that don't by a widening margin. A literacy divide, emergent, with a timestamp you can point at.
all.what_selects: Three layered pressures. Individual: calories and temperature, same as Emberlisp. Tribal: winter and predation cull tribes whose library lacks storage and defence; a tribe that drops below 3 members merges into a neighbour or dies out and its library dies with it. Inter-tribal: contact events resolve by comparing the executing programs' outcomes — a tribe with better tools wins raids, takes carriers, and grows. The selection unit that actually matters is the LIBRARY, and libraries compete by being learnable (shallow, teachable, robust to death) as much as by being powerful. That is a real and interesting tension: the deepest abstraction is the most powerful and the least transmissible, so there is genuine evolutionary pressure toward flattening and re-factoring the library for teachability. Watching a tribe refactor its own tech tree for pedagogy is the kind of thing you cannot author.
all.changing_worlds: The map moves: sea level shifts on a long cycle, connecting and severing islands, which switches tribes between isolation (divergence, novel libraries) and contact (convergence, transplant). Storms and blights hit specific biomes. And there is a slow one worth building: abandoned settlements leave marks and works behind, so a migrating tribe can encounter another tribe's ruins and attempt to decode them — archaeology as a search problem, where the goal predicate is 'reconstruct an abstraction whose behaviour matches these marks'. Human perturbation slots in naturally as a tenth actor: web visitors to the public page are 'the Sea People', and each unique visitor deposits a small resource cache or a rumour (a partial abstraction body) at a random coastal site. Strangers become a genuine, cheap non-stationarity, and the visit log becomes a historical record.
all.novelty_detector: Tuned for this idea's specific drama. (1) FORGETTING EVENTS: the last carrier of an abstraction dies — always push, with the abstraction's name, its age in nights, and the count of dependent entries it just invalidated. 'The Reed clan has forgotten TWIST-CORD (age 611 nights, 9 dependents orphaned)' is a devastating notification. (2) REDISCOVERY: a new abstraction is accepted whose behaviour (evaluation vector on the standard probe set) matches a previously-deleted one but whose body differs — convergent re-invention, and reporting the body diff is fascinating. (3) TRANSPLANT SUCCESS: first time an abstraction executes in a tribe that did not invent it. (4) DIVERGENCE INDEX: pairwise Jaccard over tribes' abstraction behaviour-signatures, tracked nightly; push on a changepoint (the moment the archipelago's traditions split or merge). (5) The Emberlisp signals (first-ever event bloom filter, MDL shock, depth increase) all still apply, scored per-tribe. Sonification is the passive companion: a generative radio where each tribe is a voice in a nine-voice drone, pitch mapped to library depth, timbre to biome, volume to population — and when a tribe forgets something, a voice drops a note. You can leave it playing and hear a dark age happen from the next room.
all.phone_view: Nine tiles in a 3x3 grid, one per tribe, each showing name, population, library size, and a single colour bar for library health (fraction of entries with more than one carrier — the redundancy of their knowledge, which is the real vital sign). Under the grid: tonight's headline events in one line each, colour-coded — green for invented, blue for taught/traded, red for FORGOTTEN. That is the 30-second read and it is genuinely readable at arm's length. Tap a tribe for its abstraction DAG with carrier counts on each node (you can see at a glance which technologies are one funeral away from extinction). Tap an event for the replay. A second tab is the comparative view: all nine DAGs overlaid, shared abstractions in the centre, divergent ones on the rim, which after a few months is a beautiful and legitimately informative picture.
all.hardware_use: Nine tribes is nine independent searches, which is the perfect shape for the 64GB machine: run each tribe's enumerative search in its own process pinned to a core or two, each with its own observational-equivalence bank (a few GB each at depth, which is exactly why the 64GB matters and why this would not fit on a 16GB machine). Stitch is called nine times per night and is still a rounding error. The GPU holds one Qwen3.5-4B Q4 instance shared by all nine tribes for naming and chronicle — batch the nine naming requests into one nightly pass. Sonification is WebAudio in the browser, zero cost. Nothing here needs training. Determinism discipline is doubly important because inter-tribal outcomes must not depend on which process finished first: give every tribe an identical node budget per night, resolve contact events in a fixed tribe-id order, and seed each tribe's RNG from (world_seed, tribe_id, night) so the entire nine-way history replays bit-identically on a cold laptop.
all.input_cadence: Read the morning grid. The one thing worth doing occasionally, maybe fortnightly, is seeding a tenth tribe from a saved library snapshot to see whether an old tradition can survive in the current world — thirty seconds of typing, and it produces a week of interesting outcomes. The public page needs no maintenance once the visitor-as-Sea-People hook is in. Genuine chore, and it is small: when a tribe goes extinct you may want to decide whether to reseed the slot or let the map depopulate; automate it with a rule and forget it.
all.tech: Everything from Emberlisp plus: multiprocessing with one process per tribe and a single SQLite writer process (WAL mode, or hand writes to one coordinator to avoid lock contention — nine writers on SQLite will bite you, plan for it on day one). Tables gain `knows(agent, abstraction, fidelity)`, `tribes`, `contacts`, `transplants`, `forgettings`. The behaviour-signature for rediscovery detection is just the evaluation vector on a fixed probe set of 64 world-states, stored as a blob and indexed. Sonification via a small WebAudio synth in the PWA driven by the same nightly JSON — no audio generated server-side, which keeps it free.
all.first_weekend: If you have Emberlisp's substrate, this is one weekend on top. Saturday: `knows` table, teaching primitive, and the deletion cascade when the last carrier dies. Two tribes only. Sunday: run it overnight Saturday and spend Sunday building the nine-tile phone view and the red FORGOTTEN event line. If you are starting from scratch, budget two weekends and cut teaching fidelity to a constant for v1. The delight moment is very reliable here and it arrives fast: the first time you get a red line saying a tribe lost a technology it had for hundreds of nights, the sim stops feeling like a program.
all.six_months_later: Nine traditions with visibly different shapes, a documented history of at least a few dark ages and re-derivations, and — if the mark/read composition ever lands — a literate tribe pulling away from illiterate neighbours. The comparative DAG view becomes the artifact you show people. What keeps it alive at six months is that forgetting makes the history non-monotonic: unlike a tech tree, this world can go backwards, so there is never a state where everything is unlocked and nothing is at stake.
all.honest_ceiling: Convergence is the enemy. Nine tribes under identical physics tend to find the same abstractions, and after a couple of months the diversity can become cosmetic — the same technology with nine different generated names. The biome-differentiated material abundance is the main defence and you should push it harder than feels natural (make biomes genuinely incompatible, not merely differently weighted). Second, the writing event may simply never happen. `(mark)` + `(read)` composing into a durable, decodable, dependency-preserving encoding is a hard synthesis problem and there is a real chance the search never finds it in six months; if you decide it must happen you will be tempted to author it, and the moment you author it you have a tech tree again. My honest recommendation is to leave it undiscovered and let it be a genuine open question about your own world. Third, nine parallel searches means one-ninth the node budget per tribe versus Emberlisp, so each individual tribe's library grows noticeably slower — this idea buys drama with depth. Fourth, the SQLite contention and determinism-under-parallelism problems are the kind of bug that eats a whole weekend and produces no visible progress.
all.research_notes: Verified: iterated learning as the standard formalism for cultural transmission, with recent work reporting a per-generation communication bandwidth constraint on cultural accumulation and a threshold effect around 8-10 bits per channel below which cumulative learning fails to beat singleton copying (summarised at emergentmind.com/topics/iterated-learning-model) — that result is the direct justification for making teaching fidelity fall in abstraction depth, and it predicts your tribes will face real pressure to refactor deep libraries into shallow teachable ones. 'Artificial Generational Intelligence: Cultural Accumulation in Reinforcement Learning' (2024) establishes that performance reliably increases across generations of agents that pass advice forward. 'Mutual benefits of social learning and algorithmic mediation for cumulative culture' (arxiv.org/pdf/2410.00780, PMC11978438) models per-timestep acquisition of a cultural trait by either copying or innovation — close to the copy-or-search choice each agent makes here. 'High Selection Pressure Promotes Increase in Cumulative Adaptive Culture' (PMC3906051) supports tying invention rate to survival pressure rather than to slack. Stitch (github.com/mlb2251/stitch) is cheap enough to call nine times a night without thinking about it. On the parallel-SQLite point: WAL mode plus a single writer is the well-trodden answer and worth setting up before you have nine processes.

audit.name: The Long Teaching
audit.ceiling: Shallower than Emberlisp by construction and they half-admit it: nine tribes on one machine is ~1/9 the node budget each, on top of an enumerator that was already the bottleneck, and forgetting actively destroys accumulated depth. Expect per-tribe library depth 3-4 and 20-40 live abstractions, plateauing at week 3-6, with the aggregate looking busier than any individual tribe is deep. Convergence, which they name as the enemy, is worse than stated: contact plus trade plus raid are all homogenising forces, and nine tribes under one shared rule set will hold maybe 6-10 genuinely distinct abstractions between them by month two, wearing nine different generated names. The headline rung (writing) does not have a ceiling — it has a floor it never reaches; see below.
audit.authored_content_risk: Low for the tech itself, and the forgetting/rediscovery machinery is the most genuinely unauthored dynamic in the whole document — a non-monotonic history really cannot be faked with a tech tree, and 'rediscovered with a different body, same behaviour signature' is a real, computable, unspoofable result. But the risk is concentrated and acute at exactly the rung they are selling: WRITING. `(mark site material)` + `(read site)` composing into a durable, decodable, dependency-preserving encoding of a library entry is not a hard search problem, it is an out-of-horizon one. There is no task predicate that rewards it: the payoff of writing accrues to a DIFFERENT AGENT AFTER THE INVENTOR IS DEAD, and a per-night node budget searching against survival predicates has no credit-assignment path to a multi-generational return. On top of that the program itself — an encoder over a 14-symbol alphabet plus a parser that reconstitutes an s-expression — is deeper than anything else in the ladder by a wide margin. It will not happen in six months, or six years. Their own honest_ceiling says 'if you author it you have a tech tree again', which is correct and is precisely the trap this design walks toward. Score the idea on the rungs below it, because rung 5 is fiction.
audit.compute_honesty: GPU: honest (one shared 4B, nine naming requests batched nightly — genuinely cheap). CPU/RAM: nine processes each with 'a few GB' of bank is the claim, and the memory arithmetic is fine on 64GB, but again the constraint is evaluation throughput, not residency, and it is now divided nine ways. Also under-costed: the deletion cascade. When the last carrier of A dies, every abstraction transitively referencing A is invalidated and every stored program re-inlines — that is a corpus-wide rewrite plus a forced re-run of Stitch, and on a bad night several tribes do it at once. Budget for it. The SQLite multi-writer warning is correct and they should be believed; WAL plus a single writer process, day one.
audit.semantic_risk: Moderate — lower than Emberlisp on abstractions that survive, because teachability and carrier count act as a second filter that MDL junk tends to fail (nobody bothers teaching a coincidence), and higher on the chronicle, because a red FORGOTTEN line for an abstraction that never meant anything reads exactly like a tragedy. The rediscovery detector (same behaviour signature, different body) is the one signal in this document that cannot be fooled by a naming model, and it should be the centrepiece rather than a bullet.
audit.dubious_claims: (1) The '8-10 bits per channel threshold below which cumulative learning fails to beat singleton copying' is the weakest citation in the set. It traces to arXiv 2511.18220 ('Lossy communication constrains iterated learning', Nov 2025) via an AI-generated emergentmind topic page, and the summary states the inequality in the OPPOSITE direction from the pitch ('below ~8-10 bits/channel, cumulative learning exceeds singleton copying'). Read the paper, not the topic page. Either way it is a rate-distortion result about BITS on a Bayesian chain, and it licenses nothing about making teaching fidelity fall in DAG DEPTH — depth is not bits, and the substitution is a design choice dressed as a finding. (2) 'Artificial Generational Intelligence' (Cook et al., NeurIPS 2024) is real and correctly characterised. (3) RAF/iterated-learning framing aside, the claim that biome-differentiated abundance defends against convergence is asserted, not supported; nine tribes sharing 12 physics rules converge in behaviour signature even when their materials differ, because the abstractions that matter are about leverage, containment and sequencing, not about which rock. (4) 'Stitch nine times a night is a rounding error' — true for compression, false once you count the re-inline cascades it triggers.
audit.one_change: Give marks an INTRAGENERATIONAL payoff so the search can actually find them. Make external marks readable as cheap working memory within a single agent's lifetime — e.g. an agent executing a deep abstraction whose dependencies it only partially knows can pay ticks to `read` a site-mark and skip part of the re-derivation cost, right now, in this program, scored by this night's budget. Writing then arrives by exaptation (a within-lifetime cost-saver that happens to outlive its author) instead of requiring the search to solve a multi-generational credit-assignment problem it structurally cannot see. This is also how writing actually arose — as tallies and receipts, not as archives — so it is the historically honest fix as well as the computationally possible one.

all.name: Glyphworks
all.pitch: Discovered abstractions do not just enter the library — they can be BUILT INTO THE LAND, becoming place-bound primitives that are cheap only where they stand. The tribe's own past inventions physically reshape which programs are affordable, so the task distribution is generated by the civilization itself rather than by you, and the map slowly becomes a readable technosphere of kilns, weirs, and ruins.
all.world: A river valley of ~400 sites with elevation, flow, and a substrate identical in spirit to Emberlisp (materials as property records, physical rules over them, a typed survival lisp). The one structural difference is that SITES CAN HOLD WORKS. A works is a built object that carries a program: it exposes a primitive `(use-works site args...)` whose semantics are a stored abstraction body and whose interpreter-step cost is a fraction (say 1/8) of executing that body by hand. Works have material requirements, maintenance costs, a decay rate, and destructibility (flood, fire, raid). Works can reach physical regimes bare hands cannot: a hearth works can hold a temperature the `heat` primitive alone never sustains long enough, which means a works genuinely extends the reachable state space of the physics rather than merely making things cheaper. Adjacent works compose: a program at a site can reference the works there AND at neighbouring sites in one call, which is how a workshop, then a village, then something like a factory falls out without any of those words existing in the code.
all.invention_engine: Wake-sleep as in Emberlisp, with a fourth phase, SLEEP-B (building), inserted after abstraction. After Stitch returns accepted abstractions, each is tested for STATIONARITY — does its body operate on a fixed site, and is its interpreter-step cost above a threshold? Stationary expensive abstractions become WORKS BLUEPRINTS: a new task automatically enters the distribution, 'construct works W at site S', with material costs derived from the abstraction's body (an abstraction that references heating a lot needs refractory material; one that references water needs an excavation). Once built, the works installs `(use-works S)` into the DSL as a place-indexed primitive, and — this is the crux — the enumerator's cost model changes at that site. Programs that were over budget become in-budget. New solutions appear. Those new solutions go into the next Stitch pass. Those abstractions become new works. The loop is closed and the world is now the thing that grows the search space. Two extra mechanisms make it rich: DECOMPILATION (a ruined works can be read by a program, recovering a partial abstraction body — archaeology as synthesis-from-partial-evidence), and WORKS COMPOSITION (an abstraction whose body calls two adjacent works can itself become a works, giving you multi-stage installations emergently).
all.why_unbounded: This is the strongest unboundedness claim of the six, and the reason is that it does not rest only on program-space combinatorics. In Emberlisp, abstractions make things CHEAPER; the reachable state space is fixed by the physics. Here, works make things POSSIBLE — a sustained-temperature works reaches a region of the material property space that no hand-executed program can reach at any budget, and the composites produced there have property vectors that then unlock further physics. That is Kauffman's adjacent possible with a mechanism: each realised technology expands the boundary of what is realisable next, and the boundary is computed, not enumerated by a designer. Add place-indexing and the DSL is no longer one grammar but a family of grammars indexed by location, so the same tribe has different affordances in different parts of its own valley and geography becomes a variable in invention. Honest bound: works can only compose the physics rules you wrote, so the reachable regime is still ultimately capped by the rule set — but because works can stack (a works built out of materials only another works could make), the depth of that stacking is what carries you, and stacking depth is limited by material property dynamic range rather than by an authored list.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: hand-executed programs only, plus one hardcoded works type to prove the cost-model rewiring works. You watch a search that failed at 10M nodes succeed at 200k nodes because a works exists. Rung 2 (~night 50): the first EMERGENT works — an abstraction the compressor found, judged stationary, built by the tribe, and now standing on the map with a generated name. Your map has a building on it that you did not design. Rung 3: works that only work together; the enumerator starts preferring sites with two adjacent works, and agents cluster. A settlement forms for a computational reason. Rung 4 (~night 200): a works built from a material that only another works can produce — second-order infrastructure, which is the real threshold between tools and industry. Rung 5: catastrophe and archaeology. A flood destroys the lower works; the tribe's programs break; a later generation decompiles the ruins and rebuilds along a different route, and the DAG now has a visible scar. Rung 6 / wildest plausible: a works whose stored abstraction is itself a search procedure over the library — a place where thinking is cheap. The tribe builds a library, in both senses, and the sites near it out-invent everywhere else. That is not a stretch given higher-order primitives; it is what the cost model rewards.
all.what_selects: Survival as elsewhere, but with a distinctive pressure: MAINTENANCE. Works decay and cost upkeep in materials and agent-ticks, so a civilization can over-build and starve. That is a real and rarely-modelled selection pressure and it produces genuinely interesting behaviour — the pruning of infrastructure, the abandonment of a periphery, retreat to a defensible core. Works are also the thing rivals want, so they are what raids target. And because works are place-bound, geography selects: a tribe that built its whole stack in a floodplain is playing a different game than one on a terrace. Abstractions are still garbage-collected by use-it-or-lose-it; works are garbage-collected by the world.
all.changing_worlds: The river is the clock: it meanders on a long cycle, floods on a stochastic one, and both rewrite which sites are viable, so the tribe's own infrastructure is periodically invalidated by geology. This is non-stationarity that is neither random nor scripted — it interacts with what was built. Longer term, the valley's mineral strata deplete: a works that consumes ore will exhaust its site, and the map's economic centre migrates. And because works persist after their builders are gone, a fresh tribe seeded a thousand nights later inherits a landscape of ruins it must decode — which is the most evocative version of 'the world changes' available, because the change is legible as history.
all.novelty_detector: Spatially-aware signals. (1) FIRST WORKS OF A KIND: any works type built for the first time — always push, with its name, its blueprint's parent abstractions, and a small rendered map thumbnail of where it stands. (2) SECOND-ORDER CONSTRUCTION: a works whose material requirements can only be met by the output of another works — this is the industry threshold and it should be a loud, distinct notification. (3) REGIME BREACH: the sim tracks the maximum value achieved on each physics dimension (temperature, pressure, sustained-duration, composite complexity); pushing past a previous all-time maximum means the civilization has reached a physical regime it never has, which is a clean, computable definition of a technological first. (4) SETTLEMENT FORMATION: changepoint detection on the spatial entropy of agent positions — when agents stop being uniformly distributed, a place has become a place. (5) DECOMPILATION SUCCESS: a ruin read and rebuilt, with a diff between the original abstraction body and the reconstruction. An e-ink frame on the wall showing today's technosphere map — works as glyphs, ruins in grey — is the right physical artifact for this one; refresh once a day at dawn.
all.phone_view: The map IS the check-in. A single rendered valley, works drawn as small distinct glyphs (the local model can even pick a unicode/emoji glyph per works type at naming time), ruins in grey, agents as dots, the river in blue. Above it, one line: `NIGHT 340 · POP 41 · WORKS 19 (+1) · LIB 112`. Below it, at most three event lines. You can read the state of a civilization from a map in about four seconds, which beats any dashboard. Tap a works to see its stored abstraction, its parents, its build date, its total lifetime call count, and how much the local cost model changed when it went up. Tap-and-hold for a time-lapse scrubber of the whole map history, which is the hour-long binge and is genuinely mesmerising.
all.hardware_use: CPU-bound as elsewhere, with one extra memory cost: the enumerator now needs a per-site cost model, so the observational-equivalence bank is effectively partitioned by location context.
