Do not materialise a bank per site — key programs by (evaluation vector, works-context signature) where the context signature is a small bitset of which works are in reach, and only branch the bank when contexts genuinely differ. This is the single most important performance decision in the design and getting it wrong will cost you 64GB fast. Naming and glyph-picking is one nightly batched call to Qwen3.5-4B Q4 on the GPU. Map rendering is client-side canvas; the e-ink frame is a Raspberry Pi Zero or an old tablet pulling the same PNG the PWA renders. Budget everything in node expansions and interpreter steps, never seconds, because works are a cost-model change and if your cost model has any wall-clock component the whole economy becomes thermally dependent.
all.input_cadence: Watch the map with coffee. Optional monthly nudge: add a physical rule that opens a new regime (a pressure dimension, a fermentation rule) and watch the works stack grow a storey. One real chore: the stationarity heuristic that decides which abstractions become works blueprints will need tuning a few times in the first month — too loose and the map fills with junk buildings, too tight and nothing gets built. Once tuned it is set-and-forget.
all.tech: Emberlisp's stack plus: a `works(id, site, abstraction_id, built_tick, decay, upkeep)` table and a `site_context(site, works_bitset)` index; the enumerator takes a context parameter and consults a per-context cost table. Rendering is canvas 2D with a fixed tile atlas plus generated glyphs; the daily PNG for the e-ink frame comes from the same code path via headless Chromium or a small Pillow renderer. Everything else — Stitch, SQLite, llama.cpp with GBNF, ntfy, Tailscale Serve, GitHub Pages — is unchanged.
all.first_weekend: Weekend one is honestly Emberlisp's weekend; this idea's distinctive part needs that substrate underneath. Given it: Saturday, the works table, the cost-model override at a site, and one hardcoded works to prove the loop; get a task that was unsolvable to become solvable purely because a building exists. Sunday, the stationarity heuristic and automatic blueprint tasks, so the tribe builds something YOU did not pick, plus the map view. The delight moment is specific and strong: a building appears on your map with a name from the language model and a body from the compressor, and the search behaviour visibly changes around it.
all.six_months_later: A valley with a hundred-odd works in visible clusters, a couple of abandoned districts, a river that has moved, and a technosphere map that reads like a real historical landscape. The time-lapse of six months of map history is the single most shareable artifact of any of these six ideas. Substantively, the second-order and third-order works stacks are what keep arriving — the invention rate does not fall off as fast as Emberlisp's because the world keeps expanding its own affordance surface.
all.honest_ceiling: The engineering is the hardest of the six and I want to be blunt about it: place-indexed enumeration with context-partitioned observational equivalence is a genuinely tricky piece of systems work, and if you get the context signature wrong you either blow memory or silently share banks across incompatible contexts and get wrong results that are very hard to debug. Expect the first month to be the enumerator, not the watching. Second, works can trap the civilization in a local optimum — cheap infrastructure makes the enumerator lazy, it stops exploring expensive-but-better routes, and the tribe ossifies. This actually happens in real economies and it is interesting the first time and tedious the fifth; the flood cycle is your designed antidote and you will need to tune its frequency. Third, the underlying physics rule set still caps the works stack; if your rules only support three regimes you get three storeys and then it is over. Realistically the interesting-new-kind rate holds up for two to three months here versus four to ten weeks for Emberlisp — better, but not forever, and the fix is still 'add physics'.
all.research_notes: Verified conceptual grounding: niche construction and the adjacent possible are the right frames, and the specific formal link is 'Emergence of autocatalytic sets in a simple model of technological evolution' (arxiv.org/pdf/2204.01059, published in J Evol Econ 2023, link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00191-023-00838-2) which combines Kauffman-style TAP (theory of the adjacent possible) combinatorial technology models with RAF autocatalytic-set detection and finds that product transformation networks from combinatorial models have a high probability of containing self-sustaining sets — that is exactly the 'works that make the materials for other works' threshold this design detects. W. Brian Arthur's 'The Nature of Technology' (technology as combination) is the informal backbone. On the engine: Stitch (github.com/mlb2251/stitch, POPL 2023) is unchanged and still the compressor; the place-indexed cost model is a modification to the search, not to Stitch, since Stitch only ever sees s-expression strings. For the equality-modulo-rewrites variant of abstraction discovery — useful if you want works to be recognised as equivalent despite different bodies — babble (e-graphs + anti-unification, par.nsf.gov/biblio/10401739) and egglog-python (github.com/egraphs-good/egglog-python, equality saturation with a typed Python API) are the live options; egglog is actively maintained in 2026 and has real Python bindings via PyO3.

audit.name: Glyphworks
audit.ceiling: The best real ceiling of the six, and for the right reason: works change what is POSSIBLE, not just what is cheap, so the reachable region of the physics genuinely grows with the built environment. But it grows in STOREYS, and you author how many storeys exist. Each 'new regime' (sustained temperature, then pressure, then whatever) is one authored rule-guard relaxation; with ~12 rules you get roughly 3-5 qualitative storeys, and each storey takes a few weeks to climb. Expect genuinely new KINDS for 6-10 weeks (better than Emberlisp's 3-6, worse than the pitch's 2-3 months), after which the map keeps filling with more works of already-known types — quantitative sprawl that photographs beautifully and means nothing. Second ceiling, arriving earlier: the context-partitioned observational-equivalence bank. Works are built and decay, so the works-context signature at a site MUTATES over time, which invalidates bank entries keyed to it. They present this as a static partitioning problem; it is actually a cache-coherence problem, and the first month is the enumerator, exactly as they say, possibly the first two.
audit.authored_content_risk: Lower than Emberlisp on the tech itself, because works must be built, maintained, and pay for themselves — an economic filter MDL alone does not have. But there are two authored seams and they are load-bearing. (1) The STATIONARITY HEURISTIC that decides which abstractions become blueprints is a hand-written classifier standing exactly where the designer's taste re-enters, and 'you will need to tune it a few times in the first month' means 'you will tune it until it promotes the buildings you were hoping for'. (2) Worse: 'material costs derived from the abstraction's body (references heating -> needs refractory material; references water -> needs excavation)' is a hand-authored mapping from program syntax to build costs. That table IS a recipe book. It is small and it is not a tech tree, but it is the point where you get to decide what a kiln costs, and therefore which stacks are affordable.
audit.compute_honesty: GPU: honest (nightly batched 4B for names and glyphs, ~4GB). CPU/RAM: the most likely of the six to actually blow 64GB, and they say so. Their own warning — key by (eval vector, works-context bitset) and branch only when contexts differ — is correct and insufficient, because it does not address invalidation on build/decay. Concretely: adopt an epoch counter per site and treat bank entries as valid only within an epoch, or accept silent cross-context contamination that produces wrong search results which are, as they note, extremely hard to debug. Also note the per-site cost model multiplies enumerator work by the number of distinct contexts in reach, so the throughput problem from Emberlisp is not merely inherited, it is multiplied.
audit.semantic_risk: Lowest of the library-learning trio. A works has to be built out of real materials, maintained, and called enough to justify itself, so an MDL coincidence that gets promoted to a blueprint dies visibly rather than sitting in a list wearing a name. The map view also makes junk legible in a way a DAG does not — a field of never-used buildings is self-evidently a bug, whereas a list of 90 named abstractions looks like success. That is a real design virtue and worth stating: THIS IDEA'S UI IS ITS BEST BULLSHIT DETECTOR.
audit.dubious_claims: (1) 'The strongest unboundedness claim of the six' — true relative to 1, 2 and 4, but the Kauffman adjacent-possible framing oversells it. TAP-style unboundedness requires that combination generate new PRIMITIVES; here combination generates new CACHED COMPOSITES over a fixed rule set, and the rule set is the boundary. The design's own honest_bound says this; the pitch language does not. (2) arXiv 2204.01059 / J Evol Econ 2023 is real and the RAF-in-technology-networks framing is legitimate, but that paper's high-probability result comes from combinatorial models with randomly assigned transformation networks; it says nothing about whether YOUR 12 hand-written rules contain a self-sustaining set, and it should not be cited as evidence that second-order works will appear. (3) babble (POPL 2023) and egglog-python are real and correctly described; e-graph equality-modulo-rewrites is genuinely the right tool for recognising works equivalence, but it is a second systems project bolted onto the hardest systems project in the set — do not attempt it in year one. (4) 'The interesting-new-kind rate holds up for two to three months versus four to ten weeks for Emberlisp' is directionally right but both numbers are optimistic by roughly a factor of two given the enumerator throughput problem inherited from Emberlisp.
audit.one_change: Let a works instantiate a PARAMETERIZED RULE SCHEMA, not just cache an abstraction body. Rewrite the 12 physics rules as ~6 schemas with open constants (a threshold, a duration, a coupling coefficient, a participating material class); a works then declares a schema instance with constants it can physically sustain, and those instances are locally active. Now the built environment extends the RULE SET rather than reaching further along a fixed one, the storey count stops being something you authored, and stacking depth becomes limited by material dynamic range — which is the thing the pitch claims and the current mechanism does not deliver. Bonus: it deletes the authored syntax-to-build-cost table, because a schema instance's cost falls out of the constants it has to hold.

all.name: The Slow Kiln
all.pitch: Instead of authoring materials, you author a dozen reaction RULES over a combinatorial substance space — so nobody, including you, has a list of what can be made. Programs are process recipes, the compressor names the recurring fragments (that is how 'smelting' and 'quenching' get invented), and a RAF detector watches for the night a set of processes becomes self-sustaining, which is the moment a civilization crosses from craft into industry.
all.world: A settlement on a mineral-rich slope. The substrate is an ARTIFICIAL CHEMISTRY, not a list of nouns. A substance is a record: a composition multiset over 12 elemental tokens (up to size ~8), a structure tag from a small set (crystalline, amorphous, fibrous, colloidal, gaseous, molten), and derived properties computed by fixed functions of composition and structure — hardness, melting point, toughness, density, reactivity, opacity, calorific value. You author roughly 15 REACTION RULES, not recipes: oxidation, carbon reduction, eutectic melting of mixtures, precipitation from solution, polymerisation, fermentation by a biotic agent, calcination, fluxing, quench-vs-anneal structural divergence, and so on. Each rule is a guarded transformation with conditions on temperature, duration, and the presence of a catalyst substance. The environment supplies a handful of raw feedstocks (ores, clays, plant matter, water, air) at sites. Agents have calories and temperature and die; a civilization needs substances with particular property thresholds to survive winter and to eat.
all.invention_engine: The DSL is a process language: `(hold X temp duration)`, `(mix A B)`, `(quench X medium)`, `(grind X)`, `(filter X)`, `(seal X vessel)`, `(wait X n)`, plus control flow. A program is a recipe; running it against the rule engine deterministically yields a substance (often a useless one). Wake: enumerative search for programs producing substances that satisfy a survival predicate ('a substance with hardness above H and toughness above T', 'a substance with calorific value above C that is not toxic'), the predicates coming from world needs, not from a materials wishlist. Sleep-G: Stitch over the corpus of successful recipes finds the fragments that recur across many products — and those fragments are exactly the named unit processes of real metallurgy and chemistry: a reduce step, a flux step, a temper step. The compressor discovers process engineering. The second engine, and the reason to build this one, is RAF DETECTION. Maintain the reaction network as a directed hypergraph (substances as nodes, executed process-abstractions as hyperedges from input multisets to output multisets) and run a RAF (Reflexively Autocatalytic and Food-generated) algorithm over it nightly: find the maximal subset of processes such that every process's inputs are either environmental feedstock or produced by another process in the subset, AND every process's required catalysts/tools are produced within the subset. When a non-trivial RAF first appears, an industry has bootstrapped itself — the settlement can now make the things it needs to make the things it needs, from dirt. That is a computable, non-arbitrary, genuinely surprising threshold event, and it is the best push notification in this entire document.
all.why_unbounded: The substance space is combinatorial and enormous: multisets of size up to 8 over 12 elements crossed with 6 structure tags is on the order of 10^7-10^8 distinct substances before you count process history effects. The REACHABLE subset is gated by achievable temperature, duration, and catalyst availability — all of which are themselves products of earlier discoveries, so the reachable frontier expands as a consequence of what has been made. You did not write the product list; you wrote the rules, and the rules generate a space neither of you has seen. On top of that sits the usual L^d program-space growth over the process DSL. The compression argument that matters here: because properties are computed functions of composition, the system can produce substances with property combinations you never anticipated, and the survival predicates will select the useful ones without you having to judge. This is the idea where you are most likely to be genuinely surprised by an OBJECT rather than by a program.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: the rule engine plus enumerative search over a 6-primitive process DSL against one predicate ('produce something with calorific value above C'). The tribe discovers charcoal-analogues. Rung 2: Stitch names its first unit process — a hold-at-temperature fragment that appears in forty recipes. You now have a word for 'roasting' that you did not write. Rung 3 (~night 60): reduction. A recipe that mixes an oxide feedstock with the tribe's own charcoal-analogue at temperature yields a metal-analogue with hardness nothing else has. Tools follow immediately because the survival predicates were already asking for hardness. Rung 4: quench-vs-anneal divergence — the same composition with two structure tags and wildly different toughness. The compressor finds both branches and names them separately, and the tribe has heat treatment. Rung 5 (~night 150-300): the first RAF. Some set like {char, flux, reduce, cast} closes on itself. Rung 6 / wildest plausible: a second, disjoint RAF using different feedstocks appears, and the two compete for site resources — two industries, endogenously defined, in economic conflict. Beyond that, catalysis by a produced substance means a process can make itself cheaper, and you get the runaway that the RAF literature predicts.
all.what_selects: Survival predicates are the fitness function and they are property thresholds, never named goods: winter needs a substance with insulation above X in quantity; hunting needs hardness and toughness above thresholds simultaneously (which is the whole difficulty of metallurgy, honestly modelled); storage needs impermeability and non-toxicity; illness pressure needs an antimicrobial property. Recipes compete on interpreter-step cost, feedstock scarcity, and yield. Processes compete on how many products they appear in — which is precisely the MDL objective, so the compressor and the economy are optimising the same thing, which is elegant. Failure mode with teeth: a settlement that specialises on a feedstock and then exhausts the deposit must re-derive its entire stack on a different chemistry.
all.changing_worlds: Deposits deplete and are non-uniform, so the accessible feedstock vector drifts and the settlement must migrate or re-derive. A cheap and very effective second axis: run several settlements on slopes with DIFFERENT elemental abundance, so their chemistries diverge — a tin-poor valley never finds bronze-analogues and goes somewhere else entirely. Slower still, and worth building: perturb one rule's threshold constants per world (a world where carbon reduction needs 200 degrees more) and you get chemically distinct histories from identical code. Weather affects achievable temperature, which affects which regimes are open in winter versus summer, which makes the seasonal cycle chemically meaningful.
all.novelty_detector: This idea has the best natural signals of the six because chemistry gives you objective firsts. (1) FIRST RAF, and every subsequent RAF expansion — the closure event, reported with the member processes and the feedstocks it eats. (2) PROPERTY RECORD: any substance that sets an all-time maximum on a property dimension, or that occupies a previously-empty cell in a coarse 2D property grid (hardness x toughness, say) — this is MAP-Elites-style illumination of substance space used as a novelty measure, and it directly answers 'is this genuinely new or just another sludge'. (3) MDL shock on the process library, as elsewhere. (4) CATALYTIC CLOSURE: a substance that catalyses a process that produces it. (5) A boredom guard specific to this idea: track the rate of new substances that are USED (appear in an accepted survival solution) versus merely produced; if the used-rate collapses while the produced-rate stays high, the system is making sludge and should be told to push exploration toward empty property-grid cells. Sonification works well here — map the property grid to a stereo field and each new substance to a struck tone, so a productive night sounds like rain on a roof and a RAF closure sounds like a chord.
all.phone_view: The headline object is the PROPERTY GRID: a small heatmap, hardness on one axis, toughness on the other, cells shaded by how recently something landed there, with tonight's new substances as bright dots. It is instantly legible and it shows progress as territory. Above it: `NIGHT 188 · SUBSTANCES 2,417 (+31, 4 useful) · PROCESSES 22 · RAF: yes (5 members)`. That RAF line is the one you check. Below: named new processes with docs. The binge view is the reaction hypergraph — feedstocks on the left, everything derived flowing right, RAF members highlighted in a cycle — plus a substance browser where you can tap any of the thousands of things your world has made and see its composition, its properties, the shortest recipe, and whether anything ever used it.
all.hardware_use: Chemistry is cheap: rule application is a few multiset operations, and you can evaluate millions of recipes per minute per core in plain Python if you intern substances by a canonical hash and memoise reaction results aggressively (this is the Infinite Craft cache lesson applied to a local rule engine — every pair-and-conditions tuple gets computed once, ever). 64GB is what lets you keep the entire substance table and the reaction memo resident, which is the difference between a fast sim and a slow one. RAF detection is a fixpoint iteration over the hypergraph, near-instant at these sizes. GPU: only the 4B namer, batched nightly, ~4GB. No training. Determinism is free here because chemistry is a pure function; budget search in node expansions and you get bit-identical replays regardless of laptop temperature.
all.input_cadence: Coffee and the property grid. The high-value nudge, which is genuinely fun and takes ten minutes, is ADDING A RULE — one new guarded transformation opens a whole region of substance space and the following week is visibly more productive. Do it monthly at most or you are just designing a tech tree slowly. Chore: none really, though you will want to skim the substance browser occasionally to check that the useful-fraction is not collapsing.
all.tech: Python with substances interned as canonical tuples in a dict and reactions memoised (this is the whole performance story). Stitch over recipe s-expressions for the process library. RAF detection is ~50 lines: iteratively remove processes whose inputs or catalysts are not producible, until fixpoint. SQLite for substances, recipes, processes, RAF snapshots. The property grid and hypergraph render in canvas. llama.cpp + Qwen3.5-4B Q4 with GBNF for process naming — and this is where naming really earns its keep, because 'the process that holds a carbon-bearing mixture above 900 for 6 ticks' becoming `reduce-with-char` is what makes the chronicle readable. ntfy + Tailscale Serve + GitHub Pages as usual.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: 12 elements, 15 rules, substance interning, and the reaction memo. Write no recipes. Then a brute-force random walk of 100k recipes to see what your rules actually generate — this alone is a delightful afternoon, because you will discover products you did not anticipate before any agent exists. Sunday: the survival predicate, enumerative recipe search, one Stitch pass, and the property grid rendered to a PNG on your phone. Delight moment: a named process and a substance in a grid cell you did not know was reachable. This is the fastest of the six to a genuine surprise, because the chemistry surprises you before the agents do.
all.six_months_later: Tens of thousands of substances catalogued, a couple of dozen named unit processes forming a real process library, at least one and probably several RAFs, and a property grid with a distinctive filled shape that differs between your parallel settlements. What stays interesting is the frontier: there are always empty cells in the property grid and always a question of whether they are reachable. That is a genuinely open question about your own creation, six months in, which is the definition of what the builder is asking for.
all.honest_ceiling: Chemistry space is vast but FLAT, and this is the honest failure mode: the overwhelming majority of the 10^7 reachable substances are useless, and without discipline you get a beautiful mountain of sludge with a survival story bolted on. The property grid and the used-versus-produced ratio are the defences and you must build them early, not later. Second, rule-based chemistries have attractors — a handful of thermodynamically favoured products that everything collapses into — and you will notice by week three that 60% of recipes end in the same three substances. Fixing that means tuning rule guards, which is fiddly and is real work. Third, the RAF event may come early and then never recur meaningfully; one industry bootstrap is thrilling, and if the feedstock diversity is too low there is never a second. Fourth, be honest that the chemistry is a toy — it will produce things that are chemically absurd, and if you care about plausibility you will spend time on rules rather than on the civilization. My advice is to not care about plausibility at all and treat it as an alien chemistry, which also removes any temptation to author the outcomes you already know.
all.research_notes: Verified: the RAF framework (Reflexively Autocatalytic and Food-generated sets, Hordijk & Steel) is well established and the specific paper that fuses it with combinatorial technology models is 'Emergence of autocatalytic sets in a simple model of technological evolution' (arxiv.org/pdf/2204.01059; J Evol Econ 2023, link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00191-023-00838-2), which reports that product transformation networks arising from combinatorial innovation models have a high probability of containing autocatalytic sets — i.e. the threshold event this design detects is a real, studied phenomenon and is likely to actually occur rather than being aspirational. 'Autocatalytic Sets Arising in a Combinatorial Model of Chemical Evolution' (PMC9695903, PubMed 36362857) gives the conditions under which they arise from random catalysis assignment. For the substrate style, Hiroki Sayama's Hash Chemistry line ('Non-Spatial Hash Chemistry as a Minimalistic Open-Ended Evolutionary System', arxiv.org/pdf/2404.18027, and 'Structural Cellular Hash Chemistry', arxiv.org/pdf/2412.12790) is the live precedent for computationally cheap open-ended artificial chemistry and is worth reading before you design your rules. On caching: the Infinite Craft architecture is exactly the pattern — the backend keeps every previously-combined pair in a cache and only novel pairs go to the expensive path (quuxplusone.github.io/blog/2024/02/08/infinite-craft/), with public datasets of 200k+ recipes existing; here the expensive path is your rule engine rather than an LLM, so caching makes it essentially free. Stitch (github.com/mlb2251/stitch) handles the process-library compression unchanged, since recipes are just s-expressions.

audit.name: The Slow Kiln
audit.ceiling: Fastest to a genuine surprise, cheapest to run, and the most honest about its own failure mode — but the ceiling is nearer than the 10^7-substance figure implies, and it is in a different place than they think. The binding limit is not the size of composition space, it is the ARITY AND NONLINEARITY OF THE AUTHORED PROPERTY FUNCTIONS. Properties are fixed functions of composition and structure tag, so the property grid is a smooth image of a space you wrote down; filling it is hill-climbing a known landscape, and its Pareto frontier is determined the moment you write the functions. Expect the frontier to be essentially mapped in 3-6 weeks. The PROCESS library — the actual claimed tech tree — saturates harder and sooner: real metallurgy has a few dozen unit operations and so will this, so budget 20-40 named processes by week 6-10 and then permanent recombination. Also: reachability from ~5 feedstocks under 15 guarded rules is typically a few hundred to a few thousand substances, not tens of thousands, and most of those differ by one composition token. 'Tens of thousands of substances catalogued' at six months is off by roughly an order of magnitude unless the rules are far more generative than 15 guarded transformations usually are.
audit.authored_content_risk: Lowest of the six, genuinely. Authoring rules rather than recipes is the correct move and it does produce objects the designer has not seen — the Saturday-afternoon 'brute-force 100k recipes and look at what came out' exercise is real discovery and it happens before any agent exists. Two caveats. First, the property functions are where taste re-enters invisibly: you choose hardness and toughness as axes because you know the metallurgy story you want, and then the survival predicates ask for hardness and toughness. Second, the RAF is at high risk of being an authored artifact rather than a discovery — with 15 rules and a handful of catalyst conditions, a self-sustaining set is usually either present from night one (char catalyses reduction which makes more char) or structurally impossible, and which one you get is decided by you when you write rule 7. A threshold event that fires once, early, and never again is a screenshot, not a mechanism.
audit.compute_honesty: The only fully honest one in the set, and by a distance. Recipes are PURE functions of a substance record, so observational-equivalence dedup and memoisation are cheap in exactly the way DreamCoder's are and Emberlisp's are not — this is the single biggest architectural advantage in the document and it is barely mentioned. Interning substances by canonical hash plus memoising (rule, inputs, conditions) makes rule application effectively free after the first evaluation; millions of recipes per core-minute in plain Python is believable here in a way it is not anywhere else. RAF detection is a fixpoint over a hypergraph of a few thousand nodes: milliseconds. GPU: one 4B namer, ~4GB, batched nightly. Nothing needs the 8GB except the namer, and nothing needs a datacenter. Zero objections.
audit.semantic_risk: Split, and the split matters. SUBSTANCES: high — they concede the sludge problem and are right; worse, rule-based chemistries have thermodynamic attractors and you will find 60% of recipes terminating in three products by week three, which is real work to tune and is fiddly in a way that resembles content authoring. PROCESSES: LOW, and this is the idea's strongest claim. A recurring 'hold above T for D then quench' fragment is meaningful because the physics makes it meaningful, not because a language model named it — MDL and physical significance genuinely coincide when the corpus is process recipes over a reaction engine. Of the six ideas, this is the one where a compressed fragment is most likely to be a real thing rather than a syntactic coincidence.
audit.dubious_claims: (1) The RAF citation is the overreach. arXiv 2204.01059 / J Evol Econ 2023 finds high probability of autocatalytic sets in product transformation networks generated by COMBINATORIAL models with RANDOM catalysis assignment, and PMC9695903 gives conditions under random catalysis. Neither transfers to 15 hand-written guarded rules — the probability argument is over an ensemble you are not sampling from. Presenting 'the threshold event this design detects is likely to actually occur rather than being aspirational' as verified is not supported; it is exactly as aspirational as the writing event in idea 2, just cheaper to check. (2) '10^7-10^8 distinct substances' conflates the composition space with the REACHABLE set; report reachability from feedstock closure instead, and do it on the first Saturday, because that number decides whether this idea is interesting. (3) Sayama's Hash Chemistry papers (2404.18027, 2412.12790) are real and the right prior art, but note they achieve open-endedness through hash-based fitness with no property semantics at all — the opposite design choice from authored property functions, and worth confronting rather than citing. (4) The Infinite Craft caching analogy is apt and the blog post is real; the pattern is correct.
audit.one_change: Stop authoring 15 rules and 7 property functions; author a GENERATIVE CORE of ~50 numbers instead — a per-element table of affinity, valence, mass, electronegativity-analogue and enthalpy contribution — and derive both the reaction guards and the property values from it by fixed formulas. Three payoffs at once: attractors become tunable by nudging numbers rather than by rewriting rule guards; adding a 13th element multiplies the reaction set instead of adding one recipe; and the chemistry becomes a MUTABLE GENOME, so the monthly 'add a rule' chore that this design depends on for longevity becomes an automatic axis (and composes directly with Thousand Dawns' outer loop). It also removes the smooth-authored-function problem — properties emerge from element interactions rather than from a landscape you already know the shape of.

all.name: Thousand Dawns
all.pitch: Run thirty-two worlds at once, each with a mutated physics genome and its own tribe and its own library, and keep a MAP-Elites archive over WORLDS so compute flows to the ones still inventing. Then transplant libraries between worlds: a technology that survives transplant is a law, one that dies is a local trick — which gives you a computed, unauthored measure of how deep an invention actually is.
all.world: A world is a genome: ~20 physics knobs (carrying cost, ignition threshold, melt thresholds, decay rates, day length, seasonal amplitude, predator pressure, resource abundance vector over 14 materials, water availability, terrain roughness) plus a terrain seed. Each world instantiates the Emberlisp substrate — property-record materials, ~12 physical rules, a typed survival lisp, one tribe, real death. Thirty-two of them run in parallel on the laptop, each cheap because each is a small grid with a few dozen agents. The knobs are not cosmetic: raising the ignition threshold past what percussion can deliver means FIRE IS IMPOSSIBLE IN THAT WORLD, and its tribe must find another way to be warm, or another way to eat, or die. Some worlds are unsurvivable and that is fine and informative.
all.invention_engine: Two nested searches. INNER: standard wake-sleep per world — enumerative synthesis over that world's library, Stitch compression into named abstractions, recognition model on fantasies. OUTER: MAP-Elites over world genomes. The archive is a grid indexed by behaviour descriptors computed from each world's HISTORY rather than its parameters: (library depth reached, number of physics dimensions the tribe's programs actually exploit, log time-to-first-abstraction-of-depth-3, count of distinct abstraction behaviour-signatures). Each cell holds the elite world for that behavioural niche, scored by an open-endedness metric rather than by survival — specifically, the rate of accepted novel abstractions over the last 200 nights. Every N nights: cull worlds whose invention rate has flatlined, and reseed those slots by mutating an elite's genome. Compute is thus continuously redirected toward worlds still producing. The third mechanism, which is the distinctive one, is TRANSPLANT TESTING: periodically inject a library entry (with its dependency closure) from world A into world B's tribe and record whether it executes, whether it helps, and whether it earns call-sites. Every abstraction accumulates a GENERALITY SCORE — the fraction of foreign worlds in which it remains useful. High-generality abstractions are laws of the substrate (leverage, containment, insulation, sequencing). Low-generality ones are parochial hacks that depended on one world's abundance draw. You did not label any of them; the archive computed it.
all.why_unbounded: Three stacked sources. (1) Program space over each world's library: L^d, growing as before. (2) Physics space: 20 continuous knobs is a large space and MAP-Elites explores it adaptively rather than by grid search, so when a region of physics stops producing invention the archive moves. (3) The cross product: the same DSL primitive means something different under different physics, so an abstraction discovered in a high-gravity world can be transplanted into a low-ignition world and compose with ITS abstractions into hybrids neither lineage would reach. Crucially, this is the only one of the six ideas where the task distribution is refreshed STRUCTURALLY rather than by you: when a world saturates, you do not add physics by hand, the archive spawns a mutated world whose task distribution is different by construction. That is the honest answer to the DreamCoder plateau, and it is why this idea has the longest half-life.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: four worlds, hardcoded genome differences, no archive — just four Emberlisp runs side by side and a page that compares their libraries. Already interesting, because the divergence is visible immediately. Rung 2: the MAP-Elites archive, cull-and-mutate, and the first time compute gets pulled off a dead world onto a live one automatically. Rung 3 (~week 3): the first transplant, and the first abstraction that FAILS to transplant — you learn something real about your own substrate the moment that happens. Rung 4: generality scores stabilise and you can sort the union of all libraries by universality; the top of that list is the substrate's genuine physics-level technology set, discovered by thirty-two independent civilizations, and reading it is a legitimate scientific pleasure. Rung 5 (~month 2): a world where fire is impossible invents something structurally different at the same depth — fermentation for calories, or insulation-by-composite for warmth — and the comparative chronicle writes itself. Rung 6 / wildest plausible: hybrid vigour — an abstraction that only exists because two transplanted foreign entries composed, achieving something no single-world lineage reached at any budget. And the endpoint that would genuinely astonish: the archive discovering a physics genome whose worlds reliably out-invent all others, i.e. your system finding what makes a universe generative.
all.what_selects: At the agent level, survival as always. At the world level, INVENTION RATE, not survival: a world where the tribe lives comfortably forever and stops inventing gets culled, which is the correct and slightly cruel selection pressure for this project, and it is directly borrowed from the open-endedness literature. At the abstraction level, generality across transplants. Three selection levels, all computed, none authored. The interaction between them is where the interest lives — comfortable worlds are boring, lethal worlds die before inventing, and the archive spends its time on the knife edge, which is exactly where you would want to be watching.
all.changing_worlds: This idea IS the changing-worlds requirement, taken literally: worlds are born, mutate, and die on a schedule, and you can watch the population of universes turn over. Within a world, the Emberlisp non-stationarity (seasons, geology) still applies. And this is the natural home for human perturbation: the public page shows the archive, and anonymous visitors get one action per day — they can 'bless' a world (a small resource shower) or 'sunder' one (a drought), or vote a culled world back into the pool. Visitors become a slow, unpredictable environmental force acting at the level of universes, the guestbook becomes a record of divine intervention, and it gives the public artifact a genuine reason to exist. Anonymous, rate-limited, logged, and mechanically bounded so it can nudge but never break.
all.novelty_detector: Archive-aware. (1) NEW NICHE FILLED: a world lands in a previously-empty MAP-Elites cell — a behavioural mode of civilization the system has never produced. Always push, with the world's genome diff from its parent. (2) TRANSPLANT SURPRISE: an abstraction that was useless in twelve worlds suddenly earns call-sites in the thirteenth — parochial tech turning out to be general is a great story and it is exactly what a generality score surfaces. (3) DIVERGENT SOLUTION: two worlds solve the SAME task predicate with abstractions whose behaviour signatures differ beyond a threshold — convergent problem, divergent technology, which is the comparative-history payoff. (4) ARCHIVE STAGNATION ALARM, the boredom detector as a first-class citizen: if no cell has been newly filled and no world's invention rate has exceeded its trailing baseline for K nights, the system tells you it is bored, widens genome mutation variance automatically, and only pings you if that fails too. (5) The per-world signals from Emberlisp, but scored against the ARCHIVE-WIDE distribution rather than the world's own, so a discovery only counts as new if thirty-one other civilizations have not already made it. That last point is what makes this the strongest novelty detector of the six — you have a population baseline, so 'genuinely new' is measurable rather than heuristic.
all.phone_view: The archive as a grid of tiles, one per world, each a tiny sparkline of library size with a colour for status (green inventing, amber plateaued, grey dead, white newly seeded). Thirty-two tiles fit on a phone screen and the whole state of your multiverse reads in five seconds. Header: `DAWN 44 · 32 WORLDS · 7 NICHES FILLED (+1) · 214 ABSTRACTIONS, 19 UNIVERSAL`. One headline card underneath for tonight's single most surprising event. Tap a world for its Emberlisp view (DAG, map, chronicle). Second tab, and this is the hour-long binge: the UNIVERSAL LIBRARY — every abstraction across all worlds sorted by generality score, each showing which worlds found it independently and how their bodies differ. That page is a comparative history of thirty-two civilizations and it gets better every week without you touching it.
all.hardware_use: This is the design that actually uses the 64GB and all the cores properly. Thirty-two small worlds at maybe 1-1.5GB of resident program bank each is a real fit for the machine, and it is the reason this idea would be impossible on a 16GB laptop. Run worlds as separate processes with a node budget each; allocate budget proportional to archive score, which is your compute-flows-to-interesting mechanism and costs nothing to implement. Stitch is called 32 times a night, still trivial. One shared Qwen3.5-4B Q4 instance on the GPU serving all naming requests in a nightly batch (~4GB, plenty of headroom). Absolutely no training, no finetuning; the recognition models are tiny per-world MLPs on CPU. Benchmark hygiene is CRITICAL here in a way it is not elsewhere: worlds compete for archive slots, so if fitness had any wall-clock component the thermal state of the laptop would decide which universes survive. Budget everything in node expansions, cost everything in interpreter steps, seed RNGs from (world_genome_hash, night), and the entire multiverse replays deterministically.
all.input_cadence: Read the tile grid with coffee; tap into whichever tile changed colour. Nudges: hand-author a world genome you are curious about and inject it into the archive (thirty seconds, high fun); pin a world so the culler cannot kill your favourite. One real chore, monthly at most: the behaviour descriptors that define the archive's axes will need one or two revisions as you learn what actually varies, and changing them resets the archive, so think before you do it.
all.tech: Emberlisp's whole stack, times 32, orchestrated by a simple scheduler process. MAP-Elites is ~100 lines (a dict from discretised descriptor tuple to elite, with mutation by Gaussian perturbation of the genome vector). One SQLite per world plus one archive DB, which sidesteps the multi-writer contention problem entirely — a much better arrangement than The Long Teaching's shared DB. Transplant is a library-entry copy with dependency closure and a scored trial period. Frontend is the same PWA reading a single generated archive JSON; visitor actions go through a tiny node endpoint behind Tailscale Funnel or a Cloudflare Worker writing to a queue the sim drains at dawn.
all.first_weekend: Only attempt this after Emberlisp exists — it is a multiplier on that substrate, not a from-scratch weekend. Given Emberlisp: Saturday, parameterise the physics as a genome vector, run four worlds with different genomes in four processes, build the tile grid. Sunday, transplant: copy an abstraction with its closure from world 1 into world 2, run a trial, record whether it earns call-sites. The delight moment here is unusually intellectual and unusually strong: you watch a technology fail to work in a different universe, and you realise you now have an experimental apparatus for your own physics.
all.six_months_later: Hundreds of world-generations turned over, an archive with most niches filled and a documented map of which physics regimes produce generative civilizations, and a universal library where the top twenty entries are the genuine invariants of your substrate — found independently by dozens of tribes, and readable as a discovered periodic table of technology. This is the idea most likely to still be producing genuinely new things at six months, because it does not depend on you adding physics; it mutates its own.
all.honest_ceiling: The genome is finite: 20 knobs, and MAP-Elites will have illuminated the interesting corners within a few months. When that happens, novelty falls off across the whole archive at once rather than world by world, which is a starker plateau than Emberlisp's. Adding knobs is cheap but is a chore and each addition resets some archive structure. Second and more fundamental: the BASE DSL AND THE PHYSICS RULES ARE THE ONE THING THAT NEVER VARIES, and every technology in every world is ultimately a composition over those authored primitives. Transplantability only means anything because the base is shared. So the deepest honest statement about this whole family of ideas is that you author the alphabet and the system authors the literature — the literature is unbounded, the alphabet is not, and if the alphabet is impoverished the literature will be too. Spend your design effort on the base primitives, not on content. Third, per-world node budget is 1/32 of a single-world run, so each civilization is individually much shallower; you are trading depth for breadth, and if what you want is one tribe going far, this is the wrong idea. Fourth, the visitor-perturbation endpoint is the only piece of internet-facing surface in these designs and it needs rate limiting and bounded effects or someone will find it entertaining to break your multiverse.
all.research_notes: Verified: MAP-Elites (Mouret & Clune) and Novelty Search with Local Competition are the two standard QD archive designs — MAP-Elites uses a static discretised mapping, novelty search an unstructured expanding archive; MAP-Elites supports both bounded and unbounded descriptor axes, which matters because library depth is unbounded (emergentmind.com/topics/map-elites-algorithm). ASAL, 'Automating the Search for Artificial Life with Foundation Models' (Kumar et al., Sakana AI + MIT + OpenAI + IDSIA + Ken Stanley, arxiv.org/abs/2412.17799, code at github.com/SakanaAI/asal, published in Artificial Life 31(3)) is the direct precedent for exactly this outer loop: searching a SPACE OF SIMULATIONS for temporally open-ended novelty and for illumination of a diverse space, demonstrated over Boids, Particle Life, Game of Life, Lenia and neural CAs — read this one before building the archive, it is the closest published thing to the outer loop here. 'Quality Diversity in the Amorphous Fortress' (arxiv.org/pdf/2312.02231) applies QD to evolving 0-player game complexity, which is nearly this project's genre. 'DejaQ: Open-Ended Evolution of Diverse, Learnable and Verifiable Problems' (arxiv.org/pdf/2601.01931) is recent work on evolving the problem distribution itself, which is the plateau fix. Inner loop unchanged: DreamCoder (PLDI 2021) + Stitch (POPL 2023, github.com/mlb2251/stitch, seconds on one CPU core, so 32 nightly calls are free). Hardware: 32 processes is the right shape for 64GB; the GPU only ever holds one Qwen3.5-4B Q4 (~3.4GB) for batched naming.

audit.name: Thousand Dawns
audit.ceiling: The distinctive mechanism does not work as described, and the arithmetic is not close. MAP-Elites needs 10^4-10^6 evaluations to illuminate even a modest descriptor space; here ONE EVALUATION IS A CIVILIZATION RUN OF HUNDREDS OF SIMULATED NIGHTS. With 32 slots and a cull-and-reseed every N nights, you get on the order of 10-50 world-evaluations per month against a 20-dimensional continuous genome. That is not quality-diversity, it is random search with a leaderboard, and 'the archive discovers a physics genome whose worlds reliably out-invent all others' is unreachable by three to four orders of magnitude. Compounding it: the descriptors are computed from HISTORY, so each evaluation is expensive, noisy and non-i.i.d., which is the regime where MAP-Elites archives are known to fill with lucky seeds (elite inflation) — your archive will confidently report niches that a rerun would not reproduce. And per-world node budget is 1/32 of Emberlisp's, which was already the binding constraint, so each civilization stalls at depth 2-3 in the first fortnight. Ceiling: interesting for ~3 weeks (the four-worlds-side-by-side comparison), then 32 shallow libraries and a scoreboard that is mostly seed noise.
audit.authored_content_risk: Their own honest_ceiling contains the correct diagnosis and then does not act on it: 'the base DSL and the physics rules are the one thing that never varies'. Twenty scalar knobs is not a physics space, it is a parameter sweep of ONE physics. Every technology in all 32 worlds is a composition over the same 28 primitives and the same 12 rules, which means the celebrated 'universal library sorted by generality' is largely a list of which compositions are robust to constant-tuning — real, computable, mildly interesting, but a much smaller claim than 'the discovered periodic table of technology'. The transplant test itself is the one part I would defend without reservation: it is cheap, it is honest, it produces an unauthored classification, and it is the single best measurement idea in the entire document. It just does not need MAP-Elites, or 32 worlds, to work.
audit.compute_honesty: GPU: honest and trivial (one 4B, batched). CPU: this is where the pitch quietly overspends. 'Thirty-two small worlds at 1-1.5GB resident each' fits 64GB, fine — but a consumer laptop has ~8-16 usable cores, so 32 worlds is roughly HALF A CORE EACH, and the enumerator throughput problem from Emberlisp is now divided by 32 rather than merely being present. 'Allocate budget proportional to archive score' partially rescues this by starving dead worlds, but it also means most slots are near-frozen, which further reduces the effective evaluation count feeding the outer loop. The claim that this design 'actually uses the 64GB and all the cores properly' is backwards: it is the design most likely to be simultaneously RAM-comfortable and compute-starved. No datacenter or API bill is hidden here — the dishonesty is about what the available compute can accomplish, not about where it runs.
audit.semantic_risk: Moderate, with one specific hazard: the ARCHIVE-WIDE novelty baseline is genuinely the strongest anti-nonsense signal in the document — 'new only if 31 other civilizations have not found it' is a real population baseline and it is worth stealing for whichever idea gets built. But it only means something once the per-world libraries are deep enough to differ, and at 1/32 budget they are not. Early on, every world's library is the same six shallow abstractions, generality scores are all ~1.0, and the universal library reads as profound while containing nothing. Expect that state to persist for the first month and to be very easy to mistake for success.
audit.dubious_claims: (1) 'MAP-Elites supports both bounded and unbounded descriptor axes' — wrong as stated, and the citation is an AI-generated topic page. Canonical MAP-Elites requires a bounded, discretised grid; unbounded axes need CVT-MAP-Elites, expanding/unstructured archives, or novelty-search-with-local-competition. Since library depth is explicitly one of their axes and is unbounded, this is a real design bug, not a nitpick. (2) ASAL (arXiv 2412.17799) is real and IS published in Artificial Life 31(3) — verified, credit where due, and it is the right prior art. But note what ASAL actually searches: simulation parameters evaluated by a VLM over RENDERED FRAMES, with each evaluation costing seconds. The analogy breaks precisely on evaluation cost, which is the thing that kills the outer loop here. (3) DejaQ (arXiv 2601.01931, Röpke/Coward/Lupu/Foster/Rocktäschel/Foerster, Jan 2026) is real — verified — but it evolves synthetic MATH PROBLEMS against an LLM's learnability during RL training, with cheap verifiable evaluation. Citing it as 'the plateau fix' for a system whose problem instances cost a civilization-run each is an analogy, not a precedent. (4) 'Amorphous Fortress' (2312.02231) is real and genuinely the closest genre match. (5) 'This is the idea most likely to still be producing genuinely new things at six months' is the claim I would bet hardest against: it plateaus ACROSS THE WHOLE ARCHIVE AT ONCE, which they concede, and it gets there sooner than the single-world ideas because each world is shallower.
audit.one_change: Put the ALPHABET in the genome, not the constants — and cut to 6-8 worlds. Make physics RULE SCHEMAS and base primitives mutable (add/remove/reparameterise a rule, add a primitive, change a type signature), so that different worlds genuinely have different languages rather than the same language with different thresholds. That does two things nothing else in this design does: it makes the transplant/generality test measure something deep (does this technology survive a change of PHYSICS, not a change of ignition threshold), and it means the outer loop can escape the 20-knob box that otherwise caps everything at a few months. Fewer worlds also gives each 4-5x the node budget, which is the difference between libraries that can differ and libraries that cannot. Accept that the result is no longer MAP-Elites — with ~30 evaluations a month it never was — and run it as an explicit, hand-read tournament of 8 physics variants instead.

all.name: The Dreaming Stone
all.pitch: A single long-lived tribe consults an oracle — a local 4B model, grammar-constrained so it can only ever speak valid programs and machine-checkable goals in the tribe's own evolving language — and everything it says must survive execution in the world before it counts. Strangers on the internet write in a guestbook that the oracle formalises into the civilization's research agenda, so the tribe's future is literally set by prayers from people it will never meet.
all.world: A single valley, the Emberlisp substrate (property-record materials, ~12 physical rules, typed survival lisp, permanent death), one tribe, running for months without reset. At the valley's centre is the Dreaming Stone: a site where an agent can spend ticks to 'dream', which in implementation means the tribe gets to consult the local language model. Dreaming is metered — a scarce in-world resource, so the tribe's LLM budget is itself part of the economy and a tribe that spends all its time dreaming starves. Around the stone, marks accumulate: the guestbook. Anonymous web visitors leave text; that text is visible in-world as inscriptions on the stone, and it is the raw material for the oracle's task proposals.
all.invention_engine: LILO with the world as the verifier, plus a task generator that is the honest fix for the DreamCoder plateau. Three grammar-constrained roles for the model, none of them trusted, all of them checked. (1) PROGRAM PROPOSER: given a task predicate and a rendered view of the current library (names + generated docs + type signatures), the model emits 8 candidate programs. It is decoded under a GBNF grammar AUTO-GENERATED FROM THE CURRENT DSL — regenerated every night as the library grows — so it is structurally incapable of emitting a syntactically invalid program or of calling a primitive that does not exist. Candidates are executed; failures are discarded silently; survivors are added to the corpus AND used to reweight the enumerative searcher's proposal distribution. The LLM is a proposal distribution, the world is ground truth, and nothing it hallucinates can enter the library. (2) ABSTRACTION PROPOSER: after Stitch's MDL pass, the model gets to suggest additional abstractions that are semantically meaningful but not maximally compressive — LILO's finding is that LLM-proposed, auto-documented abstractions produce more interpretable and more USABLE libraries than pure MDL. Each proposal must compile to base DSL and must earn call-sites within 20 nights or it is demoted. (3) TASK PROPOSER: this is the important one. Given the library docs, the current world state, and the guestbook, the model emits goal predicates — again grammar-constrained, so every proposed task is a machine-checkable predicate over world state, never prose. Proposals are filtered to those currently UNSOLVED but within a heuristic reach horizon (the Voyager auto-curriculum condition, plus DreamCoder's adjacent-possible framing), and scored later on whether they were eventually solved. A task proposer that only emits impossible or trivial goals gets its proposals downweighted. Optional fourth engine, the Ouroboros piece: weekly, take every verified (task, library-view, program) triple and QLoRA-finetune the 4B on its own wins; the new checkpoint must beat the old on a held-out set of last month's tasks measured in INTERPRETER STEPS TO SOLVE (deterministic, thermally invariant) or it is discarded.
all.why_unbounded: Program space over a growing library is unbounded as in all of these, but the distinctive claim here is about the TASK distribution, which is where the other ideas plateau. An LLM reading a library of named, documented technologies will propose goals that reference those technologies, so the goal distribution grows with the library — a self-referential curriculum. When the tribe invents `bank-the-coals`, the oracle starts proposing tasks about carrying fire, storing fire, trading fire, hiding fire. That is a genuinely different plateau profile from pure MDL wake-sleep. Layered on top, the guestbook injects goals from outside the system entirely — a source of non-stationarity with no computational bound at all, because it is other people. Honest counterweight: the model is a 4B and its proposals are shallow; the grammar constrains syntax, not sense; and the reach-horizon filter is doing a lot of work. But the mechanism is real, it is the published LILO/Voyager finding, and it directly addresses the failure mode of ideas 1 through 4.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: no LLM at all — Emberlisp's search plus one hardcoded task. Then bolt on the namer and get your first generated technology name. Rung 2: the GBNF grammar auto-generated from the DSL, and the program proposer; measure how often its candidates beat pure enumeration (they will, on deep tasks, and the measurement is the fun part). Rung 3: the task proposer, and the moment the tribe starts working on a goal that neither you nor the world's need-generator produced. Rung 4 (~week 4): the guestbook. Someone on the internet writes 'they should learn to bury their dead', the oracle formalises it into a checkable predicate, the tribe eventually satisfies it, and the chronicle records that a stranger's prayer was answered on night 312. That is a genuinely moving thing to build. Rung 5: the weekly QLoRA loop, with the held-out step-count eval as the gate — the oracle measurably gets better at its own world's language. Rung 6 / wildest plausible: the model's proposals become good enough that it starts suggesting REFACTORS — abstractions that do not compress the corpus but do make it teachable and composable, which is what a real engineer does and what MDL alone will never find. And the endpoint worth aiming at: the tribe develops a stable technical vocabulary that the model uses fluently, so the chronicle reads like a culture describing itself in its own invented words.
all.what_selects: Survival as always, plus three verifier gates that are the whole design philosophy: a program counts only if it executes and satisfies the predicate; an abstraction counts only if it earns call-sites within a window; a finetuned checkpoint counts only if it beats the incumbent on held-out interpreter-step cost. Nothing the model says is taken on faith at any level, which is what makes an LLM-in-the-loop design honest rather than a vibes machine. Dreaming is metered by an in-world resource so the oracle competes with food for the tribe's time — a nice pressure that makes consultation a strategic choice the search has to make.
all.changing_worlds: Seasons and geology as in Emberlisp, but the primary non-stationarity here is HUMAN. The guestbook is a live external process: it changes when you post the link somewhere, it changes when a friend finds it, it goes quiet for a month and then a stranger writes something strange. That is genuinely unpredictable input that no amount of compute could have generated. Secondary: every ~4000 nights the valley resets with new terrain but the library, the oracle checkpoint, and the guestbook-scripture persist — so the tribe carries its technology and its religion into a new land, and you find out which parts of each still work.
all.novelty_detector: (1) PRAYER ANSWERED: a guestbook-derived task predicate satisfied for the first time, reported with the original human text alongside the formalised predicate and the program that satisfied it. This is the flagship notification and it will be the one you screenshot. (2) The Emberlisp battery: first-ever event bloom filter, MDL shock, abstraction depth increase, long-unsolved-now-solved. (3) ORACLE SURPRISE: a program from the LLM proposer that the enumerative searcher had not found within its full node budget — i.e. the model contributed something search could not reach, which is the measurement that tells you whether the LLM is earning its keep. Track this as a running percentage; it is the honest metric for the whole hybrid design. (4) VOCABULARY DRIFT: embed the generated abstraction names nightly with a small local embedder and detect when the library's naming cluster structure shifts — the culture's technical vocabulary reorganising. (5) A hard rule for the feed: at most three pushes per day, ranked by surprise, everything else archived. Physical artifact fits this idea best of the six — a thermal receipt printer on the desk printing the dawn chronicle each morning, one paper strip: the date, the three events, any answered prayer with the stranger's words quoted. Sub-forty-pound printer, a few lines of ESC/POS over USB, and the check-in becomes a physical ritual with no screen at all.
all.phone_view: Deliberately quiet and text-forward, because this idea's payload is language. Top: `NIGHT 312 · POP 19 · LIB 94 · ORACLE v7 (won 31% of tasks search missed)`. Then, if there is one, the answered-prayer card: the stranger's original sentence in quotes, the formalised predicate underneath in monospace, and the solving program. Then up to two more event lines. Then a single button, 'leave a mark', which is the guestbook — so the phone view is also the input surface and visitors get the same page you do. Binge view: the full chronicle as a scrolling text history with the abstraction DAG inline, readable like a book. The guestbook history is its own page and over months it genuinely becomes scripture — a list of what strangers wanted from a civilization that cannot see them.
all.hardware_use: The most GPU-dependent of the six, and still comfortably inside 8GB. Qwen3.5-4B or Qwen3-4B at Q4_K_M, ~3.4-4.6GB resident, ~40 tok/s, running continuously as a llama.cpp server with the library dump kept in the KV cache across the night's calls (regenerate the cached prefix only when the library changes, which is once per night — this makes the per-call cost tiny). GBNF grammar regenerated nightly from the DSL; note the documented caveat that llama.cpp does runtime token checking for grammars and that this adds real overhead, so keep the grammar tight and expect maybe 25-30 tok/s under constraint rather than 40. Nightly volume of ~50-100k tokens local is free and takes under an hour. The weekly QLoRA on a 4B in 8GB is FEASIBLE BUT TIGHT and I want to be honest: Unsloth-style 4-bit QLoRA with gradient checkpointing, sequence length capped around 1024, batch size 1 with accumulation, expect 2-4 hours and expect to hit OOM the first few attempts. It is optional; the library is the real asset and the finetune is a garnish. If you want a stronger oracle occasionally, Claude Haiku 4.5 at $1/$5 per Mtok with prompt caching (cache hits at one tenth of input, batch API at 50% off) means a weekly hard-case pass with a 20k-token cached library prefix and a few thousand output tokens costs cents; a whole month of weekly calls is a couple of dollars. Everything timed for fitness is in interpreter steps, never seconds, which also means the QLoRA eval gate is unaffected by GPU thermals.
all.input_cadence: Coffee and a paper strip from the printer. The one genuinely enjoyable recurring act is leaving your own mark in the guestbook and seeing whether the tribe ever answers you. Chores, honestly: the weekly QLoRA will need babysitting the first few times (OOM tuning), and the guestbook needs a profanity/abuse filter and rate limiting since it is public and its content will be quoted onto your phone and your printer — build that on day one of making it public, not later. After the first month, near-zero.
all.tech: Emberlisp's substrate and stack, plus: llama-cpp-python running a persistent server with a nightly-regenerated GBNF grammar derived programmatically from the library's type signatures; a `proposals` table recording every LLM output with its verification outcome so you can measure the model's hit rate over time; a `guestbook` table with raw text, formalised predicate, moderation state, and satisfaction tick; Unsloth + PEFT for the optional weekly QLoRA with the held-out step-count eval as the accept gate; python-escpos for the receipt printer. Public surface via Tailscale Funnel or a small Cloudflare Worker queue that the sim drains at dawn, so the laptop never takes direct inbound traffic.
all.first_weekend: Assumes Emberlisp's substrate. Saturday: llama.cpp server, GBNF grammar generated from your DSL's type signatures, and the program proposer — then measure, on ten tasks, how many the model solves that enumeration alone did not. That measurement is the whole thesis of the idea and you can have it in an afternoon. Sunday: the task proposer with the machine-checkable-predicate grammar, and the guestbook as a single text box writing to SQLite with the oracle formalising entries at dawn. Delight moment: type a wish into your own guestbook on Sunday night, wake Monday to a formalised predicate the tribe is now working on.
all.six_months_later: A tribe with a hundred-plus named technologies, an oracle that has been finetuned a dozen times on its own verified wins and speaks the civilization's invented vocabulary fluently, a guestbook that has become a genuinely strange document, and a shoebox of receipt strips. The thing that keeps it alive is the human input channel — the guestbook does not saturate, because people keep being unpredictable, and that is one non-stationarity source no other idea here has.
all.honest_ceiling: A 4B model is not smart. Its program proposals will be worse than enumeration on shallow tasks and only occasionally better on deep ones; the 'won X% of tasks search missed' metric might sit at 10-20% and you should be prepared for it to be low enough that the LLM is decoration. Measure it early and honestly, because if that number is near zero the whole idea reduces to Emberlisp with a nice namer — which is still good, but is not this. Second, the task proposer degenerates: LLMs asked repeatedly to propose goals converge on the same handful of themes, and after a few weeks you will see the same shapes of task recycled. The reach-horizon filter and the was-it-eventually-solved scoring help but do not fix it; the guestbook is the real defence, which means this idea's long-term novelty is partly dependent on other people showing up, and if nobody visits your page it plateaus like the others. Third, QLoRA on 8GB is a real time sink for uncertain gain; treat it as strictly optional and do not let it become the project. Fourth, public input means moderation, and quoting stranger text onto a physical printer in your house is a decision to make deliberately. Fifth, grammar-constrained decoding has known overhead and there is published work on how tokenisation interacts badly with grammar constraints, so expect some fiddling to get valid, fluent DSL out rather than valid, stupid DSL.
all.research_notes: Verified: LILO, 'Learning Interpretable Libraries by Compressing and Documenting Code' (Grand, Wong et al., ICLR 2024, arxiv.org/abs/2310.19791) is the direct precedent — it integrates Stitch compression with LLM-generated auto-documentation in a search-compress-document loop and reports solving more complex tasks and learning richer libraries than DreamCoder; this is the published version of roles (1) and (2). LAPS (Wong et al., ICML 2021, code at github.com/lio-wong/laps_dreamcoder) is the language-guided-abstraction predecessor. Voyager (Wang et al., arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291, voyager.minedojo.org) supplies the auto-curriculum + ever-growing executable skill library + iterative prompting with execution-error feedback and self-verification — role (3) and the retry loop. Recent successor framing: skill-library agents with RL-based acquisition (SAGE) and the 2026 survey 'Agent Skills for Large Language Models' (arxiv.org/html/2602.12430) describing skills as bundles of instructions, scripts, docs and metadata loaded on demand. Grammar constraints: llama.cpp GBNF (github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/grammars/README.md) supports arbitrary custom DSL grammars and there is a good worked example of constraining a model to a custom assembly language (jamesdrandall.com/posts/gbnf-constrained-generation/); the documented caveat is runtime per-token checking overhead, and 'Lost in Space: Optimizing Tokens for Grammar-Constrained Decoding' (arxiv.org/html/2502.14969v1) covers the tokenisation pitfalls. Models: Qwen3-4B / Qwen3.5-4B Q4_K_M ~3.4-4.6GB, 40+ tok/s on 8GB, described as solid for coding on constrained hardware; Qwen3.5-9B Q4_K_M ~6.6GB is possible but leaves little room for context. Costs if you supplement with the API: Claude Haiku 4.5 is $1 input / $5 output per Mtok, prompt caching gives cache hits at one tenth of base input (5-minute and 1-hour cache writes at 1.25x and 2x), and the Batch API is 50% off — so a cached-library weekly pass is genuinely a few cents. Phone/push: ntfy.sh behind Tailscale is the standard hobby pattern and the ntfy web UI is itself installable as a PWA (docs.ntfy.sh/integrations); Tailscale Serve gives HTTPS with a stable URL and no router config.

audit.name: The Dreaming Stone
audit.ceiling: Correctly identifies that the task distribution is where every other idea plateaus, then hands the fix to the one component that cannot deliver it. A 4B model, GBNF-constrained to a DSL that DID NOT EXIST DURING ITS TRAINING and whose primitive names were invented last week by a 4B model, has no prior to contribute. That is the crux and it is worth stating precisely: LLM priors are valuable in program synthesis exactly when the DSL is human-legible and maps onto world knowledge the model already has (this is why Voyager works — it writes JavaScript against a Minecraft API documented all over the internet). Here you have deliberately stripped every noun out of the substrate, so the model sees `(prop> (bank-the-coals x) 3)` and has nothing to reason with. The predicted 'won 10-20% of tasks search missed' is optimistic; expect 0-5%, and expect the wins to be on shallow tasks enumeration would have reached anyway. Grammar constrains SYNTAX, not sense. Strip the proposer and the finetune and what remains is Emberlisp with a namer and a guestbook — which is a nice project, and is not this one. Ceiling for the distinctive mechanism: measurable in the first week, and the measurement is the honest thing they should build first, exactly as their own first_weekend says.
audit.authored_content_risk: Inverted from the other five, and more insidious. The tech is not authored — the MEANING is. Two places. (1) The task proposer's reach-horizon filter is a hand-tuned heuristic that decides which LLM goals are 'within reach'; that filter, not the model, determines the curriculum, and tuning it is content authoring with extra steps. (2) The guestbook, which is the emotional centre of the pitch, is the worst offender: a 4B asked to formalise 'they should learn to bury their dead' into a predicate over calories, core temperature, position and property records will emit something syntactically valid, semantically unrelated, and eventually satisfiable — and then the system will print 'PRAYER ANSWERED' on a receipt, quoting a stranger, with a program that has nothing to do with burial. That is not discovery revealed in random order; it is manufactured meaning, and it is more corrosive than an authored tech tree because it is designed to be moving. Build the mapping so a human can inspect and reject it, or do not ship the printer.
audit.compute_honesty: The most GPU-dependent design and still comfortably honest on 8GB — ~4GB resident for a 4B Q4, prefix-cached library dump, 25-30 tok/s under GBNF (their overhead estimate is realistic), ~100k tokens a night in about an hour. Two under-costings. (1) Volume: 8 candidates x N tasks x ~300 tokens scales faster than they budget; at 50 active tasks that is 120k OUTPUT tokens, which is over an hour of pure generation before the searcher gets a turn. Cap candidates per task, not tasks. (2) The QLoRA is worse than 'feasible but tight'. Qwen3.5-4B is a hybrid Gated-DeltaNet/gated-attention architecture with a vision path — Unsloth/PEFT support for that stack is not something to assume, and 'expect to hit OOM the first few attempts' will become 'expect to spend a weekend on kernel and adapter-target compatibility'. Separately, a weekly harvest of a few hundred verified triples is far too little data to move a 4B in any direction except overfitting, and the held-out interpreter-step gate will (correctly) reject nearly every checkpoint. Their advice to treat it as optional is right; my advice is to delete it. Also correct and worth repeating: costing fitness in interpreter steps rather than seconds is the right call and makes the whole thing thermally reproducible.
audit.semantic_risk: Highest of the six. Every other idea risks meaningless abstractions with plausible names; this one adds meaningless GOALS with plausible names, then a finetune that trains the model to produce more of them, then a receipt printer that renders the output as scripture. The three verifier gates (executes, earns call-sites, beats incumbent on steps) are genuinely good and I want to credit them — they make this the most epistemically careful LLM-in-the-loop design I have seen in a hobby spec. But note what they check: that a program RUNS and that a predicate is SATISFIED. Nothing checks that the predicate means what the words said, and the guestbook path makes that the load-bearing question.
audit.dubious_claims: (1) LILO (ICLR 2024, 2310.19791), LAPS (ICML 2021) and Voyager (2305.16291) are all real and correctly characterised. But LILO's LLM operates over Python-like DSLs with English-adjacent semantics and Voyager's over documented JavaScript APIs; neither is evidence for a 4B on an invented property-record lisp, and the design leans on them as if it were. (2) 'Agent Skills for Large Language Models' (arXiv 2602.12430) — February 2026, I cannot verify it and it is doing no load-bearing work; drop it. (3) 'Lost in Space' (2502.14969) on grammar-constrained tokenisation is real and the caveat is right — expect valid, stupid DSL, which is exactly the failure mode. (4) Qwen3.5-4B/9B: verified real (Mar 2026), sizes as stated. (5) Claude Haiku 4.5 at $1/$5 per Mtok with 0.1x cache reads, 1.25x/2x cache writes and 50%-off batch: correct, and it is the most useful fact in the entire research_notes — see below. (6) 'A source of non-stationarity with no computational bound at all, because it is other people' assumes visitors; a hobby page linked nowhere gets zero entries a month, and this idea's stated long-term novelty then reduces to the same plateau as the others. They admit this in the last paragraph, which is to their credit and should be read as the actual forecast.
audit.one_change: Move the PROPOSER off the 4B and onto a weekly batched frontier-model call, and have it reason over a HUMAN-LEGIBLE rendering of the world rather than the invented DSL. Concretely: each week, render the last 7 nights as English (what the tribe tried, what killed them, what the new abstractions do, what the guestbook said), send it as a cached prefix to a batch API call, and ask for goals in natural language plus a mapping into a small FIXED predicate algebra that you wrote and can read. Their own numbers say this costs a couple of dollars a month. Three things change: the model now has priors that actually apply (it knows what winter, storage and burial mean, even if your primitives do not), the formalisation step becomes inspectable rather than a 4B's private guess, and the 'oracle won X% of tasks search missed' metric has a chance of being non-zero. Keep the local 4B for naming, where a small model is sufficient and its errors are cosmetic. And run that measurement on day one, before building anything else — if the number is still near zero with a strong model, the whole LLM branch is decoration and you should go build Glyphworks instead.

all.name: Embertongue
all.pitch: A cold basin where technology is literally a library of named programs that agents discover, and every entry lives in specific people's heads until someone invents writing. DreamCoder's wake/sleep compression loop is the tech tree: nightly, Stitch compresses the tribe's successful action-programs into new named primitives, and those primitives become tomorrow's vocabulary — forever.
all.world: A 96x96 hex basin, deterministic, 1 tick = 1 hour, seeded RNG, no authored recipes anywhere. The substrate is CONTINUOUS FIELDS plus typed matter: a heat field, an airflow field, a moisture field, a load/stress scalar per structure, and ~9 element-ish material tags (carbon, silica, clay-mineral, iron-oxide, tallow, cellulose, keratin, water, salt). Every physical object is a struct: {mass, temp, composition_vector, hardness, plasticity, porosity, wetness, integrity, decay_rate}. Physics is ~400 lines of threshold rules over those numbers — clay above 900C for 4h becomes irreversibly hard; cellulose heated with airflow below a threshold becomes carbon-dense charcoal instead of ash; iron-oxide + carbon + airflow above 1200C yields a bloom. You never write "pottery" or "iron" as a concept; the sim only knows numbers, and the tribe names what it notices. Agents are bodies (kcal, core temp, injury, age, pregnancy, skill floats) plus a MIND: a memory stream (generative-agents style, but 90% of entries are sim events not prose) and a personal library of program entries each with a mastery float. All actions are programs in a typed DSL over the substrate: heat, strike, bind, twist, soak, dry, bury, cover, carry, wait, place, split, mix, plus control flow (seq, repeat_until, if_state).
all.invention_engine: Wake/sleep library learning, straight out of DreamCoder (Ellis et al., PLDI 2021) with Stitch (Bowers et al., POPL 2023) as the compressor. WAKE: an agent has a need (cold, hunger, broken tool, a child dying). It searches for a program that reduces that need.
