Unsloth's VRAM table is roughly right; the December-2025 3x/30% claims are unverifiable marketing. arXiv 2605.23054 'Model Collapse as Cultural Evolution' (Guo, Wu, Yiu, 21 May 2026) is real and actually SUPPORTS the design better than cited: its finding is that compositionality follows a non-monotonic trajectory under self-training and is sustained only by TASK-GROUNDED filtering, not random filtering — that is a direct argument for the survival gate, so cite it as justification, not merely as a risk. PNAS 2025 iterated learning establishes only weak systematic generalization at very large data scale; do not lean on it for weight-level iterated learning at this scale. Project Sid (2411.00114) is a non-peer-reviewed industry report with heavily scaffolded emergent-religion/specialization claims — weak support for 'make tribe minds differ'.
audit.one_change: Change the training objective. Imitating your own surviving trajectories is self-distillation on a satiable task: it saturates in two or three rounds and collapse is the documented endpoint. Train instead on a dense, non-satiable objective — next-state and outcome PREDICTION over sim transitions the tribe has observed (a tribe-specific world model) — and keep survival only as the acceptance gate. Prediction error never runs out, it improves planning rather than mimicking it, the corpus is ~100x larger, and tribes that have lived in different places end up with genuinely different world models, which is a far better mechanistic account of culture than copying whoever failed to die. Ship the within-tribe null control in the same commit.

all.name: Marginalia
all.pitch: A civilization whose entire technology lives in physical, decaying, hand-copied texts — so the mutation operator of its evolution is the scribal error, and the selection operator is whether the misread recipe kills you. Strangers on the internet can drop one line a day into the world, and you will watch a joke become scripture and then become a working technique.
all.world: A river valley of three or four settlements, deterministic hourly tick, ordinary hard survival economy (kcal, warmth, injury, childbirth, seasons, floods). What is unusual is where knowledge lives. Every piece of knowledge is a TEXT OBJECT: {content (a program in a survival DSL, plus prose gloss), medium_id, location, legibility 0..1, decay_per_day, copy_of_id, generation}. Media are physical and differ: bark (decay 0.01/day), fired tablet (0.0001), hide (0.002), stone (~0). A text exists at a place. To use knowledge, an agent must be AT the text, with enough light, and be literate (a learned skill with a mastery float), OR have it in personal memory from having been taught (also lossy, also decaying). Copying is an action costing 3-8 labor-hours that produces a child text with errors. Nothing about competence is free-floating: an illiterate valley with a burned archive is genuinely back at zero, and the sim will show you that.
all.invention_engine: COPY ERROR + INTERPRETATION, which together form a complete evolutionary algorithm over a program population. VARIATION: the scribal error model, drawn from real paleography and delightfully cheap to implement — dittography (a line copied twice), haplography (a line skipped), homoeoteleuton (the eye jumps between two lines with the same ending — devastating and very real), transposition, numeral corruption (a temperature or duration digit changes), and marginal gloss absorption (a later copyist's note gets copied INTO the body as if it were part of the recipe, which is historically the single most productive corruption there is). Error rates scale with legibility, scribe mastery, light, and fatigue. HEREDITY: copy_of_id gives you an exact stemma — a manuscript family tree — for free. SELECTION: a corrupted recipe is executed in the hard sim. Mostly it fails or kills someone. Occasionally the dropped step or the changed numeral produces something BETTER, and that variant gets copied more because it works. INTERPRETATION, which is where the LLM earns its keep and where genuine novelty enters: when an agent reads a damaged or corrupted text, the local Qwen3-4B must turn ambiguous marks into an EXECUTABLE program, grammar-constrained by the DSL. It is filling gaps, guessing at a smudged numeral, reconciling a gloss with the body. Interpretation of noise is a creative act, and it is a cheap, high-yield source of variation that is unlike random mutation — it is BIASED toward things that make sense given the reader's prior knowledge, which is exactly how real reinterpretation works. Then reality adjudicates, with no appeal. CANON: texts accumulate copy counts. When a text's copy count and geographic spread cross thresholds it is flagged CANONICAL, and canonical texts get copied preferentially (a rich-get-richer rule with one line of code), which produces a canon, an apocrypha, and eventually a schism when two settlements' canonical versions of the same ancestor text have diverged past a similarity threshold. Institutions — a scriptorium building that lowers error rates, a scribal caste, a rule against copying non-canonical texts — emerge from cost-benefit thresholds, not from authored content.
all.why_unbounded: It is an evolutionary algorithm over programs, with a mutation operator (scribal error), an interpretation operator (a language model filling gaps), and a fitness function (survival). Program space is unbounded; the population is a library. What keeps it from converging is that the fitness landscape moves (seasons, floods, migration) and that the interpretation operator injects structured, prior-biased variation rather than white noise. HONEST BOTTOM: this is hill-climbing with a clever mutation operator, and hill-climbing on a fixed landscape plateaus. Marginalia is genuinely deeper on TRANSMISSION than on INVENTION — the tech tree it grows will be shallower than Embertongue's unless you pair them. And you should pair them: run Embertongue's DSL and its nightly Stitch compression as the invention engine, and Marginalia as the transmission layer. Then the abstractions are minted by compression AND corrupted by copying, and you have the best of both. As a standalone, expect the depth to come from the corpus dynamics, not the technology height, and price your expectations accordingly.
all.depth_ladder: WEEK 1: agents scratch marks on bark, most of it rots, someone copies something and gets it slightly wrong, and the first person dies of a misread. REAL RUNGS: the first text that survives its author; the first COPY that outperforms its parent (push-worthy, always); the discovery that fired tablets outlast bark, which reorganises the whole economy around clay; a scriptorium; a canonical text with 20+ descendants and a visible stemma; a settlement-level schism from divergent canon; the first CRITICAL act — an agent who owns two divergent copies and reconciles them into a third (textual criticism, emerging because reconciliation measurably improves outcomes); an INDEX (a text whose content is the locations of other texts, which mechanically multiplies retrieval and is a genuine phase change); and a marginal gloss absorbed into a recipe body that turns out to be an improvement, which is my favourite possible event in any of these six designs. WILDEST PLAUSIBLE ENDPOINT: a library building whose destruction in a flood causes a measurable multi-generation technological regression that the survivors partially recover from by collecting outlying copies from other settlements — i.e. you get to watch a dark age and a renaissance, mechanically, with numbers.
all.what_selects: Ordinary mortality plus a very specific pressure: knowledge that is not copied dies with its medium, and copying costs labor-hours that could have been food. So a settlement is constantly choosing between eating and remembering, which is a real and beautiful tension and it is one line of the labor allocator. Between settlements: the one with better transmission infrastructure recovers faster from shocks, and shocks are frequent. Texts themselves are under selection — copy count is fitness, and legibility, usefulness, and brevity all raise it.
all.changing_worlds: Floods (destroy caches, and are the engine of dark ages), fires, and migration to new valleys where the ecology differs so inherited recipes are wrong. The strongest world-change lever here is MEDIUM: introduce a new material with a different decay rate and the entire information economy reorganises. VISITORS AS PERTURBATION, and this is the best public hook of the six: the public site has a guestbook where an anonymous visitor may leave one line per day. That line is deposited into the world as a SKYFALL TABLET at a random location — a stone with words on it that no one wrote. Agents may find it, fail to read it, copy it, misread it, gloss it, and canonise it. The sim treats its content as a text like any other, so a visitor's line can end up in a recipe body via gloss absorption. You will get scripture from strangers, and it costs you nothing but a rate limiter and a moderation call.
all.novelty_detector: (1) A copy outperforms its parent on the sim's fitness measure — the core event, always pushed. (2) Canon formation: copy count crosses threshold, or a text hits 50 descendants. (3) Schism: two settlements' canonical versions of a common ancestor drop below a similarity threshold (normalized edit distance on the AST, not the prose). (4) A 'classic': a text transmitted N generations with fewer than k mutations — rare and remarkable, and worth a push. (5) Skyfall canonisation: a visitor's line entered a canonical text. (6) Assembly index of the deepest reliably-reproducible artifact, as elsewhere. (7) Bayesian surprise over everything else. This idea has the richest and most legible novelty signals of the six because textual events are inherently narrative.
all.phone_view: Card: 'Ashwater · Day 903 · 4 settlements · 88 alive'. Headline: 'A MISCOPY WORKS. Line 3 of *emberkeep* was skipped by a tired scribe; the result cooks faster. 6 copies of the error now exist; 2 of the original.' Then: canon size, literacy rate, and total surviving text-mass sparklines (text-mass is a gorgeous civilizational health metric — it drops during floods and famines). Then one line: 'Skyfall tablet from visitor "hannah" was inscribed into the Book of Rains.' Tap → the STEMMA VIEWER, a manuscript family tree of any text, with diffs between versions highlighted, which is the single most binge-able screen in any of these designs. You will lose an hour to it.
all.hardware_use: Very light. The local 4B does interpretation (read damaged text → emit program, grammar-constrained, ~150 output tokens) and short teaching dialogues. Interpretations happen maybe a few thousand times a day; at 4B Q4 on a 5070 with -np 6 that is well under an hour of GPU. Everything else — copying, decay, stemma tracking, similarity metrics — is CPU string work and is free. 64GB RAM means the entire corpus with full version history stays in memory. Haiku: the daily chronicle written IN THE VOICE OF A LATER HISTORIAN working from the surviving texts (which is a genuinely great constraint — give it only the texts that survived, not the ground truth, so the chronicle is itself lossy and sometimes WRONG, and you can diff the chronicle against the sim's truth for extra delight), plus moderation of guestbook lines. ~50 calls/day, well under $0.30. You could run four valleys.
all.input_cadence: Zero. Optional god-nudges: burn an archive, flood a settlement, gift a new medium, or drop your own skyfall tablet. The guestbook means OTHER people supply the nudges, which is the point.
all.tech: Python sim + SQLite (texts, copies with copy_of_id, media, readings, literacy, settlements, canon_flags, guestbook). The DSL and executor shared with Embertongue (this is the shared-substrate argument in action — one DSL, two projects). Error model: ~120 lines. Stemma: recursive CTE in SQLite, rendered as a d3-less hand-rolled canvas tree in the PWA (your home turf). Similarity: normalized tree edit distance on ASTs. llama.cpp + Qwen3-4B with GBNF. Public mirror on GitHub Pages with a tiny serverless guestbook (or a Tailscale Funnel endpoint with a rate limit and a cheap Haiku moderation call). ntfy for push. RECEIPT PRINTER: this is the idea that most deserves one — a cheap ESC/POS thermal printer on USB, printing one text per morning (the day's most-copied passage, with its corruptions marked) on a strip of paper you find with your coffee. That is the physical artifact, and for a manuscript civilization it is exactly right.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: the survival sim, the DSL, texts as physical objects with decay, and the copy action with three error types. No LLM. Sunday: give agents a starting text that works, let them copy it for 200 sim-days, and render the stemma. The delight moment is watching a family tree of a recipe form, seeing branches die, and finding the one branch where a dropped line accidentally improved things. Sunday afternoon: add LLM interpretation of damaged texts and watch it invent readings. Very achievable.
all.six_months_later: A corpus of thousands of texts with a deep, browsable stemma. A canon, an apocrypha, at least one schism, at least one dark age with a partial recovery. A guestbook-derived scripture that regular visitors recognise and contribute to. The historian's chronicle, which is sometimes wrong in interesting ways because the evidence rotted. A shoebox of receipt-printer strips.
all.honest_ceiling: Standalone, the TECHNOLOGY plateaus in roughly 6-10 weeks because copy-error hill-climbing exhausts the local optima of whatever DSL you shipped; the CORPUS dynamics stay interesting much longer (6+ months) because they are driven by mortality, geography and visitors, which do not converge. So the honest description is: a great transmission simulator with a mediocre invention engine, which is why the strong play is to bolt it onto Embertongue's compression engine and let the two operate on the same DSL. Second honest note: the interpretation step can produce garbage that is neither interesting nor fatal, and you will need a quality floor (reject interpretations that fail static type checks) or the corpus fills with noise. Third: guestbook moderation is a real ongoing obligation the moment the site gets any traffic — automate it on day one, not after.
all.research_notes: VERIFIED CONTEXT: iterated learning / cultural transmission with a bottleneck is the mechanism this idea mechanises — Kirby's framework, plus PNAS 2025 'Compositionality and systematicity emerge from iterated learning in deep linear networks' (doi 10.1073/pnas.2509739123) and 'From Signals to Structure' (arXiv 2607.00233), which together establish that transmission NOISE plus a learnability pressure is a generative force, not just degradation. Generative agents' memory-stream/reflection architecture (Park et al., arXiv 2304.03442) is the ancestor of the per-agent memory here, but note that the original Smallville study cost thousands of dollars in API calls; Affordable Generative Agents (arXiv 2402.02053) and Lyfe Agents (arXiv 2310.02172) report 30-100x cost reductions via aggressive caching and cheap policies — the design principle I have applied throughout is that the LLM should be called only at the moment of INTERPRETATION, never for bookkeeping. Program-population evolution with library compression as the complementary engine: DreamCoder (PLDI 2021) + Stitch (github.com/mlb2251/stitch, pip stitch_core). Assembly index for artifact depth: Sharma et al., Nature 2023 (arXiv 2206.02279). Scribal error types (dittography, haplography, homoeoteleuton) are standard textual-criticism categories and are trivially implementable; stemmatics gives you the family-tree rendering for free. llama.cpp GBNF grammars keep every interpretation type-valid: github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/grammars/README.md.

audit.name: Marginalia
audit.ceiling: Correctly self-diagnosed, and the correct diagnosis is severe: this is hill-climbing whose mutation operator is line-level edits to ASTs. Program space has no smooth genotype-phenotype map — a dropped line is almost always type-valid and useless — so the beneficial-mutation rate sits orders of magnitude below what evolutionary intuition suggests. Worse, the beneficial mutations you DO get are overwhelmingly deletions of redundant steps: efficiency, not capability. The promised recurring headline ('A MISCOPY WORKS') arrives a handful of times, says 'it cooks faster', and the technology curve is flat by week 4-8 at whatever local optima the shipped DSL contains. LLM interpretation adds prior-biased variation, which beats white noise, but it is variation toward what the model expects a recipe to say — regression toward plausibility is a contracting operator, not an expanding one. What genuinely does NOT converge: stemma structure, canon/apocrypha, schism, literacy rate, text-mass. Those are low-order statistical processes (preferential attachment, drift, spatial isolation) that reliably produce structure and keep producing it past six months. This is the design most likely to actually deliver its promised screens — they are just philological screens, not technological ones.
audit.authored_content_risk: Mixed, and worth being blunt. The corruption operator is genuinely unauthored and is the best mutation model in the six — dittography, haplography, homoeoteleuton, numeral corruption and especially marginal-gloss absorption are real, cheap, and structurally productive. But the INSTITUTIONS are authored: 'a scriptorium emerges from cost-benefit thresholds' means he wrote a scriptorium building with an error-rate modifier and a cost and agents found it worth building; canon is a rich-get-richer rule he wrote; schism is a threshold he chose on tree-edit distance. These will feel emergent and are mostly parameterized authorship. And the base recipes are borrowed outright — Marginalia has no invention engine at all, only a transmission engine, exactly as stated.
audit.compute_honesty: Yes, genuinely light and correctly costed: a few thousand 150-token interpretations/day is well under an hour of GPU, and decay/copying/stemma are CPU string work. One undersized item: normalized tree edit distance is roughly O(n^2) per pair and schism detection wants it pairwise over a growing corpus — cache or sample aggressively or it becomes the CPU hot spot by month two. The historian-chronicler-restricted-to-surviving-texts idea is free and is the best writing constraint in any of the six documents.
audit.semantic_risk: Low-moderate. Type-checked interpretations keep the corpus executable and the prose glosses stay anchored to programs. The real hazard is pollution by interpretations that are neither interesting nor fatal (he flags it): you need a UTILITY floor, not just a static type check, or the stemma viewer fills with noise variants and the schism metric starts firing on garbage lineages. Also note the risk that the most-cited emergent events (canon, schism) are threshold artifacts — vary the thresholds and confirm the phenomena persist before believing them.
audit.dubious_claims: Same iterated-learning caveats as Saltmark: PNAS 2025 (doi 10.1073/pnas.2509739123) shows only WEAK systematic generalization requiring very large data, and arXiv 2607.00233 is about memory architecture in two-agent Lewis games, not 'transmission noise plus a learnability pressure is a generative force' — that claim traces to Kirby et al. 2015. The generative-agents cost figure and the AGA (2402.02053) / Lyfe (2310.02172) reduction claims are roughly right, and the derived principle (call the LLM only at interpretation) is the soundest engineering instinct in the whole batch. Scribal error taxonomy is accurate paleography. Unstated risk: the skyfall guestbook is the best public hook here and moderation is a permanent adversarial obligation — 'a cheap classifier call' is not sufficient for a public write endpoint feeding a corpus you publish.
audit.one_change: Make texts carry CLAIMS about the world, not just recipes. Let a text assert a testable proposition — a threshold, a numeral, a condition ('clay holds at four hands of heat') — and let agents test claims against the physics. Then copying, reconciliation of two divergent copies, and index-building do real epistemic work: the corpus becomes a growing, testable model of the world instead of a population of programs stuck at a local optimum, textual criticism becomes measurably profitable instead of a scripted rung, and depth is bounded by the physics rather than by DSL local optima. It also makes the lossy historian's chronicle diffable against ground truth in a way that means something.

all.name: The Ark of Constants
all.pitch: The unbounded space here is not the tech tree — it is the space of WORLDS. An LLM writes new physics modules as code, a mechanical filter keeps only the ones that are survivable-but-not-trivial, and civilizations migrate between them carrying an ark of knowledge, most of which turns out to be wrong. What they keep doing anyway becomes ritual, and ritual has a measurable cost.
all.world: A world is a Python module implementing a narrow, frozen interface: resource fields and their regeneration, a reaction/threshold table over material properties, hazard schedules, seasonality, and a small set of affordances. Everything else — agents, bodies, the DSL, hunger, death, teaching, the library — is SHARED and fixed across all worlds. So a world is a few hundred lines of constants and rules, and the space of worlds is the space of those programs. Worlds are generated, validated, frozen, and then absolutely deterministic forever. Between worlds are GATES; a civilization can send an ARK through a gate: a chosen subset of its library, its lexicon, its written texts, and a handful of living elders. The rest is left behind and is playable later as a ruin.
all.invention_engine: TWO LEVELS, and the outer one is the point. INNER (per world): whatever engine you like — I would use Embertongue's Stitch-compression library, so within a world the tribe genuinely invents. OUTER (across worlds): OMNI-EPIC applied to physics. Haiku writes a candidate world module as CODE, given (a) the fixed interface, (b) a description of the archive of existing worlds and what makes them different, and (c) an explicit instruction to produce something LEARNABLE and INTERESTING relative to the current civilization's competence. Then MECHANICAL VALIDATION, which is what makes this honest rather than vibes: the module must import, must be deterministic under replay (run it twice from a seed and diff), must be survivable — a scripted baseline agent must last at least N days — and must NOT be trivial — the same baseline must NOT thrive without inventing anything. Fail → one repair round with the traceback, then discard. Pass → the world is frozen, hashed, and added to the archive. To stop the archive from converging to desert/ice/volcano variants, keep it as a MAP-Elites grid over a behavioural characterization computed by RUNNING the baseline, not by reading the prose: axes like (resource sparsity, hazard tempo, minimum reaction depth to reach a survivable calorie source, material-property variance). A new world is only admitted if it fills an empty cell or beats the incumbent in its cell. That is a real novelty archive, not an LLM saying 'this one is interesting'. THE CULTURAL PAYOFF — RITUAL AS A MEASURABLE OBJECT: when an ark arrives, every inherited library entry is silently re-evaluated against the new physics. Entries that still improve fitness are KNOWLEDGE. Entries that no longer do anything, but are still taught and still performed, are RITUAL — and the engine labels them automatically, tracks ritual_labor_hours as a fraction of total labor, and lets that fraction impose a real cost. High ritual load makes a tribe poorer, which creates selective pressure for reform; reform means an agent stops teaching an ancestral practice, which other agents may punish (a social-cost rule). So you get orthodoxy, reformation, and schism as consequences of an accounting identity. That is the most grounded route to emergent religion I know of.
all.why_unbounded: The space of world-generating programs is unbounded in the same way any program space is, and OMNI-EPIC (ICLR 2025) is the existence proof that an LLM plus an interestingness filter can keep producing new, learnable, non-repeating environments rather than sampling from a narrow authored distribution. And the CROSS-WORLD dimension adds something no single-world design has: the quantity being optimised over time is TRANSFERABLE knowledge, which is a strictly harder and more interesting target than knowledge that works here. HONEST BOTTOM, and it is a real one: LLM-generated worlds DO converge in flavour — you will see the desert/ice/tidal/toxic-atmosphere cluster within the first twenty. The MAP-Elites behavioural archive is what fights this, and it only partly wins, because the model's prior shapes what code it writes no matter what you ask for. Expect the archive to fill its easy cells fast and then produce diminishing returns; expect to hand-write two or three genuinely alien worlds yourself to reseed the distribution, and consider that a feature (you get to be a god who occasionally makes a world by hand). Second honest bound: the shared interface caps what a world can BE. A world cannot introduce a new physical dimension you did not put in the interface, so the interface design is the real creative act and it is yours, not the model's.
all.depth_ladder: WEEK 1: two hand-written worlds, one gate, one tribe that walks through and immediately does badly. REAL RUNGS: the first automatically-generated world that passes validation without repair; the first ark arrival where you can see the transfer score (what fraction of the library still works) — this number is the project's heartbeat; the first RITUAL detected automatically (they still cure hides with a plant that does not exist here, using a substitute that does nothing); ritual load crossing 10% of labor and a reformer emerging; a schism where half the tribe goes back through the gate; a world that DEFEATS a civilization entirely, and the ruin left behind; a later ark finding that ruin and recovering part of a lost library from its written texts. WILDEST PLAUSIBLE ENDPOINT: a civilization that has crossed eight worlds and whose library has been filtered by eight independent physics — what survives that gauntlet is, by construction, ABSTRACT knowledge (search strategies, teaching methods, how to test a hypothesis) rather than concrete recipes, because only the abstract transfers. Watching a culture become epistemically sophisticated because concreteness kept failing is the wildest and most plausible endpoint of all six ideas, and it falls straight out of the mechanism.
all.what_selects: Survival in each world, plus the cross-world pressure: arks are small, so a civilization must CHOOSE what to carry, and that choice is made by the culture's own valuation (most-taught, most-used entries get carried) which may be wrong. Ritual load is a direct fitness tax. Between civilizations: run 2-3 arks through the same archive on different paths and compare their transfer scores over time — the one that learned more abstractly wins, measurably.
all.changing_worlds: This IS the changing-worlds idea; it is the answer to that part of the ask. Three timescales: within a world (seasons, hazards), between worlds (gate crossings every few sim-generations), and the archive itself growing as new worlds are generated nightly. You can also RETURN to a world you left, hundreds of years later, and find your ruins and your left-behind population, because worlds are frozen and deterministic and can be resumed from a snapshot.
all.novelty_detector: (1) TRANSFER SCORE on arrival — the fraction of the library that still improves fitness. A high score means the world is similar (less interesting); a very low score means a crisis (very interesting). Push on both tails. (2) Automatic ritual detection — a new entry crossing from knowledge to ritual is a story every time. (3) Archive cell fills — 'a world unlike any before it' is literally 'a previously empty MAP-Elites cell', which is a rigorous claim you can make on the phone. (4) Inner-world novelty from the borrowed engine (assembly index records, first-ever programs). (5) Extinction and ruin-discovery events. (6) Reformation/schism events triggered by the ritual-load accounting. Push volume: 1-3 a day.
all.phone_view: Card: 'Ark of the Weft · World 14 "Saltglass" · day 61 in-world · 34 alive'. Headline, always the transfer score on a fresh arrival: '61% of their library still works here. Fire-hardening now does nothing. They still do it — 4% of all labor.' Then a horizontal strip of the world archive as small tiles colored by whether an ark survived there, which is the single best 30-second civilizational overview I can imagine: you see the whole multiverse and where your people died. Then the ritual-load gauge and the chronicle sentence. Tap → the archive map (MAP-Elites grid, hover a cell to see the world's generated description and its baseline stats), and the ark's library colored knowledge/ritual/dead.
all.hardware_use: Sim and validation are CPU-bound and parallel — with 64GB RAM you can validate 8 candidate worlds concurrently in separate processes, and validation is a few minutes each. The local 4B does the inner-world agent thinking as in Embertongue (~3-4GB VRAM, GBNF-constrained, comfortable). World GENERATION is the only thing that wants a strong model: Haiku writing a world module is ~1.5-3k output tokens plus a repair round. At 2 new worlds a day that is maybe 8-10 calls, ~25k output tokens = ~$0.06 batched. Add the chronicle and transfer analysis: total well under $0.50/day, so this is one of the cheaper designs despite feeling like the most ambitious. Note: you MUST sandbox generated world code — run it in a subprocess with a restricted import set, a CPU/memory rlimit, and no network. Do not skip this; it is 30 lines and it is the difference between a fun project and a bad evening.
all.input_cadence: Zero. The best optional nudge in any of these six: WRITE A WORLD YOURSELF. Drop a hand-written module in the worlds directory and it enters the archive alongside the generated ones, and your ark may wander into it. Also: open a gate manually, force a migration, or resurrect a dead world's population.
all.tech: Python throughout (generated world modules are Python, so the interface must be small and typed — use a Protocol plus a validation harness). Subprocess sandbox with resource limits. SQLite for the archive, arks, transfer scores, ritual ledger, lineage. MAP-Elites grid: a dict keyed by discretized behavioural characterization, ~80 lines, no library needed. Inner engine: Embertongue's DSL + stitch_core, shared code. llama.cpp + Qwen3-4B for agents; Haiku (Batch API) for world generation and chronicle. PWA over Tailscale + nightly GitHub Pages static export + ntfy. Determinism test in CI: every world module must produce identical event hashes on replay, and this test is what keeps the whole multiverse trustworthy.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: the world interface, TWO hand-written worlds, the shared agent/survival layer, and a gate. Get an ark to walk from world A to world B and compute the transfer score — even with a library of six hand-written entries, seeing '3 of 6 still work' is the delight moment and it is a Saturday-night result. Sunday: the ritual detector (it is genuinely about 20 lines: entry is taught AND performed AND its measured fitness delta is ~0), then one Haiku call to generate world C, and the validation harness. If a generated world passes validation and your ark survives 30 days in it, you are done for the weekend and you have already built the outer loop.
all.six_months_later: An archive of 100-300 worlds with a filled MAP-Elites grid you can browse like a star map. Two or three ark lineages with divergent histories, several extinctions, a couple of ruins rediscovered. A civilization whose surviving library is visibly more abstract than it was in world 1, with the transfer-score curve to prove it. A ritual ledger that reads like a religion. You will have hand-written five worlds yourself because it is fun.
all.honest_ceiling: World-generation flavour convergence at roughly 20-40 worlds; the MAP-Elites archive keeps admitting new cells for a while but the model's prior is a real limit and the marginal world gets less surprising. Interface expressiveness is the hard wall, same as Embertongue's physics wall but one level up. Inner-world depth is inherited from whichever inner engine you pick, with its own ceiling. Validation is a genuine cost: a few CPU-minutes per candidate and a nonzero rate of subtly-broken worlds that pass validation and are just tedious. And the biggest honest risk is DILUTION — with a hundred worlds, no single world gets enough sim-time for a deep civilization, so you must choose: many shallow worlds or few deep ones. My recommendation is a hard rule of at most three active arks and long residencies (weeks of wall-clock per world), with the archive growing in the background as a place to GO rather than a treadmill. Get that dial wrong and this becomes a screensaver.
all.research_notes: VERIFIED: OMNI-EPIC — Faldor, Zhang, Cully, Clune, 'Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness with Environments Programmed in Code', ICLR 2025, arXiv 2405.15568, repo github.com/maxencefaldor/omni-epic. Its core claim is exactly this design's outer loop: foundation models autonomously generate CODE specifying the next learnable (not too easy, not too hard) and interesting task/environment, escaping the manually-predefined narrow environment distributions that limited prior work. The learnability filter (a baseline must partially succeed) is theirs and it is the load-bearing piece. Darwin Gödel Machine (arXiv 2505.22954, github.com/jennyzzt/dgm) supplies the archive lesson — keep every variant, branch from anywhere, because open-ended archives beat greedy improvement; that is why dead worlds and dead arks stay resumable here. MAP-Elites / quality-diversity is the standard way to keep a generated archive diverse along behavioural axes rather than along an LLM's self-report. Inner engine: DreamCoder (PLDI 2021) + Stitch (github.com/mlb2251/stitch, pip stitch_core). Cultural-transmission-across-environments framing and the emergence of religion/memes in agent societies: Project Sid, arXiv 2411.00114 (agents spread cultural memes and a religion across a 500-1000 agent population; specialization required social awareness). Cost: Haiku 4.5 at $1/$5 per MTok with Batch API 50% off (anthropic.com/claude/haiku) makes 2 worlds/day cost pennies. Sandboxing generated code is not optional — subprocess + rlimits + import allowlist.

audit.name: The Ark of Constants
audit.ceiling: Two hard stops and one self-inflicted wound. (a) The archive is a MAP-Elites grid over FOUR axes he chose, so 'a world unlike any before it' means 'an empty cell in a space I defined'. The unbounded space of world-programs is projected onto a bounded grid, and the grid fills — easy cells in 2-4 weeks, diminishing returns after; his 20-40-world flavour-convergence estimate is right and the archive measures the convergence rather than preventing it. (b) The frozen interface is Embertongue's expressiveness wall one level up, and worse, because generated worlds can only permute constants inside it. (c) The self-inflicted wound: the outer loop SUBTRACTS depth. The brief asks for fire, then houses, then tools, then something wild — which requires long uninterrupted residency and accumulated library depth. Gating a civilization into a new world every few generations, where 40% of its library stops working, is an explicit anti-accumulation mechanism. His dilution warning understates it: this is not a dial to tune, it is a direct conflict between the headline mechanism and the stated goal.
audit.authored_content_risk: The world modules are genuinely unauthored, and OMNI-EPIC is a real existence proof for LLM-generated code environments under a learnability filter. But the validation filter is very weak — 'baseline survives N days AND does not thrive without inventing' admits an enormous space of tedious worlds, and nothing checks that a world is LAWFUL rather than arbitrary. Meanwhile the ritual mechanic is the single best idea in all six documents and is not authored at all: knowledge-vs-ritual as an accounting identity (taught AND performed AND measured fitness delta ~ 0), with ritual_labor_hours as a real tax producing orthodoxy, reform and schism as consequences rather than as content, is about 20 lines and I have not seen it done. Extract that mechanic and put it in whichever design actually gets built.
audit.compute_honesty: Honest on tokens (2 worlds/day is pennies) and the sandboxing requirement is correctly stated and non-negotiable. Undersized: the INNER engine is the expensive part and now runs in N worlds; validation at a few CPU-minutes each, x8 concurrent, at a rate high enough to fill a grid, is a permanent background load competing with the sims he actually cares about. Every generated module is also a maintenance surface — subtly-broken-but-valid worlds pass validation, and debugging someone else's generated physics is the least fun failure mode in the batch.
audit.semantic_risk: The specific risk is ARBITRARINESS, and it silently kills the payoff. Transfer score is the project's heartbeat and its interpretation depends entirely on worlds sharing latent structure. If Haiku samples constants and rules freely, '61% of their library still works here' is a draw from a random distribution and carries no information about the civilization's epistemics. Worse, the marquee endpoint — a culture becoming abstract because only abstract knowledge transfers — requires learnable cross-world regularity to abstract TOWARD. Random worlds select for nothing; they merely delete libraries. As specified, the mechanism cannot produce its own best outcome.
audit.dubious_claims: OMNI-EPIC (2405.15568, ICLR 2025) is real and fairly described, but it generates ROBOT TASKS in a fixed simulator, filtered by a model of human interestingness, using frontier-class code models; extrapolating to 'Haiku writes coherent civilizational physics modules' is a substantial stretch, and its learnability filter was calibrated to a single RL agent's partial success, not to a multi-agent civilization. Darwin Godel Machine (2505.22954) is real and the archive lesson is fairly drawn. Project Sid (2411.00114) is a non-peer-reviewed industry report; citing it for emergent religion is unnecessary here, since the ritual accounting in this very design is more rigorous than anything in that paper. Assembly index carries the usual caveats (NP-complete exactly; contested as a selection detector). MAP-Elites is described correctly.
audit.one_change: Stop generating free-form world code. Define ONE shared generative physics with a structured parameter space — identical constitutive laws everywhere, worlds differing in constants, topology, resource distributions and which couplings are active — and let the LLM sample within that family (writing flavour, and proposing new couplings for human review). Then cross-world invariants genuinely exist, abstract knowledge genuinely transfers better than concrete recipes, transfer score becomes an informative measurement instead of a random number, validation collapses to bounds-checking instead of executing untrusted code, and the 'epistemically sophisticated civilization' endpoint becomes reachable rather than rhetorical. Pair it with a hard residency rule (at most 3 active arks, weeks of wall-clock per world) so depth has time to accumulate.

all.name: KINDLING
all.pitch: A gridworld with real physics and zero crafting recipes, where a tribe's technology is a growing library of named, executable behavior programs that a nightly compressor carves out of whatever kept them alive. Fire is not an item you unlock; it is a lambda term the system discovered, named, and can now call.
all.world: 96x96 toroidal grid, struct-of-arrays cells: material_id (uint8), temperature (f16), moisture, integrity, occupancy. Materials come from a per-world table of ~24 types x 8 continuous properties (hardness, ignition_temp, conductivity, calorific value, density, friability, toxicity, decay). Nothing is named 'flint' in code — flint is whatever material happens to be hard and spark-prone this world. Agents: 3-8 tribes x 8-24 bodies; body = pos, facing, 2 hand slots, stamina, core_temp, hunger, hp, 8 int8 memory registers. Plants regrow on a moisture/heat curve; prey with flee policies; mineral outcrops; deadwood that dries with heat and wets with rain. A coarse 16x16 climate lattice advects heat/moisture with a 3000-tick seasonal cycle.
all.invention_engine: Nested wake/sleep. WAKE (GPU, nightly, JAX): each tribe carries a Library L of typed lambda terms over a base DSL of ~22 primitives — MOVE(d), TURN, GRAB, DROP, STRIKE(a,b), RUB, PLACE, DIG, EAT, THROW, WAIT, SENSE_TEMP(d), SENSE_MAT(d), SENSE_AGENT, IF, bounded WHILE, SEQ, REPEAT(n), LET, GOTO_NEAREST(pred), numeric ops. The controller is a tiny conv+GRU policy (~300k params) whose action head does NOT emit primitives — it emits an index into L ∪ base plus arguments. PPO (purejaxrl single-file style) over 2048 parallel worlds. Adding an abstraction literally enlarges what one decision can do: that is the compounding. SLEEP (CPU, ~20 min, while the GPU cools): expand top-quartile survivors' action traces to base primitives, run Stitch (stitch_core, Bowers et al. POPL'23) for top-k abstractions by MDL. Admit any that saves > tau bits and is not alpha-equivalent to an existing entry; do net surgery (new row in the action head, initialized near the mean of its constituent primitives' rows); name it with a one-shot local Qwen3-4B call that sees the term plus a 6-frame render of it executing ('BANK_THE_COALS'). The name is cosmetic; the term is the technology. Verification is the sim: re-run on 256 held-out world seeds; if reward drops, roll the library edit back. That is Ouroboros Forge's rejection-sampling hygiene transplanted onto physics instead of unit tests.
all.why_unbounded: Two arguments. (i) Compression compounding: abstractions are built from abstractions, so after n nights the set of behaviors expressible in <=8 tokens grows super-exponentially in |L|. This is DreamCoder's argument and it is empirically demonstrated. (ii) The target is not a task list — it is survival in procedurally regenerated physics, so the adjacent possible moves as the world moves. Where it honestly bottoms out: the PHYSICS, not the library. With 8 material properties and 22 primitives I expect a few hundred qualitatively distinct useful behaviors, not infinity. Mitigation is to grow the physics on a slower clock than the library (add a field — pressure, charge — every few weeks), but be clear-eyed: that is you adding physics, not the system inventing it.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: grid + PPO + base DSL, no library learning. Agents seek food and huddle on warm cells at night; first unauthored thing is dragging deadwood into sunlit cells to dry it — you never wrote 'dry'. Weeks 2-3: Stitch loop on, first 5-10 abstractions (GATHER_NEAREST_EDIBLE, DRY_AND_STACK, STRIKE_REPEAT). Somewhere here, ignition: hold hard-material, strike against hard-material, adjacent to low-moisture high-calorific material, temperature crosses ignition_temp. Fire, unauthored. Month 2: fire-dependent abstractions — KEEP_FIRE_ALIVE (feed before integrity hits 0), COOK, SMOKE_OUT_PREDATOR; shelter as PLACE patterns that lower a cell's heat loss; WINDBREAK. Months 3-4: 40-80 abstractions, 3-4 levels of nesting, a recognizable toolchain where abstractions produce intermediates other abstractions consume; sustained high temperature transforms materials if you add a small temp/pressure phase map (one function, not a tech tree). Wildest plausible at 6-12 months: tribes specializing (extraction vs fabrication), trade emerging as an abstraction (GIVE + EXPECT), and a library entry that is ABOUT other entries — TEACH(x), which runs an abstraction slowly beside a naive agent. Ceiling of the ladder: agriculture, metallurgy-as-phase-change, proto-teaching. Not writing, not electricity.
all.what_selects: Hunger drains per tick with a cold penalty proportional to (comfort_temp - core_temp). Night predators spawn away from heat sources. A 3000-tick winter zeroes plant regrowth — only stored/cooked food and heat survive it. Tribes share one map: flint outcrops and dry deadwood are finite and contested, and a tribe that burns a forest denies fuel to its neighbour (real niche-construction externality). Tribe hits zero members: its library is archived as a ruin (dead branch in the DB) and its territory reseeds. Fitness = tribe-ticks survived across a held-out seed set. Deterministic tick budget, never wall-clock — this laptop thermally throttles and any timing-based fitness would silently drift with ambient temperature.
all.changing_worlds: Three levers. (1) A world genome per run: material property table, climate amplitude, predator aggression, all seeded. Every Sunday the outer loop spawns a new genome and forces surviving libraries to transfer cold; abstractions that survive transfer are the DEEP ones, and the archive records 'portable' vs 'parochial' technologies — itself a great phone stat. (2) POET-style co-evolution: keep an archive of world genomes, mutate those where the current library is neither trivially winning nor hopeless. (3) Concurrent shards: 4 worlds at once are just vmap batches with different property tables, so you get parallel civilizations to compare.
all.novelty_detector: Three signals ANDed before any push. (a) MDL: Stitch reports bits saved; require bits_saved > tau and a canonical de Bruijn hash never seen before. (b) First-ever world-event ledger: a small set of physics predicates (a cell exceeded ignition_temp with an agent adjacent; a manufactured material appeared; a tribe survived a whole winter) each carrying a 'first time in project history' flag in SQLite. (c) Usage gate: an abstraction only becomes a TECHNOLOGY once it appears in >=5% of surviving-tribe traces for 3 consecutive nights — this kills the flood of one-off compressions. The morning ntfy is at most 3 lines and often says nothing, which is the point.
all.phone_view: One screen. Top: a 200x200 PNG of last night's most eventful tick. Middle: the tech tree as an actual growing DAG (abstraction -> children) in SVG, newest node pulsing. Bottom: three counters — living tribes / library size / nights since last genuine novelty. Tap a node for the lambda term, its Qwen-given name, a 3-second GIF of an agent executing it, and its birth night. Served static over `tailscale serve`, mirrored to GitHub Pages each morning so friends can look.
all.hardware_use: Ideal 8GB workload. Obs is an 11x11xC int8 egocentric patch, policy ~300k params, 2048 parallel envs sits under 3GB. Craftax-Classic does 1B env steps in under an hour on one GPU and Craftax-MA does 250M steps in 57 min on an L40S, so an 8-hour overnight run on a 5070 laptop realistically lands 1-3B steps. Stitch is Rust on CPU, seconds-to-minutes on thousand-program corpora — perfect use of 64GB RAM and an idle GPU. Qwen3-4B Q4_K_M is ~3GB and only runs during the naming pass after RL stops; never concurrently. Blackwell caveat: sm_120 needs CUDA 12.8+ wheels and PyTorch only got there via nightlies (pytorch/pytorch#164342) — budget a full setup day and keep a CPU-JAX fallback (64GB RAM runs a 64x64 world at tens of thousands of steps/s, enough to debug).
all.input_cadence: Fully autonomous nightly. Optional god-nudges: add one physics field or one base primitive when the tree visibly plateaus (a 20-line change); veto a degenerate library entry from the phone (writes to a blacklist table); hand-author a world genome when you want to see something specific ('make flint rare').
all.tech: Python + JAX, single-file purejaxrl-style PPO, Flax or Equinox for the net, a hand-written grid env (do NOT fork Craftax — its fixed recipes are exactly what you are removing; read it for structure only), stitch_core for compression, SQLite for the lineage/event DB, llama.cpp + Qwen3-4B-Instruct GGUF for naming only, FastAPI + vanilla-JS PWA, ntfy.sh, Tailscale. This is the shared substrate for everything else: sim core + SQLite event/lineage DB + PWA chronicle + push.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: the env (grid arrays, 6 materials, heat diffusion as a 3x3 conv, agent step, hunger/cold) plus a random-policy renderer writing GIFs. Sunday: purejaxrl PPO with a flat base-primitive action space, the SQLite event ledger, and a cron-pushed static page with last night's GIF and the first-time-ever list. You already get an unauthored moment: agents learning to spend nights on sun-warmed rock.
all.six_months_later: 60-150 abstractions across a handful of lineages; a visibly branched DAG where two isolated worlds independently found ignition via different terms (convergent invention, a genuinely thrilling push); a set of portable technologies that survive world-genome swaps and a graveyard of parochial ones. You will be adding physics fields occasionally and each one buys weeks of new branches.
all.honest_ceiling: The library grows forever but interestingness per abstraction decays. Realistically 4-6 qualitatively distinct capability tiers with a 22-primitive DSL and 8 material properties: forage/thermoregulate, object and material manipulation, fire and heat management, shelter/construction, transformed materials (cook / fire-harden / smelt-as-phase-change), crude social tech (share, defend, teach). Anything resembling writing, selective agriculture, or machines needs physics you do not have. Expect novelty pushes to get sparse around month 3-4 unless you feed new physics. Also honest: PPO over a GROWING action space is finicky — real debugging time will go into net surgery and into abstractions that get learned then catastrophically forgotten.
all.research_notes: Craftax (arXiv 2402.16801, craftaxenv.github.io): 1B env interactions in under an hour on a single GPU, ~250x faster than Python Crafter — this is the speed budget the whole idea rests on. Multi-Agent Craftax (arXiv 2511.04904, github.com/BaselOmari/MA-Craftax): 250M steps in 57 min on one L40S with 4 agents; also confirms IPPO/MAPPO/PQN all fail its long-horizon credit assignment, so do not expect a stock algorithm to just work. Stitch (Bowers et al., POPL 2023, mlb2251.github.io/stitch.pdf): 3-4 orders of magnitude faster and 2 orders less memory than DreamCoder's compressor, with equal or better compressivity — this is what makes a nightly CPU sleep phase realistic on a laptop. LILO (arXiv 2310.19791) is the precedent for using an LLM to name/document a Stitch-learned library. purejaxrl for the PPO skeleton. Avoid Neural MMO: 2.0 soft-launch, env repo last active Aug 2024, baselines Jul 2024, no 3.0 — do not build on it. sm_120 friction: pytorch/pytorch#164342, cu128 required.

audit.name: KINDLING
audit.ceiling: Hard stop is architectural, not physical, and it is earlier than the pitch says. Stitch consumes typed lambda terms with variables, IF and WHILE; what you feed it is a FLATTENED execution trace. Flattening destroys exactly the structure DreamCoder compounds over — a trace records the branch taken, not the IF; the unrolled body, not the WHILE; a concrete argument, not a binder. So the library can only ever contain straight-line macro-actions (options / action n-grams). That is a well-trodden and famously flat literature: macros buy a constant-factor horizon reduction, never compositional growth. 'Behaviors expressible in <=8 tokens grows super-exponentially in |L|' is true of a lambda library and false of a macro table. Practical stop: useful macro-actions over 22 primitives and 8 material properties saturate around 30-60 entries. Forage/thermoregulate by week 2, ignition weeks 3-6, fire-tending + shelter + cook by weeks 8-14, then the DAG keeps adding nodes that are re-parameterizations of existing ones. Novelty pushes go sparse at ~week 10-14, earlier than the stated month 3-4, and PPO net surgery on a growing head will cost you weeks of the interval by forcing re-exploration each time a row is added.
audit.authored_content_risk: Medium-low, and honestly disclosed. Fire really is a consequence of a property table rather than a recipe — that part is legitimate and is the best thing in the design. But the set of possible KINDS of outcome is exactly the authored physics: every tier in honest_ceiling maps 1:1 to a function you will write (heat diffusion, ignition, the temp/pressure phase map). The system discovers routes, not outcomes. Sharper problem in the notification layer: the world-event ledger is a list of hand-written predicates, so you can only ever be surprised by things you already wrote a detector for. Qwen naming is correctly labelled cosmetic.
audit.compute_honesty: Partly dishonest by an order of magnitude, in the throughput claim rather than the memory claim. 2048 envs x 300k params x 11x11 int8 obs under 3GB: fine. Stitch on CPU: fine. Qwen3-4B after RL releases the GPU: fine. But '1-3B steps overnight' borrows Craftax's single-agent number for a sim with 3-8 tribes x 8-24 bodies (up to ~190 agents per world). The right reference is the paper this idea itself cites: Craftax-MA does 250M interactions in under an hour with FOUR agents on an L40S, and a 5070 laptop is roughly a quarter of that card. Realistic overnight budget: 20-80M multi-agent steps, one to two orders below the stated figure — which matters, because the whole depth-per-night argument is built on the larger number.
audit.dubious_claims: (1) 'Avoid Neural MMO, no 3.0, dead since Aug 2024' is WRONG. Neural MMO 3 is alive and is a headline showcase of PufferLib (PufferLib 2.0, RLC 2025; continued NMMO3 work through 2025). You may still not want to build on it, but not for the stated reason. (2) 'DreamCoder's compounding argument is empirically demonstrated' — demonstrated on curated task suites with an expensive enumerative wake search, never on RL traces, and no published result shows super-exponential growth of USEFUL behaviors. (3) Craftax-MA (2511.04904) is real and does report existing algorithms failing on long-horizon credit assignment, but its published throughput figure is '250M interactions in under an hour'; the '57 min on one L40S with 4 agents' precision is an unverified paraphrase and it argues against your speed budget, not for it. (4) The pytorch sm_120 issue is a red herring for a JAX stack — jaxlib cu12 wheels are the actual dependency.
audit.semantic_risk: Low for drivel, high for triviality. Every library entry is executable and sim-verified against 256 held-out seeds, so nothing meaningless can survive — but nothing forces entries to be interesting either, and a macro table fills with GRAB-then-MOVE-then-EAT micro-motifs. The 5%-of-traces-for-3-nights usage gate is the right instrument and will correctly leave most mornings silent.
audit.one_change: Stop flattening. Log the PROGRAM the policy executed, not the action sequence it produced: have the action head emit a small parameterized sketch (primitive + argument + optional sensor guard) so traces retain conditionals and binders, and Stitch has real structure to abstract over. That single change is the difference between a macro table that saturates at ~50 entries and a library that actually compounds — it is the load-bearing assumption of the entire idea and right now the pipeline destroys it before Stitch ever sees it.

all.name: JOINTMAKERS
all.pitch: Agents in a real 2D rigid-body world whose only superpower is joining things together — a technology is an evolved physical assembly plus the policy that wields it, and one search discovers both. Hammers, levers, deadfall traps and catapults come out of a MAP-Elites archive, not a recipe list.
all.world: Jax2D (the physics engine inside Kinetix, FLAIROx) — deterministic impulse-based rigid-body sim in pure JAX: circles, polygons, revolute and fixed joints, thrusters. The arena has terrain polygons, scattered loose bodies (stones of varying density, sticks of varying length and stiffness), and food nodes gated by physics rather than by inventory: a nut needing >40 N impact, a burrow slab needing a 3-body lever to lift. An agent is itself a small articulated ragdoll (3-5 bodies, 2-4 motorized joints), so morphology is part of the genome and bodies co-evolve with brains.
all.invention_engine: Genome = (morphology graph, attachment policy, control policy). Two verbs beyond locomotion: WELD(hand, body) instantiates a real joint constraint in Jax2D, CUT(joint) removes one. An agent can therefore build an assembly from loose bodies, attach it to itself or to the ground, and must then LEARN to use it. Search is MAP-Elites whose behaviour descriptors are physical: peak impulse delivered, reach, assembly mass, joint count, energy per unit work. Elites' controllers are refined by short PPO bursts — this is PGA-MAP-Elites, which already exists in QDax. A technology is an archive cell's elite: a canonicalized joint graph with parameters. New technology = a newly filled cell, or a >15% improvement to an occupied one. Crucially, assemblies persist in the world after their builder dies, so a clan inherits its infrastructure and can steal or demolish a rival's.
all.why_unbounded: The design space is (graph topology x continuous geometry x attachment points x control policy). Kinetix's own claim is that this substrate procedurally contains tens of millions of distinct TASKS; the assembly space is strictly larger than the task space, and a joint graph over n bodies has super-exponentially many topologies each carrying continuous edge parameters. There is no enumerable list. Where it bottoms out honestly: the physics is 2D, rigid, frictional — no chemistry, no fields, no fluids. The FUNCTIONAL space is mechanics: leverage, impulse storage (springs via joint stiffness), containment, projectile launch, traps, wheeled transport. That is about three real capability tiers. Genuinely unbounded in variation, genuinely bounded in kind, and I would rather say that plainly than sell you a tech tree.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: Jax2D arena + PPO locomotion + a nut needing impulse; agents learn to body-slam. Weeks 2-3: WELD enabled; first tool is pick up heavy stone, weld to limb, swing. It looks exactly like a hammer. Month 2: leverage (stick welded to a fulcrum stone to lift a slab) and the deadfall — an assembly storing potential energy that releases on contact, i.e. a machine that works while the agent is elsewhere. Months 3-4: multi-agent assemblies (two agents cooperatively hold and weld a structure neither can build alone), inherited infrastructure (a bridge across a chasm that outlives its builder, and a clan that only survives because a dead ancestor built it). Wildest plausible: a wheeled sledge for hauling heavy food, a torsion catapult, and counter-technology — a clan evolving assemblies specifically to demolish a rival's bridge. Physical arms races.
all.what_selects: A caloric economy where the high-value food is only accessible above a force or height threshold. A chasm separating rich from poor terrain. Rival clans sharing an archive but holding separate territory. Joint fatigue means assemblies decay, so infrastructure must be maintained or lost. And POET-style pressure: arenas live in their own co-evolving archive, so a clan that solves everything is handed a harder arena.
all.changing_worlds: Kinetix arenas are just data — mutate gravity, friction, body density distributions, terrain. Run an explicit POET loop: an archive of (arena, clan) pairs, mutate arenas, transfer clans across arenas, keep pairs scoring in a goldilocks band. Multiple worlds is free, they are vmap batches. Publicly, let visitors vote weekly on one arena mutation ('raise gravity 10%', 'make sticks brittle') — cheap non-stationarity with a human story attached to it.
all.novelty_detector: Canonical hash of the assembly's joint graph (Weisfeiler-Lehman hash on the labelled graph, continuous params bucketed) plus archive-cell events. Push when: a never-seen graph hash becomes an elite; a previously empty archive region gets colonized; or a functional first fires — first assembly delivering >100 N, first assembly that continues doing work with no agent touching it. That last predicate is a one-line detector for 'they built a machine', and it is the best notification in this design.
all.phone_view: A 6-tile grid of last night's newest elites, each a 2-second autoplaying WebM of the assembly in use, labelled with its archive cell and the record it broke. One headline line: 'Clan Basalt built something that works without them.' Beneath it, the archive heat-map as a raw 2D image (behaviour space coloured by fitness) — that single image is a 3-second read of six months of progress.
all.hardware_use: Jax2D is the entire reason this fits 8GB: Kinetix trains general agents through billions of steps on a single GPU. Keep bodies per scene <=12 and parallel scenes <=1024; VRAM is not the binding constraint here, wall-clock is. The MAP-Elites archive lives in RAM, where 64GB is luxurious (a 50k-cell archive of small genomes is nothing). Video encoding on CPU overnight. Same sm_120/CUDA-12.8 setup tax as any JAX project on this laptop.
all.input_cadence: Autonomous. Nudges: add a body type (rope? a soft joint?), add one verb, or hand-place a puzzle arena you want solved and see whether the archive can reach it.
all.tech: Jax2D + Kinetix (github.com/FlairOx/Kinetix), QDax for PGA-MAP-Elites, JAX/Flax, evosax if you want ES variants, SQLite for archive metadata and lineage, ffmpeg for clips, the shared PWA + ntfy + Tailscale stack.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: install Kinetix, get its arena editor running, hand-build the nut arena, train PPO to smash it. Sunday: implement WELD/CUT as env actions, run vanilla MAP-Elites over three descriptors, export the top 6 elites as GIFs to a static page. This idea has the fastest delight-to-effort ratio of the six — welding a rock to your arm and hitting things is instantly legible on a phone.
all.six_months_later: An archive of a few thousand distinct assemblies with a scrollable visual museum, several convergently rediscovered classics (hammer, lever, deadfall, ramp) plus a long tail of things you have no name for, and inter-clan demolition wars. The museum page is the artifact strangers will actually share.
all.honest_ceiling: 2D rigid-body mechanics, full stop. Hammers, levers, traps, bridges, sledges, catapults — yes. Fire, chemistry, agriculture, writing, electricity — never, the substrate has no channel for them. Three realistic tiers (held tool -> static structure -> energy-storing machine), and from month 4 you are mostly getting variation inside tier 3. Second warning: MAP-Elites archives cheat. OpenAI's hide-and-seek agents famously exploited physics (box surfing, ramp abuse) and yours will too — budget for a physics-exploit blacklist and a hard cap on joint impulse, or your museum fills with infinite-energy joints.
all.research_notes: Kinetix (arXiv 2410.23208, ICLR 2025 Oral; github.com/FlairOx/Kinetix; kinetix-env.github.io) — introduces Jax2D, a deterministic impulse-based 2D rigid-body engine in pure JAX, procedurally generates tens of millions of physics tasks, trains a general agent that zero-shot solves unseen human-designed levels, all on accelerator hardware. QDax provides MAP-Elites, CVT MAP-Elites, PGA-MAP-Elites and CMA-MEGA in JAX. evosax (arXiv 2212.04180, github.com/RobertTLange/evosax) has 30+ ES implementations under a jit/vmap ask-eval-tell API if you want ES rather than PG refinement. OpenAI's emergent tool use / hide-and-seek is the precedent that pure multi-agent competition produces ramp use, box locking AND documented physics exploits — treat the exploits as an expected outcome, not a bug you failed to prevent.

audit.name: JOINTMAKERS
audit.ceiling: Two hard walls the pitch does not name. (1) Jax2D is statically shaped: every scene compiles to fixed-size arrays with a maximum shape and joint count (Kinetix's largest preset is on the order of a dozen shapes and a handful of joints). Runtime WELD must consume a preallocated joint slot, so maximum assembly complexity is a compile-time constant, realistically 6-8 joints. Your catapult has a hard part count and there is no version of this design with a 30-part machine. (2) MAP-Elites over a FIXED 5-descriptor space has a literal, countable ceiling: the number of cells. Once coverage saturates, 'new technology' degenerates into the >15% fitness-improvement clause, i.e. grinding. Illumination is not accumulation — nothing lets assembly A become a reusable component of assembly B with A's controller intact, so the archive gets wider forever and deeper never. Hammer week 2-3, lever and deadfall month 2, coverage saturating month 3-4, and from there it is variation inside tier 3, which the author already concedes.
audit.authored_content_risk: Lowest in the set alongside BYTE REEF, and the pitch is honest about kind-boundedness. The one real authorship: the five behaviour descriptors ARE the coordinate system of the tech tree. 'New technology = newly filled cell' means new point in a space you drew, and peak-impulse/reach/mass/joint-count/energy-per-work is a compact statement of what you already expect mechanics to be about. Multi-agent cooperative welding (two agents holding a structure neither can build alone) is asserted with no mechanism and is a much harder joint-exploration problem than anything else in the ladder — treat it as speculative, not month-3.
audit.compute_honesty: The weakest 'it fits on 8GB' claim of the six, and the framing hides where the cost is. VRAM is genuinely not binding; the binding cost is that PGA-MAP-Elites means per-elite PG refinement across an archive of thousands. With morphology in the genome, every genome has a different observation and action shape, so you cannot vmap one policy over the archive without padding to a max morphology and masking, and each variation batch is a fresh short PPO run with its own optimizer state. Filling a 5-D archive plus refinement is days-to-weeks per frontier, not one overnight. Citing OpenAI hide-and-seek as precedent compounds this: that result took on the order of hundreds of millions of episodes on a large distributed cluster, and it is used here as evidence for what a laptop will produce.
audit.dubious_claims: Kinetix claims check out: arXiv 2410.23208, ICLR 2025 Oral, Jax2D, 'tens of millions of procedurally generated tasks', 'billions of environment steps' — all confirmed (repo is FLAIROx/Kinetix, not FlairOx). The unsupported step is the inference from those numbers: 'the assembly space is strictly larger than the task space' is true and irrelevant, because reachability under MAP-Elites is bounded by descriptor cells and joint slots, not by the size of the underlying space. The hide-and-seek citation is used for two opposite purposes at once (proof emergence works, warning that exploits happen) and only the second is safe.
audit.semantic_risk: Low nonsense, high exploit — and the two interact badly. Runtime joint creation in an impulse solver is a textbook energy-injection bug: welding overlapping bodies produces an instantaneous penetration-resolution impulse. Since 'peak impulse delivered' is itself a descriptor, the archive will actively select for the solver artifact. Your museum's top exhibits will be free-energy joints unless the impulse cap and an overlap check land before the first long run, not after.
audit.one_change: Add composition. Let a finished elite be inserted into a new genome as a single reusable macro-part (its body subgraph plus its trained controller, frozen and callable), with a hierarchical or nested archive over parts-of-parts. That is the only route past both walls at once — it converts illumination into accumulation, and it sidesteps the joint-slot cap because a composed part occupies one slot in the parent genome.

all.name: THE KILN
all.pitch: Embodied tribes run physical processes — heat this, crush that, soak the other for a while — and when a process produces a combination nobody has ever made, a language model is asked, once and forever, what it becomes and what its properties are. The model never decides what happens next; it only expands the periodic table, and everything downstream is ordinary physics.
all.world: 2D JAX grid. Every substance is a 12-float property vector (density, hardness, melting_pt, ignition_pt, conductivity, toughness, calorific, toxicity, reactivity, opacity, elasticity, decay). The world begins with 14 base substances. A PROCESS is a situation the sim can detect: substances A and B co-located in a cell whose (temperature, pressure, moisture, duration, mechanical work) falls in a bucketed region. The sim quantizes that into a key. Key present in the SQLite recipes table -> apply the cached outcome. Key absent -> enqueue an oracle query. Tribes are PPO policies with bodies, hunger, tool durability, and territory.
all.invention_engine: The oracle, tightly leashed. One batched call per night over all cache misses, with a rigid structured-output schema: given the two input property vectors, their discovered names, and the process conditions, return {product_name, product_property_vector, yield_fraction, byproducts}. Three guardrails keep it from being slop: (a) conservation — mass in >= mass out, and a hard clamp so no property may exceed the max of its inputs by more than 1.5x unless the process supplied the energy for it; (b) two independent samples must agree within tolerance on the property vector or the pair is marked inert (Ouroboros Forge's mechanical verifier, applied to physics); (c) once written, a recipe is immutable and cached, so the world's physics is append-only and consistent forever. The embodied half is the actual game: the LLM tells you THAT sustained 900 degrees on high-reactivity ore yields a hard tough substance; the tribe still has to independently learn, via PPO, to build a structure that holds 900 degrees for 400 ticks. Knowing a recipe and being able to perform it are separate problems, and only the second one kills you.
all.why_unbounded: The recipe space is |substances|^2 x |condition buckets|, and |substances| grows with every accepted recipe, so reachable space grows super-quadratically with discoveries. Infinite Craft is the existence proof that this does not run out — its community-mined recipe dataset already exceeds 200k entries. Where it genuinely bottoms out is not size but COHERENCE: LLM-invented property vectors drift toward cool-sounding things with high numbers, and after a few thousand recipes you get a smooth gradient of super-materials with no interesting structure. The two mitigations that actually help are the conservation clamp and a usage tax: any substance no tribe has physically used in 20 nights is deleted and its recipes marked dormant. Physics nobody uses is not physics.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: grid + 14 substances + 6 hand-written recipes; PPO tribes learn to stay warm. Week 2: oracle wired in, 30-50 cache misses a night; the first LLM-born material appears (usually charcoal-like, then a ceramic). Months 1-2: tribes discover that MAINTAINING conditions pays — the first kiln, which is a wall geometry the policy learned because it holds heat. Month 3: two-stage processes, where a product becomes an input to another process. That is the moment the tech tree stops being flat. Month 4+: material lineages tens deep, tribes specializing, trade emerging because one territory has the ore and another has the fuel. Wildest plausible: a material with a genuinely weird vector — very high conductivity, very low density — and a tribe whose entire survival strategy reorganizes around it. You will read that push and laugh out loud.
all.what_selects: Durability. Tools wear at a rate set by hardness and toughness, so better materials are a survival edge rather than a score. Winters, predators, and finite ore veins that EXHAUST — which is what makes tribes migrate and fight. A tribe that loses its kiln loses the ability to make the material its tools depend on and visibly regresses; technological collapse becomes a legible, filmable event rather than a stat.
all.changing_worlds: Geological eras every ~2 weeks: veins exhaust, new strata expose, the climate band shifts. Public perturbation: the world has a sky that anonymous web visitors influence — a guestbook where each visitor's message is hashed into a small weather nudge (rain, heat, wind), and the accumulated messages render on the site as the world's omen log. Cheap non-stationarity plus an actual reason the page is public.
all.novelty_detector: Three tiers. (a) A cache miss is a candidate, not news. (b) A new substance is news only if a tribe USED it to survive — present in a surviving tribe's tool or structure for 3 consecutive nights. (c) Rank survivors by property-vector novelty: k-NN distance in the normalized 12-d space against every existing substance, and push the top one per night as a rendered material card. That yields roughly one interesting message per morning and silence on boring ones.
all.phone_view: A materials trading card: new substance name, radar chart of its 12 properties, the process that made it, the tribe that first used it, and a thumbnail of the structure they used it in. Plus one sparkline — substances discovered versus substances actually used. The gap between those two lines is the honesty metric of the whole project, and watching it is oddly compelling.
all.hardware_use: The RL half is small (same profile as KINDLING; 8GB is plenty). The LLM is the scheduling problem: run it only after the RL job releases the GPU. Local Qwen3-4B Q4_K_M is ~3GB at 40+ tok/s, so 50 recipes a night at ~300 output tokens each is about 7 minutes, free. If you would rather have coherence, claude-haiku-4-5 is $1/MTok in and $5/MTok out: a query with a cached system prompt is roughly 600 in / 250 out, about $0.0019 each, so 50/night is ~$0.10/night, ~$3/month — and the Batch API halves that while prompt caching (cached reads at ~0.1x) makes the fixed physics-rules prefix nearly free. This is the rare LLM-in-the-loop design whose bill is genuinely rounding error.
all.input_cadence: Autonomous. Nudges: tighten or loosen the conservation clamp, kill a runaway super-material from the phone, or hand-write a recipe when you want to seed a direction.
all.tech: JAX grid env + PPO; SQLite tables substances / recipes / process_keys / usage; llama.cpp with Qwen3-4B GGUF, or the anthropic Python SDK with output_config.format structured outputs plus prompt caching plus the Batch API; shared PWA + ntfy + Tailscale stack.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: grid, substances-as-vectors, the process-key quantizer, six hardcoded recipes, a PPO tribe that survives one night. Sunday: swap the hardcoded table for the oracle behind an aggressive cache, and watch the first non-authored material get born and written into SQLite. That is a hell of a Sunday-night moment and it is reachable.
all.six_months_later: Several hundred substances, maybe 60-100 of them load-bearing; a materials wiki that generated itself; tribes with genuinely different technological identities per world; and a graveyard table of deleted materials nobody ever used. The self-written wiki is the shareable artifact.
all.honest_ceiling: The LLM will eventually produce mush — expect visible coherence decay past roughly 500 substances without the usage tax, and even with it the property space is 12 floats and everything eventually becomes interpolation. Realistic tiers: fuels and fire, fired ceramics, alloys and composites, one or two genuine exotics. Four tiers, not twenty. The bigger risk is temptation: it is very easy to start letting the LLM adjudicate BEHAVIOUR too, and that is the exact moment the project turns into a chatbot playing pretend. Keep the model strictly on the property-vector side of the line, forever.
all.research_notes: Infinite Craft's architecture is the precedent: the backend asks an LLM what a combination produces, then caches it permanently, so only genuinely new pairs cost anything; community-mined datasets of 200k+ recipes exist. Open clones to read before building: github.com/bufferhead-code/opencraft, github.com/CharlesFauman/infini-craft, and github.com/ngruychev/finite-craft (explicitly runs on a laptop without a good GPU). Pricing verified: claude-haiku-4-5 at $1.00/$5.00 per MTok, claude-sonnet-5 at $3.00/$15.00, cached input reads ~0.1x with ~1.25x write cost and a ~1024-token minimum cacheable prefix, Batch API at 50%. Local alternative: Qwen3-4B Q4_K_M fits ~3GB VRAM; 8B Q4_K_M hits 40+ tok/s on 6-8GB cards, so 4B is comfortable. Theory being operationalized: Kauffman's adjacent possible and W. Brian Arthur's 'technology is combination'.

audit.name: THE KILN
audit.ceiling: Two ceilings, and the near one is not the one the pitch worries about. The pitch fears coherence decay past ~500 substances; the real failure is DIMENSIONAL COLLAPSE at 30-80 substances, weeks 3-6. Twelve floats are only real if the sim implements consequences for each. Realistically hardness and toughness feed tool wear, calorific and ignition feed fire, density and conductivity feed heat — opacity, elasticity, toxicity and reactivity are decoration unless you write dynamics for them, which is as much work as the rest of the sim. So the effective material space is ~4-D, and the conservation clamp makes it monotone and bounded. Every new material is then a point on a scalar quality ladder: to the simulator, 'bronze' and 'unobtainium' are the same object with slightly better numbers. That is a stat progression, not a tech tree, and it stops climbing when the clamp ceilings bind. Two-stage processes (month 3, the claimed moment the tree stops being flat) do not fix this — a chain of processes that each nudge four numbers upward is still one dimension of progress.
audit.authored_content_risk: Fatal, and it is precisely the flaw the brief warns about — with the twist that the author is a language model rather than the designer. Ask any competent model 'high-reactivity ore, sustained 900C, with charcoal' and you get metallurgy, because it memorised Wikipedia. The recipe table is human technological history retrieved from pretraining and revealed in the order the tribes happen to physically explore. The pitch calls this 'expanding the periodic table' as if that were the harmless half; expanding the periodic table IS the tech tree. The verifier does not save it: two samples agreeing is self-consistency, not truth — models are mode-collapsed at low temperature, agreement is near-guaranteed, and it measures nothing. Ouroboros-style rejection sampling works because the unit tests are an oracle independent of the generator; here there is no independent oracle at all. What IS genuine discovery is the embodied half — learning a wall geometry that holds 900C for 400 ticks is real, unauthored, and the best moment in the design. But that is one discovery, re-run against a retrieved catalogue.
audit.compute_honesty: Yes — the most honest budget in the document, and the numbers are essentially right.
