Verified: claude-haiku-4-5 is $1.00/$5.00 per MTok, claude-sonnet-5 $3.00/$15.00, Batch API 50%, cached reads ~0.1x with ~1.25x write cost, minimum cacheable prefix ~1024 tokens. ~$0.10/night at 50 recipes is correct in magnitude. One self-contradiction: at the stated 600-in/250-out per query the request is BELOW the ~1024-token cacheable minimum, so prompt caching cannot engage at all — you would have to pad the physics-rules prefix past 1024 tokens for the 'nearly free prefix' claim to be true, which also raises the uncached cost of the first call. Local Qwen3-4B at ~3GB after the RL job releases the GPU is fine.
audit.dubious_claims: Infinite Craft precedent and the 200k+ community recipe datasets are real, but the precedent proves the wrong thing: Infinite Craft never runs out because it is a naming game with no simulator downstream, so nothing has to MEAN anything. Here everything downstream is physics that reads four numbers. 'Recipe space is |substances|^2 x buckets, so growth is super-quadratic' counts syntactically distinct keys, not distinguishable outcomes — the honest count is the number of reachable points in the sub-space of properties the sim actually consumes. 'Mechanical verifier' is a misuse of the Ouroboros Forge analogy as described above.
audit.semantic_risk: High — but the failure mode is not gibberish, it is plausible-sounding interpolation. You will get an unbroken gradient of reasonable-looking materials with monotonically nicer stats and no structure, which reads as depth on a trading card and is flat in the simulator. The usage tax (delete anything unused for 20 nights) is a genuinely good instrument and the discovered-vs-used sparkline is the most honest telemetry proposed anywhere in this document — it will show the gap widening, which is the correct diagnosis arriving too late to fix the architecture.
audit.one_change: Invert the oracle so the model cannot retrieve. Two coupled moves, one idea: never show it names or human-legible property labels (feed anonymised input vectors and bucketed conditions), and restrict its output to a RULE in a tiny closed algebra you wrote — which conserved quantity moves where, which phase boundary is crossed, what fraction transfers — from which the product vector is derived mechanically. Novelty then comes from your algebra composing rather than from the model's memory, the result can surprise the model, and the tree stops being a walk through human metallurgy in a random order.

all.name: PALIMPSEST
all.pitch: An archipelago of small worlds where a technology only exists as long as someone alive can perform it and someone young is watching — inventions are memes with a physical carrier, and the drama is transmission, drift, loss and rediscovery. The tech tree is a phylogeny, not a checklist, and it has dark ages.
all.world: 5-9 island grids, each 64x64, all vmapped as one batch, separated by water. Each island holds one lineage of 12-40 embodied agents with real lifespans (~2000 ticks), age, and death. The physical substrate is KINDLING's — materials with property vectors, heat, moisture, food, predators — but the invention engine is completely different.
all.invention_engine: Three coupled mechanisms. (1) Individual innovation: an agent occasionally mutates a program it knows (subtree swap in a small behaviour DSL) at a low base rate that RISES with hunger — necessity as the mother of invention, literally parameterized. Most mutations are useless; the sim is the only filter. (2) Transmission with a real bottleneck: knowledge is never shared by copying parameters. A knower must physically PERFORM the program adjacent to a learner, repeatedly, and the learner runs a small behavioural-cloning update on the observed (obs, action) pairs — DeepMind's cultural-transmission 'starter kit' of memory, expert dropout, and attentional bias toward the expert. The copy is noisy. That noise IS cultural drift and it is the source of variation. (3) External storage: an agent can inscribe a program onto a carved token at a cost. A token is a real physical item — carried, traded, stolen, buried, burned. Reading one gives a cleaner copy than watching a person. So writing is not a milestone you author; it is a strategy that either pays or does not, and you find out by watching.
all.why_unbounded: The space is programs, which is combinatorially open as in KINDLING, but what makes it never settle is the DYNAMICS: transmission noise plus finite lifespans plus island isolation means each lineage random-walks a different region of program space, and contact events (rafts, storms carrying a body between islands) horizontally transfer memes into contexts that recombine them. This is exactly the iterated-learning / cultural-accumulation regime that 'Artificial Generational Intelligence' formalizes. It bottoms out where the DSL and physics do — the same honest bound as KINDLING — but the HISTORY it generates is far richer per unit of technology, because the same 40 technologies produce a different story on every island every month.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: one island, agents with lifespans, one hand-seeded skill held by one agent — watch it die out when the knower dies. Technology visibly going extinct is the first delightful moment and it arrives in days. Week 2: imitation channel on; measure whether a skill survives 5 generations (the standard cultural-transmission metric). Weeks 3-4: innovation on; the first lineage-original technology. Month 2: multiple islands, first contact event, first horizontal transfer. Month 3: dark ages — a famine kills Island 3's elders, fire-making is lost for 40 generations, then independently reinvented by a different term. That single push is the best notification anything in this document can produce. Month 4+: inscription becomes adaptive on some islands and not others, and a literate island out-accumulates its neighbours in a way the phylogeny makes visible. Wildest plausible: a token economy, tokens as inter-island trade goods, and an island whose survival strategy is acquiring other islands' tokens — emergent cultural imperialism.
all.what_selects: Individual death from hunger, cold, predation. Lineage extinction at population zero, after which the island reseeds from a neighbour's raft — itself a transmission event. Teaching has an explicit opportunity cost: the elder is not foraging. That creates the innovate/imitate/forage tradeoff which the cultural-accumulation literature says is the precondition for accumulation to happen at all. Islands differ in resource richness, so poor islands are innovation-pressured and rich islands are conservative, and you can watch that difference in the phylogeny.
all.changing_worlds: The archipelago IS multiple worlds, changing independently. Sea level oscillates slowly: low sea level opens land bridges (mass contact, tech homogenization), high sea level isolates (divergence). Visitors are travellers — an anonymous web visitor may once a day 'sail', and the site picks a random agent and moves it, with everything it knows, to another island. And the guestbook literally becomes scripture: a visitor's message is inscribed on a token that enters the world as a physical object, and the site shows which islands currently hold which human-written tokens. That is a genuinely good reason for the page to be public and for strangers to come back.
all.novelty_detector: Run it on the phylogeny, not the world state. Push on: (a) convergent invention — two lineages independently reach behaviourally equivalent programs with different terms, compared by action-trace equivalence on a fixed probe set rather than by syntax; (b) resurrection — a technology extinct for more than N generations reappears; (c) horizontal transfer — a meme's first appearance in a lineage whose ancestors never had it; (d) lineage collapse — meme-pool entropy dropping more than 30% in one night. Each is one SQL query over the meme table and each produces a headline a human actually wants to read.
all.phone_view: The archipelago as a small map, each island tinted by meme-pool size, plus one headline event. Below it a CHRONICLE: reverse-chronological one-sentence historical events auto-generated from the event table, phrased by a Qwen3-4B pass — 'On night 214, the last woman who knew how to bank a fire died on Ashen Isle.' The chronicle is the binge-for-an-hour artifact, and it is exactly what a thermal receipt printer wants: a $30 printer on the desk emitting the previous night's three chronicle lines every morning is the best off-screen check-in ritual of any idea here.
all.hardware_use: Tiny. Islands are vmap batches of a small grid; imitation is a few BC gradient steps per teaching event, not a training run. This is the idea that most comfortably runs 24/7 on 8GB while leaving room for the LLM chronicler to share the GPU. 64GB RAM matters more than VRAM: the meme lineage DB and per-agent program stores are the memory hogs and they live CPU-side.
all.input_cadence: Autonomous; the phone action is READING, which is the point. Nudges: trigger a catastrophe, seed a technology onto one island to see whether it spreads, change the sea-level period.
all.tech: JAX for the island sims, Flax or PyTorch for the small BC updates, SQLite with a memes table (id, parent_id, lineage_id, term_hash, born_night, died_night) — a real queryable phylogeny — networkx or d3 for rendering it, Qwen3-4B for chronicle phrasing, python-escpos driving a USB thermal printer, shared PWA + ntfy + Tailscale stack.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: one island, agents with age and death, one hardcoded skill held by one agent, and the imitation channel. Sunday: the meme table, the extinction detector, and a page that prints the chronicle. You will watch a technology die on Sunday evening, and that alone justifies the weekend.
all.six_months_later: A phylogeny of thousands of meme nodes across 9 lineages, a chronicle holding a year of readable history, several documented dark ages and rediscoveries, and a visible difference between islands that a stranger perceives in ten seconds. The chronicle, printed and bound, is a physical book of a world's history.
all.honest_ceiling: The technologies themselves stay simple. This design spends its complexity budget on transmission dynamics rather than depth of invention, so expect 20-40 distinct technologies per lineage at the fire/shelter/tool tier and no further. If you want deep tech AND deep culture you must merge this with KINDLING's Stitch loop — the meme becomes the abstraction, which is a real and attractive option but roughly doubles the build. Second honesty: imitation learning between tiny agents is fiddly, and getting transmission fidelity into the goldilocks band (not zero, not one) will take real tuning. Too faithful and you get no drift, no loss, and no story at all.
all.research_notes: DeepMind's cultural transmission line: 'Learning few-shot imitation as cultural transmission' (Nature Communications 2023) and 'Learning Robust Real-Time Cultural Transmission without Human Data' (arXiv 2203.00715) — the ablations identify the minimal sufficient starter kit (memory, expert dropout, attentional bias toward the expert, automatic domain randomization), which is exactly what to implement. 'Artificial Generational Intelligence: Cultural Accumulation in Reinforcement Learning' (arXiv 2406.00392) makes the key point for this design: accumulation appears only when social learning and independent learning are BALANCED, and existing generational algorithms fail to capture the open-ended nature of it — that gap is the room this project lives in. Stitch (POPL 2023) if you take the merge-with-KINDLING option. Craftax/JaxMARL confirm the multi-agent-in-JAX scaling; JaxMARL (NeurIPS 2024 D&B) reports up to 12,500x speedups over CPU MARL pipelines and is worth reading for its vmapped multi-agent patterns even if you write your own env.

audit.name: PALIMPSEST
audit.ceiling: The invention engine is the weakest of the six and it collides with the transmission channel. Random subtree mutation over a behaviour DSL, filtered only by survival, is genetic programming with a sparse, noisy, credit-free fitness signal: it finds programs of a few nodes and stops. Meanwhile transmission is lossy BY DESIGN. For a program of L nodes copied at per-node fidelity f, retention goes as f^L, so the technologies most worth accumulating are precisely the ones transmission cannot hold. That is a built-in complexity cap, and it is low: expect single-digit-node programs, maybe 5-15 durable memes per lineage rather than the claimed 20-40, with invention plateauing around month 2. Note this is a ceiling on TECHNOLOGY only — the history keeps generating indefinitely, and that is a genuinely different and defensible product from the one the brief asked for.
audit.authored_content_risk: Low on the sim side — lineage-original programs are real discoveries, extinction and rediscovery are real dynamics, and the sea-level/contact machinery is honest non-stationarity. The authorship creeps in at the chronicler: a Qwen pass turning event rows into 'the last woman who knew how to bank a fire died on Ashen Isle' will confabulate significance for statistically trivial events, and the chronicle is the headline artifact. Gate it to templated facts with the model only choosing phrasing, or the project's most shareable output becomes its least trustworthy one. Separate design incoherence worth fixing before week 1: memes are simultaneously DSL terms with a term_hash in a phylogeny table AND transferred by behavioural cloning into a neural policy. BC yields weights, not terms — after one update the learner has no term to hash, so parent_id becomes an inference from probe-trace clustering rather than a fact, and your 'real queryable phylogeny' is a fuzzy clustering wearing a schema.
audit.compute_honesty: Yes, the most honest of the RL designs — vmapped 64x64 islands, a few BC gradient steps per teaching event, no training run in the loop. The uncosted risk is not compute but bootstrap: DeepMind's cultural-transmission results depended on a scripted expert bot to imitate, plus ADR and large-scale training. Here generation 0 has nothing worth copying, so the transmission machinery has no signal until innovation has already succeeded, and innovation is blind mutation. Two weak mechanisms mutually bootstrapping is the real schedule risk, not GPU hours.
audit.dubious_claims: The citations are accurate: 'Learning few-shot imitation as cultural transmission' (Nat Comms 2023), arXiv 2203.00715, arXiv 2406.00392, JaxMARL's up-to-12,500x figure. The interpretation is where it slips. 2406.00392's actual finding — accumulation appears only when social and independent learning are balanced, and existing generational algorithms fail to be open-ended — is cited as 'the room this project lives in'; it reads at least as well as evidence the effect is fragile and narrow, and the pitch takes the optimistic reading without argument. The DeepMind 'starter kit' is presented as a recipe to implement, but its ablations were run with a privileged expert present by construction, which this design does not have.
audit.semantic_risk: Low. Memes are executable and filtered by survival, so nothing meaningless persists. The risk is the opposite: the surviving memes will be so simple that naming them technologies overstates them, and the drama (loss, drift, rediscovery) will be doing all the narrative work.
audit.one_change: Give innovation a search engine. Replace blind subtree mutation with a within-lifetime hill-climb — an agent tries small variants of a program it knows against a hunger/energy proxy over a few hundred ticks and keeps the better one — so that what enters the transmission channel is worth transmitting. That raises the complexity of the thing being copied, which is the only quantity that moves this design's ceiling; fidelity tuning cannot, because it only decides how fast simple things are lost.

all.name: BYTE REEF
all.pitch: A spatial soup where every agent IS a short program executing on a tiny VM, eating energy and rewriting itself and its neighbours — technology is whatever code motif evolution keeps, found by mining the genome corpus for reused subroutines and proving function by ablation. No fitness function, no tech tree, no authored anything.
all.world: A 256x256 lattice; each site holds a 64-byte tape and a program counter. The instruction set is a Brainfuck derivative extended with six world verbs — SENSE_ENERGY, MOVE, EAT, EMIT(byte), READ_NEIGHBOR, WRITE_NEIGHBOR. That extension is the crucial modification to BFF: the programs are EMBODIED. They have a position, a metabolism, and can act on a shared spatial resource field, rather than only self-copying in a formless soup. Energy diffuses and regrows spatially, every executed instruction costs energy, running out is death, and accumulating enough triggers fission.
all.invention_engine: Nothing but selection and self-modification, which is the entire point — all the engineering goes into the DETECTOR. Nightly: mine the corpus of living genomes for frequent subsequences (generalized suffix automaton, or SPADE-style sequential pattern mining, over the population). Then test each candidate motif for FUNCTION by ablation — splice it out of 200 living genomes and measure survival delta in a short sandboxed rerun. A motif with a significant negative ablation delta is a TECHNOLOGY: a discovered subroutine the organism needs. Then build the dependency graph over motifs and run the RAF algorithm on it to find autocatalytic clusters — motif sets that collectively sustain each other. Those clusters are 'civilizations' in the only sense this substrate can offer, and they are detected, not authored.
all.why_unbounded: The substrate is Turing-complete and genome length is unbounded if you allow growth, so the space of discoverable programs is literally infinite with no authored ceiling of any kind. This is the only idea here with no designed tech tree even implicitly. The honest counterweight is that unbounded does not mean interesting: BFF gets self-replicators in ~40% of runs within 16k epochs and Avida reaches logic operations, but nobody has ever gotten a legible civilization out of a code soup and you probably will not either. What you WILL reliably get is genuine unfaked open-endedness at the motif level plus parasites, hyperparasites and immunity — the classic Tierra arc — which is real emergent arms racing.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: the VM, the soup, energy; replicators appear. This is a known-reproducible result, so week 1 has a near-guaranteed payoff. Week 2: spatial embodiment via MOVE/EAT — now replicators must also forage, and you get motility. Weeks 3-4: motif mining plus ablation testing; the first named technology, usually a compact copy loop. Month 2: parasites (genomes exploiting a neighbour's copy loop), then resistance. Month 3: RAF clusters — motif groups that only function together. Wildest plausible: spatial territoriality, a signalling motif via EMIT that coordinates neighbours, and multicellular-ish clumps of specialized genomes.
all.what_selects: Energy, and nothing else. No reward function anywhere in the codebase. Spatial energy regrowth creates patches, patches create competition, competition creates everything else. Death is running the tape with an empty battery.
all.changing_worlds: Mutation rate as a slow oscillation; periodic cosmic-ray bursts; instruction-set drift as an epoch event (retire an opcode, add another); and merging two independently-evolved soups, which is the single most interesting experiment this substrate offers — a real contact-between-worlds event with a measurable, gambleable outcome.
all.novelty_detector: Four signals. (a) Selective sweep detection: a motif whose population frequency derivative crosses a threshold — something just won. (b) First-ever motif by canonical hash WITH a significant ablation delta. (c) RAF closure events: the first detection of a new autocatalytic set. (d) A complexity proxy: gzip size of the population's genome corpus, normalized — a step change means the population just got structurally richer. Report at most one per morning, ranked.
all.phone_view: The soup itself as a 256x256 image, hue = genome hash, brightness = energy. It is genuinely beautiful and different every night, so the 30-second check-in is just 'look at the reef'. One headline: the night's top motif, its ablation delta, and a hex dump. Sonification is the killer feature here and this is the substrate that most deserves it — map EMIT bytes plus birth/death events to a generative Web Audio stream (or an icecast stream off the laptop) and you have a soup radio you leave running. Most passive check-in possible.
all.hardware_use: Cheapest of the six by far. A 65k-cell soup of 64-byte tapes is 4MB; VM steps vectorize beautifully in JAX (numba or plain numpy also works). No neural network at all, so 8GB is barely touched and you could run 20 soups concurrently. The 64GB RAM is what you actually want, for the genome corpus archive and the motif mining. Best hardware fit of the six and the worst legibility — those two facts are related.
all.input_cadence: Fully autonomous. The interesting nudges are experiments rather than maintenance: merge two soups, retire an opcode, spike the mutation rate. Each is a one-line config change with a genuinely unpredictable outcome.
all.tech: JAX or numba for the VM, SQLite for genome snapshots and motif tables, a suffix-automaton motif miner (pure Python is fine at this scale), a short RAF implementation, a Web Audio PWA for the radio, ntfy, Tailscale.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: the BF VM, a random soup, the copy-and-mutate loop. You will likely see replicators emerge by Saturday night — an unusually strong first-weekend payoff because the result is already reproducible in the literature. Sunday: energy, space and EAT, plus the soup-image renderer and a cron that pushes the nightly image and starts the radio stream.
all.six_months_later: A large motif library with ablation-verified function, documented parasite/host arms races, detected RAF clusters, and a year of soup images that make a gorgeous time-lapse. Whether any of it looks like CIVILIZATION is genuinely uncertain — that is the bet you would be making.
all.honest_ceiling: Highest-variance idea in the set. The realistic ceiling is ECOLOGY, not civilization: replication, parasitism, resistance, motility, maybe signalling. Two, perhaps three capability tiers, and they are biological rather than technological. If what you want is cavemen discovering fire, this will not give it to you, and I would rather you know that now than discover it in month 3. Build it if the appeal is genuine unfaked open-endedness plus beautiful images and a radio station; skip it if the appeal is watching a civilization.
all.research_notes: 'Computational Life: How Well-formed, Self-replicating Programs Emerge from Simple Interaction' (arXiv 2406.19108, Agüera y Arcas et al., 2024): random Brainfuck programs interacting with no fitness function, no selection pressure and no designer produce self-replicators in roughly 40% of runs within 16k epochs, mostly via self-modification, with or without background mutation; the same holds on real Z80/8080 instruction sets with ecosystem-like dynamics. Follow-up 'BFF: Simple explanations for complex phenomena' (arXiv 2607.01483) and 'Self-replication and Computational Universality' (arXiv 2510.08342). 'Non-Spatial Hash Chemistry as a Minimalistic Open-Ended Evolutionary System' (arXiv 2404.18027) for the minimal-substrate framing. RAF theory: 'A Concise and Formal Definition of RAF Sets and the RAF Algorithm' (arXiv 2303.01809) gives a short implementable spec; Hordijk & Steel's detection algorithms (Algorithms for Molecular Biology 2015) for the analysis side. Sakana's ASAL (arXiv 2412.17799, github.com/SakanaAI/asal, MIT Press Artificial Life 31(3)) is the modern precedent for automated open-endedness detection across Boids, Particle Life, Game of Life, Lenia and NCA — its temporal-open-endedness score is directly borrowable if you would rather score novelty in a foundation-model representation space than hand-roll the gzip proxy.

audit.name: BYTE REEF
audit.ceiling: The most damaging fact in the whole document, and this pitch does not mention it: Avida's rise in complexity is DRIVEN BY AUTHORED REWARDS — explicit energy bonuses for computing NAND, AND, and the rest of the logic ladder. Strip the reward ladder and Avida populations do not climb; they optimise replication speed and their genomes SHRINK. Tierra likewise settles into a parasite/host ecology within days. 'Energy and nothing else' is exactly the regime that has never produced a complexity ratchet in thirty years of the literature. Worse, the energy-per-instruction metabolism actively selects against the unbounded genome growth the pitch relies on: longer programs cost strictly more per replication cycle. Expect replicators week 1 (genuinely reproducible), genome shrinkage weeks 2-4, parasites and resistance month 2, and then a stable ecology forever. Two tiers, biological, permanently.
audit.authored_content_risk: Lowest of the six — effectively zero. There is no authored content anywhere and the pitch is admirably direct that no one has ever gotten a legible civilisation out of a code soup. The honesty is real and should be credited. The problem is that the brief asked for cavemen discovering fire and this substrate has no channel for it, which the pitch also says.
audit.compute_honesty: Fully honest and the cheapest here by a wide margin. A 65k-cell soup of 64-byte tapes is ~4MB, VM steps vectorise, no neural network anywhere, 20 concurrent soups is realistic, and the 64GB of RAM is correctly identified as the resource that matters for corpus mining. Nothing in the hardware section needs correcting.
audit.dubious_claims: (1) The 40%-of-runs-within-16k-epochs figure is real but cherry-picked: it holds at one specific background mutation rate (~0.024%), and the same paper reports state transitions as rare as 3 in 1000 under a different condition. Quoting it as the headline reproducibility number oversells the week-1 payoff. arXiv 2607.01483 (BFF: Simple explanations for complex phenomena) does exist, as does 2406.19108. (2) The Avida claim — 'Avida reaches logic operations' — is stated as though it supports a no-fitness-function design when it is the strongest single piece of evidence against it. (3) Methodologically, three of the four detectors are broken as specified: ablation by excision from a BF-like genome shifts every downstream offset and unbalances brackets, so nearly every ablation is lethal and the detector will label essentially all motifs technologies — you need a length-preserving in-place scramble control and a matched null distribution. RAF over a 'motif dependency graph' is a category error: RAF is defined on a catalytic reaction network with a food set and explicit catalysis relations; motifs do not catalyse one another's production, so you would be inventing the relation and then discovering properties of your own invention. And gzip over the corpus mostly tracks clonality and diversity, so it DROPS during a selective sweep even when the winner is structurally richer.
audit.semantic_risk: Highest of the six, though not in the usual way — nothing generated is meaningless, but nothing is interpretable either. A hex-dump motif called a technology is a naming decision, not a finding, and the RAF clusters as specified would be beautiful artefacts of an invented graph. The sonified soup radio and the nightly image are genuinely excellent and are the actual product; the technology layer is decoration on top of an ecology.
audit.one_change: If you want a complexity ratchet you must make length pay. Make energy release conditional on non-trivial computation: spatially varying 'locks' that pay out only to a genome whose EMIT byte is a specified non-trivial function of a byte it sensed, with the function class drifting on a slow clock. That is Avida's logic-task reward reintroduced as a physical resource rather than a score, it is the only lever known to produce a complexity ratchet in code soups, and it costs you authoring a function class rather than a tech tree. Be clear-eyed that it is a partial retreat from the purity that is this idea's main selling point.

all.name: LOAM
all.pitch: A world where the technology IS the landscape — tribes survive by irrigating, burning, terracing and above all breeding plants and animals whose genomes are themselves evolving, so domestication is a real evolutionary process the tribes drive rather than a recipe they unlock. The tech tree is written into the terrain and you can read it from orbit.
all.world: 256x256 raster in JAX. Layers: elevation (fixed), water (shallow-water cellular flow), soil nutrients, soil moisture, fire fuel load, biota. Each plant or animal carries a 16-gene vector — growth rate, water need, nutrient need, seed dispersal distance, toxicity, edible yield, palatability, and for animals flee distance, aggression, herd affinity, reproduction rate. These genomes mutate and are selected by the environment continuously: a real evolving ecosystem that runs whether or not agents exist. Tribes are PPO policies with bodies living on top of it.
all.invention_engine: Niche construction as a co-evolutionary loop between two coupled searches. AGENT SIDE: tribes have a small verb set that writes permanently into the raster — DIG (moves elevation and therefore water), BURN, PLANT(seed_in_hand), CULL(target), HERD, DAM, FENCE, CARRY_WATER. There is no 'irrigation' technology anywhere in the code; there is only digging, and irrigation is a PATTERN of digs a policy discovers because it raises yield. BIOTA SIDE: when a tribe selectively harvests the palatable plants and replants genomes it carried, it applies directional selection to the local plant genome distribution. Over hundreds of generations the plants in its territory BECOME domesticated — higher yield, lower toxicity, lower seed dispersal — which is precisely the archaeological signature of domestication, arising because the tribe's behaviour is the selection pressure. Nothing in the code says 'domestication'. The technology is therefore jointly a learned spatial pattern of world-modification (mined as recurring spatial motifs) and a genome cluster in biota space. Both are searched, both compound, and each reshapes the other's fitness landscape.
all.why_unbounded: The invention space is the cross product of raster configurations (astronomically large, and unlike a tech tree it has no discrete states) with the biota genome space (16 continuous genes under agent-driven selection, an open evolutionary search against a moving target). Co-evolution is the unboundedness argument: the agents change the biota's selective environment, the biota changes the agents' resource landscape, and neither has a fixed optimum to converge to. It bottoms out at the resolution of the verb set — with eight verbs you get roughly the neolithic package and no further, because there is no channel for materials or mechanisms. This idea is deep in exactly one direction (ecology, landscape, domestication) and shallow in every other, and that is the trade.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: raster, water flow, plants with genomes, no agents — watch an ecosystem run and watch plant genomes drift to fit the terrain. Already hypnotic. Week 2: tribes plus forage PPO; they overharvest and crash, which is the first real story. Weeks 3-4: PLANT and BURN enabled; the first fire regime appears, because burning raises nutrients after a delay so a burn-then-plant policy beats one that does not. That is slash-and-burn, discovered. Month 2: DIG and water — the first irrigation channel shows up as a visible line on the map and the 'look at the map' check-in becomes addictive. Month 3: measurable domestication — plot mean yield-gene inside versus outside tribal territory and watch the curves separate. That chart is the single strongest evidence-of-depth artifact in this whole document. Month 4+: herding and animal domestication (flee-distance gene falling inside herded populations — tameness, evolved), terracing on slopes, erosion as a consequence of over-digging, and a tribe that collapses from its own success. Wildest plausible: two tribes with incompatible landscape strategies — one irrigator, one pastoralist — in resource conflict, and a landscape a stranger can read as 'someone lives here'.
all.what_selects: Nutrient depletion, erosion, drought cycles, and the biota's own evolution. That last one gives you a free emergent failure mode: over-selecting for yield drives down the toxicity gene that was protecting the plant from a co-evolving pest, and the crop collapses. Real agricultural pathology, no authoring required. Tribes compete for watershed position, and an upstream tribe damming a river is a direct act of war.
all.changing_worlds: A slow climate oscillation (500-night period) in rainfall and temperature, plus rare catastrophes — volcano, flood, pest bloom — drawn from a table whose TIMING is voted on by web visitors. And the world genuinely never resets: this is the one idea where the world's own accumulated history is the content, so run one long-lived world plus a couple of control shards rather than reseeding weekly.
all.novelty_detector: Learning-progress surprise, done properly. Train a tiny conv net (a few hundred k params) to predict tomorrow's raster from today's, continuously fit on the world's own history. Push when its prediction error SPIKES — a Schmidhuber-style compression-progress signal that fires exactly when the world does something structurally new: the first channel, the first burn scar, the first terrace, the first collapse. Supplement with two explicit statistics: a domestication index (t-statistic on mean gene value inside versus outside territory) and spatial-motif mining that clusters recurring 8x8 patterns of agent-caused change and reports a new cluster.
all.phone_view: One image: the map in false colour with a diff overlay showing what changed last night in a hot colour. That is the entire 30-second check-in and it is genuinely great, because you see the SHAPE of what they built. Below it the domestication chart and one headline. The physical artifact that fits perfectly here is an e-ink frame on the wall showing the map, refreshed each morning — a slowly changing landscape is exactly what e-ink is good at, and the daily glance becomes ritual.
all.hardware_use: Raster sims are the cheapest thing a GPU does. 256x256 by ~10 float layers plus a few thousand biota entities in JAX is a few hundred MB; PPO on small conv policies fits easily; you can run 8 world shards in parallel inside 8GB. The surprise model is tiny. This will never be VRAM-bound — it is bound by how fast you want simulated years to pass, which makes 24/7 operation the actual feature rather than a workaround.
all.input_cadence: Autonomous. Nudges: add a verb — the highest-leverage knob in the whole design, since each new verb opens a technological direction — trigger a catastrophe, or fork the world to run a counterfactual.
all.tech: JAX raster sim (shallow-water flow is a ~30-line stencil), PPO, a small Flax conv surprise-model, SQLite for the event and genome-stats DB, canvas or matplotlib for the map render, a Raspberry Pi Zero driving an e-ink panel (or just a pinned phone page), shared PWA + ntfy + Tailscale stack.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: raster layers, the water-flow stencil, plants with genomes reproducing and mutating; render a PNG every 100 ticks and stitch a time-lapse. That alone is a satisfying screensaver by Saturday night. Sunday: one tribe with FORAGE and PLANT, plus the nightly map-diff push. The unauthored moment lands immediately — plant genomes adapting to the terrain's moisture gradient without a line of code about adaptation.
all.six_months_later: A landscape with centuries of legible history — old channels, abandoned terraces, forest that is now grassland — plus quantified domestication of two or three species, and a time-lapse of a year of world history that is the best possible thing to show another human being.
all.honest_ceiling: The neolithic, and that is it. Fire regime, irrigation, terracing, plant and animal domestication, maybe rudimentary land tenure and conflict over water. There is no path from here to metallurgy or machines without bolting on a different substrate entirely. Roughly four tiers and the last arrives around month 4. The other honest risk is balance: the ecology needs careful tuning, an unbalanced biota either goes extinct in week 1 or fills everything by week 2, and getting the parameters into a regime that stays interesting for months is real fiddly work no paper will do for you.
all.research_notes: Niche construction theory (Odling-Smee, Laland, Feldman) is the framing — organisms modifying their own selective environment is the mechanism this whole idea instantiates. Speed budget verified via Craftax (arXiv 2402.16801: 1B steps under an hour on one GPU) and Craftax-MA (arXiv 2511.04904: 250M multi-agent steps in 57 min on an L40S) — a raster sim is cheaper than either. purejaxrl for the PPO skeleton; JaxMARL (NeurIPS 2024 D&B, blog.foersterlab.com/jaxmarl) for vmapped multi-agent rollout patterns. Schmidhuber's compression-progress / learning-progress formulation is the basis for the surprise detector; Sakana's ASAL (arXiv 2412.17799, github.com/SakanaAI/asal, code public) is the modern precedent for automated novelty scoring over ALife renders and its temporal-open-endedness objective is directly borrowable if you would rather run a small CLIP over map images than train your own predictor. OMNI-EPIC (arXiv 2405.15568, jennyzhangzt.com/omni-epic) is the reference for the archive-plus-model-of-interestingness pattern if you later want an LLM proposing catastrophes and challenges rather than a fixed table.

audit.name: LOAM
audit.ceiling: Genuine mechanism, but the ladder splits in two and only the bottom half is safe. The domestication half will work: directional selection on a gene distribution driven by agent harvesting preference needs no clever policy, only a preference, and it produces a measurable archaeological signature. That is the most honest discovery mechanism in the entire document. The landscape-engineering half is the part most likely never to arrive. Burn -> delayed nutrient -> plant, or dig a 20-cell channel -> water arrives -> yield rises 300 ticks later, is a sparse-reward, long-horizon, spatially extended construction problem where a HALF-BUILT channel pays strictly negative (stamina spent, no water yet). Vanilla PPO is famously defeated by exactly this shape — Craftax exists to demonstrate it, and Craftax-MA's own conclusion is that IPPO/MAPPO/PQN all fail its long-horizon credit assignment. So expect week 2 (overharvest and crash) and month 3 (measurable domestication) to land, and months 2-4 (irrigation, terracing, the map a stranger can read) to be at serious risk of never landing. Even if they do, the verb set caps you at 6-10 recurring motifs and the neolithic, as stated.
audit.authored_content_risk: Lowest of the six. There is no authored tech tree even implicitly; irrigation is a pattern of DIG and domestication is a shift in a gene distribution, and neither word appears in the code. The only authoring is the verb set itself, which the pitch correctly identifies as the highest-leverage knob and the honest bound. The catastrophe table is authored but is weather, not technology.
audit.compute_honesty: Honest and, if anything, over-modest — except for one backwards claim. 'A raster sim is cheaper than Craftax' is wrong per tick (655k cells x ~10 layers of stencil work vs Craftax's small per-agent grid ops), though both are trivial on a GPU and 8 shards in 8GB is right. The uncosted item is not FLOPs, it is numerics: explicit shallow-water flow on a 256^2 raster is CFL-limited and 'a ~30-line stencil' will go unstable or silently lose mass, and mass non-conservation quietly corrupts the moisture field that the domestication signal is measured against. Budget a week there, and add a mass-conservation assert on every tick.
audit.dubious_claims: Citations are sound (Craftax 2402.16801, Craftax-MA 2511.04904 confirmed real with 250M interactions in under an hour — the L40S/57-minute precision is unverified paraphrase; ASAL 2412.17799 and OMNI-EPIC 2405.15568 both real; niche-construction framing is used correctly). The dubious piece is the novelty detector, not a citation: a continuously-refit predictor of tomorrow's raster on a world with stochastic weather and a 500-night climate cycle is a noisy-TV machine. Prediction ERROR will spike on rain fronts, fire stochasticity and its own optimiser's non-stationarity far more often than on the first channel, and you will be paged every morning. Schmidhuber's actual quantity is compression PROGRESS — the derivative of error measured on a held-out replay of past rasters — and the design as written uses the wrong statistic.
audit.semantic_risk: Lowest in the set, essentially nil. Every technology here is a physical pattern in a raster with a measurable consequence on yield, water or erosion. Nothing can be drivel, and the domestication chart (mean yield-gene inside vs outside territory) is the single strongest evidence-of-depth artifact proposed anywhere in these six ideas.
audit.one_change: Fix credit assignment so landscape engineering is reachable: give agents an option layer — a small library of parameterised multi-tick construction routines (dig-a-line-of-length-n-toward-lower-elevation, burn-a-patch-then-return) searched by quality-diversity over spatial-signature descriptors rather than by gradients, so a channel is one decision instead of four hundred. That is the difference between shipping an ecology simulator and shipping a map on which a stranger can see that someone lives there, and it is the same missing layer that limits KINDLING.

all.name: Twelve Anvils
all.pitch: Twelve planets with different physics constants each get a tribe that survives by writing programs in a survival DSL; every night the system compresses its successful programs into new named primitives — those primitives ARE the technologies, and they differ per planet. The product is the comparative atlas: which worlds invented fire, which never could, and what they invented instead.
all.world: Twelve seeded planets, each a hex-globe (icosphere, ~8k cells) with its own PhysicsVector: gravity, day length, atmospheric O2 partial pressure, ignition threshold, water phase boundaries, thermal conductivity of a per-world material table, ore abundance curves, growing-season length, predator pressure. Agents are tribes (population count, kcal store, held materials, known library). Resources are cell-local material stacks with property vectors (hardness, density, melt point, calorific value, toxicity) drawn from the world's material table — so 'flint' on world 3 may be soft, and world 7 has no free O2 so open fire is physically unreachable.
all.invention_engine: DreamCoder wake/sleep, stripped to what one person can build. Data structures: (a) Program = typed lambda term over ~25 base primitives (gather, hold, strike(a,b), heat(x,T), quench, wait(d), plant, weave, carry, if-then over sensed state); (b) Library = list of {name, typed term, MDL cost, usage count, world_id}; (c) TaskSet = survival tasks auto-derived from the world state ('produce >=1800 kcal/person for 14 days at 260K given only cells reachable in 2 days'). WAKE: type-directed bottom-up enumeration with a unigram/bigram prior over library entries, budget measured in NODE EXPANSIONS not wallclock (thermal throttling must never change fitness), plus a local Qwen3.5-4B proposing candidate skeletons that get typechecked and executed against the deterministic world simulator — traceback means retry with the error string, Homunculus-style. SLEEP-ABSTRACTION: greedy MDL compression over the corpus of solutions (simplified Stitch: anti-unify subtrees, score by corpus-bits saved, accept the top candidate, repeat 5x/night). Accepted abstraction gets a name from the local model ('heat(clay,900K)->quench' becomes 'firing') and enters the library permanently. SLEEP-DREAM: sample programs from the library, run them in the world, keep any that produce a novel useful material or surplus — those become new tasks. A civilization's tech = its library. Losing the tribe deletes it.
all.why_unbounded: The search space is the space of typed programs — infinite. What makes it compound rather than merely infinite is that each accepted abstraction rewrites the search distribution: a 12-node program becomes a 3-node program, so the same node budget now reaches depth-40 behaviours it could never enumerate before. That is the same ratchet DreamCoder demonstrated across domains (PLDI 2021), and the abstraction set is not authored by me — I authored only the 25 base primitives and the type system. Twelve different PhysicsVectors mean twelve different compression optima: the libraries provably diverge because the corpus of successful programs differs. Where it actually bottoms out: the abstraction wall. Once the shortest unsolved task needs ~8 more nodes than the budget can enumerate even with the best library, progress stops until the task generator produces an intermediate rung. That is why the changing climate matters — it manufactures intermediate rungs for free.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: 25 primitives, one world, tasks are 'get 1200 kcal'; the library learns 'gather-then-eat' and 'strike(stone,stone)->sharp' and you watch a two-entry library form. Week 2-3: MDL compression starts naming things you did not author — a 'cordage' abstraction that is really weave(strip(bark),twist) appearing on 3 of 12 worlds independently. Month 2: hierarchical entries — 'firing' built on 'sustained-heat' built on 'fuel-stack'; the atlas shows world 7 (no O2) routing around fire entirely via a 'pressure-forge' abstraction using volcanic vents. Month 4: libraries reach depth 6-8 and inter-world comparison gets genuinely interesting — convergence rates per abstraction, 'inventions unique to one world'. Wildest plausible endpoint at a year: a world where an abstraction is discovered, lost in a famine (tribe dies, library dies), and re-derived 4000 sim-years later in a structurally different form, and the novelty detector flags the re-derivation as a near-duplicate at the MDL level but not at the syntax level. That is a real result about convergent evolution of technology that nobody authored.
all.what_selects: Calories, warmth, injury, and childbirth. Each tick a tribe must cover kcal demand (scaled by population and temperature) and survive hazard rolls whose probability the library reduces (a hardness-4 tool cuts butchery time; a shelter cuts cold deaths). Population grows on surplus and crashes on deficit. Below ~40 people, complex library entries start failing transmission rolls and are DELETED — Henrich's Tasmania effect, so technology is genuinely lossy. Between worlds there is no combat (they never meet), so competition is against the planet and against your own past best: each world's fitness is tracked as max sustained population and library MDL depth.
all.changing_worlds: Two layers. Slow: each world runs a Milankovitch-ish climate oscillator (three sine terms with per-world periods and amplitudes) driving temperature bands and sea level, plus a tectonic drift that migrates ore seams and opens/closes mountain passes on a 50k-year cycle. Fast: stochastic catastrophes with per-world rates (bolide, supervolcano, plague, decade drought). The critical design point is that climate change INVALIDATES LIBRARY ENTRIES — an abstraction whose preconditions include 'liquid water in cell' silently stops solving tasks when the cell freezes, which fires a re-search and usually produces a different abstraction. The world is the task generator.
all.novelty_detector: Three signals, combined into one surprise score. (1) FIRST-EVER: every event is emitted with a structured signature (event_type, argument type-hashes); a global seen_signatures table across all twelve worlds means 'first time in the multiverse' is a one-line query. (2) MDL DELTA: when a new abstraction reduces total corpus description length by more than 6%, that is objectively a big idea, not a tweak — this is the best novelty measure in the whole set of ideas because it is a number the compressor already computes. (3) DISTRIBUTION SHOCK: nightly z-score of per-world summary stats (population, library depth, kcal margin) against a 30-night rolling baseline. Push to ntfy only the top 3 by score per day, hard-capped; everything else goes in the chronicle for bingeing.
all.phone_view: Twelve tiles in a 3x4 grid, one per world, each tile: a 40x40 climate sparkline, population number, library depth as a stack of bars, and a one-line 'newest technology: FIRING (day 8,214)'. Red border = a world is dying. Tap a tile for that world's library as a scrollable tree with each entry's discovery date, current usage count, and the exact program text; tap an entry for the three-frame animation of the tribe executing it on the hex map. The daily push is one sentence: 'World 7 compressed a new primitive (-11% corpus MDL): PRESSURE-FORGE. No other world has it.'
all.hardware_use: This one barely needs the GPU, which is why it is the safest first build. The simulator and the program search are pure Python/NumPy and CPU-bound: 12 worlds = 12 worker processes on the laptop's cores, each with its own SQLite file in WAL mode; 64GB RAM is plenty since the biggest object is the program corpus (tens of MB). The 5070's 8GB runs llama.cpp with Qwen3.5-4B-Instruct at Q4_K_M (~3GB weights, tens of tok/s on a laptop Blackwell) for skeleton proposals and naming — called maybe 2k times a night, entirely optional; kill it and the system still works, just searches blinder. Nothing here needs PyTorch, so the sm_120 toolchain risk is zero. Benchmark hygiene: all budgets in node expansions and all costs in simulated days, never seconds.
all.input_cadence: Zero chores. Weekly nudge, 10 minutes: a 'primitive proposals' page shows the 3 abstractions the compressor most wants to accept and lets you veto (rarely needed, but it is the good kind of tinkering); plus a slider to add a 13th world with a physics vector you pick by hand, which is the most fun button in the project.
all.tech: Python 3.12, NumPy, SQLite (one DB per world + multiverse.db for cross-world signatures), msgpack event log, uvicorn+FastAPI serving a vanilla-JS canvas PWA, Tailscale serve for phone access, nightly rsync of a static snapshot to GitHub Pages so it works when the laptop sleeps, ntfy.sh for push. llama.cpp server with GBNF grammar for constrained JSON. Optional: python-escpos to print the daily 'first-ever' events on a thermal receipt printer.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: hex world, 8 materials with property vectors, one tribe, kcal accounting, and the typed DSL with 25 primitives plus an interpreter. Sunday morning: bottom-up enumerative search that solves 'feed the tribe' and logs solutions. Sunday afternoon: the anti-unification compressor — 60 lines, find the most-compressive shared subtree, name it 'skill_001', add to library, re-run search. The delightful moment is watching skill_001's definition print and realising you would have called it 'a cutting tool' and you never typed those words. Sunday night: kick off 12 worlds, wake up to twelve different libraries.
all.six_months_later: Libraries 200-600 entries deep per world with 6-9 levels of nesting; a cross-world convergence matrix showing which abstractions are universal and which are physics-contingent; a graveyard page of technologies lost in population crashes with the exact famine that killed them. You will have rewritten the search prior at least twice (unigram to bigram to a small learned recognition model) and added primitives when the abstraction wall bit. The surprise at month 6 is mostly comparative: not 'they invented X' but 'seven worlds needed X to get to Y and world 4 didn't'.
all.honest_ceiling: It plateaus when enumeration cannot reach the next rung even with a good library — realistically around library depth 8-10, or 3-5 months in, unless you keep feeding it harder tasks. Two honest weaknesses: the base primitive set is mine, so the vocabulary of possible thought is authored even though the abstractions are not (world 7 can only 'route around fire' in ways expressible in 25 primitives); and MDL compression rewards frequent patterns, which is not the same as rewarding important ones — you will get elegant abstractions for boring things. Mitigations exist (weight compression by task value, mint new primitives from LLM-written+tested functions), but be clear that this is a compounding ratchet with friction, not perpetual motion.
all.research_notes: Verified via search: DreamCoder wake-sleep library learning is real and published (PLDI 2021, dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3453483.3454080; NSF PAR 10320121) — abstraction sleep uses refactoring/E-graph matching to extract common sub-components and accepts them by MDL. Stitch formulates library induction as greedy MDL optimisation over a program corpus and is much simpler to reimplement (arXiv 2211.16605, 'Top-Down Synthesis for Library Learning'); LILO (arXiv 2310.19791) shows LLM-assisted variants that also auto-document abstractions, which is where the naming step comes from. TAP / adjacent-possible formalism for combinatorial invention: arXiv 2204.14115 and arXiv 2307.15083. Local model for 8GB: Aug-2026 guides converge on Qwen3.5-4B (or Gemma 3 4B) at Q4_K_M as the standard fit for 8GB VRAM (canitrun.dev/guides/best-llms-for-8gb-vram, atomic.chat/blog/guides/best-local-llm-8gb). Planet-gen priors worth stealing from: github.com/MightyBOBcnc/nixis (Python, icosphere, tectonics+climate+biomes) and github.com/FreezeDriedMangos/realistic-planet-generation-and-simulation.

audit.name: Twelve Anvils
audit.ceiling: Real ratchet, but it stalls far earlier than claimed. The binding constraint is not the enumeration wall they name — it is corpus homogeneity. MDL compression only finds subtrees that RECUR, and every task here is one scalar objective ('get N kcal, don't freeze'). A single-objective task family produces a near-homogeneous solution corpus, so after the first ~10-25 abstractions the marginal corpus-bits-saved collapses and their own 6% MDL-delta trigger stops firing. Expect a library of 15-40 entries at nesting depth 3-4, flat by week 3-6 — not '200-600 entries at depth 6-9 by month 6'. Second wall behind it: each accepted abstraction buys a constant-factor reduction on the exact pattern compressed, not an exponential; type-directed bottom-up enumeration on ~1 core/world reaches maybe 10^6-10^7 nodes/night, i.e. effective program size ~12-16 nodes. Climate invalidation manufactures re-search, but re-search over the same primitive set and the same kcal objective mostly re-derives cousins of existing entries — which their own novelty detector will correctly flag as MDL near-duplicates, and that is a ceiling symptom being reported as a headline result.
audit.authored_content_risk: The abstractions are genuinely not authored — this is the least fake discovery in the set. But the SEMANTICS are fully authored: the 25 primitives, the type system, and above all the world simulator's material-transformation table. 'Fire' is discoverable only because someone wrote combustion into heat(); world 7's 'pressure-forge' is discoverable only because someone wrote vent chemistry. So library depth is bounded by the depth of the authored state space, and the depth ladder's late rungs (writing, trade, institutions) have no representation at all — nothing in the DSL can express them, so 'eventually something wild' is unreachable by construction, not by search budget. The honest framing is: the abstractions are found, the vocabulary of possible thought and the set of reachable world-states are both hand-written.
audit.compute_honesty: Mostly honest, one significant understatement. Hashing-free pure-Python/NumPy sim and SQLite are fine, and putting budgets in node expansions rather than wallclock is the right call. But 'barely needs the GPU / it is the safest first build' hides that DreamCoder's cost is CPU enumeration, and the published experiments used tens of cores per domain for hours-to-days per wake cycle. Twelve worlds on one laptop means roughly one core per world — order 1-2% of a single published DreamCoder domain run, and Python-interpreted enumeration is another 10-50x behind their OCaml enumerator. The wake phase will be starved, which is exactly the regime where the ratchet does not start. The LLM side is genuinely optional and cheap (~2k Qwen-class calls/night at Q4_K_M fits 8GB easily).
audit.dubious_claims: Sourcing is unusually good; the problems are misuse, not fabrication. (a) 'the abstraction set is not authored by me' is true but oversold — see above. (b) Stitch is described as 'greedy MDL optimisation'; it is a top-down branch-and-bound/beam search over abstraction space, and the 60-line anti-unification weekend version will be materially weaker than either Stitch or DreamCoder's version-space refactoring. (c) The Henrich/Tasmania 'complex entries fail transmission below ~40 people' mechanism is presented as settled; the population-size-drives-complexity result is contested (Vaesen et al. 2016 PNAS; Read's critiques) and here it is a designer-set knob that directly caps depth. (d) DreamCoder is cited as evidence of a compounding ratchet 'across domains' — true, but always with a human-authored, difficulty-ordered task curriculum, which is precisely the ingredient this design replaces with a calorie threshold. That substitution is the whole risk and the notes do not acknowledge it.
audit.semantic_risk: Low-moderate, and the lowest in the set. Every abstraction executes against a deterministic simulator, so entries mean something mechanically. Two leaks: the 4B model's names are flattering fiction over terms like (lambda (strike x x)) and will make a shallow library read as deep — log the term next to the name always; and their own admission that MDL rewards frequency not importance is correct and severe (you will get an elegant abstraction for 'walk two cells then pick up').
audit.one_change: Replace the calorie-threshold task generator with an autotelic goal generator over the world's state space — goals as unreached regions of the material-property / settlement / population-structure space, with each accepted abstraction seeding new goals that use it as a precondition. Corpus heterogeneity, not search budget, is what keeps MDL delta above zero; this is the single change that converts a 1-D curriculum into an open one and it is where the whole ceiling lives.

all.name: Ashfall Chemistries
all.pitch: Every planet is seeded with its own deterministic pseudo-random chemistry — a hash function that says what happens when you combine any two substances under any conditions — and tribes discover it by experiment, building recipe DAGs that are their technology. No LLM in the loop and no authored recipe table, so a hundred thousand substances per world costs nothing but CPU.
all.world: Six to twelve planets, each a 256x128 equirect grid with elevation, temperature, precipitation, and a crust composed of ~40 primitive substances whose abundance map is generated per world (volcanic worlds are metal-rich and sulfur-heavy; a water world hides everything under ocean). A substance is an integer id plus a 16-dim property vector: hardness, density, melt point, boil point, calorific value, conductivity, toxicity, reactivity, opacity, tensile strength, elasticity, solubility, magnetism, radioactivity, nutrition, decay rate. Tribes are villages with population, stores, a kiln/hearth with a max attainable temperature, and a personal recipe DAG. Everything a civilization can physically do is: bring substances together at some temperature, pressure, and duration, with or without a catalyst.
all.invention_engine: A keyed artificial chemistry plus an experiment scheduler. react(world_seed, sorted(a,b), temp_bucket, pressure_bucket, catalyst) = BLAKE2b hash -> a deterministic branch: 65% no reaction, 20% mixture (property vector = mass-weighted blend), 10% new compound (property vector = a NONLINEAR mix — element-wise blend plus a hash-seeded rotation matrix and a hash-seeded 'emergent bonus' on 1-2 dims), 5% decomposition into fragments. Because it is a hash, the chemistry is infinite, deterministic, reproducible from a 64-bit seed, requires zero storage until discovered, and is DIFFERENT ON EVERY PLANET. Discovery: each village runs an experiment scheduler — a UCB bandit over untried (pair, condition) cells, scored by expected information gain and by proximity to an unmet need ('we need hardness>6', 'we need something that burns above 900K'). Successful reactions are appended to a recipe DAG in SQLite. A technology is a named sub-DAG that reliably produces a substance crossing a need threshold. Two special detectors run nightly: AUTOCATALYTIC SET DETECTION (find cycles in the DAG where a product is a catalyst for its own precursors — this is the moment a craft becomes an industry, and it is a graph query, not a vibe) and PROPERTY FRONTIER tracking (a pyribs MAP-Elites archive whose behaviour dims are hardness x melt point x calorific value; a substance that lands in an empty cell is genuinely new capability).
all.why_unbounded: The reachable substance graph branches at roughly (discovered substances choose 2) x condition buckets per generation, so the frontier grows super-exponentially in the TAP sense — Kauffman's adjacent possible with an efficiency factor. Crucially the space is not authored: I write the mixing function, not the products, and the seed makes each world's chemistry a different draw from the same generative law. Where it honestly bottoms out: hash chemistry is unbounded in COUNT but flat in MEANING — substance #91,000 is not more interesting than #900 unless deep combinations are systematically better. The design fix, and you must build it deliberately: emergent bonuses are only granted to products whose precursor DAG is deeper than the current median, and need thresholds escalate with population and cold, so the civilization is always chasing a property value it cannot reach with shallow recipes. With that, depth is selected for. Without it, you get a very large pile of grey sludge, and I'd rather say that up front.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: 40 substances, one village, random pairwise experiments; you watch the first compound get discovered and named by property ('a hard, dense, high-melt solid'). Week 2: needs and thresholds — the village that finds hardness>5 gets better tools and outgrows its neighbour. Month 1: multi-step recipes and the first kiln temperature ceiling, so an entire branch of chemistry is gated behind discovering a better fuel — the first real tech-gate the system generated itself. Month 2: autocatalytic cycle detected; a substance whose production catalyses its own precursor means the village can mass-produce, population doubles, and the event is worth a push notification with a graph picture. Month 3-4: cross-planet comparison — 'metallurgy' (a cluster in property space) is reached on 5 of 8 worlds by wildly different DAGs, and on the sulfur world the equivalent cluster is reached through what is functionally biochemistry. Wildest plausible endpoint: a world discovers a substance with high calorific value AND low decay, i.e. storable fuel, which decouples them from the growing season entirely and produces a visible hockey-stick in their recipe count — self-generated industrial revolution from a hash function.
all.what_selects: Villages compete for grid cells with the substances they need. Fitness is population supported, which depends on tools (hardness), warmth (calorific value + shelter), food preservation (decay rate), and defence. Villages fight or trade on contact; a village with better material properties wins raids and absorbs the loser's recipe DAG (partial — 30-60% of entries transmit, weighted by how many people knew them). Starvation deletes recipes: any recipe not executed within N years and known by fewer than K people is forgotten. Between planets there is no contact; the competition there is your own dashboard leaderboard.
all.changing_worlds: Geology gates chemistry, and geology moves. Ice ages (a global temperature oscillator with per-world period and amplitude) change what temperature a hearth can reach ambient-relative and freeze water-mediated reactions entirely; sea level change exposes or drowns mineral-rich shelf cells; volcanism spawns high-temperature, high-pressure vent cells that unlock a condition bucket no hearth can reach, making volcano-adjacent villages temporarily the most advanced on the planet until the eruption kills them. Tectonic collision raises mountains that expose new crust layers with substances absent from the surface for 10,000 years. Migration matters concretely: the same chemistry hash is global to the planet, but ABUNDANCE is local, so moving to a new continent means a different reachable subgraph.
all.novelty_detector: MAP-Elites archive occupancy is the primary signal and it is beautifully cheap: a new substance that fills a previously empty cell of the hardness x melt-point x calorific-value grid is genuinely new capability, and 'cells filled' is a single number per world you can plot forever. Secondary: first-ever autocatalytic cycle, first-ever recipe of depth N, first cross-planet convergence (two worlds independently reach the same archive cell), and a substance whose property vector is Pareto-non-dominated by everything discovered anywhere. Nightly ranking pushes the top 2. Everything else is chronicle.
all.phone_view: A 2x4 grid of planets; each tile is that planet's MAP-Elites archive rendered as a tiny heatmap — literally a picture of how much of the possible-materials space that civilization has illuminated, filling up over months. Under it: population, recipe count, deepest recipe. Tap through to a scrollable substance codex sorted by discovery date with property bars and the DAG path that made it, plus a 'reactions tried / reactions that did something' ratio which is the civilization's science efficiency. Push text: 'Ashfall-3 filled a new frontier cell: hardness 8.2, melts at 1740K, made from 6 steps starting with river silt.'
all.hardware_use: Pure CPU, and that is a feature: 8-12 worlds as separate Python processes with NumPy for the grid layers, hash chemistry via hashlib/BLAKE2b (fast enough at millions of calls per night), pyribs for archives, SQLite per world. 64GB RAM lets you keep every discovered substance and every experiment result in memory. The GPU is free for other projects, or optionally runs a 4B local model purely to write flavour names and codex prose for discovered substances (cached forever, keyed by substance id) — pure garnish, removable.
all.input_cadence: Effectively none. Monthly, if you feel like it: mint a new planet by choosing an abundance profile and a chemistry seed, or hand-place a 'need' (declare that this world's winters now demand insulation) and watch the experiment scheduler re-aim. There is also an irresistible optional toy: a web page where visitors pick two substances from a world's codex and the result of their experiment is injected as a wandering-stranger event.
all.tech: Python 3.12, NumPy, hashlib.blake2b, pyribs for MAP-Elites, SQLite WAL, networkx (or hand-rolled) for cycle detection in the recipe DAG, FastAPI + vanilla-JS canvas PWA, Tailscale, GitHub Pages static mirror, ntfy.sh. Sonification option: map each planet's archive occupancy to a drone chord and each discovery to a plucked note via sounddevice — leave it playing in the room; you hear industrialisation as the note density rises.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: grid world, 40 substances with property vectors, the hash reaction function, and a village with needs. Sunday: the bandit experiment scheduler, the recipe DAG in SQLite, and a codex page. The moment: you set hardness threshold 5 for good tools, walk away for an hour, come back and the village has a four-step recipe involving heating a mineral you never thought about with a plant ash you added as a decoration, and it works because the hash said so and the property blend crossed the line.
all.six_months_later: Eight planets with 20k-200k discovered substances each, archives visibly different in shape, several autocatalytic industries, at least one civilization that industrialised and one that got stuck for 50,000 years because its crust lacked a high-calorific fuel and never broke the kiln temperature ceiling. The comparative page — 'which property frontiers are universally reachable and which are planet-locked' — is the artifact you show people.
all.honest_ceiling: Two real limits. First, meaningfulness saturates: without the depth-gated emergent bonus and escalating needs, discovery count keeps rising while nothing important happens, and you will feel that around week 3 if you skip the fix. Second, there is no agency in the invention itself — the bandit is a good searcher but nobody is REASONING about chemistry, so you never get the satisfying 'they had a theory' moment. You can bolt on a theory layer (villages fit a linear model predicting product properties from precursors and use it to aim experiments; a village with a good model outcompetes one without, and you can literally watch science emerge as predictive accuracy) — that is the single best extension and it is maybe two weekends. Even so, this plateaus as a materials-discovery sim, not a full civilization.
all.research_notes: Verified: TAP / adjacent-possible combinatorial innovation math (arXiv 2204.14115, 'The TAP equation: evaluating combinatorial innovation'; arXiv 2307.15083 'Reaction Diffusion TAP') — these give the actual growth equations for 'new things made from combinations of old things with an efficiency factor', including the hockey-stick regime. Autocatalytic-set framing traces to Kauffman and is well covered in the ALife literature; Flow-Lenia (MIT Press Artificial Life 31(2), 2025, Plantec/Hamon/Etcheverry/Chan/Oudeyer/Moulin-Frier) is the current state of the art for intrinsic open-ended evolution in continuous CA and is worth reading for how they force mass conservation to keep the sim honest — the same discipline (conserve mass across reactions) makes this idea's economy real. MAP-Elites/QD tooling: pyribs (bare-bones Python QD library) is the right choice on CPU; QDax (JMLR v25, 23-1027) is the JAX one if you later go GPU. Infinite Craft's caching trick (store every combination result so the same pair always yields the same output) is documented on its Wikipedia page and reimplemented in github.com/bufferhead-code/opencraft and github.com/sshh12/llm_alchemy — this idea replaces the LLM with a hash and keeps the determinism.

audit.name: Ashfall Chemistries
audit.ceiling: Count is unbounded; meaning stops in week 2-4 and the design already knows it. The fatal detail is that the author's own fix is the disease: 'emergent bonuses are only granted to products whose precursor DAG is deeper than the current median' means every expansion of the property frontier is produced by a designer-written depth reward. Strip that clause and the frontier saturates almost immediately, because the stated composition rule (mass-weighted blend + hash-seeded rotation) is a contraction toward the corpus mean with isotropic noise — repeated blending regresses properties inward, so deep chains are on average LESS extreme than shallow ones. So: with the bonus, the tech tree is a hand-authored difficulty gradient wearing a hash costume; without it, the MAP-Elites archive fills its reachable envelope in days and then nothing happens for six months. Concretely: hardness/melt/calorific archive occupancy plateaus within the first week or two of real running, and substance count keeps climbing into the hundreds of thousands as pure decoration.
audit.authored_content_risk: Inverted from the usual failure. The products are not authored, but they are also not meaningful, so what carries the appearance of a tech tree is the authored part: need thresholds, the escalation schedule, the depth-gated bonus, the kiln-temperature gate. Those four hand-tuned curves are the tech tree. 'Metallurgy reached on 5 of 8 worlds' is a statement about a labelled region of a property grid, not about a technology — nothing in the sim distinguishes a bronze age from a substance whose hardness float crossed 6.
audit.compute_honesty: Fully honest — the best of the six on this axis. BLAKE2b at millions of calls/night is trivial, pyribs archives are cheap, 8-12 CPU processes and SQLite are well within one laptop, and the GPU is genuinely unused. No hidden datacenter, no API bill. The compute plan is the only part of this idea that does exactly what it says.
audit.dubious_claims: (a) TAP is misused. The TAP equation counts combinations of existing things; its hockey stick is a statement about cardinality, not about usefulness or depth. Citing it as the unboundedness argument is exactly the count-vs-meaning conflation the idea then admits to. (b) Flow-Lenia's mass conservation is invoked to make 'the economy real' — Flow-Lenia conserves mass in a continuous CA to prevent pattern blow-up; it is not evidence that a hash chemistry with conserved mass produces meaningful technology, and Flow-Lenia itself demonstrates open-ended pattern evolution, not open-ended invention. (c) Infinite Craft is cited for the caching trick, correctly, but its actual observed behaviour — rapid convergence to absurd noun soup — is evidence against this design's semantics and goes unmentioned. (d) The proposed best extension ('villages fit a linear model predicting product properties from precursors, and you watch science emerge') is close to provably weak in this design: the hash-seeded rotation is engineered to destroy exactly the precursor→product mutual information a linear model would need. You have built an unlearnable universe and then proposed learning as the headline upgrade.
audit.semantic_risk: Highest in the set. A 16-dim vector blended through a random rotation has no compositional structure, so there is no fact of the matter about what any substance IS. The DAG is real, the properties are real numbers, and none of it composes into a technology; substance #91,000 differs from #900 only in bonus tag. The autocatalytic-cycle detector is a graph query that will fire on hash coincidences and be narrated as 'a craft became an industry'.
audit.one_change: Delete the hash and give the chemistry compositional structure: a few dozen typed element tokens, conserved stoichiometry, and a small randomly-seeded rule algebra so a product's property vector is a deterministic FUNCTION of its composition and conditions. Then products are predictable in principle (theory formation becomes possible and can be selected for), depth means structural distance rather than a bonus tag, and you can drop the authored depth reward entirely — which is the only way this stops being an authored gradient.

all.name: Winterforge
all.pitch: The planet is an adversary with a learning algorithm: an ACCEL-style level editor mutates geology and climate specifically to maximise the tribe's regret, while the tribe is a neural policy trained across thousands of GPU-parallel worlds. Technology here is the set of open-ended crafting recipes a lineage reliably reproduces and teaches, and the world's whole job is to break them.
all.world: A JAX gridworld in the Craftax lineage: 64x64 tiles, biomes, seasons, day/night, resources, hazards, and a tribe of 4-16 embodied agents with hunger, warmth, health, and an inventory. The world is defined by a level vector (elevation seeds, biome bands, resource density per type, glacier extent, monsoon phase, predator density, catastrophe schedule) that is fully mutable — that vector is what the adversary edits. Thousands of these worlds run simultaneously on the GPU as a batched tensor; a 'civilization' is a lineage of policy weights plus a recipe book that survives across level mutations.
all.invention_engine: Two layers, deliberately hybrid because pure RL is bad at long invention chains and I will not pretend otherwise. (1) OPEN CRAFTING: there is no recipe table. craft(item_a, item_b, verb, station, temperature) returns an item whose 8-dim attribute vector is a deterministic procedural composition (hash-seeded matrix blend, with the station and verb selecting the blend operator) plus a validity test — most combinations return junk. So the recipe space is combinatorial and untabulated exactly like Ashfall's chemistry, but embodied. (2) DISCOVERY: a symbolic experiment layer sitting above the RL policy — each tribe holds a small MCTS/bandit over craft attempts using items it currently possesses, weighted by unmet need; discovered recipes go in the lineage's recipe book, and the RL policy is conditioned on the book (recipes as an embedding set), so learning to USE technology is RL's job and FINDING it is search's job. That split is the design's whole trick. (3) THE ADVERSARY: an ACCEL/PLR-style level buffer scored by positive value loss as a regret proxy; the top-regret levels get mutated by geological edit operators (raise range, shift monsoon 30 degrees, advance glacier, delete an ore type, schedule a bolide at step 4000) and the mutants go back in the buffer. The teacher therefore learns which catastrophes actually hurt this civilization, which is the most viscerally 'the world is the antagonist' mechanic available.
all.why_unbounded: Two separate unbounded-ish spaces multiplied together: the craft-composition space (combinatorial in items x verbs x stations, and items are themselves craftable, so recipe DEPTH is unbounded) and the level space (continuous level vector under unlimited mutation, which is the standard UED premise that a teacher can generate an infinite curriculum). The honest part: RL policies in 8GB are small, and small policies plateau at a competence ceiling regardless of how open the environment is. The invention space is vast; the AGENT'S reach into it is the binding constraint, and it is the reason the symbolic experiment layer exists. Also honest: procedural attribute composition is combinatorially vast but semantically shallow — an item is 8 floats, and there are only so many ways 8 floats matter. Depth comes from chains and gating, not from the attribute space itself.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: Craftax-style env running batched, one tribe, hand-picked levels, PPO learning to eat and not freeze. Week 2: open crafting swapped in for the recipe table plus the bandit experiment layer; the tribe finds a two-item recipe you never wrote. Month 1: PLR level buffer with regret scoring — you see the curriculum auto-order itself from easy to brutal, which is the first genuinely uncanny moment. Month 2: ACCEL mutations, so the world starts targeting the tribe's dependencies: they lean on a fuel type, the editor deletes that ore, and the recipe book has to route around it. Month 3-4: lineage persistence and teaching — recipe books transmit imperfectly between tribes, and you get technology loss under population stress.
