Wildest plausible endpoint: a documented arms race where the editor's mutation distribution visibly co-evolves with the recipe book — a plot of 'which world edit was most damaging' over time that shows the planet learning to attack whatever the civilization most recently invented.
all.what_selects: Direct survival: freeze, starve, get eaten, or persist. Regret (value-loss) selects LEVELS, not agents. Agents are selected by episodic return and lineage survival; recipe entries are selected by usage — an entry unused for K episodes and known by <2 tribes is dropped. Across the batch, lineages compete for a fixed number of persistent slots, so a lineage that solves harder levels displaces one that only handles easy worlds.
all.changing_worlds: This idea's non-stationarity is the point and it operates at three timescales: within-episode seasons and weather; across-episode level mutation from the ACCEL editor (the slow geological pressure); and a scheduled 'era shift' every N million steps where the base generator's priors change wholesale (an ice age era where all levels are colder, a greenhouse era, a volcanic era). Additionally I would run 4 divergent BRANCHES from the same lineage checkpoint under different era schedules — that is the multiple-worlds product here: same starting civilization, four climate futures, compare their technology books at the end. That is a real comparative experiment and it is exactly what UED tooling makes cheap.
all.novelty_detector: First-ever recipe signatures (hash of the item-attribute-cluster produced, so functionally-equivalent rediscoveries collapse); recipes of record depth; the regret ranking itself ('the world found a new way to hurt them' — a mutation operator that jumps to the top of the regret buffer for the first time is a great notification); and behaviour-descriptor novelty via a QD archive over (calorie strategy, mobility, aggression, tech depth) so a lineage occupying a new cell is flagged. Rate-limited to the top 2 per night.
all.phone_view: A live 'regret weather map': four branch worlds side by side, each showing the current top-regret level as a tiny rendered map thumbnail, the tribe's survival rate as a big number, tech-book depth, and what the editor changed most recently ('advanced the glacier 12 tiles'). Tap for a 6-second replay GIF of the most surprising episode of the night, pre-rendered at 4am so the phone never renders anything. Push: 'Branch C lost fire: the editor deleted surface coal and survival fell 41% in one generation. They have not recovered.'
all.hardware_use: This is the GPU-heaviest idea and the one where 8GB actually bites. Realistic plan: JAX with a small CNN policy (<2M params), 1024-4096 parallel envs, batched PPO — Craftax reports enormous throughput for exactly this shape of workload, and the bottleneck at 8GB is activation memory for the rollout buffer, so keep rollout length modest (128) and observations small (symbolic local view, not pixels). Expect single-digit-hours per meaningful training run, which fits the overnight rhythm perfectly. Real risk to check on day one: jaxlib CUDA wheels on Blackwell sm_120 — PyTorch got stable sm_120 wheels from 2.7 with CUDA 12.8, and JAX CUDA12 wheels generally work on recent drivers, but VERIFY with a two-line matmul before building anything, and have the fallback ready (drop to a smaller CPU-side env count, or port the env to PyTorch which definitely supports sm_120).
all.input_cadence: Weekly: glance at the regret buffer and optionally hand-author one nasty level to inject (this is fun and takes two minutes). Monthly: fork a new branch with a different era schedule. Otherwise nothing; runs continuously.
all.tech: Python, JAX + Flax + Optax, PureJaxRL-style PPO, env written from scratch in the Craftax mould (do not fork it — the brief wants a from-scratch world, and writing a JAX gridworld is a genuinely good learning arc), level buffer with prioritised replay by positive value loss, SQLite for lineage/recipe/event history, offline GIF rendering with Pillow, FastAPI + PWA, Tailscale, ntfy.sh. Benchmark hygiene: all comparisons in environment steps and gradient steps, never wallclock; log GPU clocks and temperature alongside runs so a thermally throttled night is visible in the chronicle rather than silently polluting a comparison.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: the JAX env — grid, resources, hunger, temperature, batched step function, and a random policy running 1024 worlds at once (seeing that number scroll is its own reward). Sunday: PPO from PureJaxRL patterns, plus the open-craft composition function. The first delightful moment is smaller than in the other ideas and arrives later — realistically end of week 2 when the level buffer starts ordering the curriculum by itself. Be honest with yourself that this is the slowest ramp of the six.
all.six_months_later: Four branch civilizations with divergent recipe books shaped by their climate era, a regret history showing the editor's evolving attack strategy, and a set of held-out 'exam' levels the lineages are periodically tested on so capability growth is measurable rather than vibes. You will also have a real RL debugging skillset, which is either a bonus or a warning depending on your mood.
all.honest_ceiling: The hard ceiling is agent capability: a 2M-param policy on 8GB will learn foraging, shelter, seasonal migration, and short tool chains, and will not learn 12-step technological reasoning no matter how open the crafting space is — that gap is why the symbolic layer carries the invention load, and it means the 'civilization' is thinner than in the symbolic ideas. Expect the interesting curve to flatten around month 3 without a redesign. Also: RL is the least debuggable thing here; a bug and a plateau look identical for days. Pick this one only if you actively want to learn JAX/RL — as a pure product bet, ideas 1, 2, or 5 dominate it.
all.research_notes: Verified: Craftax (arXiv 2402.16801, craftaxenv.github.io) is a JAX open-ended RL benchmark reporting 169-257x speedups over CPU Crafter with an end-to-end GPU pipeline via PureJaxRL — that establishes the throughput claim. Multi-Agent Craftax exists too (arXiv 2511.04904) if tribes-as-multiple-agents appeals. Kinetix (arXiv 2410.23208) is the open-ended physics-task-space cousin and its level-mutation machinery is the closest published template for a geological editor. UED background: PLR/ACCEL regret-based curricula, plus current work — 'Efficient Unsupervised Environment Design through Hierarchical Policy Representation Learning' (arXiv 2602.09813), 'Improving Regret Approximation for Unsupervised Dynamic Environment Generation' (arXiv 2601.14957), and 'Imagined Autocurricula' (arXiv 2509.13341) which induces UED curricula over world-model-generated worlds. JaxLife (arXiv 2409.00853, github.com/luchris429/JaxLife) is the single most relevant precedent for this exact fantasy: JAX-native embodied agents evolving with programmable Turing-complete 'robots', reported to show rudimentary communication, agriculture, and tool use. Hardware: PyTorch stable sm_120/CUDA 12.8 wheels from 2.7 onward (pytorch/pytorch issue #164342); Unsloth documents Blackwell/RTX 50 fine-tuning with TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0.

audit.name: Winterforge
audit.ceiling: Two ceilings arrive before the interesting part. (1) The invention carrier is the symbolic bandit over hash-composed crafts — 8 floats, procedural blend, validity test — which is Ashfall's shallow space with less room, so the same meaning-saturation applies within weeks. (2) The RL side plateaus where Craftax says it plateaus: the paper's own headline is that PPO baselines reach only a small fraction of achievements after ~1e9 steps on the full benchmark, and long-horizon credit assignment is the named open problem. Their honest_ceiling says 'flattens around month 3'; the more likely story is that a 2M-param policy on a from-scratch env plateaus on forage/shelter/short-chain within the first few overnight runs, and everything after is debugging. There is also a third, non-stationarity ceiling nobody flags: PPO against an ACCEL-mutated level distribution AND a growing recipe-book conditioning set AND scheduled era shifts is three simultaneous distribution shifts; catastrophic forgetting will make capability curves non-monotone and indistinguishable from bugs.
audit.authored_content_risk: Moderate on invention (craft composition and validity are procedural, not tabulated) but high on narrative. 'The planet learns to attack whatever you invented' is a misreading of the mechanism: positive value loss is a learnability/regret PROXY that scores levels where the critic is wrong — it does not identify dependencies. Worse, an edit operator like 'delete an ore type' can make levels unsolvable, and PVL happily ranks unsolvable levels high, which is the classic regret-proxy collapse mode. The evocative plot 'which world edit was most damaging over time' will largely be a plot of where the value function was undertrained. The story is authored even though the levels are not.
audit.compute_honesty: The least honest of the six, in a specific and checkable way. Craftax's 169-257x figure comes from an end-to-end jitted pipeline where the ENTIRE env step is a pure tensor op. This design bolts a per-tribe MCTS/bandit over craft attempts, a growing per-lineage recipe book, lineage bookkeeping and SQLite writes on top. None of that is jittable as described; if any of it runs host-side per-env-per-step across 1024-4096 envs, throughput drops by two to three orders of magnitude and 'single-digit hours per meaningful run' becomes weeks. 8GB is survivable for a small CNN at rollout 128 with symbolic obs, but XLA fragmentation plus a growing recipe-embedding set will bite. Also unaddressed: the batch is the parallelism, so 'four divergent branches' quarters an already-marginal step budget. Day-one sm_120 verification is the right instinct but it is the smallest risk here.
audit.dubious_claims: (a) Craftax cited for throughput while its capability result — which directly contradicts the depth pitch — is omitted. (b) JaxLife is cited as showing 'rudimentary communication, agriculture, and tool use'; those are small-scale qualitative observations in a preprint, generously labelled, and are not evidence that this shape of system produces technology chains. (c) UED references check out (2410.23208 Kinetix, 2402.16801 Craftax, 2511.04904 Multi-Agent Craftax, 2602.09813 all real), but ACCEL's published wins are on navigation/physics task spaces with solvable-by-construction mutations, not on 'delete a resource type from an economy'. (d) 'the recipe book as an embedding set conditions the policy' is asserted, not argued; a 2M-param CNN will functionally ignore a set input that grows into the hundreds.
audit.semantic_risk: High. An item is 8 floats; a station and verb pick a blend operator; 'most combinations return junk'. Nothing about a depth-9 item is qualitatively different from a depth-2 item, so recipe DEPTH is bookkeeping, not capability. Embodiment adds physical plausibility to USING items, which is real, but it does not make the item space mean anything.
audit.one_change: Cut PPO entirely. Keep the JAX env and the ACCEL editor, and make the tribe a search/planning agent (MCTS over craft+act against the simulator) rather than a policy network. You immediately get a capability you can measure, deepen and debug; the adversary then attacks a real dependency structure instead of a critic's error; and you stop paying the throughput tax that the symbolic layer imposes on the jitted pipeline. If you want to learn JAX/RL, that is a legitimate reason to build this — but say that out loud, because as a depth bet it is dominated by ideas 1 and 5.

all.name: The Ninefold Constitution
all.pitch: Nine worlds, each with its own procedurally written laws of physics, and a local 4B model adjudicates every novel invention against that world's constitution plus its own case law of prior rulings. Identical ideas resolve differently on different worlds — fire burns violet and eats salt on world 4 — and every ruling is cached forever, so the unbounded space costs almost nothing.
all.world: Nine planets. Each has (a) a CONSTITUTION: ~300 tokens of procedurally composed physical law drawn from a generator over clause templates with randomized constants ('liquid water boils at 340K here', 'metals are brittle below 300K', 'no free oxygen; combustion requires the sulfur cycle', 'the long night lasts 90 days'), and (b) a machine-readable shadow of that constitution as typed constants the engine actually simulates. Terrain, climate, and resources are generated consistently with those constants. Inhabitants are tribes with population, needs (kcal, warmth, safety, water), a settlement, and an inventory of INVENTIONS — each invention being a named thing with a typed effect record the engine executes every tick.
all.invention_engine: LLM-as-physics, but fenced so the engine never loses coherence. A tribe proposes an experiment: ingredients (things it has), a method verb, a station, conditions. The adjudicator prompt = world constitution + the k=6 nearest PRECEDENTS retrieved by embedding similarity from that world's ruling table (case law: the model sees how it ruled on similar attempts before, which is what actually keeps a small model consistent) + the proposal. Output is constrained by a GBNF/JSON schema to a typed EFFECT RECORD: {name, description, requires:[typed preconditions], produces:[resource deltas], modifies:[need_multipliers], durability, failure_modes}. The engine typechecks it, sanity-bounds the numbers, and only then admits it. Every ruling is cached in SQLite keyed by (constitution_hash, sorted ingredients, method, station, condition bucket) so it is computed exactly once ever and is deterministic thereafter — the Infinite Craft trick. The escape hatch from 'effects can only be what my grammar expresses': a tribe that reaches sufficient sophistication can trigger a MECHANISM proposal where the model writes an actual small Python function (sandboxed, fixed signature, must pass generated property tests: conserves mass, terminates, monotone where declared) that becomes a new engine-level effect primitive — Homunculus's tested-skill loop, but the skill is a law of nature and the tribe that funded it owns it.
all.why_unbounded: The proposal space is natural language over an ever-growing set of held things, which is combinatorially open in the strict sense — this is the Infinite Craft argument, and caching makes it affordable. Two things keep it from being noise: the constitution makes rulings world-specific (so the same combination is nine different technologies across the multiverse), and the effect grammar makes every ruling mechanically executable, so an invention either helps the tribe survive or it does not, and the engine decides that, not the model. The grammar is the real ceiling — mechanical novelty is capped by what the effect language can express — which is exactly why the mechanism-proposal escape hatch matters: it lets the model extend the effect language itself, with tests, which is a genuine unbounded ratchet on top of a bounded one. Honest failure mode: LLM drift toward generic fantasy nouns. Precedent retrieval plus the mass/energy sanity checker fights it; it does not fully win.
all.depth_ladder: Weekend 1: one world, hardcoded constitution, 12 starting resources, local model adjudicating combinations into effect JSON, tribe survives or starves. Week 2: nine constitutions generated, nine caches, and the first delicious divergence — 'clay+fire' rules differently on the sulfur world. Month 1: precedent retrieval kills the consistency problem and you can read a world's ruling log as a coherent legal history. Month 2: needs escalate with climate, so inventions must chain (the model starts requiring a tool from a prior ruling as a precondition, unprompted, because the precedents taught it to). Month 3: mechanism proposals — the model writes and passes tests on a new effect primitive, e.g. a preservation mechanic nobody's grammar had. Month 4+: the constitutions AMEND (see changing worlds) and whole invention branches are invalidated. Wildest plausible endpoint: nine complete divergent technological histories readable as nine books, with a cross-world index showing which inventions are constitution-independent (universal) and which are contingent — plus a handful of engine primitives that were written by the system, tested, and are now part of your simulator's physics.
all.what_selects: Needs vs supply, per tick, per tribe. An invention only spreads if executing its effect record improves the tribe's survival margin; useless inventions are recorded in the codex as curiosities and never used again (and the codex of failed inventions is one of the funniest pages). Tribes on the same world compete for territory and trade inventions; a conquered tribe's codex is partially absorbed. Population collapse deletes inventions not written down — and 'writing down' is itself an invention the model can rule into existence, which is a delightful bootstrap.
all.changing_worlds: Constitutions AMEND on a slow schedule: every few sim-millennia one clause mutates (the sun dims by 8%, the ocean acidifies, the long night lengthens) and every cached ruling whose preconditions touch the changed clause is invalidated and re-adjudicated lazily. Technologies stop working, and the tribes must re-derive. Layered on top: normal climate cycles, migration, and island isolation (a tribe cut off by sea level develops a divergent codex from the same world's constitution — allopatric technological divergence within a world, which is a nice second-order effect). Public perturbation: the web page lets anonymous visitors leave one line in a guestbook; nightly, the highest-voted line is injected into one world as an OMEN, prepended to that world's adjudication prompts for a day ('the sky spoke of iron'), which measurably tilts what gets invented and slowly accretes into that world's scripture. Cheap non-stationarity and the best reason for the artifact to be public.
all.novelty_detector: Cache-miss rate is the baseline heartbeat (a world whose miss rate spikes is doing something new). Ranked novelty combines: embedding distance of a new invention from every prior invention on that world and across all nine; whether its effect record is Pareto-non-dominated on the need axes; first-ever precondition depth; and any accepted mechanism proposal (always pushed — a new law of nature is always news). Contradiction detection runs weekly: a cheap hosted model audits sampled ruling pairs for inconsistency, and contradictions become an in-world event ('the laws were revised') rather than a bug report, which is a lovely way to turn model error into content.
all.phone_view: Nine cards, each showing the world's one-line constitutional summary, tribe count, and the single newest invention with its emoji and effect summary ('SALT-SMOKE RACK — preserves meat 40 days, requires hardness-3 blade + sustained low heat'). A 'divergence bar' shows how far this world's codex has drifted from the multiverse median. Tap into a world for the codex (chronological, searchable), the ruling log (its case law), the amendment history, and the scripture page of accreted visitor omens. Push: one line, at most three a day, always naming the world.
all.hardware_use: Comfortable fit. llama.cpp serving Qwen3.5-4B-Instruct at Q4_K_M (~3GB) with a GBNF grammar for the effect schema leaves headroom on 8GB for a small embedding model (bge-small/gte-small, ~130MB) used for precedent retrieval — both resident simultaneously. Nine world simulators are CPU processes and near-free. Throughput reality: expect tens of tokens/sec, so budget adjudications rather than spamming them — a few thousand per night is plenty, and the cache means the steady-state miss rate falls fast (that decay curve is itself a plot worth watching). Hosted models are optional and cheap: with the Aug-2026 price floor around $0.10-0.20 per million input tokens for small models, the weekly contradiction audit and the occasional high-stakes ruling run to single-digit dollars a month; you can also run zero-cost by keeping everything local.
all.input_cadence: None required. Optional weekly: read the contradiction report and hit 'ratify' or 'strike' on a disputed ruling — you are the supreme court, which takes three minutes and is genuinely fun. Optional: hand-write a tenth constitution.
all.tech: Python 3.12, llama.cpp server (GBNF-constrained JSON), fastembed or llama.cpp embeddings for precedents, SQLite per world (rulings, codex, events) + multiverse.db, a sandboxed exec harness for mechanism proposals (subprocess, no imports, CPU/time limits, generated property tests), FastAPI + vanilla-JS PWA, Tailscale serve, GitHub Pages nightly static mirror, ntfy.sh push. The public guestbook is a static page posting to a tiny rate-limited endpoint.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: the engine — resources, needs, ticks, tribe death, plus the typed effect record and its typechecker (build this BEFORE touching the model; the grammar is the project). Sunday: llama.cpp with a JSON grammar adjudicating combinations, SQLite cache, and two worlds with different hand-written constitutions running the same tribe start. The moment lands Sunday evening when the same combination produces two different technologies on two worlds and both are mechanically real — the tribe on one world actually survives winter because of it.
all.six_months_later: Nine codices of several thousand inventions each, readable as histories; an amendment log showing technologies going extinct when physics changed; a scripture page shaped by strangers; a handful of engine primitives written by the system itself. The cross-world index is the thing you will show people: 'the wheel-equivalent appears on 7 of 9 worlds; on the two heavy-gravity worlds nothing like it ever appears'.
all.honest_ceiling: A 4B model is the weak link and it will show: rulings get repetitive, descriptions get flowery, and around invention 500 on a world you will notice the model reaching for the same tropes. Precedent retrieval delays this a lot; it does not cure it. The effect grammar caps mechanical depth until mechanism proposals work, and mechanism proposals are the hardest part of the build (sandboxing plus test generation is a weekend of unglamorous work). Also be honest that the invention space's openness is linguistic, not physical — the model can rule anything into being, so the world's coherence is a maintained property, not a guaranteed one. Realistic plateau: month 4-5, unless you upgrade the adjudicator or lean harder on mechanism proposals.
all.research_notes: Verified: Infinite Craft (Neal Agarwal) uses LLMs to generate new elements and caches every combination in a database so the same pair always yields the same result for everyone — that caching pattern is the affordability argument, documented on its Wikipedia page. Working open clones to read for the plumbing: github.com/bufferhead-code/opencraft, github.com/sshh12/llm_alchemy (elements+recipes+art), github.com/Fus3n/infinite-sides (local LLM via Ollama), github.com/CharlesFauman/infini-craft (local Llama-2-7B-GPTQ). Local model choice for 8GB in Aug 2026: Qwen3.5-4B or Gemma 3 4B at Q4_K_M is the consensus fit (canitrun.dev/guides/best-llms-for-8gb-vram, atomic.chat/blog/guides/best-local-llm-8gb); llama.cpp is the hobbyist-standard server with GGUF+grammar support, SGLang/vLLM are the throughput options if you outgrow it. Hosted-model economics: as of Aug 2026 the mainstream floor is roughly $0.10-0.20 per million input tokens for small models, with several cheaper (pricing trackers modelgrep.com/pricing, costgoat.com/compare/llm-api) — verify before wiring any paid call. Precedent-retrieval-for-consistency is the same idea LILO (arXiv 2310.19791) uses when it documents library abstractions so later prompts stay coherent.

audit.name: The Ninefold Constitution
audit.ceiling: This is the purest case of authored content revealed in random order, and the author's own plateau estimate is off by roughly an order of magnitude. At tens of tok/s with ~2k-token precedent-laden prompts and 200-400 token effect records, you get maybe 2-5k rulings a night across nine worlds — 200-500 per world per NIGHT. Their admitted trope-collapse point ('around invention 500 on a world') therefore arrives in the first week, not month 4-5. After that, precedent retrieval makes it worse, not better: rulings condition future rulings, so the system locks into its own early vocabulary and the ruling log becomes a self-reinforcing mode. Structural ceiling underneath the model ceiling: every technology is an effect record of {resource deltas, need multipliers, preconditions}. That ontology makes all technology isomorphic to 'multiply a need by k, given a list' — a 12-step chain and a 1-step invention differ only in precondition bookkeeping. There is no structural depth for depth to accumulate in.
audit.authored_content_risk: Maximal, and disguised twice over. The author is not the builder — it is a 4B model's pretraining prior, which IS the human tech tree. Asked what happens when you fire clay, it will produce pottery; asked for sulfur-cycle combustion, it produces fire with a violet reskin and a salt flavour note. Nine constitutions do not change the nearest neighbour in the prior; they change the adjective. So 'nine divergent technological histories' will be one history in nine costumes, and the cross-world index ('the wheel-equivalent appears on 7 of 9 worlds') is measuring the model's prior, not the worlds. The second disguise: the model emits the numbers, and 'the engine sanity-bounds them' means the builder's clamp is the only thing making the economy coherent — the balance is authored, the fiction is free.
audit.compute_honesty: Honest about hardware, quietly dishonest about which part carries the depth. Qwen-class 4B at Q4_K_M plus a bge/gte-small embedder co-resident on 8GB is a correct fit, and the caching argument genuinely makes the steady state cheap. But the ONLY unbounded mechanism in the design — mechanism proposals, where the model writes a tested Python effect primitive — is a frontier-model task. A 4B model will not reliably author novel, terminating, mass-conserving simulation primitives that pass generated property tests; you will get a very high rejection rate and the accepted ones will be trivial. So the ratchet needs a hosted frontier model, and if it runs often enough to matter it is no longer pennies; if it runs rarely enough to stay cheap, it is not a ratchet. The sandbox-plus-test-generation work is also correctly called the hardest part and is the part most likely never to ship.
audit.dubious_claims: Citations largely check out (Infinite Craft caching, the clone repos, LILO, the Qwen3.5-4B/Gemma-3-4B 8GB fit — though canitrun.dev and atomic.chat are SEO-shaped sources, not authorities). The misuses: (a) Infinite Craft is offered as the affordability precedent while its most famous property — convergence to incoherent noun soup — is the exact failure mode here and goes unmentioned; (b) LILO's documentation-for-consistency is cited to justify precedent retrieval, but LILO documents abstractions that are VERIFIED PROGRAMS, whereas here precedents are unverified prior rulings, so retrieval propagates errors as well as consistency; (c) 'the model can rule anything into being, so coherence is a maintained property' is admirably honest and should be read as a concession that this is not a physics, it is a narrator; (d) the weekly hosted-model contradiction audit will find contradictions faster than you can adjudicate them — turning them into in-world 'the laws were revised' events is charming but it means model error is now unbounded content.
audit.semantic_risk: Moderate on the surface, severe underneath. Individual inventions will read beautifully — the effect grammar and the clamp guarantee mechanical executability, which is genuinely better than most LLM-crafting toys. But the tech tree's SHAPE is a language model's associative neighbourhood, so you get plausible-sounding technology in an order that is neither discovered nor physical. That is the most seductive failure in the set: it is the one that will look best on the phone and mean least.
audit.one_change: Move the model from adjudicator to proposer. Make it emit PROGRAMS in a typed DSL over engine primitives with conservation laws (borrow Twelve Anvils' interpreter wholesale); the engine executes them, measures the survival delta, and accepts or rejects. The constitution becomes the interpreter's constants rather than prompt text. That keeps the model's strength (proposing plausible combinations) and removes its fatal weakness (inventing outcomes and numbers), and it is the only version where a world can invent something that is not in the model's prior.

all.name: Landbridge
all.pitch: One planet, one million years, at fifty years a tick: plate tectonics and ice ages open and close land bridges while technology — stored as a genome of executable recipes — mutates, recombines, transmits imperfectly, and goes extinct. The product is a technology phylogeny you can scroll: allopatric divergence of tools on isolated islands, and hybridisation spikes when the glaciers drop the sea and the continents touch.
all.world: An icosphere planet (~10k cells) with real-ish deep-time machinery: 8-14 tectonic plates on Voronoi regions drifting with per-plate velocity vectors, collision raising mountains and subduction opening volcanic arcs, elevation feeding a cheap climate model (latitude + altitude + a simple orographic rainfall pass + ocean-distance), and global ice volume driven by a three-term Milankovitch-style oscillator that sets sea level. Cells flip between land, shelf, and ocean as sea level moves by up to 120m. Agents are CULTURES: a population, a territory of cells, a subsistence mode, and a tech genome. Time: 1 tick = 50 years, 20,000 ticks = a million years, and a full run takes a night.
all.invention_engine: Genetic programming over a survival DSL, with per-culture MDL library extraction, plus lossy cultural transmission. Data structures: (a) Recipe = typed program over resource/action primitives (same shape as Twelve Anvils' DSL but simpler), with a complexity score = node count; (b) TechGenome = a set of recipes plus a per-culture library of extracted abstractions; (c) a PhyloDB recording every recipe's parents, birth tick, birth culture, and death. Mechanisms: MUTATION (point-edit a recipe: change a constant, swap a primitive, graft a subtree) and RECOMBINATION (crossover between two recipes, including recipes acquired from a neighbouring culture — this is where contact makes technology explode). Every candidate is mechanically verified by executing it against the culture's actual local resources and climate: does it terminate, is it feasible here, does it yield surplus kcal / reduce mortality? Only survivors enter the genome. Every 200 ticks, each culture runs MDL compression over its genome to extract shared abstractions (its 'craft traditions'). TRANSMISSION is the cruel part and the best part: copying a recipe of complexity C to a neighbour succeeds with probability that falls with C and rises with the number of people who know it and contact frequency — so complex technology cannot survive in small isolated populations and is genuinely LOST, with the loss event recorded in the phylogeny as an extinction.
all.why_unbounded: Program space is infinite and recombination is the engine, so the reachable set grows with the diversity of contacted genomes — the space is not merely large, it is a function of the population structure, which the geology keeps rearranging. Isolation creates divergence (two islands explore different regions of program space), contact creates hybridisation (crossover between distant lineages produces recipes neither could reach alone), which is textbook allopatric-then-secondary-contact dynamics applied to technology rather than to genes. That is a structurally different unboundedness argument from every other idea here and it is the one most tightly coupled to a changing world: the tech tree's shape is literally the planet's connectivity graph over time. Honest bottoming-out: GP bloat (programs get big without getting better) and fitness saturation (once a culture covers its needs, selection goes flat). Countermeasures that actually work: MDL/parsimony pressure in the fitness, and climate that keeps moving the needs so the fitness landscape never stops sliding.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: icosphere, plates drifting, sea level oscillating, and a map that animates a million years in 30 seconds — this alone is worth the weekend and it is a gorgeous phone view. Week 2: cultures, kcal, migration to adjacent habitable cells, population dynamics. Week 3: the recipe DSL, mutation, verification, and the first invention. Month 2: transmission with complexity-dependent loss, plus the phylogeny DB — you get your first technology extinction and it will hurt. Month 3: a glacial maximum drops sea level, a land bridge opens between two continents that have been separate for 300,000 years, and the recombination rate spikes; you watch a hybridisation burst in the phylogeny. Month 4-6: MDL library extraction per culture gives named traditions; a supercontinent assembles and the whole planet's tech pool merges. Wildest plausible endpoint: a run where an isolated island culture holds the only surviving copy of a deep abstraction lost everywhere else during a bottleneck, the bridge opens 80,000 years later, and it reseeds the mainland — and your novelty detector flags it because that recipe's signature had been marked extinct.
all.what_selects: Carrying capacity. Each cell yields calories as a function of climate, biome, and the culture's applicable recipes; population grows toward capacity and crashes past it. Mortality comes from cold, drought, disease (population-density dependent), and conflict at borders. Cultures expand into empty or weaker-held cells; a culture that loses its territory is dead and its genome dies with it unless a neighbour already copied entries. Small populations lose complex tech automatically via the transmission rule, so 'being cut off on a small island' is a slow technological death sentence — which makes migration decisions genuinely load-bearing.
all.changing_worlds: This is the deep-time engine, so change is constant and multi-scale: tectonic drift over hundreds of thousands of years reshaping continents; Milankovitch cycles at ~20k/40k/100k years driving ice volume and sea level, hence connectivity; volcanic arcs and flood basalts as punctuated catastrophes; bolide impacts on a Poisson schedule with a decade-scale impact winter. The connectivity graph over cells is recomputed each tick and it is the single most important derived quantity in the sim because it decides who can teach whom. For multiple worlds: run 4-6 planets with different orbital eccentricity, axial tilt, land-to-ocean ratio, and plate count — a high-tilt world has violent seasons and (hypothesis) faster storage technology; an ocean world with tiny islands should produce maximal divergence and maximal loss. That comparison is the science.
all.novelty_detector: The phylogeny gives objectively good signals: first-ever recipe motif (structural hash, so cosmetically different rediscoveries collapse), record-depth abstraction, an extinction of a recipe that had survived >100k years, a resurrection (extinct signature reappears), a hybridisation burst (crossover-origin recipes exceeding a rolling z-score after a bridge opens), and a culture crossing a carrying-capacity regime it had never reached. Plus the MDL-delta measure from library extraction. Nightly the top 3 by surprise go to the phone; the rest fill the chronicle.
all.phone_view: The hero view is a single animated globe thumbnail showing 'last night's million years' with ice sheets pulsing and coastlines breathing, and beneath it three numbers: cultures alive, deepest tech, technologies lost. Second tab is the phylogeny — a vertical time-scrolling tree where each branch is a recipe lineage, colour-coded by culture, with extinctions as terminated lines; scrolling it for ten minutes with coffee is the binge experience. Third tab: the atlas of 4-6 planets with their divergence statistics. Push: 'Landbridge opened at tick 14,220 (sea level -108m). Two isolated tech pools met after 340,000 years; 61 hybrid recipes in 3,000 years — highest recombination burst ever recorded.'
all.hardware_use: CPU and RAM, which suits this perfectly: the globe is ~10k cells x 20k ticks, all NumPy, and a full million-year run is minutes to an hour per planet. Run 6 planets as 6 processes and still have cores spare; 64GB RAM comfortably holds the full event log and phylogeny in memory before it is flushed to SQLite. The GPU is entirely optional — a local 4B model writing the chronicle prose for each night's headline events (cached, ~100 calls a night) is the only use, and pure garnish. No PyTorch, no sm_120 risk, and no timing-based fitness anywhere so thermals cannot corrupt results.
all.input_cadence: Zero. Optional monthly: mint a new planet by choosing tilt/eccentricity/land ratio/plate count, or drop a hand-placed catastrophe at a chosen tick to see counterfactuals (the sim is deterministic from a seed, so you can re-run the same million years with and without a meteor — a counterfactual button is trivially available and enormously fun).
all.tech: Python 3.12, NumPy, a hand-rolled icosphere + spherical Voronoi (scipy), SQLite for cultures/recipes/phylogeny/events, msgpack event stream, offline frame rendering to a small mp4/webp per night with Pillow or matplotlib, FastAPI + vanilla-JS canvas PWA (the globe view is a canvas orthographic projection — right in your wheelhouse), Tailscale, GitHub Pages mirror, ntfy.sh. Sonification is exceptionally natural here: map global ice volume to a drone pitch, population to density, and each invention to a note — one hour of audio per simulated million years, left playing in the background as ambient radio.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: icosphere, plates, drift, collision, elevation, sea level oscillator, and a canvas globe that animates deep time. Sunday: cultures, calories, migration, and the simplest possible recipe genome with mutation and verification. The moment: run a million years, then look at the map of who ended up where and notice that the cultures on the two sides of a strait that closed 400k years ago have different recipe sets — and you did not write a single line of divergence logic. Geology did it.
all.six_months_later: Six planets, each with a complete phylogeny of thousands of recipe lineages; a comparative study of how orbital parameters shape technological trajectories; a library of counterfactual runs (same seed, one meteor changed); and an ambient audio archive. The phylogeny is the artifact — a picture of invented history that nobody authored, scrollable on a phone.
all.honest_ceiling: GP over programs bloats and stalls; expect the fitness curve to flatten within each run unless climate keeps sliding the needs, and expect to spend real time on parsimony pressure and typing. The cultures have no minds — there is no reasoning, only variation and selection, so you never get 'they figured it out', you get 'it was selected for', which is a different and colder pleasure. Also, deep-time realism is a rabbit hole with no bottom; the climate model will always be embarrassingly crude next to the geology, and you must decide early that it is a toy physics you keep cheap. Plateau: the invention engine flattens around month 4, but the comparative-planet layer keeps generating new questions long after — this is the idea with the longest tail per unit of effort, and the least raw invention depth.
all.research_notes: Verified: solid open-source priors for the planet layer — github.com/MightyBOBcnc/nixis (Python, icosphere planet-scale maps, plate tectonics + hotspots, precipitation, climate/biome derivation), github.com/FreezeDriedMangos/realistic-planet-generation-and-simulation (tectonics + weather + ocean currents, with a live web demo), PyPlatec (used by WorldMachina, github.com/SAED2906/WorldMachina) for tectonic heightfields, and github.com/weigert/SimpleTectonics for the convection-based approach. Cultural-loss-in-small-populations (the Tasmania effect) is the Henrich demographic model of cumulative culture and is the mechanism that makes technology genuinely lossy here. Library extraction from a corpus by MDL: Stitch (arXiv 2211.16605) and DreamCoder (PLDI 2021) as above. For quality-diversity framing of divergence across islands, pyribs on CPU or QDax (JMLR v25) on GPU. Note on 'the wheel': the comparative claim only works because the sim is deterministic per seed — same seed, same million years, so counterfactuals are exact.

audit.name: Landbridge
audit.ceiling: The most intellectually honest idea here, and the one whose ceiling is provable rather than empirical — because the designer built it deliberately and called it realism. The transmission rule (copy success falls with recipe complexity C, rises with number of knowers) is Henrich's model, and Henrich's model has a closed-form maximum sustainable complexity as a function of effective population. So recipe depth is not open-ended; it converges to f(N), and N is bounded by cell carrying capacity. Second, self-inflicted cap: they add MDL/parsimony pressure to fitness to fight GP bloat, which is the same pressure that punishes depth — you cannot use parsimony as the anti-bloat mechanism and expect deep programs. Third, the fitness function is scalar carrying capacity with saturating returns, so once local calories are covered selection goes flat and everything after is neutral drift. Realistic stop: typed recipes of depth 3-6, per-culture libraries of a handful of 'traditions', flat by month 1-2. The phylogeny, the counterfactual button and the comparative-planet layer keep generating interest long after invention stops — which is the correct read of 'longest tail, least raw depth'.
audit.authored_content_risk: Low on divergence, which is the real achievement: nobody writes the divergence logic, geology does, and 'two sides of a strait closed 400k years ago have different recipe sets' is a genuine emergent result. Authored: the primitive set, the resource/climate model, and — decisively — the shape of the fitness landscape. The hybridisation-burst headline is the weakest claim: crossover between two typed programs from lineages that diverged 300k years ago mostly yields verification failures, so '61 hybrid recipes in 3,000 years' will largely be a burst of neutral variants caused by having more parent material in the pool, not a qualitative capability jump. Report accepted-and-USED hybrids with a fitness delta, or the flagship moment is an artifact of the counter.
audit.compute_honesty: Honest about the planet layer, silently wrong about the invention layer. 10k cells x 20k ticks of NumPy in minutes-to-an-hour is right. But that estimate omits the GP inner loop: tens of cultures x 20k ticks x candidate programs mutated, crossed over and EXECUTED against local resources is easily 10^7-10^9 interpreted program executions per planet-run. In Python that is not 'a night for six planets', it is days per planet unless you cut candidate counts per tick to single digits — at which point the mutation-selection process is too weak to climb anything. Either amortise invention (run GP every Nth tick, on a subsample of cultures) and say so, or write the interpreter in something fast. Zero GPU need and no timing-based fitness are both correct and admirable.
audit.dubious_claims: (a) Tasmania/Henrich presented as the mechanism that makes technology 'genuinely lossy' — the empirical claim that population size drives cultural complexity is actively contested (Vaesen et al. 2016 PNAS; Read), and here it functions as an analytic depth cap rather than realism. (b) 'Program space is infinite and recombination is the engine, so the reachable set grows with contacted diversity' — true of the reachable set, false of the SELECTED set, which is bounded by a saturating scalar fitness. (c) Planet-layer repo citations (nixis, PyPlatec, SimpleTectonics) are plausible and appropriate; the DreamCoder/Stitch citations are being used for a much weaker per-culture MDL pass than those systems do, so do not expect their compression quality. (d) 50-year ticks mean there is no within-lifetime learning anywhere — the notes never say this, but it forecloses 'they figured it out' at the level of the clock, not just the algorithm.
audit.semantic_risk: Low-moderate. Recipes execute against real local resources and climate, so every entry means something concrete. The catch is that everything they can mean is 'acquire, process, eat, shelter' — you get a gorgeous, scrollable phylogeny of calorie routines. The structural-hash novelty signals (extinction, resurrection, record depth) are objectively computed and genuinely trustworthy, which is rare in this set.
audit.one_change: Replace the scalar carrying-capacity fitness with a quality-diversity objective — MAP-Elites over subsistence behaviour descriptors (diet breadth, mobility, storage horizon, processing depth, biome tolerance) maintained per culture — and demote parsimony from the fitness function to a tie-break. Scalar saturating fitness is the thing that flattens GP; illuminating a behaviour space keeps selection rewarding NEW KINDS of solutions after calories are covered, and it composes perfectly with the phylogeny you are already recording.

all.name: Bureau of Comparative Worlds
all.pitch: An agent-scientist runs your multiverse as a controlled experiment: it forms hypotheses about what makes civilizations invent, designs the night's batch of worlds with paired seeds and ablations, runs them while you sleep, and publishes a paper with figures to your phone by morning. Its predictions are pre-registered and scored, so you wake up to a finding and a calibration curve, not a feed.
all.world: A parameterised world generator is the substrate — use Twelve Anvils' library-learning worlds or Ashfall's chemistry worlds as the engine (this idea is the meta-layer and deliberately reuses one of them, which is also the 'one shared substrate across projects' play). What matters here is the WORLD PARAMETER SPACE as the independent variable: ~20 knobs (gravity, ore abundance and clustering, climate variability amplitude, catastrophe rate, island fragmentation, growing-season length, predator pressure, initial population, contact frequency between tribes). A 'world' is a point in that space plus a seed; a civilization is whatever the underlying engine grows there.
all.invention_engine: Two engines stacked. The object-level invention engine is inherited (library learning by MDL compression, or hash-chemistry discovery — pick one and do not build both). The meta-level engine is the interesting part and it is the actual product: a HYPOTHESIS REGISTRY in SQLite with columns {hypothesis text, formal form (parameter -> outcome metric), pre-registered predicted direction and effect size, planned N, seed list, status, result, replication status}. The nightly loop, driven by a Claude Code agent with a fixed toolset: (1) read yesterday's results and the current registry; (2) propose 1-3 new hypotheses, each with a pre-registered numeric prediction; (3) DESIGN the batch — paired seeds with common random numbers so the only difference between world A and A' is the one knob under test, plus one-factor-at-a-time ablations and a couple of random exploration worlds; (4) launch 12-16 worlds across CPU workers; (5) at dawn compute bootstrap CIs, effect sizes, and a Brier/calibration update for its own predictions; (6) write the paper — abstract, one claim, two figures, methods, limitations — and mark any finding as UNREPLICATED until it survives a fresh-seed rerun scheduled automatically. The agent cannot mark a finding confirmed without that replication; that rule is enforced in code, not in the prompt.
all.why_unbounded: The object-level unboundedness is inherited from whichever engine you pick (program-space compression or combinatorial chemistry — both argued above). The meta-level adds a different kind of open-endedness: the space of QUESTIONS about a 20-dimensional world-parameter space with interaction effects is astronomically larger than the space of worlds, and each answered question suggests new ones (mechanism questions follow correlational ones; 'why' follows 'whether'). This is the only idea here where the thing that keeps growing is understanding rather than artifacts, which is also its honest weakness: understanding of a simulator you wrote is bounded by the simulator's own richness. If the underlying engine is shallow, the Bureau publishes true findings about a boring world, forever. Pick a deep engine or this is elegant machinery around nothing.
all.depth_ladder: Week 1: the batch runner — 12 worlds on 12 processes, a results table, and a single hand-written hypothesis tested with a paired-seed design. Week 2: the agent writes the nightly report from the results table (Claude Code on a cron, or a local model for the prose with the stats computed in Python — always compute stats in Python, never let a model do arithmetic). Week 3: pre-registration and the Brier scoreboard; the first time it predicts an effect direction and gets it wrong is the moment the project becomes addictive. Month 2: automatic replication scheduling and a 'findings' page with confirmed/unreplicated/refuted status. Month 3: interaction hunting — the agent starts testing 2-factor designs because main effects are exhausted. Month 4-6: a mechanism layer, where a finding must come with a proposed causal story that is then tested by an intervention (knock out the mediating variable and see the effect vanish). Wildest plausible endpoint: a genuinely non-obvious, replicated, mechanistically explained law of your multiverse — something like 'invention rate peaks at intermediate climate variability, and the mechanism is that low variability never invalidates library entries while high variability kills the population before compression can run' — that you did not know and could not have guessed, with the figures to prove it.
all.what_selects: Two selection pressures, which is what makes this fun. In-world: whatever the underlying engine uses (calories, cold, competition). Meta-world: HYPOTHESES compete — a hypothesis that fails replication is retired to a graveyard page, and the agent's calibration score (Brier on its own pre-registered predictions) is a public, permanent number on the dashboard. There is no way to fake it, because pre-registration happens before the runs and is timestamped in SQLite. A hypothesis-generation strategy that keeps producing refuted predictions gets down-weighted in the proposer.
all.changing_worlds: Worlds change within runs (the inherited engine's climate cycles and catastrophes) and BETWEEN runs by design — the batch designer deliberately samples non-stationary schedules as an experimental factor: constant climate vs. cyclic vs. punctuated, mild vs. severe. 'Does catastrophe accelerate or destroy technology?' is the flagship question and it is exactly the sort of thing that needs many worlds run in parallel with paired seeds to answer honestly. Long-running 'cohort' worlds persist across nights so the Bureau also has longitudinal subjects, not just fresh batches — and a cohort world getting wiped out is a real loss, which gives the meta-layer stakes it would otherwise lack.
all.novelty_detector: Novelty here is statistical by construction, which is the cleanest version in this set: an effect is newsworthy if its bootstrap CI excludes zero AND the pre-registered prediction was wrong (surprise = the agent's own miscalibration, which is the correct definition of learning something), or if an interaction term is large. Object-level first-evers from the inherited engine feed in as a second channel. Anti-noise discipline is enforced structurally: preregistration, replication before promotion, a cap of one push per night carrying the single best finding, and a visible count of tests run so p-hacking is legible on the dashboard rather than hidden.
all.phone_view: One card, and this is the tightest 30-second check-in of all six: today's headline finding in a sentence, a single small figure (paired dot plot or effect-size bar with CI), a status chip (CONFIRMED / UNREPLICATED / REFUTED), and the agent's running calibration number. Swipe for the findings archive, the graveyard of refuted hypotheses, and the multiverse map (a 2D projection of world-parameter space with dots coloured by outcome, which after months becomes a genuinely informative picture). The physical artifact fits perfectly here: a receipt printer on the desk prints the abstract every morning — a one-paragraph paper on thermal paper next to the coffee, which is the best version of the ritual you described.
all.hardware_use: CPU-dominant and ideal for 24/7: 12-16 world processes overnight, each a few hundred MB, well inside 64GB. Stats in NumPy/SciPy. The GPU is used only if the inherited engine wants a local 4B model, or optionally to run the report prose locally instead of via a hosted agent. Cost honesty: if the nightly scientist is a hosted agent, one report a night at a few thousand tokens of context is pennies-to-low-dollars per month at Aug-2026 small-model prices; if you use a frontier model for the reasoning it is still dollars, not tens of dollars, because it runs once a night. Benchmark hygiene is critical here since this idea is all about comparisons: every metric must be in simulated units (ticks, node expansions, kcal) and never wallclock, and the runner should log CPU temperature and clock throttling per batch so a hot night is visible as metadata rather than silently biasing a comparison.
all.input_cadence: The lowest of all six by design: read a paragraph with coffee. Weekly, optionally, add a hypothesis of your own to the registry and race the agent on calibration — a human-vs-agent Brier scoreboard is a delightful and nearly free feature. Monthly: retire a parameter or add a new one to the generator, which reopens the whole question space.
all.tech: Python 3.12, NumPy/SciPy, SQLite (registry, results, cohort worlds, calibration history), a batch runner over multiprocessing with per-run manifests capturing the exact seed and code git-hash (reproducibility is the whole point), matplotlib rendering figures to PNG at dawn, a Claude Code cron job as the scientist (or a local 4B for prose with all statistics precomputed), FastAPI + PWA, Tailscale, GitHub Pages mirror of the findings, ntfy.sh push, python-escpos for the morning receipt.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: take the simplest possible object-level engine you have (even Twelve Anvils' weekend version), wrap it in a batch runner with a manifest per run, and get 12 worlds finishing overnight into one results table. Sunday: paired-seed design for one knob, bootstrap CI, a matplotlib figure, and a templated one-paragraph report pushed to your phone at 6am. The moment arrives Monday morning: you read a sentence about your own worlds that you did not know was true and had not thought to check.
all.six_months_later: A hundred-plus findings, maybe fifteen confirmed and replicated, a calibration curve showing the agent got better at predicting its own multiverse, a parameter-space map with visible regimes, and a small body of knowledge about an invented universe. If you rotate the object-level engine (chemistry worlds this quarter, program-library worlds next), the Bureau layer transfers wholesale — this is the shared substrate you wanted, and it is the one component worth designing for reuse from day one.
all.honest_ceiling: Statistical power on one laptop is the hard wall: 12-16 worlds a night with noisy outcomes means you can detect large effects and will never resolve subtle ones, so the findings skew obvious early ('more ore, more tools'). Second wall: the garden of forking paths is real even with preregistration, because the agent chooses what to test after seeing yesterday's data — the honest fix is the enforced fresh-seed replication plus reporting the total number of tests, and you should assume some fraction of 'confirmed' findings are still noise. Third and most important: this layer cannot be more interesting than the engine underneath it, so do not build it first. Build engine 1 or 2 for a month, then add the Bureau — at which point it is maybe two weekends and it doubles the value of everything already running.
all.research_notes: Verified: UED framing (a teacher generating environments as a curriculum) is the closest published analogue to 'the world-parameter sampler as experimenter' — see 'Efficient Unsupervised Environment Design through Hierarchical Policy Representation Learning' (arXiv 2602.09813), 'Improving Regret Approximation for Unsupervised Dynamic Environment Generation' (arXiv 2601.14957), and 'Imagined Autocurricula' (arXiv 2509.13341); the Bureau differs by optimising for INFORMATION about worlds rather than agent robustness, which is a legitimately under-explored direction and a decent reason to build it. Project Sid (arXiv 2411.00114, github.com/altera-al/project-sid, Altera) is the best precedent for reporting emergent civilizational phenomena — specialisation, currency, religion spread — from many-agent runs, and worth reading precisely for how hard it is to state such results rigorously; their PIANO architecture and their metrics are the cautionary tale that motivates preregistration here. QD/illumination tooling for mapping parameter space: pyribs (CPU) and QDax (arXiv/JMLR v25 23-1027, JAX). Reproducibility practice — pin the git hash and the seed in every run manifest — is the one non-negotiable piece of engineering, since every claim the Bureau makes is a comparison between runs.

audit.name: Bureau of Comparative Worlds
audit.ceiling: Not a depth mechanism at all, and it says so: 'this layer cannot be more interesting than the engine underneath it'. It contributes exactly zero invention depth — it is instrumentation, narration and experimental hygiene wrapped around whichever engine you pick, so its ceiling is that engine's ceiling plus a calibration curve. Its own independent wall is statistical power: 12-16 worlds/night with 8 per arm against outcomes like library depth or recipe count, which are heavy-tailed with CV near 100%, means you can only resolve effects around one SD or larger. Those are the effects you could have guessed ('more ore, more tools'), and they are usually restatements of code the builder wrote — a unit test with a confidence interval. Interaction effects, which is where the genuinely non-obvious findings live, are permanently out of reach at that n. Expect the findings feed to be interesting for 3-6 weeks and then become a well-calibrated stream of tautologies.
audit.authored_content_risk: Different failure mode: not authored content revealed as discovery, but implementation details revealed as laws of nature. Every dependent variable is something the builder chose to log about a simulator the builder wrote, so 'a law of my multiverse' is at best a characterisation of one's own code. That is a real and pleasant thing to have; it is not the cavemen-to-something-wild demand. Also under-defended: the agent both PROPOSES hypotheses and is scored on predicting them, so the dominant strategy is to propose safe hypotheses — calibration improves while informativeness collapses, and there is no code-enforced fix in the design (the enforced replication rule is enforced in code, which is genuinely good; the proposal-incentive problem is not).
audit.compute_honesty: The most honest costing in the set, with one caveat. 12-16 CPU world processes overnight, SciPy bootstraps, matplotlib at dawn, one hosted agent call per night — pennies to low dollars a month is right, and the run-manifest-with-git-hash-and-seed discipline is the single best piece of engineering in all six proposals. Caveat: if the inherited engine is Twelve Anvils, giving each of 16 worlds ~half a core for 8 hours makes every world a starved DreamCoder run, so the Bureau will be doing rigorous statistics on the noise floor of an under-resourced search. Fewer, longer, better-fed worlds beat more arms here — power comes from effect size, and starved engines have none.
audit.dubious_claims: (a) UED papers are cited as the closest analogue to the world-parameter sampler; the citations are real (2602.09813 verified, 2509.13341, 2601.14957), but UED optimises a teacher for agent robustness with a regret signal — repurposing that framing for information-about-worlds is a genuinely different objective and the analogy buys less than claimed. (b) Project Sid is cited well, as the cautionary tale, but note it ran many hosted-LLM agents at a cost structure nothing like a laptop, and its emergent-civilization claims remain largely unreplicated — a good reason for the Bureau to exist, and also a warning that 'reporting emergent phenomena rigorously' may find there is nothing to report. (c) The preregistration defence is oversold: preregistering a prediction chosen AFTER seeing yesterday's data is not preregistration, it is sequential inference. The enforced fresh-seed replication does most of the real work (roughly squaring the per-test error rate) and deserves the credit instead. (d) 'the object-level unboundedness is inherited' is doing enormous load-bearing work for an idea that ships none of it.
audit.semantic_risk: Low, and this is the layer's genuine value: statistics computed in Python and prose written by a model, with an explicit rule never to let the model do arithmetic, is the correct architecture and the only one in the set that structurally resists narrative inflation. The remaining risk is prose that dresses a 1.2-sigma difference as a law; cap it by printing the effect size and n in the push text itself.
audit.one_change: Close the loop: make the Bureau OPTIMISE world-parameter space rather than only publish about it — a POET/illumination-style outer loop searching for parameter regions that maximise sustained novelty rate or time-to-plateau in the object engine, with hypothesis-testing as a readout of that search. Then the meta-layer feeds depth back into the object level instead of describing its plateau eloquently, and the answer to 'which worlds keep inventing' becomes the thing you run rather than the thing you write up. Build it second, never first — after a month of engine 1 or 5, it is two weekends and it doubles the value of everything already running.

all.name: Palimpsest
all.pitch: A civilization's technology IS a library of small programs it wrote to survive, and each night a corpus-compression pass finds the shared structure across everything every tribe did and mints it as a new named primitive — that minting event is a real invention, not a tech-tree unlock. You read it as an encyclopedia with etymologies, inventor biographies, and a citation graph you can walk backwards from 'reinforced haft-lashing' to 'strike two rocks together'.
all.world: One planet, hex map ~256x256, but the substrate that matters is a procedurally generated MATERIALS TABLE, regenerated per world: 60-200 substances, each an 8-12 dim property vector (hardness, toughness, density, melt point, fibrousness, caloric density, toxicity, reactivity class, workability) plus a generated reaction table of the form `A + B @ (temp, duration, presence-of-C) -> D`, where D's property vector comes from a fixed-seed nonlinear interaction map. You never author 'bronze'; you author 'two metals heated above both melt points interpolate nonlinearly', and world #7's specific useful alloy is a discovery. Agents are BANDS (20-200 people), not individuals: each band has a population pyramid, health, a stock vector, a territory, a lexicon, and a LIBRARY of programs. Resources are kcal, fuel joules, labour-hours, materials, water, salt. Seasons plus a stochastic hazard calendar (winter severity, flood, blight, raid, murrain).
all.invention_engine:
DreamCoder wake/sleep with Stitch as the compressor, wrapped around a deterministic materials simulator that acts as the mechanical verifier — zero LLM in the causal loop.

DATA STRUCTURES: (1) `library` table: id, band_id, canonical_body (alpha-normalized lambda term, hashed), type signature, arity, name, gloss, invented_tick, parent_ids (the library entries appearing in its body — this is the citation DAG). (2) `solution` corpus: every program that ever passed a goal predicate, with band, task, tick. (3) `task` rows auto-generated from world state, never hand-written: a generator emits (goal_predicate, initial_stock, environment) from actual pressure — `survive(40 people, -20C, 90 days)`, `cross(river, 30m, in flood)`, `store(3000 kcal, 90 days, humid)`, `kill(aurochs, at range)`.

WAKE: for each band, bottom-up type-directed enumerative synthesis over the band's current library, with observational-equivalence deduplication (Bustle/Probe style) and a bigram prior over the band's own historical library usage. Budget is measured in NODES EXPANDED, never seconds (thermal hygiene: a hot laptop must not make a tribe stupid). Critically, the node budget is proportional to the band's SURPLUS LABOUR-HOURS — thinking is a luxury good paid for by food. Every candidate is executed against the materials sim; only programs whose output satisfies the goal predicate given the band's real stock survive.

SLEEP: nightly, run `stitch` (github.com/mlb2251/stitch, POPL 2023, Rust with Python bindings, 3-4 orders of magnitude faster than DreamCoder's own compression) over the solution corpus. Stitch proposes abstractions maximizing corpus compression under MDL. Each accepted abstraction becomes a new library primitive. THAT IS THE INVENTION. It permanently reshapes the search space: what cost 100k nodes last week now costs 3.

NAMING (LILO-style, arXiv 2310.19791): local Qwen3-4B, GBNF-constrained to `{name, gloss, etymology_parents[]}`, given the abstraction body, 3-5 call sites, and the band's phoneme inventory + existing lexicon. Sound-change rules applied per generation keep the lexicon internally consistent, so words visibly drift across centuries.

DIFFUSION: trade, marriage, and conquest copy library entries with fidelity < 1. A copied abstraction can lose an argument, producing a degenerate variant that occasionally outperforms the original.

ARCHAEOLOGY: a dead band's library is written to a `ruin` row with a damage mask (holes punched by preservation rules). A later band excavating that site recovers a holey program and runs sketch-completion synthesis to fill the holes. The encyclopedia records 'reconstructed from the Tablets of Ashen Ford; three arguments conjectural.'
all.why_unbounded: The invention space is the set of well-typed lambda terms over a signature that GROWS every night, and every new abstraction can appear inside the next one. That is a countably infinite space whose measure under the learned prior keeps shifting, not a finite list. Two independent compounding axes: the term space (unbounded, self-referential) and the materials chemistry (procedurally generated per world, so the semantics are also not authored). MDL compression is the selection pressure that keeps growth in useful directions instead of random ones — an abstraction only enters the library if it pays for itself in bits across the whole corpus, which means it only becomes a 'technology' if multiple independent survival problems happened to share that structure. That is a shockingly good operational definition of a technology.
all.depth_ladder:
WEEK 1: 20 materials, 15 primitives, one band, one task (survive winter). Bottom-up enumeration finds `(heat (grind acorn) fire 2h)`; stitch names it; you watch that named thing appear inside three later solutions. First delight.
WEEK 3: 5 bands, diffusion on. Two bands independently invent something with the same canonical hash — the encyclopedia gets its first 'independently discovered at X and Y, 40 years apart' entry.
MONTH 2: citation DAG hits depth 5. Techniques exist that no human wrote, made of techniques no human wrote. Bands with better tools have more surplus, therefore bigger search budgets, therefore runaway — checked by disease scaling with density and by fuel depletion (deforestation raises the cost of every heat-based abstraction, which retroactively devalues an entire branch of the library).
MONTH 4: first cataclysm. A band dies with a 60-entry library. 200 years later someone digs it up half-legible.
ENDPOINT (plausible, not promised): a world where the encyclopedia has an entry whose etymology chain is 12 deep, whose parent techniques come from three different extinct cultures, and where the reconstruction from ruins produced a variant that is measurably better than the original because a lost argument was replaced by a constant.
all.what_selects: Starvation, mechanically. Winter kcal deficit kills people, dead people are lost labour-hours, lost labour-hours shrink the synthesis node budget, a smaller budget means fewer solutions, fewer solutions means weaker nightly compression, which means the library stops growing — a death spiral you can watch in the numbers. Competition: bands raid for stock AND for libraries (a successful raid copies 1-3 random library entries). Niche construction bites: deforestation, soil exhaustion, and game depletion are tracked per-tile and are caused by the very techniques that made the band successful, so success is self-undermining on a 100-200 year lag. Disease pressure scales superlinearly with settlement density, so the sedentary route is not a free win.
all.changing_worlds: A SHELF OF WORLDS: 3-5 worlds run concurrently under one scheduler, each with its own generated materials table and hazard climate, sharing nothing but your reading list. The encyclopedia is cross-world: an entry says 'analogous to the Bitterment of world Kesh, though there fibre came from a mollusc'. Within a world, long climate cycles (10k-tick Milankovitch-ish sine stack) plus a Poisson cataclysm (bolide, plague, volcanic winter, ~1 per 3000 ticks) that wipes 60-95% of population and creates a hard archaeological layer. Post-cataclysm bands inherit ruins, not libraries. The cross-world comparison is where the biggest reading pleasure lives: 'in 4 of 5 worlds, someone eventually invented the arch; in Kesh, nobody ever did, and here is what they built instead.'
all.novelty_detector:
Four channels, all cheap, ANDed against a hard push budget of 2 notifications/day.
(1) FIRST-EVER: an abstraction whose alpha-normalized canonical hash has never appeared in any world's library table. Trivially exact, zero false positives.
(2) COMPRESSION SHOCK: nightly MDL delta (bits saved by the new abstractions) exceeding 3 sigma of the trailing 30-night distribution — this fires exactly when a genuinely load-bearing idea lands.
(3) DEPTH RECORD: a new abstraction whose depth in the citation DAG exceeds the all-time max. Technology built on technology built on technology.
(4) ASAL-style historical novelty (arXiv 2412.17799): embed each night's world-state summary with bge-small-en-v1.5, keep the running archive, score = mean cosine distance to the k=20 nearest previous nights, push only if in the top 1% of the trailing distribution. This catches things you did not think to instrument, like a demographic pattern nobody has ever seen.
Everything else goes into the encyclopedia silently and is there when you want to binge.
all.phone_view: Lock-screen ntfy line: 'Kesh, year 4,182 — 3 new words.' Open the PWA: a single scrolling column. Top card is tonight's headline invention — its name in the band's own orthography, a one-line gloss, the inventor band's sigil, and its parent techniques as tappable chips. Below it, a 30-second strip: population sparkline per band, a 'words known' counter, and any deaths of note. That is the whole 30-second view. Tap the headline and you fall into the encyclopedia: full entry, etymology tree rendered as an SVG DAG, list of every surviving program that calls it, the biography of the band that coined it, and 'see also' links that keep you there for an hour. FTS5 search across every entry ever written, in every world.
all.hardware_use: CPU-dominant and honest about it. The synthesis search is the hot loop and it is pure CPU — 64GB RAM is the real resource here, holding the observational-equivalence tables and the full solution corpus in memory. Run 8-12 band-workers as separate processes; a 24/7 run at a few hundred thousand nodes per band-tick is comfortable. Stitch is Rust, single-digit seconds on corpora of 10^4-10^5 programs. The GPU does almost nothing: Qwen3-4B-Instruct at Q4_K_M is ~2.5GB, fully offloaded on the 5070's 8GB with room to spare, used only for naming (a few hundred calls a night at ~200 tokens each) and for the nightly prose pass. bge-small-en-v1.5 embeddings are 90MB and could run on CPU. You will never touch the 8GB ceiling in this project, which is exactly why it is a good first build for this hardware.
all.input_cadence: Zero daily chores. Read with coffee. Two genuinely god-tier nudges are available and worth doing about monthly: (a) add a primitive verb to the DSL — one line, and it opens an entire semantic continent (adding `mark(surface, symbol)` is how writing becomes discoverable); (b) hand-seed a new world with a deliberately weird materials table (no metals; one absurdly abundant fibre) and watch the encyclopedia diverge. Both are 20-minute acts with month-long consequences.
all.tech: Python 3.12 sim (numpy for stock/property vectors, no framework). `stitch` via its Python bindings for nightly compression. SQLite in WAL mode as the single event store, with FTS5 over chronicle text — one file, greppable, backed up by copying. llama.cpp server with Qwen3-4B-Instruct Q4_K_M and GBNF grammars for every structured call (naming, glossing, prose claims). sentence-transformers bge-small-en-v1.5 for the novelty archive. Nightly build step emits a static JSON bundle; PWA is vanilla JS + a service worker so it works on the train. Served over Tailscale from the laptop for the private full-fidelity version; a pruned public mirror rsynced to GitHub Pages. ntfy.sh topic for push.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: materials table generator, 20 substances, the property-vector interaction map, and the stock simulator. 15 DSL primitives, a typed bottom-up enumerator with observational-equivalence dedup, one task (`survive winter`). Get a program that passes. Saturday night: pip install stitch, run it over your ~200 passing programs, print the abstractions. Sunday: wire Qwen3 for naming, add a second band and copy-with-error diffusion, write the encyclopedia entries to SQLite, and put a dumb HTML list on localhost. The delightful moment is Saturday night, before any UI exists: stitch hands you an abstraction you did not write, and you realise it is the thing every winter solution had in common.
all.six_months_later: Five worlds, an encyclopedia of 400-900 entries, a citation DAG 10-14 deep, and a lexicon with visible sound change (the word for 'parch' in year 200 and year 4000 are cognates you can hear). You have a favourite dead civilization. You have caught yourself checking whether the arch got invented again. The public mirror has strangers reading the etymology of a word for a technique that only exists on your laptop.
all.honest_ceiling: The ~40 primitive verbs are authored, and no amount of compression invents a concept the primitives cannot express. If nothing in your DSL can carry information, writing will never be discovered no matter how long it runs. Realistically this generates five to eight distinct 'eras' of genuine depth and then settles into recombination inside a fixed physics — I would put the plateau at month 5-8. Two honest mitigations, neither a cure: seed a handful of high-leverage semantically-open primitives (`mark`, `teach`, `store_program_in_artifact`) so writing, schooling and libraries are discoverable rather than authored; and accept that extending the physics is a manual act you perform every few months, which is itself the fun part for a builder who likes the whole arc. Second real limitation: enumerative synthesis scales badly with library size — past ~150 primitives the branching factor hurts, and you will need to prune the library (a 'forgetting' mechanic, which conveniently is also good fiction). Third: stitch's abstractions are sometimes ugly, semantically arbitrary fragments; expect maybe 1 in 4 to be a satisfying 'technology' and the rest to be plumbing. Do not oversell the hit rate to yourself.
all.research_notes: Verified: DreamCoder (Ellis et al., PLDI 2021, dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3453483.3454080) — wake phase searches for programs solving tasks under the current library, sleep phase extracts common sub-expressions and admits them if they reduce total MDL. Stitch (Bowers, Olausson, Wong, Grand, Tenenbaum, Ellis, Solar-Lezama; 'Top-Down Synthesis for Library Learning', POPL 2023, dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3571234; code at github.com/mlb2251/stitch) is corpus-guided top-down abstraction synthesis, reported 3-4 orders of magnitude faster than DreamCoder's compression, with Python bindings documented as the easiest access path — this is what makes a nightly compression pass on a laptop trivially affordable, and it is the single most important dependency in this idea. LILO (arXiv 2310.19791, 'Learning Interpretable Libraries by Compressing and Documenting Code') pairs Stitch-style compression with an LLM auto-documentation step — exactly the naming layer proposed here, and evidence that LLM-naming of compressed abstractions is a working published technique rather than my invention. ASAL (arXiv 2412.17799, github.com/SakanaAI/asal, published in Artificial Life 31(3), 2025) defines open-endedness operationally as high historical novelty in a representation space at each timestep — I am reusing that formulation with cheap text embeddings instead of CLIP. llama.cpp supports guaranteed structured output via --grammar-file / GBNF and JSON-schema response_format, confirmed current in 2026 tooling guides, which is what makes LLM naming safe to automate unattended. Qwen3-4B at Q4_K_M is ~0.5-0.6GB per billion params by the standard GGUF rule of thumb, so ~2.5GB — trivially inside 8GB. Precedent for reading rather than watching: Dwarf Fortress legends are browsed like a wiki by clicking links (dwarffortresswiki.org/index.php/World_generation), and Lynn Cherny's Dwarf2Text work is the closest existing attempt at data-to-text over DF legends XML.

audit.name: Palimpsest
audit.ceiling: Real discovery, but it plateaus earlier than claimed — month 3-5, not 5-8, and for a reason the doc misses. DreamCoder only works because of a graded task curriculum; the wake phase needs tasks that are just barely out of reach. Here tasks are auto-generated from world pressure (`survive(40, -20C, 90d)`, `cross(river,30m)`), which produces a bimodal difficulty distribution: nearly all trivially satisfiable at depth 1-2, a few unreachable at any budget, almost nothing in the productive band. Enumerative synthesis is exponential in depth, so the 'surplus labour buys node budget' coupling — the design's proudest loop — buys depth logarithmically: a 10x richer band searches maybe one or two levels deeper, not ten.
