Meanwhile Stitch saturates: MDL gain per night is a decreasing function of corpus homogeneity, and a corpus drawn from ~6 task templates gets most of its compression out in the first 20-40 abstractions. Concretely: expect ~40-80 library entries by week 8, then nightly MDL delta collapsing to noise, at which point channel (2) of the novelty detector stops firing permanently. The citation DAG will still deepen — but depth in a DAG of MDL fragments is free and means nothing. Second, unflagged ceiling: the branching-factor problem arrives sooner than 150 primitives because bottom-up enumeration with observational-equivalence dedup is bounded by the OE table, and OE dedup only fires when two programs agree on the *test inputs* — with a rich materials sim, distinct programs almost never collide, so dedup buys much less than it does on DreamCoder's list/string domains where it was measured.
audit.reaches_depth_note: Strongest of the six on genuine discovery; still bounded.
audit.authored_content_risk: Lowest of the six but not zero, and the doc mislocates it. The honest_ceiling blames the ~40 primitive verbs; the real authored surface is the TASK GENERATOR. Discoverable technologies are exactly the well-typed terms that satisfy predicates the generator emits, so the generator, not the DSL, defines the space of things that can count as inventions. The `mark`/`teach` mitigation is a bluff: adding a `mark(surface,symbol)` primitive does not make writing discoverable unless the sim independently models bounded knowledge transmission, decay, and a fitness advantage to externalised memory — i.e. unless you author the entire subsystem that makes writing pay. Adding the verb without that just adds an unused primitive that inflates the branching factor. Everything below the category level is genuinely unauthored: generated materials table, MDL-mined abstractions, un-anticipated recipes. Verdict: recipes and abstractions are real discoveries; the KINDS of technology are authored, and the encyclopedia format will disguise that because Qwen3-4B will supply confident etymologies for whatever it is handed.
audit.compute_honesty: Honest — the most honest of the six alongside Apocrypha. Pure CPU hot loop, GPU used for ~a few hundred short constrained generations a night, no API bill, nothing near the 8GB ceiling. Two caveats. (1) 'a few hundred thousand nodes per band-tick' in Python: each candidate must be *executed* against the materials sim, so throughput is roughly 10^4-10^5 candidates/sec optimistically and realistically closer to 10^4 with a Python interpreter loop — that is seconds-to-a-minute per band-tick, fine overnight, but it means the effective search depth is much shallower than the node count suggests. Budget in *solved tasks per night*, not nodes. (2) The OE table and full solution corpus in RAM is fine at 10^5 programs and starts hurting at 10^7; the corpus grows monotonically and Stitch cost is superlinear in corpus size, so you will need corpus windowing by month 3 (Stitch's headline speed is measured on fixed corpora, not on an ever-growing one).
audit.semantic_risk: Moderate-high, and the doc's own '1 in 4 satisfying' estimate is optimistic. Stitch maximises compression, not meaning; typical abstractions are partial applications with hole-filled arguments that correspond to no coherent concept. The naming layer makes this worse rather than better: a constrained 4B given a body, 3 call sites and a lexicon will always produce a plausible name and etymology, so the encyclopedia's readability is uncorrelated with whether an entry is a technology or plumbing. You will not be able to tell them apart by reading, which is the failure mode that matters for a project whose product IS the reading. Mitigation the doc lacks: gate library admission on a semantic test as well as an MDL test — e.g. require the abstraction to be invoked by ≥2 bands on ≥2 distinct task templates before it earns a name; leave the rest unnamed as 'unnamed fragment #331'.
audit.dubious_claims: (a) 'pip install stitch' — the PyPI package is `stitch_core`; `stitch` is something else. Small but it will eat a Saturday. (b) Stitch's '3-4 orders of magnitude faster' is about the COMPRESSION step versus DreamCoder's compressor; it says nothing about the enumerative search, which is your actual bottleneck. The doc calls Stitch 'the single most important dependency' — it is not; the wake-phase search is. (c) ASAL 'published in Artificial Life 31(3), 2025' — arXiv 2412.17799 and the SakanaAI repo are real, but I cannot verify that journal placement; treat as unverified. (d) DreamCoder's published results used substantial multi-core compute over days per domain with hand-designed curricula; citing PLDI 2021 without citing that compute/curriculum context oversells laptop feasibility. (e) The claim that MDL compression 'is a shockingly good operational definition of a technology' is the doc's most seductive and least supported line — MDL identifies shared syntax, which correlates with shared technique only when the corpus is semantically homogeneous, i.e. exactly when the corpus is least interesting.
audit.one_change: Co-evolve the task generator with the library instead of deriving tasks from world state. Add a minimal-criterion/POET-style loop: generated goal predicates are kept only if they are currently unsolved at the standard budget but solvable at ~3x budget, and retired once cheap. This converts depth-in-time from logarithmic to roughly linear, keeps Stitch's corpus continuously heterogeneous (so nightly MDL delta never collapses), and it is maybe 150 lines on top of what is already specified. Without it, everything else in the design is correct and the project still plateaus in three months.

all.name: Reliquary
all.pitch: A world of island workshops that invent materials by experiment and objects by design, and the artifact you check is a MUSEUM CATALOGUE: accession numbers, object labels, provenance chains, conservation notes, and a gallery of things that have never existed. Every morning the receipt printer spits out one object label.
all.world: An archipelago of 30-80 islands, each holding a different random subset of the world's ~120 procedurally generated substances — the isolation is the point, because divergent material cultures plus trade is what produces hybrid artifacts worth cataloguing. Each substance has an 8-dim property vector and participates in a generated reaction network of rules `k*A + m*B @ (temperature, pressure, catalyst) -> C (+ waste D)`, where C's properties are a fixed-seed nonlinear function of the inputs. Some reactions are CATALYTIC and a few are AUTOCATALYTIC — a product that catalyses its own production, which is what gives you a bronze age that arrives suddenly rather than as a ramp. Agents are GUILDS (workshops with a master, apprentices, a stock, a reputation, and a private recipe book), plus polities that commission work and fight wars. Objects are physical: a specific axe is a real row with a material stack, a form, a maker, a decoration, a wear state, and a location.
all.invention_engine:
Two coupled engines, both mechanical, LLM confined to the label copy.

ENGINE 1 — MATERIALS, as a bandit over the adjacent possible. Maintain per-guild a FRONTIER set: every pair/triple reachable from substances the guild knows, crossed with processes it knows, crossed with the conditions it can achieve (its kiln's max temperature is a real number that improves as a technology). Experiments cost materials, fuel, labour, and carry risk (toxic, explosive, ruins the crucible). Selection of what to try next is UCB, but the exploitation term is DEMAND-PULLED: the sim emits NEEDS as target regions of property space ('something harder than obsidian that does not shatter when struck', 'a pigment that survives three summers of sun', 'a binder that sets underwater'), derived from actual failures — a boat sank, a roof fell, a dye faded on a king's robe. The guild scores frontier candidates by predicted property-vector distance to an open need, using a per-guild learned linear model over past results. Results are written to a global `reaction_cache` (Infinite Craft's exact trick: a pair is adjudicated once, ever) so the chemistry is deterministic, reproducible, and free after first evaluation.

ENGINE 2 — OBJECTS, as quality-diversity search. An object's FORM is a small tree-grammar program: haft + head + binding + haft-treatment, each node parameterised (length, taper, angle, bind-turns). Performance is computed from material properties and geometry by a deterministic physics-lite model. Each guild runs local search over form space, but globally you maintain a MAP-Elites archive per object class using pyribs, with behaviour descriptors like (mass, edge retention) or (draw weight, cost). The archive IS an exhibit: the museum literally has a gallery that is a grid of all extant blade forms, one per cell, with the guild and year that filled it. A newly filled cell is a first-of-its-kind object.

ARTIFACT IDENTITY: every object gets an accession number, a provenance chain (made by guild G in year Y, gifted to K, buried with K, looted in the sack of S, held by the collection of T), and a conservation state. Named artifacts emerge when an object accumulates a provenance chain above a threshold of eventfulness — fame is computed, not authored.
all.why_unbounded: The reachable set of a generated reaction network grows superexponentially: 120 base substances, pairs and triples, several condition axes, catalysis, and products that feed back in as inputs. Nobody enumerates it; guilds crawl it locally under a need gradient, so the crawl path is different in every world and every guild. On top of that the object design space is continuous (a tree grammar with real-valued parameters), so 'all possible axes' is an infinite set of which the MAP-Elites archive holds a diverse finite sample that keeps improving. Honest structure of the unboundedness: it is BREADTH-unbounded, not DEPTH-unbounded — see the ceiling field.
all.depth_ladder:
WEEK 1: 30 substances, one island, one guild, one need ('harder cutting edge'). The bandit finds a two-step recipe you did not author and the printer prints its label. Delight.
WEEK 2: MAP-Elites over axe forms; the archive fills; you can see a Pareto front of 'light and fragile' versus 'heavy and enduring' emerge as distinct local traditions.
MONTH 1: trade between islands. A guild that has metal meets a guild that has resin; the first composite hafting appears and spreads. First LOST TECHNIQUE — a master dies in a raid with no apprentice, and the museum now holds an object it cannot explain.
MONTH 2: an autocatalytic loop ignites on one island. Production of a substance explodes over 40 years, its price collapses, and everything downstream of it becomes cheap at once. The catalogue's 'Second Trade Age' gallery is created automatically because the material census shifted past a threshold.
MONTH 4: a forgery. A guild reproduces the FORM of a famous lost artifact with the wrong material stack; the object enters the catalogue with an authenticity note; centuries later an excavation resolves it.
ENDPOINT: a museum with thousands of objects, dozens of galleries organised by material era, a handful of genuinely famous named artifacts with 8-link provenance chains crossing four polities and two extinctions, and at least one technique that was lost, rediscovered independently, and named differently the second time.
all.what_selects: Guilds compete for commissions and die from bankruptcy: materials cost real stock, failed experiments burn it, and a guild with no commissions dissolves and its recipe book is lost unless apprentices carried it. Recipe knowledge is per-guild and transmitted with fidelity proportional to apprentice-years and to whether the culture has writing (a discoverable technology here too), so knowledge loss is a first-class mechanic rather than a scripted dark age. Polities compete militarily and objects win battles — a polity whose guilds found a better alloy actually wins wars, which redistributes commissions and accelerates the winner. Counter-pressures: resource depletion per island (the good clay bed runs out), and trade dependency (an island that specialised is ruined when its partner falls).
all.changing_worlds: Each archipelago is a world; run 3-4 concurrently, each with an independently generated chemistry, so 'the alloys of Vess' and 'the alloys of Tarn' are genuinely different sciences. The catalogue is a single museum with wings for each world, which makes comparative material culture a browsable pleasure: the same need ('binder that sets underwater') solved four different ways by four chemistries. Within a world, sea-level change over long cycles submerges and reconnects islands, which reshuffles who trades with whom — non-stationary trade topology is the cheapest source of ongoing novelty I know. Sunken workshops become underwater sites with excellent organic preservation, which is an in-fiction reason the catalogue suddenly gains a whole category of wooden objects it never had.
all.novelty_detector:
(1) UNPRECEDENTED MATERIAL: a substance whose property vector's distance to its k=10 nearest catalogued neighbours exceeds the 99th percentile of the historical distribution — genuinely outside known material space, not just a new name.
(2) DEEP SYNTHESIS: a substance whose production requires >=3 previously-invented intermediates. This is the compounding signal, and it is exactly the one that distinguishes real technological depth from a wide flat crafting tree.
(3) ARCHIVE ILLUMINATION: a MAP-Elites cell filled for the first time, weighted by how isolated the cell is. pyribs gives you this for free as archive coverage delta.
(4) PROVENANCE EVENT: an object crossing a fame threshold, or a LOST TECHNIQUE event (last holder of a recipe dies).
Push budget two per day, ranked by a single scalar that is the max of the four normalised scores. Everything else accrues silently into the catalogue.
all.phone_view: One object card. A procedurally drawn SVG silhouette of the actual artifact (the form program renders directly to SVG — this is nearly free and it is what makes the museum feel real), its accession number, a three-line label in museum voice ('Hafted adze, Fifth Kiln period. Boar-tusk lamina over cured resin. Vess, workshop of Adda-of-the-Tin. Recovered from the flooded quarter.'), and a gallery breadcrumb. Below: today's acquisitions count and a single sparkline of the material census. Tap through for provenance chain, the recipe (if known to anyone alive), conservation notes, and 'objects like this'. Binge mode is walking a gallery, then walking a provenance chain into a war, then into an obituary.
all.hardware_use: This is the CPU-only idea, and that is a feature. The reaction network, the bandit, the physics-lite object model and pyribs all run in numpy on the CPU; 64GB RAM comfortably holds a multi-million-object catalogue in memory with the archive. GPU use is optional and small: Qwen3-4B Q4_K_M (~2.5GB, easy inside 8GB) writes object labels and conservation notes for the top few dozen objects a night, maybe 20k tokens total, a couple of minutes. If you ever wanted the GPU busy you could put a tiny surrogate model on it to predict reaction outcomes and prune the frontier, but you do not need to. The honest statement: this project would run on a Raspberry Pi if you dropped the prose layer, and the 5070 is idle 95% of the time.
all.input_cadence: None required. The one worthwhile monthly nudge is to hand-write a NEED into the world ('the king wants something that glows') and watch guilds crawl toward it — you are commissioning, not designing, and the solution is still theirs. Quarterly: generate a new archipelago with a deliberately hostile chemistry (no high-melting-point substances at all) and see what a civilization does without fire-based metallurgy.
all.tech: Python + numpy sim. pyribs (docs.pyribs.org, v0.11.x) for the MAP-Elites archives. SQLite WAL with FTS5 for the catalogue; the `object`, `provenance`, `recipe`, `reaction_cache` tables are the whole data model and they are worth designing carefully on day one because they are also the shared substrate you will reuse across projects. Form-program-to-SVG renderer in ~200 lines of Python, output inlined into the PWA (no external assets, works offline). llama.cpp + Qwen3-4B with GBNF for labels. python-escpos + the escpos-printer-db device profile database for the morning receipt. ntfy.sh push, Tailscale-served PWA, GitHub Pages public mirror of a pruned catalogue.
all.first_weekend: Saturday morning: substance generator and the reaction network, 30 substances, the property interaction map. Saturday afternoon: a single guild, the UCB frontier bandit, one hard-coded need. Print discovered substances to a terminal — this already feels alive because the second-order products are surprising. Saturday night: the form grammar and the SVG renderer, so you can look at an object. Sunday: pyribs archive over one object class, SQLite catalogue, a static HTML gallery. If you own a cheap thermal printer, Sunday evening is python-escpos printing your first object label, and that is the moment the project becomes a physical ritual rather than a program.
all.six_months_later: A museum of several thousand catalogued objects across four worlds, twenty-odd galleries created by threshold events rather than by you, a dozen artifacts famous enough to have their own pages, three lost-and-rediscovered techniques, and a shelf of printed receipts by your coffee machine that reads like a real museum's daily accessions. You will have started caring about a particular workshop lineage.
all.honest_ceiling: Chemistry does not compound in ABSTRACTION the way a program library does. You get a colossally wide space of substances but the conceptual depth is capped by the number of PROCESS types you authored (heat, grind, soak, alloy, bind, ferment, precipitate — maybe ten). Once all ten are in play in all combinations, roughly month 3-5, new discoveries are new points in a space whose shape you already understand, and the catalogue starts to feel like a very good stamp collection rather than a history of ideas. Two honest patches: make process types themselves discoverable objects (a kiln is an artifact whose max-temperature parameter is under design search, so 'we can now reach temperatures nobody could reach' is a real event that opens previously-unreachable reactions); and let the object grammar be extensible by composition, so 'a thing with a haft' can become a component of 'a thing with a haft and a lever'. Even so, I would call this the widest of these six ideas and not the deepest. The second real risk: property vectors drifting into meaninglessness — nonlinear interaction maps happily produce a substance with hardness 400 and the catalogue becomes numerology. Clamp aggressively, use log-space, and sanity-check that the distribution of properties stays roughly log-normal after 10k reactions.
all.research_notes: Verified: Infinite Craft's caching architecture — the backend checks whether a pair has ever been combined, serves cached responses, sends only genuinely new pairings to the model, and flags never-before-seen results with a 'First Discovery' indicator (quuxplusone.github.io/blog/2024/02/08/infinite-craft, and independent write-ups at blog.jverkamp.com/2024/03/14/infinite-craft-bot). I am reusing the cache-and-first-discovery pattern but replacing the LLM adjudicator with a deterministic generated chemistry, which makes it free and reproducible. pyribs (pyribs.org, docs.pyribs.org v0.11.0; GECCO 2023 paper arXiv 2303.00191) is the maintained bare-bones QD library implementing the RIBS framework with Archive/Emitter/Scheduler components and CMA-ME, CMA-MAE and variants — the archive-as-exhibit idea maps directly onto its API with no custom evolutionary code. On generated chemistries: 'Maximizing the Adjacent Possible in Automata Chemistries' (Artificial Life, MIT Press, 22(1):49) is the live research thread on designing artificial chemistries so the reachable set keeps expanding, and the autocatalytic-set literature (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autocatalytic_set; PMC9695903 'Autocatalytic Sets Arising in a Combinatorial Model of Chemical Evolution'; PMC6161236 on autocatalytic sets in compartmentalised spatial worlds) supplies the mechanism for sudden regime shifts rather than smooth ramps. Physical artifact precedents that are real and maintained: python-escpos, the escpos-printer-db device database (github.com/receipt-print-hq/escpos-printer-db), chr15m/print-weather as a minimal daily-print example, and mashedkeyboard/dashday for daily summary printing on any ESC/POS device.

audit.name: Reliquary
audit.ceiling: Month 2-4 for anything that reads as depth; breadth then continues forever and will be mistaken for progress. Two specific mechanisms, one of which the doc misses entirely. (1) The MISSED one: the UCB exploitation term is demand-pulled toward property-space targets, which is a greedy hill-climb — and greedy hill-climbing in property space is an ANTI-DEPTH mechanism. If a 1-step reaction lands near the need region, the 4-step chain that lands nearer is never explored, because the bandit's regret is computed against reachable value, not against depth. Your 'DEEP SYNTHESIS (>=3 intermediates)' detector therefore fires a handful of times early (when short paths happen not to exist) and then approximately never. Depth only appears if the reaction map has hard bottlenecks that short paths cannot cross. (2) The one the doc half-sees: conceptual depth is capped by ~10 authored process types crossed with a few condition axes; once that grid is populated, everything new is a new point in a space whose shape you already know. Also note the reaction network's own ambiguity, which the doc never resolves: if rules are a generated TABLE keyed on substance identity, the reachable closure is finite and a UCB crawl exhausts the interesting part in weeks; if rules are a FUNCTION over property vectors, the closure is infinite but structureless and you get the numerology failure the doc itself fears. There is no third option specified, and the two horns have opposite failure modes, so this must be decided before day one.
audit.authored_content_risk: Split verdict. Engine 1 (materials) is genuine discovery — generated chemistry, crawled locally, un-enumerable by the designer in advance. Engine 2 (objects) is authored content in disguise and the doc does not admit it: the form grammar is `haft + head + binding + haft-treatment`, so MAP-Elites is doing continuous parameter search inside a fixed four-slot vocabulary you wrote. Every 'first-of-its-kind object' is a numerically distinct instance of a shape you already specified. Worse, the archive-illumination novelty channel measures GRID RESOLUTION, not world events: a 50x50 archive has exactly 2500 possible 'first-fill' notifications available for the lifetime of the project, most of them consumed in month 1, and the rate of firing thereafter is a property of your descriptor binning, not of the civilization. The autocatalysis knob is likewise an authored 'bronze age arrives suddenly' switch dressed as chemistry.
audit.compute_honesty: Completely honest, and the doc's self-assessment ('would run on a Raspberry Pi') is correct. numpy chemistry, pyribs archives, physics-lite object scoring — all trivial. GPU used for a few dozen label generations a night. The reaction_cache makes chemistry free after first evaluation. No hidden datacenter, no API bill. This is the cheapest-to-run idea after Apocrypha, and its costs are all in the developer's time, not the machine's.
audit.semantic_risk: High, and self-flagged. Nonlinear interaction maps over 8-dim property vectors drift into meaninglessness fast; 'hardness 400' is the visible symptom, but the invisible one is worse — property vectors that stay in range while ceasing to correspond to any coherent material. The clamping/log-space/log-normal advice is right but insufficient, because a distribution can stay log-normal while the *correlational structure* between properties dissolves (dense-and-fibrous-and-low-melting-and-hard), at which point the museum is cataloguing noise with good labels. Add a structural constraint, not just a marginal one: derive products by interpolation *within* the convex hull of input properties plus a bounded process-specific perturbation, so materials inherit family resemblance. The SVG-silhouette-plus-museum-voice presentation is exactly the kind of surface that hides semantic decay from its own author.
audit.dubious_claims: (a) 'pyribs v0.11.x' — the version number looks wrong/invented; pyribs was in the 0.7-0.8 range at last verification. The GECCO 2023 paper (arXiv 2303.00191) and the Archive/Emitter/Scheduler API description are correct. (b) Infinite Craft caching and First Discovery flag: accurate. (c) 'Maximizing the Adjacent Possible in Automata Chemistries', Artificial Life 22(1) — plausible and I believe real (Hickinbotham/Stepney lineage), but note that literature is about automata chemistries where the *rules* are themselves mutable programs; your chemistry has fixed rules, so the citation supports a stronger claim than your design makes. That gap is precisely your ceiling. (d) 'the reachable set grows superexponentially' — unsupported as stated. Superexponential growth requires products to be reliably reactive; generated property vectors will mostly produce inert or duplicate products, and the effective branching factor after dedup is likely small. Measure it in week 1 before building on it.
audit.one_change: Delete the boundary between Engine 1 and Engine 2: make every PROCESS an artifact under design search. A kiln is an object whose max temperature is an emergent property of its form and materials; a bellows, press, mold, mill, and crucible likewise. Then the process vocabulary is no longer authored — it is whatever the object archive has produced — and material progress requires instrumental progress requires material progress. That single change converts the design's only monotone ladder (achievable conditions) into the spine of the tech tree, turns the '>=3 intermediates' detector back on permanently, and is the difference between a stamp collection and a history.

all.name: The Ninefold Gazette
all.pitch: Nine small worlds with nine different generated physics, where a local 4B model acts as the adjudicator of what novel combinations produce — but only proposes, while arithmetic conservation laws clamp it and actual starvation decides whether the invention was real. You read a newspaper of the age each morning, front page chosen by a surprise metric, with foreign dispatches from the other eight worlds.
all.world: Nine worlds, each 64x64 tiles with 5-8 tribes, each initialised with a generated PHYSICS CARD: a short structured description (element inventory with real numeric properties, which processes exist, what is abundant, what is deadly, what the sky does) that is injected into every adjudication prompt for that world. World 3 has no fire but has a mineral that liberates heat when wetted. World 7's atmosphere corrodes metal in a decade. Tribes have population, stores, territory, tools, beliefs, and a market with actual prices. The nine worlds run at different speeds; a slow world is a control.
all.invention_engine:
LLM-as-physics, budgeted, cached, and — the crucial fix to Infinite Craft's emptiness — SUBORDINATE TO A SURVIVAL VERIFIER.

STEP 1, PROPOSAL: when a tribe combines known things (A, B, process P) in a way never seen in this world, ask local Qwen3-4B, GBNF-constrained to a strict JSON schema: `{result_name, tags[3..6], props:{mass_per_unit, durability, energy_yield, labour_cost, toxicity, insulation, edge, storage_life}, requires_process, plausibility}`. Every numeric field is bounded by the grammar itself. Temperature 0.8, sampled THREE times; fields where 2-of-3 agree within tolerance survive; where they disagree the item is marked UNSTABLE, which is both an honest representation of model uncertainty and a great in-world category (unstable things behave inconsistently and are feared).

STEP 2, CLAMP: a conservation engine adjusts the proposal before it enters the world. Total utility of the product is capped at (sum of input utilities x process efficiency) + a small novelty bonus; mass is conserved against inputs; energy_yield cannot exceed the chemical budget of its inputs; labour_cost has a floor derived from the process. This is ~80 lines of arithmetic and it is the entire difference between a world and a wish-granting machine.

STEP 3, CACHE: write to `adjudication` keyed by (world_id, sorted inputs, process). Never asked twice. Cache hit rate exceeds 95% within a week of a world's life, which is what makes this affordable.

STEP 4, SELECTION AS THE PHYSICS-CHECKER OF LAST RESORT: the item now exists with those numbers, and the deterministic survival sim runs. Tribes that adopt a bad item (because the model hallucinated a great-sounding but numerically mediocre thing) lose stores and die. Tribes that adopt a good one outcompete. Nobody adjudicates truth; starvation does. This is the honest answer to 'how do you stop the LLM lying': you do not, you make lies costly to the believer.

STEP 5, INVENTION PRESSURE: tribes combine under demand (a need registry like Reliquary's) plus a small random exploration rate scaled by surplus. Adoption spreads by imitation weighted by observed prosperity, so a genuinely good invention diffuses and a bad one is abandoned — and the newspaper can report both, including a great running feature: RETRACTIONS, where a celebrated invention turns out to have been useless.
all.why_unbounded: The naming and semantic space is the whole prior of a 4B language model, conditioned differently in each of nine worlds by its physics card — that is effectively unbounded and, more importantly, it is unbounded in KINDS of things rather than only in parameter values. Combinations feed back as inputs, so the reachable set is the transitive closure of a relation the model keeps extending. Nothing here bottoms out in a list. What it bottoms out in instead is described honestly below: not size, but VARIETY.
all.depth_ladder:
WEEK 1: one world, six starting elements, tribes combining under need. You watch the model invent something and then watch the tribe that adopted it die because the clamp gave it a labour cost they could not pay. That failure is the moment you know the design works.
WEEK 2: the market. Prices for every item, published as a table. A commodity price series is unreasonably fun to read and costs nothing.
MONTH 1: nine worlds live. Divergence is visible — world 3's whole material culture is built on wetted mineral heat, and its vocabulary has no word for flame.
MONTH 2: retractions and revivals; a technology abandoned in year 300 is rediscovered in year 900 under a different name because the cache keyed the same combination in a different world.
MONTH 3: visitor omens start steering worlds; a guestbook line becomes a prophecy a tribe canonises.
ENDPOINT: a newspaper archive of 200+ editions, a cross-world 'comparative technology' supplement, an obituary column you actually read, and at least one world that collapsed for a reason you can trace on the front page of an edition from forty issues earlier.
all.what_selects: Standard but tight: kcal, stores, winter, raids, disease. The distinguishing pressure here is ADOPTION RISK. Adopting a new item costs retooling (labour, stored materials, and a period of reduced output), so a tribe that adopts everything the adjudicator dreams up goes bankrupt on churn, and a tribe that adopts nothing is out-competed. The optimal adoption rate is an emergent property of the hazard climate, and different tribes land on different cultural attitudes to novelty — conservative and radical tribes arise mechanically. That is a genuinely interesting thing to read about.
all.changing_worlds: Nine is the point. Different physics cards, different speeds, different visitor exposure (three worlds public and perturbable, three private, three frozen controls), and worlds occasionally ENDING — when a world's last tribe dies, its newspaper prints a final edition and a fresh world takes its slot with a physics card generated partly from the dead world's most successful concepts, so there is inheritance across worlds. The Gazette's masthead tracks which worlds are live. Cross-world comparison is the reading pleasure: the same section header, nine different answers.
all.novelty_detector:
(1) CROSS-WORLD FIRST: an item name (normalised) that has never appeared in ANY of the nine worlds — checked against a global name table, exact and cheap.
(2) CONSEQUENCE MAGNITUDE: an item whose adoption changed a tribe's 20-year survival probability by more than X, measured by counterfactual replay (rerun 20 years with the item unavailable, seed-locked — this is expensive but you only do it for the ten most-adopted items per night, and it converts 'a thing was invented' into 'a thing MATTERED', which is the actual news).
(3) CASCADE: an item that becomes an input to three or more further inventions within 100 years.
(4) SURPRISE-VS-MODEL: keep a cheap n-gram/embedding model of what item names this world produces; flag items in the tail. This is the one that catches genuine weirdness.
Seeded counterfactual replay is the single best idea in this whole set, because it is the only novelty detector here that measures IMPORTANCE rather than mere newness — and importance is what makes a front page.
all.phone_view: A newspaper front page, mobile-first: masthead with world name and date, one headline, one paragraph of real prose, and a strip of six one-line briefs from the other worlds. Under the fold: the market table (5 rows), obituaries (2 lines each), and the almanac. Thirty seconds gets you the headline and the briefs. An hour gets you the archive: every past edition, searchable, cross-linked by item and by tribe, plus the RETRACTIONS index which is the funniest page in the paper.
all.hardware_use: This is the one that actually uses the GPU, and here is the honest arithmetic. Qwen3-4B-Instruct Q4_K_M is ~2.5GB, fully offloaded on the 5070's 8GB with a large KV cache; expect roughly 40-80 tok/s generation on a laptop Blackwell part. Each adjudication is a ~250-token prompt and ~150-token grammar-constrained completion, x3 samples, so about 4-8 seconds wall-clock per novel combination. An 8-hour overnight run therefore supports roughly 4,000-7,000 novel adjudications across all nine worlds, which sounds small until you notice that after the first week the cache absorbs >95% of combination attempts and nightly novel volume settles to a few hundred. So: the GPU is the bottleneck for the first week and nearly idle after. Do not try to run a 14B here — it fits at Q4 but halves your throughput and the extra quality does not survive the clamp anyway. Keep the prose layer separate: 3-5 Claude Haiku 4.5 calls a night for the front page ($1/MTok in, $5/MTok out, with 90% off cached prefixes) is well under a dollar a month and the writing quality difference on the ONE piece you actually read is worth it.
all.input_cadence: Nothing daily. Monthly: write a new physics card by hand for a slot that has opened (30 minutes, enormously high leverage — this is the most fun creative act in the whole project). Weekly-ish if you feel like it: read the retractions page and tighten a clamp constant if the model is inflating a particular property.
all.tech: Python sim, llama.cpp server with Qwen3-4B-Instruct Q4_K_M and per-call GBNF grammars (llama.cpp's --grammar-file / response_format JSON-schema support is what makes unattended structured adjudication safe). SQLite WAL for everything, with the `adjudication` cache as its own table so it survives sim rewrites — that cache is the world's physics and it is the most precious file you own. Claude Haiku 4.5 via the Anthropic API for the daily front-page prose only, with prompt caching on the style guide and the world bible. Newspaper rendered as static HTML per edition (a real archive of files, which is both cheap and pleasing), PWA wrapper with a service worker, Tailscale for the private version, GitHub Pages for the three public worlds. ntfy.sh for the one daily push.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: llama.cpp server up with Qwen3-4B and a GBNF grammar for the adjudication schema; get 3-sample majority voting working; write the conservation clamp. Test by hand-combining absurd things and watching the clamp refuse to grant free energy. Saturday night: SQLite cache, a 32x32 world, three tribes, a kcal loop. Sunday: the need registry and adoption dynamics, then a hideous single-column HTML newspaper with one headline. The delightful moment is Saturday night when a tribe adopts a model-invented item and the deterministic sim kills them for it — that is when it stops being a chatbot toy.
all.six_months_later: Roughly 180 editions, nine world histories with genuinely different technological vocabularies, an adjudication cache of tens of thousands of entries that IS your physics and could be shared as a dataset, a retractions index that is a comedy, and public worlds where strangers' omens are visible in the historical record. You will be able to point at a front page from month 2 and say 'that is where world 6 was doomed'.
all.honest_ceiling: LLM-as-physics converges to genre. A 4B model asked for the result of combining things reaches for 'crystal', 'rune', 'essence', 'shard' across every world within weeks, and the nine worlds will start to rhyme by month 3 — this is the real failure mode, not hallucinated numbers. Partial mitigations, all of which I would actually build: maintain a cross-world token frequency table and apply logit bias / grammar exclusions against any token appearing in more than 2% of item names; condition each world on a GENERATED phonology and a generated material vocabulary so the model is naming in a constructed language rather than in fantasy English; and periodically rotate the adjudicator model (a different 4B has a different cliché attractor). Even with all of that, expect flavour convergence to be noticeable by month 4. Second honest limit: a 4B model's proposals are shallow — it will not give you a mechanism, only a name and some numbers, so the 'why' of a technology is always thin compared to Palimpsest, where the why is literally the program. Third: the counterfactual-replay novelty detector is O(20 years of sim) per candidate; budget it hard or it eats your night. Fourth: this design is only as good as its clamp, and clamps are fiddly — expect two weeks of tuning where the world is either static or exploding.
all.research_notes: Verified: Infinite Craft's architecture — every pair checked against a cache, only novel pairings hit the model (originally Llama 2), results cached forever so the same pairing is stable for every player, with a 'First Discovery' flag on never-before-seen results (quuxplusone.github.io/blog/2024/02/08/infinite-craft; blog.freestyle.dev/posts/multiplayer-infinite-craft for a full-stack reimplementation). This is the proven affordability trick and my design depends on it. llama.cpp guarantees structured output via --grammar-file GBNF or server response_format with a JSON schema, and this works offline with any model — confirmed in current (2026) llama.cpp documentation and guides; this is non-negotiable for unattended overnight adjudication. Qwen3-4B at Q4_K_M is ~2.5GB by the ~0.5-0.6GB-per-billion GGUF rule of thumb, comfortably inside 8GB with a large KV cache; smeltcore.com's RTX 5070 recipes cover Qwen3-8B and 14B Q4_K_M on exactly this class of card if you want to trade throughput for quality. Claude Haiku 4.5 is $1.00/MTok input and $5.00/MTok output as of August 2026, with prompt caching cutting cached input to 10% of standard and the Batch API cutting both by 50% — so a nightly front-page prose pass is cents per month. On LLM-driven civilizations that actually exist: CivAgent (github.com/fuxiAIlab/CivAgent) runs LLM agents as digital players in Unciv, and Altera's Project Sid demonstrated emergent role specialisation and cultural norm propagation with large agent populations in Minecraft — both are evidence the genre works and neither delivers a readable chronicle, which is the gap this fills.

audit.name: The Ninefold Gazette
audit.ceiling: Depth never starts. Item count grows forever and will be misread as depth for about six weeks. The structural reason: every invention in this world is a NAME plus an 8-field numeric vector. There is no representation in which one technology is MADE OF another — only a parent pointer in a provenance table. So 'compounding' is a graph annotation, not a mechanism; nothing about invention #400 is cheaper, better, or differently-shaped because inventions #1-399 exist. Compare Palimpsest, where a new abstraction literally reshapes the search space. Empirically, Infinite Craft is the control experiment and it already ran: deep combination chains degenerate into modifier stacking and self-reference rather than into structure, because the model does not track what an item IS across compositions. Your clamp constrains arithmetic, which is the failure mode you can see, and does nothing about semantic decoherence, which is the one that kills you. Expect nine worlds that rhyme by month 2-3 (the doc says month 4; it is optimistic), and a front page that is entertaining prose over a flat namespace indefinitely.
audit.authored_content_risk: Maximal, and disguised better than in any other idea here. The invention space is a 4B model's pretraining prior — that is the single largest body of authored content on this list, revealed in an order determined by which tribe combined what. The physics card conditions the surface vocabulary; it does not condition the model's combinational semantics, which are learned from human text and will keep reaching for the same attractors. The doc treats this as a flavour problem to be patched with logit bias and generated phonologies; it is a substance problem, and token-level bans against 'crystal/rune/shard' will produce differently-named versions of the same three concepts. The honest description of this design is: an LLM is asked to reveal, one pair at a time, what human culture already believes results from combining things, with numbers clamped so the reveal cannot break the economy. That is the fatal flaw the brief warns about, in its purest form.
audit.compute_honesty: Honest on the per-call arithmetic, wrong on the aggregate, and the error is load-bearing. 40-80 tok/s for Qwen3-4B Q4_K_M on a laptop 5070 is a fair-to-conservative estimate; ~4-8s per 3-sample adjudication is right; 4,000-7,000 adjudications per overnight is right. But the claim that novel volume 'settles to a few hundred a night after the first week' is backwards. The number of *possible* combinations is O(n^2) in the item count and n grows monotonically; with need-pulled exploration plus a random exploration rate scaled by surplus, novel-pair encounters grow rather than shrink. Cache hit rate is high only if tribes keep retrying the SAME pairs, which is exactly what a need-driven explorer avoids. You will be GPU-bound permanently, not for a week, and the practical consequence is that you must hard-cap combination attempts per tribe-year — which caps invention rate — or accept a growing adjudication backlog. Separately, counterfactual replay at 20 sim-years per candidate for ten candidates a night across nine worlds is the other budget hole the doc flags but does not cost out. Claude Haiku for the front page really is cents/month; that part is fine.
audit.semantic_risk: Highest of the six by a wide margin. The output is a name and eight numbers, with no mechanism, no recipe, and no executable content — so 'meaningful' can only mean 'the name sounds plausible given the inputs', which is precisely what a language model optimises and precisely what carries no information about the world. The three-sample UNSTABLE category is a genuinely clever touch and the only honest signal in the pipeline, but at temperature 0.8 on a 4B, disagreement will be dominated by numeric sampling noise rather than by real model uncertainty, so 'unstable' will mostly tag boring items. Selection-as-verifier does not rescue this: starvation can kill tribes that adopt numerically bad items, but it cannot make a semantically incoherent item coherent, and it never runs on items nobody adopts — which is most of them.
audit.dubious_claims: (a) '>95% cache hit within a week, nightly novel volume settles to a few hundred' — arithmetically unsupported, see above; this is the assumption the whole affordability story rests on. (b) 'smeltcore.com's RTX 5070 recipes' — I cannot verify this source; treat as fabricated until checked. (c) Haiku 4.5 at $1/$5 per MTok with 10% cached input and 50% Batch API discount — consistent with what I can verify. (d) CivAgent (fuxiAIlab) and Altera's Project Sid are real and correctly characterised, but neither is evidence that LLM adjudication produces *technological depth*; Sid demonstrated role specialisation and norm propagation, which is a different claim than the one it is cited for here. (e) Infinite Craft's original adjudicator was Llama 2 — correct. (f) 'the naming and semantic space is the whole prior of a 4B model... effectively unbounded' — unbounded in string space, extremely bounded in concept space, and the doc conflates the two.
audit.one_change: Invert the LLM's role: stop asking it for RESULTS and start asking it for RECIPES. Constrain it to emit a program in a small typed process DSL over substances the world already has, and let the deterministic sim compute what that program produces. The model becomes a proposal distribution over structured actions — which is what LLMs are genuinely good at and where their prior is an asset rather than a contaminant — and the world's physics becomes real, compositional, and yours. This converges the design toward Palimpsest with an LLM proposer instead of enumerative search, which is a legitimately good architecture and arguably the best hybrid available on this list. Keep the clamp, the cache, the retractions page, and the nine physics cards; they all survive the change.

all.name: Strata
all.pitch: The simulation is deliberately hidden from you: civilizations rise, invent, and fall in deep time, and every night an autonomous expedition digs three trenches and publishes an excavation report built only from what physically survived. The chronicle stays fresh for months not because new things keep happening but because your understanding of what happened keeps being revised — including by a famous forgery you will not spot at first.
all.world: One planet, 12 regions, 200,000 in-world years at a coarse tick with fine-grained focus periods where interesting things happen. Civilizations arise, build, invent, exhaust their environment, and collapse; several rise on the ruins of others. The load-bearing subsystem is not the civilization sim but the DEPOSITION MODEL: every object, structure, burial, and text has a material class with a preservation function over (soil pH, waterlogging, temperature cycling, later construction, erosion, looting). Bone dissolves in acid soil. Wood survives only waterlogged or charred. Ceramics survive essentially forever but travel. Metal is recycled by later people, which means the more valuable a thing was, the less likely it survives — a beautiful and real inversion. Every site accumulates a proper Harris-matrix stratigraphy: numbered contexts, cut-and-fill relationships, intrusions, residual finds.
all.invention_engine:
Grammar-based genetic programming over a CRAFT GRAMMAR, coupled to niche construction with long lags.

A craft is a derivation in a context-free grammar whose terminals are actions over materials and whose fitness is its contribution to survival in the population that holds it. Variation is subtree mutation and crossover of derivations plus rule-level innovation (a production rule that gets used together often enough is promoted to a named non-terminal — a cheap library-learning move that gives you compounding without a full DreamCoder stack). Transmission is vertical (parent to child, high fidelity), oblique (master to apprentice), and horizontal (trade, conquest), each with different error rates.

The distinctive mechanism is NICHE CONSTRUCTION WITH DELAY. Every craft has an environmental side effect written into the tile state with a lag of 50-500 years: irrigation raises soil salinity, smelting deforests and then erodes, drainage lowers the water table, intensive cropping shifts the pollen spectrum. So a technology's fitness is high when adopted and can be catastrophically negative three centuries later, after everyone has become dependent on it. This is what makes the archaeology worth reading: the excavation report can show you the salt crust in context 14 sitting directly above the granary floor, and you get to work out the causality yourself.

And here is the actual product loop. Every night an EXPEDITION runs: a survey model picks 1-3 trenches (biased by previous finds, by a small budget, and by a rivalry between two in-world schools of archaeology with different theories), excavates, and recovers a SAMPLE — a filtered, damaged, spatially biased subset of the ground truth. Then an INTERPRETATION pass runs with access ONLY to the recovered finds and previously published claims, never to ground truth. It writes a site report and updates a CLAIMS table: statements with confidence values, supporting contexts, and an author. Later digs can raise, lower, or invert those confidences.
all.why_unbounded: Two independent sources. First, the craft grammar with rule promotion is a growing formal grammar — the space of derivations over a signature that keeps gaining non-terminals does not bottom out, and the delayed-consequence dynamics mean the fitness landscape is non-stationary, so there is no final optimum to converge on. Second, and this is the part unique to this idea: the INTERPRETIVE space is unbounded independently of the event space. Even if the sim froze forever, the archive of possible hypotheses about it, the revisions, the rival schools, and the reinterpretations under new evidence keep producing genuinely new text. Most procedural history projects die of repetition because the reader eventually sees the generator; here the reader sees a lossy channel, and lossy channels are inexhaustible.
all.depth_ladder:
WEEK 1: a toy civ, a deposition model, one trench. You dig up 40 potsherds and a posthole and the report says 'probably a structure, function unclear'. You know it was a granary. That gap is the entire feeling of the project and you get it on day one.
WEEK 2: stratigraphy proper — Harris matrix, residual finds, intrusions. The report starts making dating arguments and getting them slightly wrong.
MONTH 1: two rival schools with different priors, publishing competing interpretations of the same finds. The chronicle now has an argument in it.
MONTH 2: the first OVERTURNED CLAIM — a trench dug in a different region invalidates a confident published statement from week 3. This is the best push notification the project will ever send.
MONTH 3: niche-construction lags start landing. A civilization collapses from soil salinity and the excavation report finds the evidence 400 years later in the wrong region first.
MONTH 4: absolute dating gets invented in-fiction (the expedition develops a technique), and the entire published chronology shifts by 300 years, cascading revisions through hundreds of claims at once. A whole night of reading.
ENDPOINT: a corpus of several hundred site reports, a claims database with a visible history of scholarly consensus forming and breaking, a forgery that fooled the record for two months, and at least one civilization whose existence is inferred entirely from the absence of things.
all.what_selects: Inside the sim: carrying capacity, climate cycles, the delayed environmental costs of the civilization's own successes, and conquest. Nothing exotic — the selection pressure does not need to be clever here because the interpretive layer is where the value is. Between SCHOOLS of archaeology there is a second, funnier selection: a school's prestige rises when its claims survive later digs and falls when they are overturned, and prestige controls the excavation budget, which controls where trenches go. So a wrong-but-prestigious school digs in the wrong places for decades, which is an extremely accurate simulation of a real field and produces terrific reading.
all.changing_worlds: A SHELF of 6-9 planets, each with different geology (hence different preservation regimes) and different climate. This makes COMPARATIVE ARCHAEOLOGY the headline feature: 'in 4 of 9 worlds someone invented the true arch; in the two worlds with no suitable stone, nobody did, and here is the timber solution they used instead.' Because preservation differs by world, the same civilization type produces radically different evidence — one world is all ceramics and no organics, another is a peat bog where you get the wooden tools and the clothes. Reading the same history through different preservation windows is a pleasure nothing else on this list offers. Within a world, deep time itself is the change: the climate curve is generated, so the Holocene-equivalent of world 4 is not the Holocene.
all.novelty_detector:
Ranked by what actually makes a person want to read:
(1) OVERTURNED CLAIM: a claim whose confidence crosses from >0.8 to <0.3 (or the reverse). This is the top-priority push and it is exactly measurable.
(2) UNEXPLAINED FIND: an object whose material or form cannot be produced by any craft the current published chronology attributes to that period — an anomaly. Trivially computable by checking the recovered artifact against the claims table, and it is the single most evocative event type in the genre.
(3) FIRST EVIDENCE: earliest recovered instance of a craft class in any world.
(4) HIATUS: a site with a stratigraphic gap exceeding N years, i.e. an abandonment nobody has explained yet.
(5) ASAL-style novelty on the embedding of the night's finds assemblage, to catch what you did not instrument.
Note the elegance: novelty here is defined against the PUBLISHED RECORD, not against ground truth, which means the detector is measuring the same surprise the reader would feel. That is much better than measuring simulation-side novelty the reader has no access to.
all.phone_view: An excavation notice. 'Trench 41, Rill Bank. 3 contexts. 1 anomaly.' One photo-equivalent: a procedurally drawn section drawing (SVG, hatched layers, labelled contexts — genuinely beautiful and nearly free to render) plus a finds count by material. If a claim was overturned, that is the whole notification and it says which one and by what. Thirty seconds. The hour-long version is the site report, the Harris matrix as an interactive diagram, the claims database with confidence histories as sparklines, the school rivalry, and the comparative view across nine worlds.
all.hardware_use: CPU-only for the sim and the deposition model; 64GB RAM is genuinely useful because deep time over 12 regions at object granularity is a lot of rows and you want the recent horizon in memory. GPU is used for one thing: the interpretation pass. This should be the strongest local model you can fit, because reasoning from partial evidence is the one task here where model quality is visible in the output — Qwen3-8B at Q4_K_M (~4.5GB) fits in 8GB with a modest context and is worth the throughput hit over 4B, since you only run a handful of interpretation calls per night. Do not attempt 14B at long context on 8GB; it fits but the KV cache will push you into shared-memory swapping and the tokens-per-second collapse is brutal. Alternative worth considering: run interpretation on Claude Haiku 4.5 via the API for a few cents a night, since it is one call per trench and quality matters more here than anywhere else in these six ideas.
all.input_cadence: Zero. This is the most hands-off idea of the six because the interpretation layer generates novelty without you. Optional quarterly nudge: fund an expedition to a region you are curious about (one row in a table), or introduce a new dating technique and watch the chronology shatter and reform.
all.tech: Python sim. SQLite WAL with tables `context`, `find`, `site`, `claim`, `report`, `school`; FTS5 over reports. Harris matrix as a DAG in the contexts table with an SVG renderer for both the matrix and the section drawings — the section drawing renderer is a weekend of fun and is the visual identity of the whole project. llama.cpp with Qwen3-8B Q4_K_M for interpretation under a GBNF schema that forces every claim to cite context IDs (a claim with no citation is rejected before it is ever rendered — this is the anti-hallucination mechanism and it is mechanical, not prompt-based). Prose rendered from validated claims only. PWA + service worker, Tailscale private, GitHub Pages public.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: a crude civ sim (population, a craft grammar with 8 rules, 3 regions, collapse conditions), run 5,000 years in a few seconds. Saturday afternoon: the deposition model — material classes, preservation probabilities, a soil layer per tile. Saturday night: dig one trench, print the recovered finds table next to the ground truth, side by side. That comparison is the delight, and it happens on day one with no LLM involved. Sunday: Harris matrix, the SVG section drawing, and the claims table with a hand-written interpreter (rules, not LLM) so you can see revisions working before you add a model.
all.six_months_later: Nine worlds, several hundred published site reports, a claims database with hundreds of statements and their confidence histories, two or three overturned orthodoxies, a comparative-technology supplement across all worlds, and a section-drawing gallery you would print and frame. The thing you will not expect: you will start rooting for one of the two archaeological schools.
all.honest_ceiling: The civilization sim underneath is the weakest of the six — the craft grammar with rule promotion gives you real but modest compounding, considerably less than Palimpsest's library learning, and if you ever look directly at ground truth you may find it thinner than the reports imply. That is a genuine risk: the project's magic depends on never showing you the sim, which means if the sim is boring you will only find out slowly and painfully. Mitigation: steal Palimpsest's engine wholesale as the underlying invention mechanism and make Strata the DELIVERY layer over it — honestly, these two ideas want to be married, and if you build one build it in a way that lets the other bolt on. Second ceiling: interpretive novelty is not infinite in practice even though it is in principle; once the world's broad chronology is settled and confidence is high everywhere, revisions get rarer. Countermeasure is new regions, new dating techniques, and periodic worlds — but expect the revision rate to decay roughly as 1/t within a world, so plan on adding worlds rather than digging one forever. Third: the interpretation pass is the one place a local model's weakness shows, because reasoning from absence is hard; budget for either an 8B local model or a few cents a night of API.
all.research_notes: Verified: Dwarf Fortress generates history for a world after generating the world itself, tracking civilizations, sites and populations across up to 2,000-year histories, and those legends are read by clicking links like browsing a wiki rather than as generated prose (dwarffortresswiki.org/index.php/World_generation) — the delivery gap this idea targets. James Ryan's work is the key scholarly grounding: Talk of the Town simulates an American small town day by day for 200 years with an emphasis on social exchange and characters' internal lives, and his dissertation 'Curating Simulated Storyworlds' (UCSC, 2018; covered in detail by Emily Short at emshort.blog/2019/05/28/curating-simulated-storyworlds-james-ryan-ch-6f) names exactly the problem this idea's novelty detector solves — a simulation generates far more than anyone can read, so the hard part is SIFTING, not generating. Ryan's 'Simulating Character Knowledge Phenomena in Talk of the Town' (Game AI Pro 3, ch. 37, gameaipro.com) is directly relevant to modelling knowledge as lossy and mutable, which is the same machinery as evidence and claims here. Lynn Cherny's Dwarf2Text is the closest real precedent for data-to-text over simulated history and is worth reading for its failure modes. On grounded generation: current data-to-text practice separates content selection and planning (an intermediate plan of what to say and in what order) from surface realisation, and template approaches give strict hallucination guarantees at the cost of sounding robotic — the citation-required claims schema here is the hybrid, and blueprint/QA-plan approaches (arXiv 2503.23204) are the published version of the same idea. ASAL (arXiv 2412.17799) supplies the fallback statistical novelty channel.

audit.name: Strata
audit.ceiling: Two ceilings, and they compound. The technological one: grammar-based GP with rule promotion is real but weak compounding — it is essentially module acquisition / ADFs, which historically gives a modest constant-factor improvement rather than open-ended growth, and the doc correctly rates it below Palimpsest. That layer plateaus around week 6-10. The interpretive one is the load-bearing claim and it is overstated. 'Even if the sim froze, the hypothesis space is unbounded' is true in principle and false in practice, because your claims are schema-constrained tuples (predicate, entity, context-citation) over an authored predicate vocabulary, and the number of *distinguishable* things that can be said about a finite ground truth is finite and small. Worse, evidence accumulation is a convergent process by construction: each trench monotonically reduces posterior variance, so overturned-claim events — your best notification, correctly identified — are self-extinguishing. Expect 20-40 genuine reversals per world, front-loaded, with the rate decaying as roughly 1/t exactly as the doc predicts, and the chronology substantially settled by month 3-4. Adding worlds adds content linearly; it does not restore compounding. And the honest framing for the builder's actual brief: this idea does not deliver cavemen-to-something-wild at all. It delivers epistemics about a shallow tech ladder. That may be better reading, but it is a different product than the one requested.
audit.authored_content_risk: Medium, in an unusual place. The ground truth has genuine (if modest) emergence — the niche-construction-with-delay mechanism is excellent and produces causal structure nobody wrote. The authored risk is in the INTERPRETIVE layer: rival schools with different priors sounds emergent but is two hand-tuned prior vectors, the 'famous forgery' is a scripted event type, and 'absolute dating gets invented in-fiction, shattering the chronology' is an authored plot beat with a date on it. Those are the three most exciting items in the depth ladder and all three are content, not mechanism. The deeper structural point in this design's favour, which is real and rare: a lossy channel over even a modest generator produces more *legitimate* novelty than a rich generator shown directly, because the reader's uncertainty is a genuine resource. That insight is correct and is the best single idea in the six after seeded counterfactual replay.
audit.compute_honesty: Honest, with the best-calibrated GPU sizing on the list. Qwen3-8B Q4_K_M at ~4.5-5GB with modest context genuinely fits 8GB; the warning about 14B thrashing into shared memory is correct and is the kind of detail that indicates the author has actually done this. A handful of interpretation calls per night is nothing. CPU-side deep time over 12 regions at object granularity is the real cost and it is RAM-shaped, not FLOP-shaped — but note that object-granularity deposition over 200,000 years across 12 regions is where this design will actually bite: you must aggressively coarsen outside focus periods or the object table becomes the bottleneck long before the GPU does. The Haiku-for-interpretation fallback at cents/night is accurate.
audit.semantic_risk: Low-to-moderate for the archaeology (section drawings, Harris matrices, and finds tables are structurally constrained and will look right), but the doc makes one claim I want to flag hard: 'a claim with no citation is rejected before it is ever rendered — this is the anti-hallucination mechanism and it is mechanical, not prompt-based'. GBNF constrains FORM, not TRUTH. The grammar can force a claim to cite context 14; it cannot prevent the model from asserting something false about context 14. The mechanical guarantee you actually have is referential integrity, which is much weaker than the doc implies, and in a project whose entire premise is that the reader trusts the reports as honest inference from evidence, that gap is the one that can rot the artifact. Fix: mechanically verify each claim's *entailment* against the recovered finds with rule-based checks for the small set of claim predicates, and mark anything the checker cannot verify as 'speculative' in the rendered text.
audit.dubious_claims: (a) DF tracking 'up to 2,000-year histories' — the standard world-gen history length is considerably shorter (1050 years in the usual presets); dubious as stated. (b) arXiv 2503.23204 for blueprint/QA-plan data-to-text — I cannot verify this identifier; the underlying blueprint-models line of work (Narayan et al.) is real, so the idea is sound but the citation should be checked. (c) James Ryan's dissertation 'Curating Simulated Storyworlds' (UCSC 2018), Talk of the Town, Game AI Pro 3 ch.37, and Emily Short's coverage are all correctly cited and genuinely the right grounding — this is the best-researched notes field of the six. (d) ASAL as fallback channel: fine. (e) The unflagged research gap: the doc cites the sifting problem but not the reliability literature on LLM inference from incomplete evidence, which is where its central pass is weakest.
audit.one_change: Make the marriage the precondition, not the mitigation: build Palimpsest's library-learning engine as Strata's ground truth from day one, and build Strata strictly as a lens over it. The doc already identifies this and then files it under 'honest ceiling' — it belongs at the top of the design. It fixes both ceilings at once: the technological one (real compounding underneath) and the interpretive one (a richer ground truth supports more distinguishable claims and keeps reversals coming). Corollary that costs nothing: build a spoiler toggle that shows ground truth beside the report, and check it weekly. The doc correctly identifies that the project's magic depends on never looking — which means you will discover the sim is thin slowly and painfully, and a toggle converts that into a week-one measurement.

all.name: Scriptorium
all.pitch: Each polity's intelligence is literally a LoRA adapter that is retrained every week on only the decisions that mechanically worked, and the chronicle is written by those same models — so as the checkpoints diverge, the prose diverges, and you can read a civilization getting sharper or going senile in its own syntax. A lost adapter file recovered from a ruin is a rediscovered manuscript, and reloading it ends a dark age.
all.world: One continent, ~12 polities, coarse annual ticks over a few thousand years. Each polity has land, population, stores, armies, neighbours, a treasury, and a COLLEGE. The college is the decision-maker: at each decision point it receives a compact structured state (a few hundred tokens: harvest, stores, threats, prices, recent history) plus a retrieved handful of its own past canonical writings, and it emits, under a GBNF grammar, a structured decision plus a JUSTIFICATION in prose. The world physics is a deterministic, boring, thoroughly-tested economy-and-war sim — deliberately boring, because it is the verifier and it must be trustworthy.
all.invention_engine:
A STaR / rejection-sampling flywheel embodied as institutional memory, with two kinds of invention stacked.

INVENTION LAYER 1 (explicit, inspectable): the college's decisions include POLICY PROGRAMS — small structured plans in a policy DSL (allocate labour, set tariffs, garrison, sow, store, conscript, build). Successful policy programs are compressed weekly into named POLICIES the college can invoke by name later. This is the same library-learning move as Palimpsest but over statecraft rather than materials, and it gives you nameable inventions like 'the Threefold Store' that are actual reusable programs.

INVENTION LAYER 2 (implicit, the reason this idea exists): the model weights themselves. Weekly, for each polity: gather all (state, justification, decision) triples from the past week, score each trajectory MECHANICALLY at +20 in-world years (population, stores, territory, survival — a scalar, no LLM judge anywhere), keep the top quantile, and run an Unsloth QLoRA finetune on the polity's current adapter. The new checkpoint must beat the incumbent on a FROZEN held-out set of 200 archived world-states, scored by the same mechanical function, or it is discarded and the polity enters a DARK AGE (reverts to a weaker sampling temperature, loses access to its most recent named policies, prose quality visibly degrades). Benchmark hygiene matters and is easy to get wrong on a gaming laptop: the eval must be scored on DECISION QUALITY under a fixed token budget, never on wall-clock or throughput, and if you ever need timing, lock clocks with `nvidia-smi -lgc` and interleave A/B runs rather than running them back to back.

ARCHAEOLOGY OF WEIGHTS: every adapter is kept. They are 50-200MB files. When a polity falls, its adapter is written to a `ruin` row. A later polity that excavates the site can load it — with damage, meaning a random subset of LoRA layers zeroed or a merge at partial alpha. A recovered ancient mind that is better than yours is the single best story beat available in any of these six designs, and here it is a literal file operation.
all.why_unbounded: Two claims, and I want to be precise about which one is strong. The STRONG claim: the policy-program library compounds exactly like Palimpsest's — named policies become invocable primitives inside later policies, over a growing signature, with mechanical verification. That is genuinely unbounded and it is where the reliable depth is. The WEAKER claim, which I will not oversell: the weight-space trajectory of a 4B model under repeated self-training is high-dimensional and never repeats, so the polities keep DIVERGING indefinitely — but divergence is not the same as capability growth. The honest framing is that this project's unboundedness is in variation and specialisation, with genuine compounding only in the symbolic policy layer.
all.depth_ladder:
WEEK 1: base Qwen3-4B making decisions for three polities under a strict grammar, deterministic sim, mechanical scoring. Read three justifications for the same harvest crisis. Already interesting.
WEEK 2: first QLoRA run. Diff the same prompt through base and finetuned adapters side by side — the styles have moved apart. That side-by-side diff view is the product.
MONTH 1: twelve polities, twelve adapters, visible dialects. One polity's justifications have become terse and numeric; another's are florid and superstitious, because its winning trajectories happened to include a lot of appeals to omens.
MONTH 2: first failed gate, first dark age. A polity's checkpoint fails held-out eval, gets discarded, and the chronicle for that decade is measurably worse written. This will feel bad in a way you did not expect.
MONTH 3: policy library depth — a named policy invoked inside another named policy inside a third.
MONTH 4: first weight-archaeology event. A polity excavates a fallen rival's adapter, merges it at partial alpha, and either inherits a genuinely better decision-maker or a beautiful madness.
ENDPOINT: twelve mutually unintelligible scholarly traditions writing about the same continent, a chronicle where you can identify the author polity from three sentences with no byline, and a lineage tree of adapters that is simultaneously a family tree of minds and a directory of files on your disk.
all.what_selects: The mechanical scorer, and nothing else, which is the discipline that keeps this honest. A polity that makes bad decisions loses population, territory and stores, and a shrinking polity gets fewer decision points per year, therefore less training data, therefore weaker weekly finetunes — the same 'thinking is paid for by surplus' coupling as Palimpsest but operating on gradient steps instead of search nodes. That feedback loop is vicious and produces real death spirals. Between polities: war, trade, and adapter theft (conquest can copy the loser's adapter, so military success can import intelligence directly, which is a lovely and slightly disturbing dynamic).
all.changing_worlds: Within a run, the continent's climate and disease regime drift, so the decision distribution a college was trained on stops matching reality — a college that overfitted to a benign century fails hard when the century turns, which is model-collapse-as-plot. Across runs: keep the adapter lineage and start a NEW world seeded with adapters from the old one, so a fresh continent is settled by the intellectual descendants of a dead one. Over six months you will have a genealogy of minds spanning several worlds, which is a much stranger and better artifact than a genealogy of kings.
all.novelty_detector:
(1) STYLE SHIFT: per-polity rolling embedding of its chronicle prose (bge-small); a checkpoint whose post-finetune output embedding moves more than 3 sigma from its own trailing distribution is a genuine event — 'the College of Vann now writes differently'. This is cheap, exact, and unique to this design.
(2) GATE OUTCOMES: passed with a large margin, or failed (dark age). Both are news.
(3) POLICY-LIBRARY EVENTS: new named policy, or a policy invoked at record composition depth.
(4) DIVERGENCE RECORD: pairwise distance between two polities' outputs on the SAME held-out state hits an all-time high — the moment two traditions become mutually alien.
(5) LEXICAL INNOVATION: a token/phrase that a polity now uses at high frequency and which it never used before, and which no other polity uses. This catches jargon formation, which is exactly what real scholarly traditions do.
all.phone_view: Two paragraphs side by side, same event, two colleges, with a one-line divergence score between them. Above them, one status strip: twelve polity glyphs coloured by health, with a small crown on any that finetuned last night and a black band on any in a dark age. That is the 30-second view and it is unusually information-dense. The hour version: the full chronicle per polity, the adapter lineage tree, the held-out eval score history as a chart, the policy library with call graphs, and a 'Rosetta' page that runs the same three archived world-states through every living college so you can compare twelve minds on identical input.
all.hardware_use: This is the idea that pushes the 8GB ceiling, and I want to be blunt about it. Unsloth supports Blackwell (RTX 5070/5080/5090, sm_120) but you MUST be on CUDA 12.8+ with all dependent libraries built for it — older wheels have no sm_120 kernels and you will hit 'no kernel image is available for execution on the device'. QLoRA on Qwen3-4B in 4-bit fits 8GB with discipline: sequence length capped at 2048, batch size 1 with gradient accumulation, gradient checkpointing on, LoRA rank 16-32 on attention projections only. Expect roughly 30-60 minutes per polity-week of training, so twelve polities is a 6-12 hour weekly job — that is your Saturday night, which fits the overnight rhythm perfectly. Inference during the week uses llama.cpp with the base model plus per-polity LoRA adapters (llama.cpp supports adapter hot-swap, so you keep one ~2.5GB base resident and swap 50-200MB adapters per call rather than holding twelve models). Do NOT attempt 8B QLoRA at useful context on 8GB; it technically loads and then thrashes. If you want more headroom, drop to Qwen3-1.7B for the colleges — the divergence story works even better with a small model because small models overfit faster and more visibly.
all.input_cadence: Weekly glance at the eval-score chart, which takes 20 seconds and is genuinely interesting. One real chore exists and I will not pretend otherwise: when the CUDA/Unsloth stack breaks after an update — and it will, once or twice in six months — you lose an evening. Pin your versions, keep a working conda env tarball, and treat the finetune as optional (if the weekly job fails, the world just continues with the incumbent adapters, which is a graceful degradation you should design in from day one).
all.tech: Unsloth for QLoRA (4-bit, Qwen3-4B or 1.7B base), CUDA 12.8+, PyTorch built for sm_120. llama.cpp server for inference with per-request LoRA adapter selection. GBNF grammar forcing every college output into `{decision, policy_program, justification}`. SQLite WAL for world state, decisions, eval history, and the adapter registry (path, parent adapter, polity, week, eval score — this table is the genealogy). bge-small for style embeddings. Adapters stored on disk with a hash-named directory layout, and yes, back them up, they are the actual artifact. PWA over Tailscale, GitHub Pages mirror with the prose only.
all.first_weekend: Saturday: the deterministic economy-and-war sim with a mechanical scorer, three polities, and base Qwen3-4B making grammar-constrained decisions. Get the chronicle rendering from justifications. Saturday night: archive 200 world-states as the frozen held-out eval and score base model performance on them so you have a baseline. Sunday: the Unsloth QLoRA pipeline end to end on one polity's week of winning trajectories, the gate, and the side-by-side diff view. The delightful moment is Sunday evening, running the same prompt through base and adapter and seeing the second one sound like it has opinions.
all.six_months_later: Twelve to thirty adapters in a lineage tree spanning two or three worlds, chronicles you can attribute by style alone, at least two dark ages, one recovered ancient mind, a policy library with genuine compositional depth, and a Rosetta page that is the most interesting thing on your phone. You will have a favourite college and you will be annoyed when it loses a war.
all.honest_ceiling: A 4B model QLoRA'd on its own filtered outputs does not get meaningfully smarter at reasoning. It gets STYLISTICALLY AND TACTICALLY SPECIALISED, and past a few generations it degrades — model collapse is real, well-documented, and you should expect it rather than fight it. Design mitigations I would actually ship: always mix 30% base-era data into every finetune, keep the frozen held-out gate absolutely honest (never let it drift, never let an LLM judge it), and treat collapse as content by making it a dark age. But do not build this expecting a capability curve that goes up; the real deliverable is DIVERGENCE and SPECIALISATION, and if you are honest about that from day one it is a wonderful project, while if you are not you will be disappointed in month 2.
